print("low T: C_2/(x^2 e^{-x}) ->", limit(C2 / (x ** 2 * exp(-x)), x=oo), "; C_E/(x^2 e^{-x}) ->", limit(CE / (x ** 2 * exp(-x)), x=oo))
Output:
two-level: C = 1/96*x^6 - 1/16*x^4 + 1/4*x^2
oscillator: C = -1/6048*x^6 + 1/240*x^4 - 1/12*x^2 + 1
low T: C_2/(x^2 e^{-x}) -> 1 ; C_E/(x^2 e^{-x}) -> 1




The Sackur-Tetrode entropy can be compared with experiment. The second exercise evaluates it for argon at room conditions, where the measured value is 154.8 J/(mol K).

Exercise 56 (The entropy of argon) Evaluate S/(Nk_B) = \log\frac{V}{N\lambda^3} + \frac52 for argon (m = 6.63\times10^{-26} kg) at T = 298 K and p
= 10^5 Pa, and convert to J/(mol K).







NoteSolution





k_BT = 4.11\times10^{-21} J, V/N = k_BT/p = 4.11\times10^{-26} m^3, \lambda = 6.626\times10^{-34}/\sqrt{2\pi\cdot 6.
63\times10^{-26}\cdot4.11\times10^{-21}} = 1.60\times10^{-11} m, \lambda^3 = 4.1\times10^{-33} m^3, so V/(N\lambda^3) = 1.0\times10^7, \log = 16.1 and S/(Nk_B) = 18.6. Times R = 8.314 J/(mol K): S = 155 J/(mol K), in agreement with calorimetry: a check of the (2\pi\hbar)^{3N} and N! in the phase-space measure.



The vibrations of a molecule can be studied in the same way as those of a crystal. The last exercise computes the vibrational contribution to the free energy and heat capacity of a gas of diatomic molecules at a given temperature.

Exercise 57 (Vibrational heat capacity) For N_2 with \theta_v = 3390 K, compute the vibrational contribution to C_V/N at T = 300 K and at T = 1000 K, and the mean number of vibrational quanta per molecule at each temperature.







NoteSolution





With x = \theta_v/T: at 300 K, x = 11.3, C = x^2e^x/(e^x - 1)^2 = 127.7\cdot1.24\times10^{-5} = 1.6\times
10^{-3}, and \langle n\rangle = 1/(e^x - 1) = 1.2\times10^{-5}; at 1000 K, x = 3.39, C = 11.49\cdot
e^{3.39}/(e^{3.39} - 1)^2 = 11.49\cdot29.7/824 = 0.41, and \langle n\rangle = 0.035. The vibration is frozen at room temperature and half thawed at 1000 K.

title: Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics
text:
Identical quantum particles are indistinguishable, and a state of many of them is specified by how many particles occupy each single-particle state, its occupation numbers. Bosons may share a state in any number, fermions at most one at a time (the Pauli principle), and the grand-canonical ensemble of Definition 8 makes the orbitals independent. This section derives the Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac distributions, applies the first to blackbody radiation and to Bose-Einstein condensation and the second to the electron gas, and checks the integrals that appear, beginning with \int_0^\infty x^3/(e^x - 1)\,dx = \pi^4/15.
For more on this topic, see Strocchi (2021, Ch. 23).






Figure 4: Left: mean occupation numbers against x = (\epsilon - \mu)/T: Bose-Einstein 1/(e^x - 1) (red), Maxwell-Boltzmann e^{-x} (dashed) and Fermi-Dirac 1/(e^x + 1) (blue); the three agree for x \gg 1, the Bose occupation diverges as x \to 0^+, and the Fermi occupation is a smoothed step at \epsilon = \mu. Right: the Planck spectral energy density u(\omega) = \omega^3/(\pi^2(e^{\omega/T} - 1)) at T = 1, 3/2, 2 (\hbar = c = k_B = 1), with the maxima at \omega
= 2.8214\,T (Wien’s law); the area under each curve is \pi^2T^4/15. Generated by figures/occupation_numbers.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


For non-interacting particles the many-body energy is \sum_k n_k\epsilon_k and the grand partition function factorises over single-particle states k. Each bosonic factor is the geometric series of Example 33, and the mean occupation is the distribution named after Bose and Einstein.


Definition 12 (Bose-Einstein distribution) For an ideal gas of bosons with single-particle energies \epsilon_k in equilibrium at temperature T and chemical potential \mu < \min_k\epsilon_k, the grand partition function is \Xi = \prod_k(1 - e^{-\beta(\epsilon_k -
\mu)})^{-1}, and the mean occupation of state k is the Bose-Einstein distribution 
\langle n_k\rangle = \frac{1}{e^{\beta(\epsilon_k - \mu)} - 1}.
 The total number and energy are N = \sum_k\langle n_k\rangle and E = \sum_k\epsilon_k\langle n_k\rangle, which in a large volume become integrals over the density of states. Quanta whose number is not conserved (photons, phonons) have \mu = 0.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





A single mode of the electromagnetic field is a harmonic oscillator, and its photons are bosons with zero chemical potential. The first example identifies the oscillator occupation of Example 43 with the Bose-Einstein distribution.

Example 56 (Photons in one mode) A cavity mode of frequency \omega in equilibrium at temperature T has \langle n\rangle = 1/(e^{\omega/T} - 1) photons, the Bose-Einstein occupation with \epsilon = \omega and \mu = 0. For a microwave mode at 10 GHz and T = 300 K, \hbar\omega/k_BT = 1.6\times10^{-3} and \langle n\rangle \approx 625; for visible light at 5\times10^{14} Hz, \langle n\rangle \approx e^{-80}.

The Bose distribution makes sense only if every occupation is non-negative. The second example derives the bound on the chemical potential and what happens as it approaches the lowest energy.

Example 57 (The bound on the chemical potential) Convergence of the geometric series and \langle n_k\rangle \geq 0 both require \mu < \epsilon_0, the lowest single-particle energy. As \mu \to \epsilon_0 from below, \langle n_0\rangle = 1/(e^{\beta(\epsilon_0 - \mu)} -
1) \approx T/(\epsilon_0 - \mu) grows without bound while the other occupations stay finite: the ground state can absorb any number of particles. This is the mechanism of Bose-Einstein condensation (Definition 15).

When occupations are small the quantum statistics no longer matters. The third example shows how the Bose distribution reduces to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and when this happens for a gas.

Example 58 (The classical limit) If e^{\beta(\epsilon - \mu)} \gg 1 for all states, \langle n\rangle \approx e^{-\beta(\epsilon - \mu)} \ll 1, the classical Boltzmann occupation. For a gas, e^{\beta\mu} = n\lambda^3 (Exercise 49), so the condition is n\lambda^3 \ll 1: the left panel of Figure 4 shows the three distributions merging when x =
\beta(\epsilon - \mu) \gtrsim 3.










NoteExercises





The Bose-Einstein distribution came from summing a geometric series in the grand-canonical ensemble. The first exercise derives it a second way, from the microcanonical counting of bosons in a group of states.

Exercise 58 (Bose counting) Group single-particle states into cells of g_s states with energy \epsilon_s, holding n_s bosons. The number of ways is W = \prod_s\binom{n_s + g_s - 1}{n_s} (stars and bars, Exercise 20). Maximise \log W at fixed \sum n_s and \sum n_s\epsilon_s with Stirling’s formula, and show n_s/g_s = 1/(e^{\beta(\epsilon_s - \mu)} -
1).







NoteSolution





\log W \approx \sum_s[(n_s + g_s)\log(n_s + g_s) - n_s\log n_s - g_s\log g_s], and \partial\log W/\partial n_s =
\log\frac{n_s + g_s}{n_s}. With multipliers, \log\frac{n_s + g_s}{n_s} = \beta(\epsilon_s - \mu), so g_s/n_s =
e^{\beta(\epsilon_s - \mu)} - 1. The multipliers are identified with \beta and -\beta\mu as in Exercise 25.



Bosons tend to bunch: the fluctuations of their occupation are larger than those of independent classical particles. The second exercise computes the variance from the grand partition function of one mode.

Exercise 59 (Bunching) For one bosonic mode show that \operatorname{Var}n = \langle n\rangle(1 + \langle n\rangle), compared with \langle n\rangle for a Poisson variable. Interpret the two terms for photons in a mode with \langle n\rangle \gg
1.







NoteSolution





\operatorname{Var}n = T\partial_\mu\langle n\rangle (Exercise 32), and with \langle n\rangle = 1/(e^u -
1), u = \beta(\epsilon - \mu): T\partial_\mu\langle n\rangle = -\partial_u\langle n\rangle = e^u/(e^u - 1)^2 =
\langle n\rangle(1 + \langle n\rangle). The term \langle n\rangle is particle-like shot noise, \langle
n\rangle^2 is wave-like intensity fluctuation: for \langle n\rangle \gg 1, \Delta n \approx \langle n\rangle, the thermal light of a classical wave with random phases. This excess (Hanbury Brown-Twiss) is computed again in Exercise 60.



The occupation of a bosonic mode is geometrically distributed. The last exercise checks normalisation, mean and variance in Sage, and the corresponding results for a fermionic mode.

Exercise 60 (Moments of the occupation in Sage) For P(n) = (1 - y)y^n with y = e^{-\beta(\epsilon - \mu)}, compute \sum P, \langle n\rangle and \operatorname{Var}n in Sage and compare with \langle n\rangle(1 + \langle n\rangle); do the same for a fermionic mode, where \operatorname{Var}n = \langle n\rangle(1 - \langle n\rangle).







NoteSolution





\langle n\rangle = y/(1 - y) = 1/(e^{\beta(\epsilon - \mu)} - 1), and the variances are y/(1 - y)^2 and y/(1 +
y)^2:

n, y = var("n y"); assume(y > 0, y < 1)
P = (1 - y) * y ** n
m0 = SR(sum(P, n, 0, oo)).simplify_full(); m1 = SR(sum(n * P, n, 0, oo)).simplify_full(); m2 = SR(sum(n ** 2 * P, n, 0, oo)).simplify_full()
print("sum P =", m0, "; <n> =", m1, "; Var n =", (m2 - m1 ** 2).simplify_full(), "; <n>(1 + <n>) =", (m1 * (1 + m1)).simplify_full())
nF = y / (1 + y)    # fermions: P(0) = 1/(1 + y), P(1) = y/(1 + y)
print("fermions: <n> =", nF, "; Var n = <n^2> - <n>^2 =", (nF - nF ** 2).simplify_full(), "; <n>(1 - <n>) =", (nF * (1 - nF)).simplify_full())
Output:
sum P = 1 ; <n> = -y/(y - 1) ; Var n = y/(y^2 - 2*y + 1) ; <n>(1 + <n>) = y/(y^2 - 2*y + 1)
fermions: <n> = y/(y + 1) ; Var n = <n^2> - <n>^2 = y/(y^2 + 2*y + 1) ; <n>(1 - <n>) = y/(y^2 + 2*y + 1)










Fermions obey the Pauli principle: each single-particle state holds zero or one particle. The grand partition function of each state has two terms, as for the orbital of Example 32, and the mean occupation is a smoothed step that becomes sharp at zero temperature.


Definition 13 (Fermi-Dirac distribution) For an ideal gas of fermions with single-particle energies \epsilon_k at temperature T and chemical potential \mu, \Xi = \prod_k(1 + e^{-\beta(\epsilon_k - \mu)}) and the mean occupation is the Fermi-Dirac distribution 
\langle n_k\rangle = \frac{1}{e^{\beta(\epsilon_k - \mu)} + 1} \in (0, 1).
 At T = 0 it is the step function \theta(\mu - \epsilon_k): all states below the Fermi energy \epsilon_F =
\mu(T = 0) are filled and all above are empty; the set of filled momenta is the Fermi sea, bounded by the Fermi surface |k| = k_F.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The Fermi-Dirac step is symmetric about \mu: the probability that a state at \mu + \delta is occupied equals the probability that the state at \mu - \delta is empty. The first example draws the consequences for the shape of the distribution.

Example 59 (The smoothed step) 1 - \langle n\rangle(\mu - \delta) = \frac{1}{e^{\beta\delta} + 1} = \langle n\rangle(\mu + \delta): holes below \mu mirror particles above it. The derivative -\partial\langle n\rangle/\partial\epsilon = \frac{\beta}{4\cosh^2
(\beta(\epsilon - \mu)/2)} is a peak of width of order T and unit area, so at low temperature only states within a few T of \epsilon_F are partially occupied (the interactive panel of Figure 4 shows the step sharpening as T decreases).

At zero temperature the Fermi gas is a filled sea, and counting the states in it gives the Fermi momentum in terms of the density. The second example computes the energy and the pressure that remains at zero temperature.

Example 60 (The Fermi gas at zero temperature) Spin-\frac12 fermions of mass m in volume V fill the momentum ball |k| \leq k_F, with two spin states per momentum: N = 2V\frac{4\pi k_F^3/3}{(2\pi)^3} = \frac{Vk_F^3}{3\pi^2}, so k_F = (3\pi^2n)^{1/3} and \epsilon_F
= k_F^2/(2m). The energy is E = \frac35N\epsilon_F and the degeneracy pressure p = -\partial E/\partial V =
\frac{2E}{3V} = \frac25n\epsilon_F is non-zero at T = 0 (Exercise 62). It supports white dwarfs and neutron stars against gravity.

In a metal the conduction electrons form a Fermi gas with a Fermi energy of several electronvolts, far above room temperature. The third example explains why only a small fraction of them contributes to the heat capacity.

Example 61 (Electrons in a metal) For copper, n = 8.47\times10^{28} m^{-3} gives \epsilon_F = 7.0 eV and T_F = \epsilon_F/k_B = 8.2\times10^4 K. At room temperature only electrons within about T of \epsilon_F can be excited, a fraction T/T_F \approx 0.4\%, each absorbing energy of order T. Hence C_{\text{el}} \sim N\,T/T_F, linear in T (the Sommerfeld result is C_{\text{el}} = \frac{\pi^2}{2}N\,T/T_F), and small compared with the lattice value 3N except at low temperature, where the Debye T^3 of Exercise 46 falls faster.










NoteExercises





The symmetry of the Fermi function and its derivative are the tools of every low-temperature calculation. The first exercise proves them and shows how they give integrals near the Fermi surface.

Exercise 61 (The Fermi window) With f(\epsilon) = 1/(e^{\beta(\epsilon - \mu)} + 1), show that -f'(\epsilon) is even about \mu, integrates to 1, and has variance \pi^2T^2/3. Deduce that for a smooth g, \int g(\epsilon)(-f'(\epsilon))d\epsilon = g(\mu) +
\frac{\pi^2T^2}{6}g''(\mu) + \dots, the start of the Sommerfeld expansion.







NoteSolution





-f' = \beta/(4\cosh^2(\beta(\epsilon - \mu)/2)) is even in \epsilon - \mu, and \int(-f')d\epsilon = f(-\infty) -
f(\infty) = 1. Its second moment is T^2\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{u^2e^u}{(e^u + 1)^2}du = 2T^2\int_0^\infty u^2\,d\left(
\frac{-1}{e^u + 1}\right) = 4T^2\int_0^\infty\frac{u\,du}{e^u + 1} = 4T^2\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{12} = \frac{\pi^2T^2}{3}, integrating by parts and using the Fermi integral of Exercise 70 at s = 2. Taylor expanding g about \mu, the odd terms vanish by symmetry and the second-order term gives \frac12g''(\mu)\cdot\frac{\pi^2T^2}{3}.



The degeneracy pressure of the electron gas in a metal is enormous by everyday standards. The second exercise computes the Fermi gas in Sage and evaluates it for copper.

Exercise 62 (The Fermi gas in Sage) With Sage, compute N and E for the T = 0 Fermi gas, express E in terms of N and V, derive p = -\partial
E/\partial V and pV/E, and evaluate k_F, \epsilon_F, T_F and p for copper.







NoteSolution





E = \frac35N\epsilon_F \propto N^{5/3}V^{-2/3}, so pV = \frac23E; in copper the electron pressure is 3.8\times
10^{10} Pa, held in check by the attraction of the ions:

k, kF, V, m, N = var("k k_F V m N"); assume(k > 0, kF > 0, V > 0, m > 0, N > 0)
Nk = 2 * V / (2 * pi) ** 3 * integrate(4 * pi * k ** 2, k, 0, kF)
Ek = 2 * V / (2 * pi) ** 3 * integrate(4 * pi * k ** 2 * k ** 2 / (2 * m), k, 0, kF)
eF = kF ** 2 / (2 * m)
print("N =", Nk, "; E =", Ek, "; E/(N eps_F) =", (Ek / (Nk * eF)).simplify_full())
kF_N = (3 * pi ** 2 * N / V) ** (1 / 3)
E_NV = (3 / 5 * N * eF).subs({kF: kF_N})
p = (-diff(E_NV, V)).simplify_full()
print("p = -dE/dV =", p, "; p V/E =", (p * V / E_NV).simplify_full())
hbar, me, eV = 1.054571817e-34, 9.1093837e-31, 1.602176634e-19
nCu = 8.47e28
kFn = (3 * pi ** 2 * nCu) ** (1 / 3)
EF = (hbar * kFn) ** 2 / (2 * me)
print("copper: k_F = %.3e m^-1, eps_F = %.2f eV, T_F = %.3e K, p = %.2e Pa" % (kFn.n(), (EF / eV).n(), (EF / 1.380649e-23).n(), (2 / 5 * nCu * EF).n()))
Output:
N = 1/3*V*k_F^3/pi^2 ; E = 1/10*V*k_F^5/(pi^2*m) ; E/(N eps_F) = 3/5
p = -dE/dV = 1/5*3^(2/3)*pi^2*N^2/((pi^2*N/V)^(1/3)*V^2*m) ; p V/E = 2/3
copper: k_F = 1.359e+10 m^-1, eps_F = 7.03 eV, T_F = 8.161e+04 K, p = 3.82e+10 Pa




The occupation of a fermionic state is a Bernoulli random variable, and its variance vanishes when the state is certainly full or certainly empty. The last exercise compares this with the bosonic bunching of Exercise 59.

Exercise 63 (Antibunching) Show that a fermionic occupation has \operatorname{Var}n = \langle n\rangle(1 - \langle n\rangle), and that the fluctuations of the total number of a Fermi gas are suppressed relative to the Poisson value, \operatorname{Var}N <
\langle N\rangle. Where in energy do the fluctuations of a degenerate Fermi gas come from?







NoteSolution





n \in \{0, 1\} gives n^2 = n and \operatorname{Var}n = \langle n\rangle - \langle n\rangle^2. Independence of the orbitals in the grand-canonical ensemble gives \operatorname{Var}N = \sum_k\langle n_k\rangle(1 - \langle
n_k\rangle) < \sum_k\langle n_k\rangle = \langle N\rangle. In a degenerate gas \langle n_k\rangle(1 - \langle
n_k\rangle) = T(-\partial f/\partial\epsilon) is non-zero only in the window of width T around \epsilon_F: deep states are always full and do not fluctuate.









A cavity whose walls are kept at temperature T fills with electromagnetic radiation in equilibrium with them. The radiation is a gas of photons, bosons with zero chemical potential and two polarisations, and its spectrum is the first formula of quantum physics.


Definition 14 (Blackbody radiation) Blackbody radiation is the equilibrium state of the electromagnetic field in a cavity of volume V at temperature T. Its modes are labelled by wave vectors \mathbf k with \omega = |\mathbf k| (c = 1) and two polarisations; in a large volume the number of modes with frequency in [\omega, \omega + d\omega] is V\omega^2d\omega/\pi^2. Each mode is a thermal oscillator with \langle n\rangle = 1/(e^{\omega/T} - 1), so the energy density per unit frequency is Planck’s law 
u(\omega) = \frac{1}{\pi^2}\frac{\omega^3}{e^{\omega/T} - 1} \qquad (\hbar = c = k_B = 1),
 and the total energy density is u = \int_0^\infty u(\omega)d\omega = \frac{\pi^2}{15}T^4 (the zero-point energies are dropped, being independent of T).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





Planck’s law interpolates between two limits that were known before it. The first example derives them and shows how the quantum occupation removes the ultraviolet catastrophe of Example 51.

Example 62 (Rayleigh-Jeans and Wien limits) For \omega \ll T, e^{\omega/T} - 1 \approx \omega/T and u(\omega) \approx T\omega^2/\pi^2, the Rayleigh-Jeans law: each mode carries the classical energy T, and \int u\,d\omega diverges. For \omega \gg T, u(\omega) \approx \omega^3e^{-\omega/T}/\pi^2, Wien’s law: high-frequency modes are frozen. The peak is at \omega = 2.8214\,T, the dots of Figure 4.

The total energy density follows from one integral, and with it the energy flux through a hole in the cavity wall. The second example derives the Stefan-Boltzmann law and its constant.

Example 63 (The Stefan-Boltzmann law) u = \frac{T^4}{\pi^2}\int_0^\infty\frac{x^3dx}{e^x - 1} = \frac{T^4}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^4}{15} = \frac{\pi^2T^4}{15}. Radiation leaving a small hole has flux \frac c4u = \sigma T^4 with \sigma = \frac{\pi^2k_B^4}{60\hbar^3c^2} = 5.670
\times10^{-8} W m^{-2} K^{-4} in SI units. The Sun’s surface at 5772 K radiates \sigma T^4 = 6.3\times10^7 W/m^2.

The cosmic microwave background is the most precise blackbody known. The third example computes its photon density from the Bose integral \int x^2/(e^x - 1)dx = 2\zeta(3).

Example 64 (The cosmic microwave background) The number density of blackbody photons is n = \frac{1}{\pi^2}\int\frac{\omega^2d\omega}{e^{\omega/T} - 1} =
\frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}T^3. For the CMB at T = 2.725 K, k_BT/(\hbar c) = 11.90 cm^{-1}, so n = 0.2436\cdot
11.90^3 = 411 photons per cm^3, and u = \frac{\pi^2}{15}T^4 = 0.26 eV/cm^3; the spectrum peaks at 160 GHz (Exercise 64).










NoteExercises





The peak of the Planck spectrum depends on whether it is plotted per unit frequency or per unit wavelength, because d\lambda and d\omega differ by a factor \lambda^2. The first exercise computes both maxima in Sage.

Exercise 64 (Wien’s displacement law in Sage) Show that u(\omega) is maximal at x = \hbar\omega/T with x = 3(1 - e^{-x}) and that the spectrum per unit wavelength u_\lambda \propto \lambda^{-5}/(e^{hc/(\lambda T)} - 1) is maximal at x = hc/(\lambda T) with x = 5(1 -
e^{-x}). Solve both in Sage, compute the Wien constant b = \lambda_{\max}T, and evaluate the peaks for the Sun, the CMB and the human body.







NoteSolution





x = 2.8214 and x = 4.9651; b = 2.898\times10^{-3} m K, so the Sun peaks at 502 nm (green) per unit wavelength and the human body at 9.3 \mum (infrared):

x = var("x")
x3 = find_root(x - 3 * (1 - exp(-x)), 1, 5); x5 = find_root(x - 5 * (1 - exp(-x)), 1, 6)
print("frequency peak: x = %.6f ; wavelength peak: x = %.6f" % (x3, x5))
h, c, kB = 6.62607015e-34, 299792458, 1.380649e-23
b = h * c / (kB * x5)
print("Wien constant b = h c/(k_B x) = %.6e m K" % b)
for name, T in [("Sun", 5772), ("CMB", 2.725), ("human body", 310)]:
    print("%s, T = %s K: lambda_max = %.4g m, nu_max = %.4g Hz" % (name, T, b / T, x3 * kB * T / h))
Output:
frequency peak: x = 2.821439 ; wavelength peak: x = 4.965114
Wien constant b = h c/(k_B x) = 2.897772e-03 m K
Sun, T = 5772 K: lambda_max = 5.02e-07 m, nu_max = 3.393e+14 Hz
CMB, T = 2.72500000000000 K: lambda_max = 0.001063 m, nu_max = 1.602e+11 Hz
human body, T = 310 K: lambda_max = 9.348e-06 m, nu_max = 1.822e+13 Hz




Radiation has entropy as well as energy, and its adiabatic expansion is the cooling of the early universe. The second exercise derives the entropy and the law of adiabatic cooling.

Exercise 65 (Entropy of radiation) From f = -\frac{\pi^2}{45}T^4 (Proposition 4), derive s = \frac{4\pi^2}{45}T^3 = \frac43\frac uT and p = \frac u3. Show that in an adiabatic expansion VT^3 is constant, so that in an expanding universe with V \propto a^3 the temperature falls as 1/a.







NoteSolution





s = -\partial f/\partial T = \frac{4\pi^2}{45}T^3, and u = f + Ts = \frac{\pi^2}{15}T^4, so s = \frac43u/T; p
= -f = u/3. Adiabatic means S = sV = \text{const}, so VT^3 is constant and T \propto V^{-1/3} \propto 1/a. The CMB was emitted at T \approx 3000 K and has cooled by the factor 1100 by which the universe has expanded since.



Neutrinos are fermions, and the radiation of the early universe contained them along with photons. The last exercise computes the factor 7/8 by which a fermionic degree of freedom contributes less energy than a bosonic one.

Exercise 66 (The factor seven eighths) Show that \int_0^\infty\frac{x^3dx}{e^x + 1} = \frac78\cdot\frac{\pi^4}{15} by writing \frac{1}{e^x + 1} =
\frac{1}{e^x - 1} - \frac{2}{e^{2x} - 1}. Deduce that a gas of relativistic fermions with g internal states and \mu
= 0 has energy density \frac78g\frac{\pi^2}{30}T^4, compared with g\frac{\pi^2}{30}T^4 for bosons.







NoteSolution





The identity holds since \frac{1}{e^x - 1} - \frac{1}{e^x + 1} = \frac{2}{e^{2x} - 1}. Then \int\frac{x^3}{e^x + 1} = \frac{\pi^4}{15} - 2\int\frac{x^3dx}{e^{2x} - 1} =
\frac{\pi^4}{15}\left(1 - 2\cdot\frac{1}{16}\right) = \frac78\cdot\frac{\pi^4}{15}, substituting y = 2x. Per internal state the bosonic density is \frac{1}{2\pi^2}T^4\frac{\pi^4}{15} = \frac{\pi^2}{30}T^4, and fermions get \frac78 of it; photons (g = 2) give \frac{\pi^2}{15}T^4.









TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. The identity is checked by exact computation in Sage (figures/occupation_numbers.sage).









In a Bose gas with a conserved number of particles the chemical potential rises towards the lowest energy as the temperature falls. Below a critical temperature the excited states cannot hold all the particles, and a macroscopic number collects in the ground state. The treatment here is in outline: the ideal gas only, with the density of states of a large box.


Definition 15 (Bose-Einstein condensation) For an ideal Bose gas of N particles of mass m in volume V (one internal state), the number of particles in excited states is at most N_{\text{ex}} \leq \frac{V}{\lambda^3}\zeta(3/2), the value at \mu = 0, where \lambda =
\sqrt{2\pi/(mT)} and \zeta(3/2) = 2.6124. When n\lambda^3 > \zeta(3/2), that is, below the critical temperature 
T_c = \frac{2\pi}{m}\left(\frac{n}{\zeta(3/2)}\right)^{2/3},
 the remaining N_0 = N - N_{\text{ex}} particles occupy the single-particle ground state, a finite fraction N_0/N = 1 -
(T/T_c)^{3/2}; this macroscopically occupied state is the Bose-Einstein condensate.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The critical temperature comes from setting \mu = 0 in the integral for the number of excited particles. The first example carries out the integral with the Bose integral of half-integer order.

Example 65 (The critical density) With \epsilon = k^2/(2m), N_{\text{ex}} = V\int\frac{d^3k}{(2\pi)^3}\frac{1}{e^{\beta(\epsilon - \mu)} - 1}, an increasing function of \mu, maximal at \mu = 0: substituting x = \beta\epsilon, N_{\text{ex}} = \frac{V}{
\lambda^3}\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{1/2}dx}{e^x - 1} = \frac{V}{\lambda^3}\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\Gamma(3/2)
\zeta(3/2) = \frac{V}{\lambda^3}\zeta(3/2), using Definition 18 of Complex analysis and Definition 20 of Complex analysis. Setting this equal to N gives n\lambda_c^3 = \zeta(3/2), the formula for T_c.

Below the critical temperature the chemical potential stays pinned at zero and the excited states hold the maximum number they can. The second example deduces the condensate fraction and the energy.

Example 66 (The condensate fraction) For T < T_c, \mu = 0 (up to O(1/N)) and N_{\text{ex}} = V\zeta(3/2)/\lambda^3 \propto T^{3/2}, so N_{\text
{ex}}/N = (T/T_c)^{3/2} and N_0/N = 1 - (T/T_c)^{3/2}: 65\% at T = T_c/2. The condensate carries no energy, so E = \frac32TV\zeta(5/2)/\lambda^3 \propto T^{5/2} and C \propto T^{3/2} below T_c; the heat capacity has a cusp at T_c (Exercise 69).

Liquid helium-4 becomes a superfluid at 2.17 K. Treating it as an ideal Bose gas at the same density gives a critical temperature of the right size, which was London’s argument that superfluidity is a form of Bose condensation.

Example 67 (Helium-4) With mass density 145 kg/m^3 and m = 6.65\times10^{-27} kg, n = 2.18\times10^{28} m^{-3} and T_c =
\frac{2\pi\hbar^2}{mk_B}\left(\frac{n}{2.612}\right)^{2/3} = 3.13 K (Exercise 68), compared with the lambda point 2.17 K. The discrepancy is due to the strong interactions in the liquid; dilute alkali gases, condensed in 1995 at about 10^{-7} K, agree with the ideal-gas formula to a few percent.










NoteExercises





The integral that limits the excited population converges in three dimensions because the density of states vanishes at low energy. The first exercise shows that in two dimensions it does not, so there is no condensation.

Exercise 67 (No condensation in two dimensions) In two dimensions the density of states per unit area is constant, m/(2\pi). Show that N_{\text{ex}}/A =
\frac{m}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{d\epsilon}{e^{\beta(\epsilon - \mu)} - 1} = -\frac{mT}{2\pi}\log(1 - e^{\beta\mu}), which diverges as \mu \to 0^-. Conclude that every density can be accommodated in the excited states at any T > 0.







NoteSolution





With z = e^{\beta\mu}, \int_0^\infty\frac{d\epsilon}{z^{-1}e^{\beta\epsilon} - 1} = T\int_0^\infty\frac{z e^{-x}dx}
{1 - ze^{-x}} = T\left[\log(1 - ze^{-x})\right]_0^\infty = -T\log(1 - z). As z \to 1 this diverges, so for any n there is a \mu < 0 with N_{\text{ex}}/A = n, and the ground state is never macroscopically occupied: n\lambda^2 = -\log(1 - z) gives z = 1 - e^{-n\lambda^2} explicitly.



The numbers in the helium example come from a short computation with physical constants. The second exercise does it in Sage, together with the condensate fractions at several temperatures.

Exercise 68 (The helium estimate in Sage) With Sage, evaluate \zeta(3/2) and \zeta(5/2), compute T_c for an ideal Bose gas with the mass and density of helium-4, and tabulate 1 - (T/T_c)^{3/2} at T/T_c = 0, \frac12, 0.9, 1.







NoteSolution





T_c = 3.13 K:

print("zeta(3/2) =", zeta(3 / 2).n(digits=8), "; zeta(5/2) =", zeta(5 / 2).n(digits=8))
hbar, kB = 1.054571817e-34, 1.380649e-23
m = 4.002602 * 1.66053907e-27
n = 145.0 / m              # mass density 145 kg/m^3
Tc = 2 * pi * hbar ** 2 / (m * kB) * (n / zeta(3 / 2)) ** (2 / 3)
print("n = %.4e m^-3, T_c = %.3f K (the lambda point of helium-4 is 2.17 K)" % (n, Tc.n()))
t = var("t")
for tv in [0, 1 / 2, 0.9, 1]:
    print("T/T_c = %s: condensate fraction = %.4f" % (tv, (1 - t ** (3 / 2)).subs(t=tv).n()))
Output:
zeta(3/2) = 2.6123753 ; zeta(5/2) = 1.3414873
n = 2.1816e+28 m^-3, T_c = 3.134 K (the lambda point of helium-4 is 2.17 K)
T/T_c = 0: condensate fraction = 1.0000
T/T_c = 1/2: condensate fraction = 0.6464
T/T_c = 0.900000000000000: condensate fraction = 0.1462
T/T_c = 1: condensate fraction = 0.0000




The heat capacity of the ideal Bose gas rises as T^{3/2} up to T_c and then falls towards the classical value. The last exercise computes the low-temperature side and the value at the cusp.

Exercise 69 (Heat capacity below T_c) Using \int_0^\infty\frac{x^{3/2}dx}{e^x - 1} = \Gamma(5/2)\zeta(5/2), show that for T \leq T_c, E =
\frac32T\frac{V}{\lambda^3}\zeta(5/2), C = \frac{15}{4}\frac{V}{\lambda^3}\zeta(5/2), and that C/N at T_c equals \frac{15\zeta(5/2)}{4\zeta(3/2)} = 1.93, above the classical \frac32.







NoteSolution





E = V\int\frac{d^3k}{(2\pi)^3}\frac{\epsilon}{e^{\beta\epsilon} - 1} = \frac{V}{\lambda^3}T\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}
\Gamma(5/2)\zeta(5/2) = \frac32T\frac{V}{\lambda^3}\zeta(5/2), since \frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\Gamma(\frac52) = \frac32. With V/\lambda^3 \propto T^{3/2}, E \propto T^{5/2} and C = \frac52E/T = \frac{15}{4}\frac{V}{\lambda^3}
\zeta(5/2). At T_c, V/\lambda^3 = N/\zeta(3/2), so C/N = \frac{15\cdot1.3415}{4\cdot2.6124} = 1.926.









The integrals of this section are all of the form \int_0^\infty x^{s-1}/(e^x \mp 1)\,dx, and they are computed by expanding the denominator in a geometric series and integrating term by term. The proposition collects them with the other results behind Figure 4.


Proposition 4 (Bose and Fermi integrals)  

\int_0^\infty\frac{x^3dx}{e^x - 1} = \sum_n\frac{6}{n^4} = \Gamma(4)\zeta(4) = \frac{\pi^4}{15}. (b) The photon gas has u = \frac{\pi^2T^4}{15}, free energy density f = -\frac{\pi^2T^4}{45} = -p, so p = u/3 and s =
\frac{4\pi^2T^3}{45}. (c) Wien’s law: \frac{d}{dx}\frac{x^3}{e^x - 1} = 0 at x = 3(1 - e^{-x}), x = 2.8214. (d) \int_0^\infty\frac{x^2dx}{e^x - 1} = 2\zeta(3), so the photon number density is 2\zeta(3)T^3/\pi^2. (e) \int_0^\infty\frac{x^3dx}{e^x + 1} = \frac{7\pi^4}{120}. (f) \int_0^\infty\frac{x^{1/2}dx}{e^x - 1} = \Gamma(3/2)
\zeta(3/2), so n\lambda^3 = \zeta(3/2) = 2.6124 at T_c. (g) n_{\text{FD}} < n_{\text{MB}} < n_{\text{BE}} for x >
0, both quantum occupations approach e^{-x}, and n_{\text{BE}} - n_{\text{FD}} = 2/(e^{2x} - 1). (h) The T = 0 Fermi gas has N = Vk_F^3/(3\pi^2) and E = \frac35N\epsilon_F.








TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Exact computation (figures/occupation_numbers.sage), each integral by term-by-term integration of the geometric series and a numerical quadrature.










NoteExamples





The term-by-term method is worth seeing once in full. The first example justifies it and carries it out for the Stefan-Boltzmann integral.

Example 68 (Integration term by term) For x > 0, \frac{1}{e^x - 1} = \frac{e^{-x}}{1 - e^{-x}} = \sum_{n \geq 1}e^{-nx}, a series of positive terms, so by monotone convergence \int_0^\infty\frac{x^{s-1}}{e^x - 1}dx = \sum_n\int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-nx}dx = \sum_n
\frac{\Gamma(s)}{n^s} = \Gamma(s)\zeta(s) for s > 1. At s = 4: 6\zeta(4) = 6\pi^4/90 = \pi^4/15; at s = 3: 2\zeta(3); at s = 3/2: \frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\zeta(3/2).

The fermionic integrals have alternating series, and the alternation produces a simple factor. The second example derives it in general.

Example 69 (The fermionic factor) \frac{1}{e^x + 1} = \sum_{n \geq 1}(-1)^{n+1}e^{-nx} gives \int_0^\infty\frac{x^{s-1}dx}{e^x + 1} = \Gamma(s)
\eta(s) with the alternating zeta function \eta(s) = \sum(-1)^{n+1}n^{-s} = (1 - 2^{1-s})\zeta(s). At s = 4 the factor is 1 - \frac18 = \frac78, at s = 2 it is \frac12, and at s = 6 it is \frac{31}{32} (Exercise 70).

Part (g) orders the three occupations. The third example derives the ordering and the identity relating the Bose and Fermi occupations, which reappears in the Matsubara sums of Section 1.6.

Example 70 (Ordering of the occupations) For x > 0, e^x + 1 > e^x > e^x - 1 > 0 gives \frac{1}{e^x + 1} < e^{-x} < \frac{1}{e^x - 1}. The identity \frac{1}{e^x - 1} - \frac{1}{e^x + 1} = \frac{2}{e^{2x} - 1} says n_B(x) - n_F(x) = 2n_B(2x); together with \frac12 + n_B = \frac12\coth\frac x2 and \frac12 - n_F = \frac12\tanh\frac x2, it relates the bosonic and fermionic frequency sums of Proposition 10.










NoteExercises





The general formula covers every power. The first exercise checks it in Sage for several values of s, Bose and Fermi, against numerical quadrature.

Exercise 70 (Bose and Fermi integrals in Sage) With Sage, compute \int_0^\infty x^{s-1}/(e^x \mp 1)\,dx for s = 2, 3, 4, 6 by term-by-term integration, compare with numerical quadrature, and verify that the ratio Fermi/Bose is 1 - 2^{1-s}.







NoteSolution





The Bose values are \zeta(2) = \pi^2/6, 2\zeta(3), \pi^4/15 and 120\zeta(6) = 8\pi^6/63; the ratios are \frac12, \frac34, \frac78, \frac{31}{32}:

x, n = var("x n"); assume(x > 0, n > 0)
for s in [2, 3, 4, 6]:
    term = integrate(x ** (s - 1) * exp(-n * x), x, 0, oo)
    B = sum(term, n, 1, oo); F = sum((-1) ** (n + 1) * term, n, 1, oo)
    qB = numerical_integral(x ** (s - 1) / (exp(x) - 1), 0, 100)[0]; qF = numerical_integral(x ** (s - 1) / (exp(x) + 1), 0, 100)[0]
    print("s = %d: Bose = %s (%.10f vs quadrature %.10f), Fermi = %s, ratio Fermi/Bose = %s" % (s, B, B.n(), qB, F, (F / B).simplify_full()))
Output:
s = 2: Bose = 1/6*pi^2 (1.6449340668 vs quadrature 1.6449340668), Fermi = 1/12*pi^2, ratio Fermi/Bose = 1/2
s = 3: Bose = 2*zeta(3) (2.4041138063 vs quadrature 2.4041138063), Fermi = 3/2*zeta(3), ratio Fermi/Bose = 3/4
s = 4: Bose = 1/15*pi^4 (6.4939394023 vs quadrature 6.4939394023), Fermi = 7/120*pi^4, ratio Fermi/Bose = 7/8
s = 6: Bose = 8/63*pi^6 (122.0811674381 vs quadrature 122.0811674381), Fermi = 31/252*pi^6, ratio Fermi/Bose = 31/32




The pressure of radiation follows from thermodynamics in part (b), but it also follows from a kinetic argument about photons hitting a wall. The second exercise asks for that argument, which holds for any gas of massless particles.

Exercise 71 (Radiation pressure from kinetics) Photons of energy \omega carry momentum \omega (c = 1). Show that an isotropic gas of massless particles with energy density u exerts pressure p = u/3 on a reflecting wall, by computing the momentum transferred per unit time and area by particles with direction cosine \cos\theta > 0.







NoteSolution





Particles with energy density u\,d\Omega/(4\pi) in solid angle d\Omega hit unit area at rate \cos\theta (speed 1) and each transfers normal momentum 2\omega\cos\theta. So p = \int_{\cos\theta > 0}\frac{u\,d\Omega}{4\pi}
2\cos^2\theta = \frac{u}{4\pi}\cdot2\cdot2\pi\int_0^1\mu^2d\mu = \frac u3. For non-relativistic particles the same argument with momentum mv gives p = \frac23u, as for the ideal gas and the Fermi gas.



The Sun is close to a blackbody at 5772 K. The last exercise uses the Stefan-Boltzmann law to estimate the temperature of the Earth, a classic application of Planck’s law in radiative balance.

Exercise 72 (The temperature of the Earth) The Sun has radius R_\odot = 6.96\times10^8 m and surface temperature 5772 K, at distance d = 1.496\times10^{11} m. Treating the Earth as a black body that absorbs sunlight over its cross-section and radiates over its whole surface, show that T_\oplus = T_\odot\sqrt{R_\odot/(2d)} and evaluate it. How does an albedo of 0.3 change the result?







NoteSolution





Absorbed power \sigma T_\odot^4\frac{4\pi R_\odot^2}{4\pi d^2}\pi r^2 equals emitted power \sigma T_\oplus^44\pi r^2, so T_\oplus^4 = T_\odot^4R_\odot^2/(4d^2). Numerically \sqrt{6.96\times10^8/2.992\times10^{11}} = 0.0482, and T_\oplus = 278 K. With albedo 0.3 the absorbed power is multiplied by 0.7, and T_\oplus = 278\cdot0.7^{1/4} = 255 K; the difference from the observed mean of 288 K is the greenhouse effect.

title: Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics
text:
Water boils, iron magnetises below 1043 K and helium becomes superfluid: at a phase transition a small change of temperature changes the state qualitatively. Landau’s theory describes the transition by an order parameter that vanishes on one side and not on the other, and by a free energy that is a polynomial in it, constrained only by symmetry. This section defines order parameters, the Landau free energy and spontaneous symmetry breaking, derives Landau theory from the mean field approximation to the Ising model, and introduces critical exponents, whose mean field values are computed and whose true values are quoted. Two exactly solvable spin systems then test these ideas: the Curie-Weiss model, in which every spin interacts with every other and mean field theory is exact, and the Gaussian free field, whose correlations are sums over random walks; between them the correlation length adds the exponents \nu and \eta.
For more on this topic, see Kivelson et al. (2024, Ch. 4, Ch. 5, Ch. 6, Ch. 7), Shankar (2017, Ch. 7-8), Skačej and Ziherl (2019, Ch. 1-5) and Strocchi (2021, Ch. 21).






Figure 5: Left: the Landau free energy f(m) - f_0 = (T - T_c)m^2 + m^4 (a = b = T_c = 1) at T = 1.3\,T_c (one minimum at m = 0), at T_c (a flat quartic minimum) and at T = 0.7\,T_c (two minima at m = \pm\sqrt{0.15}, dots, and a maximum at m = 0). Right: the equilibrium order parameter against T/T_c in the mean-field Ising model, m =
\tanh(T_cm/T) (purple), and in its Landau approximation m = \sqrt{3(1 - T/T_c)} (green), which agree near T_c. Generated by figures/landau_free_energy.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


At a phase transition some thermodynamic function is not analytic in the temperature or another control parameter. An order parameter is a quantity that distinguishes the phases, and choosing it well is the first step of every theory of the transition.


Definition 16 (Order parameter) A phase transition is a point (or line) in the space of control parameters, such as (T, p) or (T, h), at which the free energy per particle is not an analytic function in the thermodynamic limit N \to \infty. It is first order if a first derivative of the free energy (entropy, volume, magnetisation) jumps, with a latent heat T\Delta S, and continuous (or second order) if the first derivatives are continuous and only higher ones are singular. An order parameter is a thermodynamic quantity that vanishes in one phase (the disordered, symmetric phase) and is non-zero in the other (the ordered phase); at a continuous transition it rises from zero continuously.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The magnetisation of a ferromagnet is the model order parameter. It vanishes above the Curie temperature and appears continuously below it, with a direction that the system chooses.

Example 71 (The ferromagnet) The magnetisation per spin m = \langle s\rangle of a ferromagnet in zero field vanishes above the Curie temperature T_c (1043 K for iron, 631 K for nickel) and is non-zero below it. In the Ising model H = -J
\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j - h\sum_is_i, s_i = \pm1, the order parameter is a real number; in the Heisenberg model the spins and \mathbf m are vectors.

The liquid-gas transition is first order except at the critical point, where the difference between liquid and gas disappears. The difference of their densities serves as the order parameter, as the van der Waals equation shows.

Example 72 (Liquid and gas) Along the coexistence curve below the critical point (Exercise 3) liquid and gas coexist with densities \rho_l > \rho_g; crossing the curve at fixed T the volume jumps (first order). The order parameter \rho_l -
\rho_g vanishes at the critical point, and near it \rho_l - \rho_g \propto (T_c - T)^{1/2} in van der Waals theory (Exercise 75), \propto (T_c - T)^{0.326} in reality.

Superfluid helium and superconductors have a complex order parameter, a macroscopic wave function whose phase is a new degree of freedom. The third example introduces it, as the order parameter of the condensate of Definition 15.

Example 73 (A complex order parameter) In superfluid helium the order parameter is a complex field \psi(x), the macroscopic wave function of the condensate, with |\psi|^2 the superfluid density. Physics is invariant under \psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi, the U(1) symmetry of particle-number conservation, and the free energy depends only on |\psi|^2; in the superconductor \psi carries electric charge 2e and the symmetry is a gauge symmetry (Spontaneous symmetry breaking).

Phase transitions need not be thermal. The next example introduces percolation, where the control parameter is a probability and the order parameter is geometric.

Example 74 (Percolation) Occupy each site of a lattice independently with probability p, and let P(p) be the probability that the origin belongs to an infinite cluster of occupied neighbours. P = 0 for p < p_c and P > 0 above: P is an order parameter, the transition is continuous, and its exponents are universal. On a chain p_c = 1 (any empty site cuts it); on the square lattice p_c \approx 0.5927, found only numerically; on a tree with z branches per node p_c = 1/(z - 1) (Boudreau and Swanson 2018, sec. 8.1 and 8.3).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.












NoteExercises





The ordered phase of the Ising model at zero temperature is its ground state. The first exercise finds it, and identifies the symmetry that relates the two possible ground states.

Exercise 73 (Ising ground states) For H = -J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j with J > 0 on a lattice, show that the ground states are the two uniform states s_i = +1 and s_i = -1, related by the \mathbb Z_2 symmetry s_i \to -s_i of H. What are the ground states for J < 0 on a square lattice?







NoteSolution





Each bond contributes -Js_is_j \geq -J, with equality iff s_i = s_j; on a connected lattice all bonds are satisfied only by the uniform states, m = \pm1. The flip s_i \to -s_i preserves H and exchanges them. For J <
0 every bond prefers antiparallel spins; on the square lattice (bipartite) the two checkerboard (Néel) states satisfy every bond, with the staggered magnetisation as order parameter.



A first-order transition has a latent heat, and the slope of the coexistence curve is fixed by it. The second exercise derives the Clausius-Clapeyron equation from the equality of chemical potentials of Exercise 13.

Exercise 74 (The Clausius-Clapeyron equation) Two phases coexist along a curve p(T) on which \mu_1(T, p) = \mu_2(T, p). Show that \frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L}{T
\Delta v}, where L = T(s_2 - s_1) is the latent heat and \Delta v = v_2 - v_1 the volume change per particle. Estimate dp/dT for boiling water (L = 2.26 MJ/kg, \Delta v \approx 1.67 m^3/kg at 373 K).







NoteSolution





Along the curve d\mu_1 = d\mu_2, and by Gibbs-Duhem d\mu = -s\,dT + v\,dp per particle. Hence (v_2 - v_1)dp =
(s_2 - s_1)dT, which is the result. For water dp/dT = 2.26\times10^6/(373\cdot1.67) = 3.6\times10^3 Pa/K: the boiling point rises by about 1 K for each 3.6 kPa, which is why water boils at about 90\,^\circC at 3000 m.



The van der Waals equation, expanded near its critical point, has the structure of a Landau theory. The last exercise performs the expansion in Sage and finds the coexistence densities.

Exercise 75 (The van der Waals critical point as a Landau theory) In reduced variables V_r = 1 + \phi, T_r = 1 + t, expand p_r = \frac{8T_r}{3V_r - 1} - \frac{3}{V_r^2} to show p_r
= 1 + 4t - 6t\phi - \frac32\phi^3 + \dots (with a 9t\phi^2 term that is subleading). Using Maxwell’s equal-area rule on the cubic, show that the coexisting phases have \phi = \pm2\sqrt{-t} for t < 0, so the order parameter exponent is \frac12.







NoteSolution





The cubic -6t\phi - \frac32\phi^3 is odd in \phi, so the horizontal line p_r = 1 + 4t cuts off equal areas, and the coexisting volumes are its outer roots \phi = \pm2\sqrt{-t}:

phi, t = var("phi t")
pr = 8 * (1 + t) / (3 * (1 + phi) - 1) - 3 / (1 + phi) ** 2
ser = pr.taylor(phi, 0, 3).expand()
keep = sum(c * phi ** k * t ** j for (c, k, j) in [(ser.coefficient(phi, k).coefficient(t, j), k, j) for k in range(4) for j in range(2)] if (k, j) in [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (3, 0)])
print("p_r to the relevant order:", keep)
print("coefficient of phi^2:", ser.coefficient(phi, 2), "(it vanishes at t = 0, and 9 t phi^2 ~ t^2 is subleading on the coexistence curve phi ~ sqrt(-t))")
# cubic isotherm p = 1 + 4t - 6 t phi - (3/2) phi^3 is odd in phi about phi = 0 at p = 1 + 4t, so equal areas give
# coexistence at that pressure with phi = +-sqrt(-4t)
cub = -6 * t * phi - 3 / 2 * phi ** 3
print("roots of -6 t phi - (3/2) phi^3 = 0:", solve(cub == 0, phi), "; equal-area integral int_{-a}^{a} =", integrate(cub, phi, -2 * sqrt(-t), 2 * sqrt(-t)))
Output:
p_r to the relevant order: -3/2*phi^3 - 6*phi*t + 4*t + 1
coefficient of phi^2: 9*t (it vanishes at t = 0, and 9 t phi^2 ~ t^2 is subleading on the coexistence curve phi ~ sqrt(-t))
roots of -6 t phi - (3/2) phi^3 = 0: [
phi == -2*sqrt(-t),
phi == 2*sqrt(-t),
phi == 0
] ; equal-area integral int_{-a}^{a} = 0










Near a continuous transition the order parameter is small, and Landau proposed to expand the free energy in powers of it, keeping only the terms allowed by the symmetry. The coefficients are smooth functions of temperature, and the transition happens where the quadratic coefficient changes sign.


Definition 17 (Landau free energy) For a real order parameter m with the symmetry m \to -m, the Landau free energy (per unit volume) is 
f(m, T, h) = f_0(T) + a(T - T_c)m^2 + bm^4 - hm, \qquad a, b > 0,
 where h is the field conjugate to m. The equilibrium value of m minimises f, and the equilibrium free energy is f(m_{\text{eq}}, T, h). The coefficients are analytic in T; only the minimisation produces non-analytic behaviour. For a complex or vector order parameter m^2 is replaced by |\psi|^2 or |\mathbf m|^2.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The minimisation is elementary, and its result is the left panel of Figure 5. Above T_c the only minimum is at zero; below it two symmetric minima appear, and the order parameter grows as a square root.

Example 75 (Minimisation at zero field) \partial f/\partial m = 2a(T - T_c)m + 4bm^3 = 4bm(m^2 - m_0^2) with m_0^2 = a(T_c - T)/(2b). For T > T_c the only real root is m = 0, a minimum. For T < T_c, m = 0 is a maximum and m = \pm m_0 are minima with f -
f_0 = -a^2(T_c - T)^2/(4b); moreover f - f(m_0) = b(m^2 - m_0^2)^2 \geq 0, a sum of squares that proves the minima global. At T = 0.7\,T_c with a = b = T_c = 1: m_0 = \sqrt{0.15} = 0.387.

A non-zero field tilts the free energy and selects one of the two minima. The second example gives the equation of state h(m, T) and the response near the transition.

Example 76 (The equation of state in a field) With h \neq 0, \partial f/\partial m = 0 gives h = 2a(T - T_c)m + 4bm^3. Above T_c and for small h, m
\approx h/(2a(T - T_c)), a susceptibility that diverges as T \to T_c^+ (the Curie-Weiss law). At T = T_c, h
= 4bm^3 and m = (h/4b)^{1/3}: the response is non-linear even for small h.

Below T_c the Landau free energy is still symmetric under m \to -m, but the equilibrium states are not: the system must choose one of two minima. This is spontaneous symmetry breaking, and the same phenomenon in field theory gives the Higgs mechanism, developed in Spontaneous symmetry breaking.


Definition 18 (Spontaneous symmetry breaking) Let a group G act on the order parameter and leave the free energy invariant, f(g\cdot m) = f(m). The symmetry is spontaneously broken when the set of minima of f does not consist of G-invariant points: each equilibrium state m_* is invariant only under its stabiliser H \subset G, and G permutes the equilibrium states, which form the orbit G\cdot m_* \cong G/H. In statistical mechanics the choice of state is made by an infinitesimal symmetry-breaking field h: the limit h \to 0 is taken after the thermodynamic limit N \to \infty, and the result depends on the sign or direction of h.

The Ising model breaks a discrete symmetry: two minima, exchanged by the flip. The first example describes the breaking and the role of the order of limits, which the exercises make quantitative.

Example 78 (Breaking of \mathbb Z_2) The Ising Hamiltonian at h = 0 is invariant under \mathbb Z_2 = \{1, -1\} acting by m \to -m. Below T_c the equilibrium states are m = \pm m_0, each with trivial stabiliser, and the orbit is \mathbb Z_2/\{1\}, two points. For a finite system, Z sums over both and \langle m\rangle = 0 by symmetry; with a field, \lim_{h \to 0^\pm}
\lim_{N \to \infty}\langle m\rangle = \pm m_0 (Exercise 79).

With a complex order parameter the symmetry is continuous, and the minima form a circle. The second example is the “Mexican hat” free energy and its flat direction.

Example 79 (Breaking of U(1)) For f = \alpha|\psi|^2 + b|\psi|^4 with \alpha < 0, the minima are |\psi| = \sqrt{-\alpha/(2b)}: a circle, the orbit of U(1) acting by phases, with trivial stabiliser, U(1)/\{1\} \cong S^1. The second derivative of f along the circle vanishes (Exercise 80): moving along the orbit costs no free energy, the origin of the massless Goldstone modes of field theory (see Definition 11 of Gauge theories later).

A vector order parameter with rotational symmetry gives minima forming a sphere. The third example identifies that sphere as a coset space, the structure that the rest of this book generalises.

Example 80 (Breaking of SO(3)) The Heisenberg ferromagnet has order parameter \mathbf m \in \mathbb R^3 and f = \alpha|\mathbf m|^2 + b|\mathbf

\mathbf e_3 is the group SO(2) of rotations about \mathbf e_3, so the set of equilibrium states is SO(3)/SO(2)
\cong S^2, a coset space (Definition 2 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles) of dimension \dim SO(3) - \dim SO(2) = 2: two flat directions, two spin-wave branches.

Example 81 (The Potts model) Each site carries \sigma_i \in \{1, \dots, q\} with energy -K\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\delta(\sigma_i, \sigma_j), invariant under the permutation group S_q acting on all spins at once. The Landau free energy of the order parameter allows a cubic invariant for q \geq 3, so mean field theory predicts a first-order transition (Exercise 78); in two dimensions the transition is continuous for q \leq 4 and first order for q > 4 (Boudreau and Swanson 2018, sec. 20.3 and Ch. 20, Exercise 10).

The Landau free energy was postulated; mean field theory derives it from a microscopic model. The idea is to replace the neighbours of each spin by their average, turning an interacting problem into a single spin in an effective field that must be determined self-consistently.


Definition 19 (Mean field approximation) For the Ising model H = -J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j - h\sum_is_i on a lattice where each site has z neighbours, the mean field approximation replaces s_is_j by m(s_i + s_j) - m^2, with m = \langle s\rangle, neglecting the correlation (s_i - m)(s_j - m). Each spin then sees the effective field h_{\text{eff}} = Jzm + h, and the self-consistency condition is 
m = \tanh\left(\beta(Jzm + h)\right).
 The corresponding free energy per spin is f_{\text{MF}}(m) = \frac12Jzm^2 - T\log\left(2\cosh(\beta(Jzm +
h))\right), whose stationary points are the solutions of the self-consistency condition.

At zero field the self-consistency condition always has the solution m = 0. A non-zero solution appears when the slope of the right-hand side at the origin exceeds one, which gives the mean-field critical temperature.

Example 82 (The critical temperature) At h = 0, m = \tanh(\beta Jzm). The right-hand side has slope \beta Jz at m = 0 and is concave for m > 0, so non-zero solutions exist iff \beta Jz > 1: T_c = Jz. For the square lattice (z = 4) mean field predicts T_c =
4J, while Onsager’s exact value is 2J/\log(1 + \sqrt2) = 2.269J; for the cubic lattice (z = 6) the prediction 6J compares with the numerical 4.51J.

Expanding the mean-field free energy in m produces exactly the Landau form, with coefficients that are now computed. The second example carries out the expansion to fourth order in m.

Example 83 (Landau theory from mean field) At h = 0, \log\cosh y = \frac{y^2}{2} - \frac{y^4}{12} + \dots gives f_{\text{MF}} = -T\log 2 + \frac{Jz}{2}
\left(1 - \frac{Jz}{T}\right)m^2 + \frac{(Jz)^4}{12T^3}m^4 + O(m^6). Near T_c = Jz the quadratic coefficient is \frac{T_c}{2T}(T - T_c) \approx \frac12(T - T_c) and the quartic one is \frac{T_c}{12}: Landau’s form with a =
\frac12, b = \frac{T_c}{12}, and m_0^2 = a(T_c - T)/(2b) = 3(T_c - T)/T_c, the green curve of Figure 5.

Mean field theory neglects fluctuations, and in low dimensions they win. The third example contrasts the mean-field prediction with the exact solution of the one-dimensional Ising chain, which has no transition at all.

Example 84 (Failure in one dimension) For the Ising chain (z = 2), mean field predicts T_c = 2J. The exact solution by transfer matrices (Exercise 127) gives m = 0 at h = 0 for every T > 0: a domain wall costs energy 2J but gains entropy \log N, so at any T > 0 walls proliferate in a long chain. Mean field theory becomes exact as z \to \infty, and its critical exponents are correct above four dimensions (Exercise 88).

Mean field theory applies to spins with more than two values too. The next example finds the critical temperature for spins taking the values -1, 0, 1.

Example 85 (Mean field for spin one) For s_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\} and H = -J\sum s_is_j, a spin in the mean field h_{\text{eff}} = Jzm has \langle s\rangle = 2\sinh(\beta h_{\text{eff}})/(1 + 2\cosh(\beta h_{\text{eff}})). Near a continuous transition thermodynamic quantities follow power laws in the distance from T_c. The exponents of these power laws are the same for very different systems, a phenomenon called universality, and mean field theory predicts definite values for them, correct in high dimensions.


Definition 20 (Critical exponent) With the reduced temperature t = (T - T_c)/T_c, the critical exponents \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta are defined by the leading behaviour near the critical point: heat capacity C \sim |t|^{-\alpha}, order parameter m \sim
(-t)^\beta for t < 0, susceptibility \chi \sim |t|^{-\gamma}, and m \sim h^{1/\delta} at t = 0. In Landau and mean field theory \alpha = 0 (a jump), \beta = \frac12, \gamma = 1 and \delta = 3. Systems with the same dimension and order-parameter symmetry share the same exponents (universality); the true exponents differ from the mean-field values below four dimensions and are computed by the renormalisation group, which is outside the scope of this chapter.

The two-dimensional Ising model was solved exactly by Onsager in 1944, and its exponents differ markedly from the mean-field values. The second example quotes them.

Mean field theory (Definition 19) is an approximation, justified by the remark that it becomes exact when every spin has many neighbours. The Curie-Weiss model makes the remark precise: every spin interacts equally with every other, the energy depends on the configuration only through the mean spin, and the partition function reduces to an integral over a single variable whose integrand is the mean-field free energy (Roland Bauerschmidt and Slade 2019, sec. 1.4).


Proposition 5 (The Curie-Weiss model) Let N Ising spins s_i = \pm1 interact pairwise with the same coupling J/N, J > 0, in a field h (the Curie-Weiss model, or mean-field Ising model): 
H = -\frac{J}{2N}\sum_{i, j = 1}^Ns_is_j - h\sum_{i = 1}^Ns_i = -N\Bigl(\frac J2\bar s^2 + h\bar s\Bigr), \qquad \bar s =
\frac1N\sum_{i = 1}^Ns_i ,
 so that H depends on the configuration only through the mean spin \bar s. Then at temperature T = 1/\beta 
Z_N = \sqrt{\frac{N\beta J}{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-NV(\varphi)}\,d\varphi, \qquad V(\varphi) = \frac{\beta J}{2}\varphi^2 -
\log\bigl(2\cosh(\beta(J\varphi + h))\bigr),
 and the canonical ensemble of the spins is the average over \varphi, distributed with density proportional to e^{-NV(\varphi)}, of the product ensemble in which the spins are independent with \langle s_i\rangle_\varphi =
\tanh(\beta(J\varphi + h)). The renormalised potential V is \beta f_{\text{MF}}(\varphi) of Definition 19 with Jz replaced by J (Roland Bauerschmidt and Slade 2019, Lemmas 1.4.2, 1.4.3 and 1.4.6).

The Curie-Weiss model has no geometry: every pair of spins is equally correlated. On a lattice the correlation of two spins depends on their distance, and near T_c it extends over distances much larger than the lattice spacing. Its decay defines two more critical exponents and explains why the susceptibility diverges (Roland Bauerschmidt and Slade 2019, sec. 1.2).


Definition 21 (Correlation length) For a ferromagnetic spin model on \mathbb Z^d at zero field and T > T_c, in the infinite-volume limit, the two-point function is \tau(x) = \langle s_0s_x\rangle, and the correlation length \xi is the rate of its exponential decay along a lattice axis, 
\frac{1}{\xi} = -\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac1n\log\tau(ne_1) .
 Near the critical point \xi \sim t^{-\nu} as t \downarrow 0, and at T = T_c the decay is a power law, \tau(x)
\sim |x|^{-(d - 2 + \eta)} as |x| \to \infty; these define the critical exponents \nu and \eta (Roland Bauerschmidt and Slade 2019, eqs. 1.2.5-1.2.10).

The covariance of the free field has a second meaning: it counts random walks. The proposition expands (-\Delta + m^2)^{-1} in walks of the symmetric random walk of Definition 12 of Probability and statistics, extended to \mathbb Z^d, and derives the critical exponents of the free field from properties of the walk (Roland Bauerschmidt and Slade 2019, sec. 1.5.2).


Proposition 8 (Random-walk representation of the free field) On \mathbb Z^d with m^2 > 0, let p_n(x, y) be the probability that the symmetric random walk started at x, which steps to each of the 2d neighbours with probability \frac{1}{2d}, is at y after n steps. Then

\to y}\Bigl(\frac{1}{2d + m^2}\Bigr)^{|\omega| + 1},
 the last sum over all nearest-neighbour walks \omega from x to y, of any number of steps |\omega|.
