NoteExamples





Part (a) proves the minima global without calculus: a sum of squares is non-negative. The first example shows the same identity at the numbers of Figure 5.

Example 108 (The figure’s minima) With a = b = T_c = 1 and T = 0.7: m_0^2 = 0.15, f(m_0) = -0.0225 and f + 0.0225 = (m^2 - 0.15)^2; the red curve of Figure 5 touches the level -0.0225 exactly at the two dots. At T = 1.3, f = m^2(0.3 +
m^2) has its only zero at the origin.

Part (c) connects Landau theory with calorimetry. The second example interprets the jump as the condensation energy being released below T_c.

Example 109 (The heat-capacity jump) Below T_c the ordered state lowers the free energy by a^2(T_c - T)^2/(4b), which is quadratic in T_c - T; its second derivative is the constant a^2/(2b), and C = -T\partial^2f/\partial T^2 jumps by a^2T_c/(2b). In the mean-field Ising model (a = \frac12, b = T_c/12 per spin) the jump is \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{12}{2} = \frac32 per spin; superconductors show such a jump, while the true Ising transition has a logarithmic peak instead.

Part (e) derives the Landau coefficients from the microscopic model. The third example compares the predicted magnetisation near T_c with the exact solution of the mean-field equation, as in part (f).

Example 110 (Mean field against its Landau expansion) At T = 0.99\,T_c the mean-field equation has the root m = 0.17251, and the Landau form \sqrt{3(1 - T/T_c)}\,T/T_c gives 0.17147; at T = 0.9\,T_c the numbers are 0.5254 and 0.4930, and at 0.5\,T_c they are 0.9575 and 0.6124 (Exercise 83). The expansion in m is accurate where m is small, as the right panel of Figure 5 shows.










NoteExercises





The coefficients of part (e) can be computed by hand from the series of the logarithm of the hyperbolic cosine. The first exercise asks for them.

Exercise 111 (Landau coefficients by hand) From \log\cosh y = \frac{y^2}{2} - \frac{y^4}{12} + O(y^6), derive the expansion of f_{\text{MF}} in part (e) and show that with Jz = T_c the quartic coefficient at T = T_c is T_c/12.







NoteSolution





With y = \beta Jzm: -T\log(2\cosh y) = -T\log 2 - \frac{T}{2}\beta^2J^2z^2m^2 + \frac{T}{12}\beta^4J^4z^4m^4 + \dots, and adding \frac12Jzm^2 gives \frac{Jz}{2}(1 - \frac{Jz}{T})m^2 + \frac{(Jz)^4}{12T^3}m^4. At T = Jz = T_c the quartic coefficient is T_c^4/(12T_c^3) = T_c/12. The \log\cosh series comes from \tanh y = y - y^3/3 + \dots by integration.



Landau theory predicts no latent heat at a continuous transition. The second exercise checks this by computing the entropy on both sides of T_c.

Exercise 112 (No latent heat) Using the equilibrium free energy of part (a), compute S = -\partial f/\partial T above and below T_c and show that it is continuous, so that the transition has no latent heat, while \partial S/\partial T jumps.







NoteSolution





Above T_c, f = f_0 and S = S_0 = -f_0'. Below, f = f_0 - a^2(T_c - T)^2/(4b) and S = S_0 - a^2(T_c - T)/(2b), which tends to S_0 at T_c: no latent heat. \partial S/\partial T jumps by a^2/(2b), which is the jump C/T of part (c); this was checked in Exercise 76.



The critical isotherm of mean field theory has \delta = 3, and the amplitude follows from expanding the hyperbolic tangent. The last exercise derives it and compares with the slope fit of Exercise 89.

Exercise 113 (The critical isotherm) At T = T_c the mean-field equation is m = \tanh(m + h) (in units T_c = 1). Expand to show h \approx m^3/3 for small m, so that m \approx (3h)^{1/3}, and compare with the Landau result m = (h/4b)^{1/3} with b = \frac1{12}.







NoteSolution





\operatorname{artanh}m = m + h and \operatorname{artanh}m = m + m^3/3 + \dots, so h = m^3/3 + O(m^5) and m =
(3h)^{1/3}. Landau theory with b = \frac1{12} gives (h/4b)^{1/3} = (3h)^{1/3}, the same. At h = 10^{-7} the exact root is 6.6943\times10^{-3} against (3h)^{1/3} = 6.6943\times10^{-3} (Exercise 89).

title: Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics
text:
The canonical density operator e^{-\beta H}/Z is the time-evolution operator e^{-iHt} evaluated at the imaginary time t = -i\beta. Thermal physics is therefore quantum mechanics in Euclidean time, and the trace in Z =
\operatorname{tr}e^{-\beta H} identifies the two ends of the Euclidean time interval: the time direction becomes a circle of circumference \beta = 1/T. This section defines Euclidean time and the thermal circle, expands fields on the circle in Fourier modes with the Matsubara frequencies (Fourier series), and makes explicit the analogy with a field on a spatial circle: a discrete tower of modes, the mechanism that compact extra dimensions use in the Kaluza-Klein theories of this book. Throughout \hbar = 1.






Figure 6: Left: the Matsubara frequencies on the imaginary frequency axis, in units of \pi/\beta: bosonic \omega_n =
2\pi n/\beta (circles, even multiples, including 0) and fermionic \omega_n = (2n + 1)\pi/\beta (diamonds, odd multiples, no zero mode). Right: two turns of the thermal circle (\beta = 1): a bosonic mode \cos(2\pi\tau/\beta) returns to itself after \tau \to \tau + \beta, a fermionic mode \cos(\pi\tau/\beta) changes sign. Generated by figures/matsubara_frequencies.sage.





Replacing real time t by -i\tau turns oscillating exponentials into decaying ones, the Wick rotation of Definition 21 of Complex analysis. Applied to the evolution operator it turns the Schrödinger evolution into a diffusion-like evolution, and the canonical density operator is that evolution over the Euclidean time \beta.


Definition 22 (Euclidean time) For a quantum system with Hamiltonian H, Euclidean (imaginary) time \tau is defined by t = -i\tau; the evolution operator e^{-iHt} becomes e^{-H\tau}, and the Heisenberg operators become A(\tau) = e^{H\tau}Ae^{-H\tau}. The canonical density operator is \rho = e^{-\beta H}/Z with 
Z = \operatorname{tr}e^{-\beta H} = \sum_ne^{-\beta E_n},
 the Euclidean evolution over the interval [0, \beta], traced. Thermal expectation values are \langle A\rangle_\beta
= \operatorname{tr}(\rho A), and the thermal (Euclidean) correlators are G_{AB}(\tau) = \langle A(\tau)B(0)
\rangle_\beta for 0 \leq \tau \leq \beta.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





For a two-level system the trace can be computed in any basis, and the matrix exponential reproduces the partition function of Example 29. The first example works it out for a spin in a tilted magnetic field.

Example 111 (A spin in a tilted field) For H = -\mu(B\sigma_3 + B_x\sigma_1) the eigenvalues are \pm E with E = \mu\sqrt{B^2 + B_x^2}, so Z =
\operatorname{tr}e^{-\beta H} = 2\cosh(\beta E) without diagonalising: e^{-\beta H} = \cosh(\beta E) +
\sinh(\beta E)(B\sigma_3 + B_x\sigma_1)/\sqrt{B^2 + B_x^2} because (B\sigma_3 + B_x\sigma_1)^2 = B^2 + B_x^2, and the Pauli matrices are traceless. The magnetisation is \langle\sigma_3\rangle = \frac{B}{\sqrt{B^2 + B_x^2}}\tanh(\beta E) (Exercise 114).

For the harmonic oscillator the trace over the number basis is the geometric series of Definition 10. The second example writes the Euclidean evolution of the ladder operators, which makes the trace computations of the next subsection possible.

Example 112 (The oscillator in Euclidean time) With H = \omega(a^\dagger a + \frac12), Z = \sum_ne^{-\beta\omega(n + 1/2)} = 1/(2\sinh(\beta\omega/2)). The Euclidean Heisenberg operators are a(\tau) = e^{H\tau}ae^{-H\tau} = ae^{-\omega\tau} and a^\dagger(\tau) =
a^\dagger e^{\omega\tau}: not adjoint to each other any more, since e^{H\tau} is not unitary. The thermal occupation is \langle a^\dagger a\rangle_\beta = 1/(e^{\beta\omega} - 1).

The thermal two-point function of the oscillator position is the Green’s function of the Euclidean equation of motion on the thermal interval. The third example computes it from the ladder operators and states its symmetry.

Example 113 (The thermal correlator of the oscillator) With x = (a + a^\dagger)/\sqrt{2\omega} and n_B = 1/(e^{\beta\omega} - 1), for 0 \leq \tau \leq \beta: 
G(\tau) = \langle x(\tau)x(0)\rangle_\beta = \frac{(1 + n_B)e^{-\omega\tau} + n_Be^{\omega\tau}}{2\omega} =
\frac{\cosh\omega(\tau - \beta/2)}{2\omega\sinh(\beta\omega/2)}.
 It satisfies G(\beta - \tau) = G(\tau), and G(0) = \langle x^2\rangle_\beta = \frac{1}{2\omega}\coth\frac{\beta
\omega}{2}, which tends to the ground-state value \frac{1}{2\omega} as T \to 0 and to the classical T/\omega^2 as T \to \infty (Exercise 117).










NoteExercises





The trace and the matrix exponential are finite-dimensional linear algebra for a spin. The first exercise computes both in Sage and checks the magnetisation of Example 111.

Exercise 114 (Thermal trace in Sage) With Sage, compute e^{-\beta H} for H = -\mu(B\sigma_3 + B_x\sigma_1) by the matrix exponential, verify Z =
e^{\beta E} + e^{-\beta E}, and compute \langle\sigma_3\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_3).







NoteSolution





The result agrees with Example 111; the trace is basis-independent, so the eigenvalues suffice for Z:

beta, mu, B, Bx = var("beta mu B B_x"); assume(beta > 0, mu > 0, B > 0, Bx > 0)
s1 = matrix(SR, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]); s3 = matrix(SR, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])
H = -mu * B * s3 - mu * Bx * s1
Z = (-beta * H).exp().trace().simplify_full()
E = sqrt(B ** 2 + Bx ** 2) * mu
print("eigenvalues of H:", H.eigenvalues())
print("tr e^{-beta H} =", Z, "; equals e^{beta E} + e^{-beta E} = 2 cosh(beta E), E = mu sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2):", bool((Z - (exp(beta * E) + exp(-beta * E))).simplify_full() == 0))
rho = (-beta * H).exp() / Z
print("<sigma_3> = tr(rho sigma_3) =", (rho * s3).trace().simplify_full())
print("check against (B/sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)) tanh(beta mu sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)):", bool(((rho * s3).trace() - B / sqrt(B ** 2 + Bx ** 2) * (exp(beta * E) - exp(-beta * E)) / (exp(beta * E) + exp(-beta * E))).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
eigenvalues of H: [-sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)*mu, sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)*mu]
tr e^{-beta H} = (e^(2*sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)*beta*mu) + 1)*e^(-sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)*beta*mu) ; equals e^{beta E} + e^{-beta E} = 2 cosh(beta E), E = mu sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2): True
<sigma_3> = tr(rho sigma_3) = sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)*(B*e^(2*sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)*beta*mu) - B)/(B^2 + B_x^2 + (B^2 + B_x^2)*e^(2*sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)*beta*mu))
check against (B/sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)) tanh(beta mu sqrt(B^2 + B_x^2)): True




The Euclidean Heisenberg equation replaces i\,dA/dt = [A, H] by a real equation. The second exercise derives it and solves it for the ladder operators.

Exercise 115 (Euclidean Heisenberg equation) Show that A(\tau) = e^{H\tau}Ae^{-H\tau} satisfies dA/d\tau = [H, A], and solve it for a and a^\dagger of the oscillator using [H, a] = -\omega a. Show that x(\tau) satisfies d^2x/d\tau^2 = \omega^2x, the Euclidean equation of motion, whose solutions are real exponentials.







NoteSolution





\frac{d}{d\tau}e^{H\tau}Ae^{-H\tau} = e^{H\tau}(HA - AH)e^{-H\tau} = [H, A](\tau). With [H, a] = -\omega a: da/d\tau
= -\omega a, so a(\tau) = ae^{-\omega\tau}; similarly a^\dagger(\tau) = a^\dagger e^{\omega\tau}. Then x(\tau) =
(ae^{-\omega\tau} + a^\dagger e^{\omega\tau})/\sqrt{2\omega} and \ddot x = \omega^2x: the real-time equation \ddot x
= -\omega^2x with t = -i\tau.



The trace over states can be rewritten as a sum over paths, which is how the thermal circle enters field theory. The last exercise outlines the time-slicing argument.

Exercise 116 (The Euclidean path integral in outline) Split e^{-\beta H} = (e^{-\epsilon H})^M with \epsilon = \beta/M, insert position eigenstates between the factors, and use \langle q'|e^{-\epsilon H}|q\rangle \approx \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi\epsilon}}e^{-\epsilon[\frac m2(\frac{q' -
q}{\epsilon})^2 + V(q)]} for H = p^2/2m + V. Show that Z = \int\prod dq_k\,\dots becomes, as M \to \infty, a sum over paths q(\tau) with q(\beta) = q(0), weighted by e^{-S_E[q]} with S_E = \int_0^\beta(\frac m2\dot q^2 +
V(q))d\tau.







NoteSolution





The trace sets q_M = q_0 and integrates over it, so the M slices form a closed chain q_0, q_1, \dots, q_{M-1},
q_0. The product of kernels is \prod_k\sqrt{m/(2\pi\epsilon)}\exp(-\epsilon\sum_k[\frac m2((q_{k+1} - q_k)/
\epsilon)^2 + V(q_k)]), and the exponent is a Riemann sum for S_E on a path periodic with period \beta. The measure \prod_kdq_k\sqrt{m/(2\pi\epsilon)} has no limit by itself, but ratios and derivatives of Z do; the Gaussian case is done exactly by the Matsubara modes of Example 118. The closed chain is the thermal circle.









The trace is cyclic, \operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA). Applied to thermal correlators, cyclicity moves an operator from the end of the Euclidean interval to its beginning, and the correlators become periodic, or antiperiodic for fermions: Euclidean time lives on a circle.


Definition 23 (Thermal circle) The thermal circle is the Euclidean time direction \tau \in [0, \beta] with its endpoints identified, a circle S^1_\beta of circumference \beta = 1/T. Thermal correlators of bosonic operators are periodic and those of fermionic operators antiperiodic on it: for 0 < \tau < \beta, 
\langle A(\tau - \beta)B(0)\rangle_\beta = \pm\langle A(\tau)B(0)\rangle_\beta \quad\text{(continued as }
\langle B(0)A(\tau)\rangle_\beta\text{)},
 the Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) condition, with + for bosons and - for fermions. Equivalently, the Euclidean path integral of a field theory at temperature T is taken over fields on S^1_\beta \times \mathbb R^d, bosonic fields periodic, \phi(\tau + \beta, \mathbf x) = \phi(\tau, \mathbf x), and fermionic fields antiperiodic, \psi(\tau + \beta, \mathbf x) = -\psi(\tau, \mathbf x).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The periodicity follows from cyclicity of the trace and the form of the Euclidean evolution. The first example derives it for any pair of bosonic operators.

Example 114 (Derivation of the KMS condition) Z\langle A(\tau)B\rangle_\beta = \operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta H}e^{H\tau}Ae^{-H\tau}B) = \operatorname{tr}(Be^{-\beta
H}e^{H\tau}Ae^{-H\tau}) = \operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta H}\,e^{\beta H}Be^{-\beta H}\,e^{H\tau}Ae^{-H\tau}) =
Z\langle B(\beta)A(\tau)\rangle_\beta. With time-translation invariance, \langle B(\beta)A(\tau)\rangle =
\langle B(\beta - \tau)A(0)\rangle, so the correlator at \tau equals the reversed-order correlator at \beta - \tau (for the oscillator, G(\beta - \tau) = G(\tau) of Example 113): the time-ordered correlator extended to all \tau is periodic with period \beta.

For fermions the time-ordered product carries a sign when the operators are exchanged, and the same cyclicity gives antiperiodicity. The second example shows it for one fermionic mode, the orbital of Example 32.

Example 115 (One fermionic mode) For H = \epsilon c^\dagger c with \{c, c^\dagger\} = 1: Z = 1 + e^{-\beta\epsilon}, c(\tau) = ce^{-\epsilon\tau}, and the time-ordered correlator G(\tau) = \langle T c(\tau)c^\dagger(0)\rangle, with T inserting a minus sign when it reorders fermions, is (1 - n_F)e^{-\epsilon\tau} for 0 < \tau < \beta and -n_Fe^{-\epsilon\tau} for -\beta < \tau < 0, n_F = 1/(e^{\beta\epsilon} + 1). Then G(\tau - \beta) = -n_Fe^{-\epsilon\tau}e^{\beta\epsilon}
= -(1 - n_F)e^{-\epsilon\tau} = -G(\tau), since n_Fe^{\beta\epsilon} = 1 - n_F: antiperiodic.

The circumference of the thermal circle is the inverse temperature, so the geometry changes with T. The third example describes the two limits, which are the starting point of the analogy with compact dimensions.

Example 116 (Large and small circles) At T \to 0 the circle becomes infinitely large, S^1_\beta \times \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R^{d+1}, and thermal correlators become vacuum correlators of the Euclidean theory. At high T the circle is small compared with the length scales of interest, and the fields become effectively independent of \tau: the (d + 1)-dimensional theory reduces to a d-dimensional one on \mathbb R^d (Example 121). In everyday units the circumference \hbar c/(k_BT) is 7.6 \mum at room temperature.










NoteExercises





The oscillator correlator can be computed as a trace in a truncated Fock space, which tests the KMS symmetry and the closed formula of Example 113 numerically. The first exercise does this in Sage.

Exercise 117 (KMS symmetry in Sage) With Sage, build the ladder operator a on the first 60 Fock states, set \omega = 1.3, \beta = 2, and compute G(\tau) = \operatorname{tr}(e^{-\beta H}x(\tau)x(0))/Z at \tau = 0, 0.3, 1, 1.7, 2. Compare with the closed form and check G(\beta - \tau) = G(\tau).







NoteSolution





The truncation error is of order e^{-60\beta\omega}, invisible at ten digits; the symmetry \tau \to \beta - \tau is exact:

Nf = 60
w, beta = 1.3, 2.0
a = matrix(RDF, Nf, Nf, lambda i, j: sqrt(j) if i == j - 1 else 0)
x = (a + a.transpose()) / sqrt(2 * w)
En = [w * (k + 0.5) for k in range(Nf)]
def G(tau):
    D = lambda s: diagonal_matrix(RDF, [exp(s * e) for e in En])
    return (D(-beta) * D(tau) * x * D(-tau) * x).trace() / sum(exp(-beta * e) for e in En)
Gex = lambda tau: cosh(w * (tau - beta / 2)) / (2 * w * sinh(beta * w / 2))
for tau in [0, 0.3, 1.0, 1.7, 2.0]:
    print("tau = %.1f: trace %.10f, formula %.10f, G(beta - tau) = %.10f" % (tau, G(tau), Gex(tau), G(beta - tau)))
Output:
tau = 0.0: trace 0.4463328860, formula 0.4463328860, G(beta - tau) = 0.4463328860
tau = 0.3: trace 0.3268774016, formula 0.3268774016, G(beta - tau) = 0.3268774016
tau = 1.0: trace 0.2264598221, formula 0.2264598221, G(beta - tau) = 0.2264598221
tau = 1.7: trace 0.3268774016, formula 0.3268774016, G(beta - tau) = 0.3268774016
tau = 2.0: trace 0.4463328860, formula 0.4463328860, G(beta - tau) = 0.4463328860




The Euclidean time circle appears also in gravity, where it determines the temperature of a black hole. The second exercise outlines Hawking’s result from the requirement that the Euclidean geometry be smooth.

Exercise 118 (The temperature of a black hole) The Schwarzschild metric continued to Euclidean time is ds^2 = (1 - \frac{2GM}{r})d\tau^2 + (1 -
\frac{2GM}{r})^{-1}dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2. Setting r = 2GM + \frac{\rho^2}{8GM}, show that near \rho = 0 the (\tau, \rho) part is \frac{\rho^2}{16G^2M^2}d\tau^2 + d\rho^2, and that it is a smooth plane in polar coordinates only if \tau is periodic with period 8\pi GM. Deduce the Hawking temperature T_H = 1/(8\pi GM).







NoteSolution





1 - 2GM/r \approx \frac{r - 2GM}{2GM} = \frac{\rho^2}{16G^2M^2} and dr = \frac{\rho}{4GM}d\rho, so (1 - 2GM/r)^{-1}
dr^2 \approx \frac{16G^2M^2}{\rho^2}\frac{\rho^2}{16G^2M^2}d\rho^2 = d\rho^2. With \theta = \tau/(4GM) the metric is d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\theta^2, smooth at \rho = 0 iff \theta \sim \theta + 2\pi, that is, \tau \sim \tau + 8\pi
GM. A quantum field on this background is therefore in a thermal state with \beta = 8\pi GM. This outline is the Gibbons-Hawking argument; the result is quoted, not derived from field theory here.



The minus sign for fermions is not a convention: the trace over a fermionic Fock space with periodic boundary conditions computes a different quantity. The last exercise identifies it.

Exercise 119 (Periodic fermions) For the single fermionic mode, compute \operatorname{tr}((-1)^Fe^{-\beta H}) with F = c^\dagger c, and explain why the path integral with periodic fermions computes this instead of Z. For a supersymmetric oscillator, H = \omega(a^
\dagger a + c^\dagger c), show that \operatorname{tr}((-1)^Fe^{-\beta H}) = 1 for every \beta.







NoteSolution





\operatorname{tr}((-1)^Fe^{-\beta H}) = 1 - e^{-\beta\epsilon}, compared with Z = 1 + e^{-\beta\epsilon}. The operator (-1)^F anticommutes with c, so inserting it in the trace flips the sign in the KMS argument: periodic fermions compute the twisted trace. For the supersymmetric oscillator, \operatorname{tr}((-1)^Fe^{-\beta H}) =
\frac{1}{1 - e^{-\beta\omega}}(1 - e^{-\beta\omega}) = 1: bosonic and fermionic excited states cancel in pairs and only the ground state counts. This is the Witten index, which does not depend on \beta.









A function on a circle of circumference \beta is a Fourier series (Definition 2 of Fourier analysis), with frequencies that are integer multiples of 2\pi/\beta; an antiperiodic function has half-odd multiples instead. These discrete frequencies are the Matsubara frequencies of finite-temperature field theory, plotted in Figure 6.


Definition 24 (Matsubara frequency) A periodic function \phi(\tau + \beta) = \phi(\tau) on the thermal circle has the Matsubara expansion 
\phi(\tau) = \frac1\beta\sum_{n \in \mathbb Z}\phi_ne^{-i\omega_n\tau}, \qquad \phi_n = \int_0^\beta\phi(\tau)e^{i
\omega_n\tau}d\tau, \qquad \omega_n = \frac{2\pi n}{\beta},
 the Fourier series of Fourier series rescaled from period 2\pi to period \beta. The \omega_n are the bosonic Matsubara frequencies. An antiperiodic function \psi(\tau + \beta) = -\psi(\tau) has the same expansion with the fermionic Matsubara frequencies \omega_n = \frac{(2n + 1)\pi}{\beta}. In both cases the modes e^{-i\omega_n\tau}/\sqrt\beta are orthonormal in L^2(0, \beta) and are eigenfunctions of -\partial_\tau^2 with eigenvalues \omega_n^2.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The Matsubara expansion is literally the Fourier series of Part I after a change of variable. The first example makes the change and states Parseval’s identity on the thermal circle.

Example 117 (From 2\pi to \beta) With x = 2\pi\tau/\beta, a \beta-periodic \phi(\tau) is a 2\pi-periodic f(x) with coefficients c_n =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-inx}dx = \frac1\beta\int_0^\beta\phi(\tau)e^{-2\pi in\tau/\beta}d\tau. With the sign convention of finite-temperature physics, \phi_n = \beta c_{-n}, and Parseval’s identity (Theorem 2 of Fourier analysis) reads \int_0^\beta|\phi|^2d\tau = \frac1\beta\sum_n|\phi_n|^2. For an antiperiodic \psi, e^{i\pi\tau/\beta}\psi is periodic, which shifts every frequency by \pi/\beta.

The Euclidean action of a free oscillator is quadratic, and the Matsubara modes diagonalise it. The second example does this, which reduces the path integral of Exercise 116 to a product of Gaussian integrals.

Example 118 (The oscillator action in Matsubara modes) For S_E = \int_0^\beta\left(\frac12\dot x^2 + \frac12\omega^2x^2\right)d\tau on periodic paths, substituting the Matsubara expansion and using orthogonality gives S_E = \frac{1}{2\beta}\sum_n(\omega_n^2 + \omega^2)|x_n|^2: each mode is an independent Gaussian variable with variance \langle|x_n|^2\rangle = \beta/(\omega_n^2 + \omega^2), and Z \propto \prod_n(\omega_n^2 + \omega^2)^{-1/2}, which after regularisation is 1/(2\sinh(\beta\omega/2)) (Proposition 10).

Summing the mode variances gives the equal-time correlator. The third example computes the Matsubara sum and finds the result of the operator calculation of Example 113.

Example 119 (A Matsubara sum) \langle x(0)^2\rangle = \frac{1}{\beta^2}\sum_n\langle|x_n|^2\rangle = \frac1\beta\sum_n\frac{1}{\omega_n^2 +
\omega^2}. With \omega_n = 2\pi n/\beta and \sum_{n \in \mathbb Z}\frac{1}{n^2 + a^2} = \frac{\pi}{a}\coth\pi a (a residue sum, Theorem 4 of Complex analysis), a = \beta\omega/(2\pi): \frac1\beta\sum_n\frac{1}{\omega_n^2 + \omega^2} =
\frac{1}{2\omega}\coth\frac{\beta\omega}{2} = \frac1\omega\left(\frac12 + n_B(\omega)\right), the zero-point fluctuation plus the thermal occupation.










NoteExercises





The fermionic sum differs by the half-integer shift of the frequencies, and the hyperbolic cotangent becomes a hyperbolic tangent. The first exercise verifies both sums in Sage, exactly and by partial sums.

Exercise 120 (Fermionic sums in Sage) With Sage, verify that \frac{1}{2\omega}\tanh\frac{\beta\omega}{2} = \frac1\omega(\frac12 - n_F(\omega)) and \frac{1}{2\omega}\coth\frac{\beta\omega}{2} = \frac1\omega(\frac12 + n_B(\omega)), and compare partial sums of \frac1\beta\sum_n\frac{1}{\omega_n^2 + \omega^2} over |n| < 2\times10^5 with these values for three choices of \beta, \omega.







NoteSolution





The identities are exact; the partial sums agree to the size of the tail \sim\beta/(2\pi^2M):

beta, w = var("beta omega"); assume(beta > 0, w > 0)
nF = 1 / (exp(beta * w) + 1); nB = 1 / (exp(beta * w) - 1)
th = (exp(beta * w / 2) - exp(-beta * w / 2)) / (exp(beta * w / 2) + exp(-beta * w / 2))
print("tanh(beta omega/2)/(2 omega) = (1/2 - n_F)/omega:", bool((th / (2 * w) - (1 / 2 - nF) / w).simplify_full() == 0))
print("coth(beta omega/2)/(2 omega) = (1/2 + n_B)/omega:", bool((1 / (th * 2 * w) - (1 / 2 + nB) / w).simplify_full() == 0))
for bv, wv in [(1.0, 1.0), (2.0, 0.5), (0.5, 3.0)]:
    M = 200000
    sF = sum(1.0 / (((2 * k + 1) * pi.n() / bv) ** 2 + wv ** 2) for k in range(-M, M)) / bv
    sB = sum(1.0 / ((2 * k * pi.n() / bv) ** 2 + wv ** 2) for k in range(-M, M + 1)) / bv
    print("beta = %s, omega = %s: fermion sum %.8f vs %.8f; boson sum %.8f vs %.8f" % (bv, wv, sF, tanh(bv * wv / 2) / (2 * wv), sB, 1 / tanh(bv * wv / 2) / (2 * wv)))
Output:
tanh(beta omega/2)/(2 omega) = (1/2 - n_F)/omega: True
coth(beta omega/2)/(2 omega) = (1/2 + n_B)/omega: True
beta = 1.00000000000000, omega = 1.00000000000000: fermion sum 0.23105833 vs 0.23105858; boson sum 1.08197645 vs 1.08197671
beta = 2.00000000000000, omega = 0.500000000000000: fermion sum 0.46211665 vs 0.46211716; boson sum 2.16395291 vs 2.16395341
beta = 0.500000000000000, omega = 3.00000000000000: fermion sum 0.10585803 vs 0.10585816; boson sum 0.26240551 vs 0.26240564




The relation between the bosonic and fermionic sums mirrors the relation between the occupations in Example 70. The second exercise derives one sum from the other by splitting the integers into even and odd.

Exercise 121 (Fermions from bosons) Let S_B(\beta) = \frac1\beta\sum_n\frac{1}{(2\pi n/\beta)^2 + \omega^2} and let S_F(\beta) be the fermionic sum. By splitting the bosonic frequencies of a circle of circumference 2\beta into even and odd n, show that 2S_B(2\beta) = S_B(\beta) + S_F(\beta), and check the identity with the closed forms.







NoteSolution





On a circle of circumference 2\beta the frequencies are \pi n/\beta: even n = 2k give 2\pi k/\beta (bosonic for \beta), odd n give (2k + 1)\pi/\beta (fermionic for \beta). So \frac{1}{2\beta}\sum_n = \frac{1}{2\beta}
\sum_{\text{even}} + \frac{1}{2\beta}\sum_{\text{odd}}, that is, S_B(2\beta) = \frac12S_B(\beta) + \frac12S_F(\beta). Check: \frac{1}{2\omega}(\coth\frac{\beta\omega}{2} + \tanh\frac{\beta\omega}{2}) = \frac{1}{2\omega}\cdot2\coth(\beta
\omega) = 2S_B(2\beta), using \coth u + \tanh u = 2\coth 2u.



The closed form of the thermal correlator is the sum of its Matsubara series. The last exercise verifies the series both ways: by computing the Fourier coefficients of the closed form, and by summing the series numerically.

Exercise 122 (The thermal Green’s function in Sage) With Sage, compute \int_0^\beta G(\tau)e^{i\omega_n\tau}d\tau for G(\tau) = \frac{\cosh\omega(\tau - \beta/2)}
{2\omega\sinh(\beta\omega/2)} and n = 0, 1, 2, -3, and check that it equals \frac{1}{\omega_n^2 + \omega^2}; then compare partial sums of \frac1\beta\sum_n\frac{e^{-i\omega_n\tau}}{\omega_n^2 + \omega^2} with G(\tau).







NoteSolution





The coefficients are exact; the partial sums converge slowly at \tau = 0, where the periodic extension of G has a corner (a jump of G'), and fast elsewhere:

tau, beta, w, n = var("tau beta omega n"); assume(beta > 0, w > 0)
G = cosh(w * (tau - beta / 2)) / (2 * w * sinh(beta * w / 2))
Ge = (exp(w * (tau - beta / 2)) + exp(-w * (tau - beta / 2))) / (2 * w * (exp(beta * w / 2) - exp(-beta * w / 2)))   # same G, exponentials
for k in [0, 1, 2, -3]:
    wk = 2 * pi * k / beta
    c = integrate(Ge * exp(I * wk * tau), tau, 0, beta).simplify_full()
    print("n = %2d: int_0^beta G e^{i omega_n tau} d tau = 1/(omega_n^2 + omega^2):" % k, bool((c - 1 / (wk ** 2 + w ** 2)).simplify_full() == 0))
bv, wv = 1.5, 0.8
for tv in [0.0, 0.4, 1.1]:
    s = sum(cos(2 * pi * k * tv / bv) / ((2 * pi * k / bv) ** 2 + wv ** 2) for k in range(-20000, 20001)).n() / bv
    print("beta = %s, omega = %s, tau = %s: series %.7f, closed form %.7f" % (bv, wv, tv, s, G.subs({tau: tv, beta: bv, w: wv}).n()))
Output:
n =  0: int_0^beta G e^{i omega_n tau} d tau = 1/(omega_n^2 + omega^2): True
n =  1: int_0^beta G e^{i omega_n tau} d tau = 1/(omega_n^2 + omega^2): True
n =  2: int_0^beta G e^{i omega_n tau} d tau = 1/(omega_n^2 + omega^2): True
n = -3: int_0^beta G e^{i omega_n tau} d tau = 1/(omega_n^2 + omega^2): True
beta = 1.50000000000000, omega = 0.800000000000000, tau = 0.000000000000000: series 1.1637622, closed form 1.1637660
beta = 1.50000000000000, omega = 0.800000000000000, tau = 0.400000000000000: series 1.0204301, closed form 1.0204301
beta = 1.50000000000000, omega = 0.800000000000000, tau = 1.10000000000000: series 1.0204301, closed form 1.0204301










A field on the thermal circle and a field on a spatial circle obey the same mathematics: periodic boundary conditions, a Fourier tower of modes, a discrete spectrum of -\partial^2. The proposition collects the computations, and the examples spell out the analogy.


Proposition 10 (Matsubara sums and the thermal spectrum)  

e^{-i\omega_n\beta} = 1 for \omega_n = 2\pi n/\beta and -1 for \omega_n = (2n + 1)\pi/\beta. (b) \frac1
\beta\int_0^\beta e^{i(\omega_p - \omega_q)\tau}d\tau = \delta_{pq} for bosonic and for fermionic modes. (c) By residues, \sum_n\frac{1}{n^2 + a^2} = \frac\pi a\coth\pi a and \sum_n\frac{1}{(n + 1/2)^2 + a^2} = \frac\pi a\tanh\pi a.
Hence \frac1\beta\sum_n\frac{1}{\omega_n^2 + \omega^2} = \frac{1}{2\omega}\coth\frac{\beta\omega}{2} for bosons and \frac{1}{2\omega}\tanh\frac{\beta\omega}{2} for fermions. (e) \frac{\partial}{\partial\omega}\log Z = -\omega\sum_n
\frac{1}{\omega_n^2 + \omega^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\omega}\left[-\log\left(2\sinh\frac{\beta\omega}{2}\right)
\right], and -\frac1\beta\log(1/(2\sinh(\beta\omega/2))) \to \frac\omega2 as T \to 0. (f) G(\tau) =
\frac{\cosh\omega(\tau - \beta/2)}{2\omega\sinh(\beta\omega/2)} satisfies (-\partial_\tau^2 + \omega^2)G = 0 on (0, \beta), G(0) = G(\beta) equals the bosonic sum in (d), and G' jumps by -1 at \tau = 0. (g) -\partial_\tau^2e^{-i\omega_n\tau} = \omega_n^2e^{-i\omega_n\tau}, so a field of mass m on S^1_\beta \times
\mathbb R^d decomposes into fields on \mathbb R^d with masses M_n^2 = m^2 + (2\pi nT)^2 (bosons), the lowest fermionic value being (\pi T)^2.








TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Exact computation (figures/matsubara_frequencies.sage), the sums in (c) also numerically with 40000 terms.










NoteExamples





Part (g) is the whole analogy. The first example states it for a scalar field and identifies the circumference of the thermal circle with that of a compact spatial dimension.

Example 120 (A tower of fields) A free scalar of mass m in d + 1 Euclidean dimensions at temperature T has action S_E = \int_0^\beta d\tau
\int d^dx\,\frac12[(\partial_\tau\phi)^2 + |\nabla\phi|^2 + m^2\phi^2]. Expanding \phi(\tau, \mathbf x) =
\frac1\beta\sum_n\phi_n(\mathbf x)e^{-i\omega_n\tau} gives S_E = \frac1\beta\sum_n\int d^dx\,\frac12[|\nabla\phi_n|^2 +
(m^2 + \omega_n^2)|\phi_n|^2]: a tower of d-dimensional fields with masses M_n = \sqrt{m^2 + (2\pi n/\beta)^2}. A field on a spatial circle of radius R gives exactly this tower with 2\pi/\beta replaced by 1/R: the thermal circle is a compact dimension of radius R = \beta/(2\pi), and its modes are the analogue of the Kaluza-Klein modes of a compact extra dimension.

The analogy has a physical consequence at high temperature, when the circle is small. The second example describes the resulting reduction of the dimension, the thermal version of the low-energy limit of a compactified theory.

Example 121 (High-temperature dimensional reduction) When T is large compared with the energies of interest, all modes with n \neq 0 have masses at least 2\pi T and decouple; the n = 0 mode, independent of \tau, remains, and the long-distance physics of the (d + 1)-dimensional theory at high temperature is that of a d-dimensional theory of the zero modes. Fermions have no zero mode, the lowest being \pm\pi T, so they decouple entirely: at high temperature the effective theory is purely bosonic.

The free energy of a field is the sum of the free energies of its modes, each an oscillator. The third example sums them for a massless scalar and recovers the blackbody result of Section 1.4.

Example 122 (The free energy of a field) Each spatial momentum \mathbf k gives an oscillator with \omega_k = |\mathbf k|, whose free energy \frac{\omega_k}2 +
T\log(1 - e^{-\omega_k/T}) is part (e). Dropping the zero-point term, the free energy density of a massless scalar in 3 + 1 dimensions is f = T\int\frac{d^3k}{(2\pi)^3}\log(1 - e^{-k/T}) = -\frac{\pi^2T^4}{90}, half the photon value -\frac{\pi^2T^4}{45} of Proposition 4, since the photon has two polarisations (Exercise 128).










NoteExercises





The Green’s function satisfies the equation of motion with a delta source on the circle. The first exercise checks this in Sage, both from the closed form and from the series.

Exercise 123 (The source of the Green’s function) Show that the jump G'(0^+) - G'(\beta^-) = -1 of part (f) means that the periodic extension of G satisfies (-\partial_\tau^2 + \omega^2)G = \delta_\beta(\tau), the periodic delta function, and that this is equivalent to the Matsubara series of Exercise 122. Why is G the inverse of the operator whose eigenvalues are \omega_n^2 + \omega^2?







NoteSolution





Away from \tau \in \beta\mathbb Z, (-\partial^2 + \omega^2)G = 0; integrating across \tau = 0, -[G']_{0^-}^{0^+} = -
(G'(0^+) - G'(\beta^-)) = 1, the weight of a delta function. The periodic delta has the Matsubara series \frac1\beta\sum_ne^{-i\omega_n\tau} (Distributions), and applying -\partial^2 + \omega^2 to the series of G multiplies each coefficient by \omega_n^2 + \omega^2, giving that series. In the orthonormal basis of modes the operator is diagonal with eigenvalues \omega_n^2 + \omega^2 > 0, and G is its inverse, with eigenvalues 1/(\omega_n^2 + \omega^2).



The thermal circle has a definite size in laboratory units. The second exercise compares it with other lengths and computes the masses of the first thermal modes at a few temperatures.

Exercise 124 (How large is the thermal circle?) Compute the radius R = \hbar c/(2\pi k_BT) of the thermal circle at T = 300 K, at the temperature T \approx
150 MeV/k_B of the quark-gluon transition, and at the CMB temperature 2.725 K. What are the masses 2\pi k_BT of the first bosonic modes at these temperatures?







NoteSolution





\hbar c = 1.9733\times10^{-7} eV m. At 300 K, k_BT = 0.02585 eV and R = 1.9733\times10^{-7}/(2\pi\cdot0.02585) = 1.
21 \mum, with first-mode mass 2\pi k_BT = 0.162 eV. At 150 MeV, R = 1.9733\times10^{-7}/(2\pi\cdot1.5\times
10^8) = 2.1\times10^{-16} m, about the size of a proton, with 2\pi T = 0.94 GeV. At 2.725 K, R = 0.133 mm and 2\pi
k_BT = 1.5 meV.



On a circle the roles of space and Euclidean time can be exchanged. The last exercise shows that the thermal free energy of a massless field in 1 + 1 dimensions and the Casimir energy on a spatial circle are the same number in two interpretations.

Exercise 125 (Space and time exchanged) For a massless scalar in 1 + 1 dimensions at temperature T on an infinite line, show that the thermal free energy density is f = T\int\frac{dk}{2\pi}\log(1 - e^{-|k|/T}) = -\frac{\pi T^2}{6}. Compare with the Casimir energy density -\frac{\pi}{6L^2} of the same field on a spatial circle of circumference L at zero temperature (Exercise 241 of Functional analysis), and explain the agreement under \beta \leftrightarrow L by rotating the Euclidean torus S^1_\beta \times S^1_L.







NoteSolution





f = \frac{2T}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\log(1 - e^{-k/T})dk = \frac{T^2}{\pi}\int_0^\infty\log(1 - e^{-x})dx = \frac{T^2}
{\pi}\cdot\left(-\frac{\pi^2}{6}\right) = -\frac{\pi T^2}{6}, using \int_0^\infty\log(1 - e^{-x})dx = -\sum_n\frac{1}{n^2}. The Casimir energy on the circle is E = -\pi/(6L), an energy density -\pi/(6L^2). In the Euclidean path integral on S^1_\beta \times S^1_L, \log Z can be computed with either circle as time: with \beta as time and L \to \infty, \log Z = -\beta Lf; with L as time and \beta as space, \log Z = -LE_0(\beta), E_0 = -\pi/(6\beta). Both give \log Z = \pi L/(6\beta).

title: Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics
text:
NoteExercises





Three exercises that combine the sections of this chapter: a Carnot engine whose working substance is blackbody radiation, the exact solution of the one-dimensional Ising model compared with mean field theory, and the free energy of a scalar field computed mode by mode on the thermal circle.
The Carnot efficiency holds for any working substance, and radiation is a substance whose isotherms are isobars. The first exercise runs the cycle with the photon gas of Proposition 4 and checks the efficiency against Exercise 8.

Exercise 126 (A Carnot engine run by radiation) Blackbody radiation in a cylinder has u = \sigma'T^4 (\sigma' = \pi^2/15), p = u/3 and S = \frac43\sigma'T^3V. Run a Carnot cycle between T_h and T_c: isothermal expansion V_1 \to V_2 at T_h, adiabatic expansion to T_c, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression. Find the volumes, the heats Q_h, Q_c, the work as \oint p\,dV, and show \eta = 1 - T_c/T_h, with Sage.







NoteSolution





Adiabats have VT^3 constant, so V_3 = V_2(T_h/T_c)^3 and V_4 = V_1(T_h/T_c)^3. On the hot isotherm Q_h = \Delta U +
p\Delta V = \frac43\sigma'T_h^4(V_2 - V_1) = T_h\Delta S, and similarly Q_c = \frac43\sigma'T_c^4(V_3 - V_4), so Q_c/Q_h = T_c/T_h. The area \oint p\,dV equals Q_h - Q_c:

Th, Tc, V1, V2 = var("T_h T_c V_1 V_2"); assume(Th > Tc, Tc > 0, V1 > 0, V2 > V1)
s = pi ** 2 / 15
p = lambda T: s * T ** 4 / 3
U = lambda T, V: s * T ** 4 * V
S = lambda T, V: 4 / 3 * s * T ** 3 * V
# A (V1, Th) -> B (V2, Th) isothermal; B -> C adiabatic to Tc; C -> D isothermal; D -> A adiabatic
V3 = V2 * (Th / Tc) ** 3; V4 = V1 * (Th / Tc) ** 3
print("adiabats: S(B) = S(C):", bool(S(Th, V2) == S(Tc, V3)), "; S(D) = S(A):", bool(S(Tc, V4) == S(Th, V1)))
Qh = U(Th, V2) - U(Th, V1) + p(Th) * (V2 - V1)       # first law on the isotherm (u depends on T only)
Qc = U(Tc, V3) - U(Tc, V4) + p(Tc) * (V3 - V4)
print("Q_h =", Qh.factor(), "= T_h Delta S:", bool((Qh - Th * (S(Th, V2) - S(Th, V1))).simplify_full() == 0))
W = Qh - Qc
print("efficiency W/Q_h =", (W / Qh).simplify_full())
# check W as the area: int p dV around the cycle, adiabat p(V) from V T^3 = const
Vv = var("Vv")
Tad1 = Th * (V2 / Vv) ** (1 / 3); Tad2 = Th * (V1 / Vv) ** (1 / 3)
Warea = p(Th) * (V2 - V1) + integrate(p(Tad1), Vv, V2, V3) - p(Tc) * (V3 - V4) - integrate(p(Tad2), Vv, V1, V4)
print("int p dV around the cycle - (Q_h - Q_c) =", (Warea - W).canonicalize_radical().simplify_full())
Output:
adiabats: S(B) = S(C): True ; S(D) = S(A): True
Q_h = -4/45*pi^2*T_h^4*(V_1 - V_2) = T_h Delta S: True
efficiency W/Q_h = -(T_c - T_h)/T_h
int p dV around the cycle - (Q_h - Q_c) = 0




The one-dimensional Ising chain is solvable by the transfer-matrix method: the partition function is the trace of a power of a 2 \times 2 matrix. The second exercise solves it and compares with the mean field theory of Definition 19, which wrongly predicts a transition.

Exercise 127 (The Ising chain) For H = -J\sum_is_is_{i+1} - h\sum_is_i on a ring of N spins, show that Z = \operatorname{tr}T^N with T_{ss'} =
e^{\beta(Jss' + h(s + s')/2)}, so Z = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N with \lambda_\pm = e^{\beta J}\cosh\beta h \pm
\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2\beta h + e^{-2\beta J}}. Check Z against a brute-force sum for N = 6 in Sage. Deduce m = T\partial_h\log\lambda_+ as N \to \infty, show m(h = 0) = 0 at every T > 0, and find the zero-field susceptibility \chi = \beta e^{2\beta J}. Compare with mean field (T_c = 2J).







NoteSolution





Writing e^{-\beta H} = \prod_iT_{s_is_{i+1}} (splitting each field term between two bonds), the sum over spins on the ring is the trace of T^N, and T is symmetric with eigenvalues \lambda_\pm. For large N, \log Z \approx N\log
\lambda_+, and m = \frac{\sinh\beta h}{\sqrt{\sinh^2\beta h + e^{-4\beta J}}}, which vanishes at h = 0 for T > 0: no spontaneous magnetisation. The susceptibility \beta e^{2\beta J} is finite at every T > 0 and diverges only as T \to 0, exponentially, unlike the mean-field pole at T = 2J (Example 84):

beta, J, h = var("beta J h"); assume(beta > 0, J > 0)
Tm = matrix(SR, [[exp(beta * (J + h)), exp(-beta * J)], [exp(-beta * J), exp(beta * (J - h))]])
lp = exp(beta * J) * cosh(beta * h) + sqrt(exp(2 * beta * J) * sinh(beta * h) ** 2 + exp(-2 * beta * J))
print("l_+ is an eigenvalue of T:", bool((Tm.charpoly()(lp)).simplify_full() == 0 or (Tm.charpoly()(lp)).simplify_full().simplify_trig() == 0) or abs(Tm.charpoly()(lp).subs(beta=0.7, J=1, h=0.3).n()) < 1e-12)
# brute force check of Z for N = 6
from itertools import product
bv, Jv, hv, N = 0.7, 1.0, 0.3, 6
Zb = sum(exp(bv * sum(Jv * s[i] * s[(i + 1) % N] + hv * s[i] for i in range(N))) for s in product([1, -1], repeat=N))
Ztr = (Tm.subs(beta=bv, J=Jv, h=hv) ** N).trace()
print("N = 6: brute-force Z = %.10f, tr T^6 = %.10f" % (Zb, Ztr.n()))
m = (diff(log(lp), h) / beta)
print("m(h = 0) =", m.subs(h=0).simplify_full())
mh = m.simplify_full()
print("m at small h: m = beta e^{2 beta J} h + O(h^3):", bool((diff(mh, h).subs(h=0) - beta * exp(2 * beta * J)).simplify_full() == 0))
for T in [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]:
    print("J = 1, h = 0.01, T = %.1f: exact chain m = %.5f" % (T, m.subs(beta=1 / T, J=1, h=0.01).n()))
Output:
l_+ is an eigenvalue of T: True
N = 6: brute-force Z = 406.0515677249, tr T^6 = 406.0515677249
m(h = 0) = 0
m at small h: m = beta e^{2 beta J} h + O(h^3): True
J = 1, h = 0.01, T = 0.5: exact chain m = 0.73750
J = 1, h = 0.01, T = 1.0: exact chain m = 0.07369
J = 1, h = 0.01, T = 2.0: exact chain m = 0.01359
J = 1, h = 0.01, T = 4.0: exact chain m = 0.00412




The last exercise assembles the thermal circle, the partition function of the oscillator and the Bose integral into the free energy of a field. It is the computation behind Example 122, and it shows the tower of three-dimensional masses that the Matsubara modes produce.

Exercise 128 (A field on the thermal circle) A free massless real scalar in 3 + 1 dimensions at temperature T: (a) argue from Proposition 10 that each momentum mode contributes the oscillator free energy \frac{\omega_k}{2} + T\log(1 - e^{-\omega_k/T}); (b) show with Sage that the thermal part integrates to f = -\frac{\pi^2T^4}{90}, using \int_0^\infty x^2\log(1 - e^{-x})dx = -\frac13
\int_0^\infty\frac{x^3dx}{e^x - 1}; (c) derive s, u and p = u/3; (d) list the masses 2\pi|n|T of the three-dimensional fields in the Matsubara tower at T = 1 and T = 10, and the lowest fermionic value \pi T.







NoteSolution






Part (e) of the proposition gives \partial_\omega\log Z for each mode, and integrating with the T \to 0 limit fixes the constant: F_k = \frac{\omega_k}{2} + T\log(1 - e^{-\omega_k/T}). (b) f = \frac{T}{2\pi^2}\int k^2\log(1 -
e^{-k/T})dk = \frac{T^4}{2\pi^2}\cdot\left(-\frac{\pi^4}{45}\right) = -\frac{\pi^2T^4}{90}. (c) s = \frac{2\pi^2T^3}
{45}, u = \frac{\pi^2T^4}{30}, p = -f = u/3. (d) The masses grow linearly with T: at high temperature only the zero mode stays light (Example 121):


k, T, x, n = var("k T x n"); assume(k > 0, T > 0, x > 0, n > 0)
# int x^2 log(1 - e^{-x}) dx = -(1/3) int x^3/(e^x - 1) dx = -(1/3) sum_n 6/n^4
I3 = sum(integrate(x ** 3 * exp(-n * x), x, 0, oo), n, 1, oo)
f = 4 * pi / (2 * pi) ** 3 * T ** 4 * (-I3 / 3)
print("f = (T^4/(2 pi^2)) int x^2 log(1 - e^{-x}) dx =", f, "; -pi^2 T^4/90:", bool(f == -pi ** 2 * T ** 4 / 90))
print("numerical check of int x^2 log(1 - e^{-x}) dx:", numerical_integral(x ** 2 * log(1 - exp(-x)), 0, 80)[0], "vs", (-pi ** 4 / 45).n())
print("s = -df/dT =", -diff(f, T), "; u = f + T s =", (f - T * diff(f, T)), "; p = -f, p = u/3:", bool(-f == (f - T * diff(f, T)) / 3))
# the tower: masses 2 pi n T of the three-dimensional fields, and the circumference 1/T
for Tv in [1, 10]:
    print("T = %s: lowest bosonic masses 2 pi |n| T =" % Tv, [(2 * pi * abs(j) * Tv).n(digits=4) for j in range(0, 3)], "; lowest fermionic pi T =", (pi * Tv).n(digits=4))
Output:
f = (T^4/(2 pi^2)) int x^2 log(1 - e^{-x}) dx = -1/90*pi^2*T^4 ; -pi^2 T^4/90: True
numerical check of int x^2 log(1 - e^{-x}) dx: -2.1646464673611323 vs -2.16464646742228
s = -df/dT = 2/45*pi^2*T^3 ; u = f + T s = 1/30*pi^2*T^4 ; p = -f, p = u/3: True
T = 1: lowest bosonic masses 2 pi |n| T = [0.0000, 6.283, 12.57] ; lowest fermionic pi T = 3.142
T = 10: lowest bosonic masses 2 pi |n| T = [0.0000, 62.83, 125.7] ; lowest fermionic pi T = 31.42

title: Classical mechanics
text:
Classical mechanics is the physics of particles and rigid bodies moving under forces. Newton’s laws state it directly; the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations restate it through an action principle and through phase space, and in doing so expose the structures (symmetries and conserved quantities, Poisson brackets, canonical transformations, normal modes) that every later theory, classical or quantum, inherits. This chapter has six sections. Newtonian mechanics introduces momentum, force and energy and solves Kepler’s problem. Lagrangian mechanics replaces forces by an action whose stationary paths are the motions, and Hamiltonian mechanics trades velocities for momenta to obtain first-order equations on phase space. Poisson brackets and canonical transformations studies the algebra and the geometry of phase space: the bracket, the transformations that preserve it, Liouville’s theorem and the Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Noether’s theorem derives conserved quantities from symmetries, and small oscillations linearises the motion about an equilibrium, ending with a particle on the sphere and on the group SU(2). Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions.


Newton’s laws describe a particle by its position \vec x(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and say how forces change its motion. This section introduces momentum and the second law, the energy of a conservative force, central forces with their conserved angular momentum, and solves the problem that founded the subject: the motion of a planet about the Sun, whose orbits are conic sections. The later sections recast all of this in a form that generalises to constrained systems, to fields and to quantum mechanics.
For more on this topic, see Knauf (2018, Ch. 11), Kotkin and Serbo (2020, sec. 1, §2) and Moretti (2023, Ch. 3-4).


The state of a particle at an instant is given by its position and its velocity, and the second law determines how the velocity changes. It is stated most economically through the momentum, which is also the quantity that is conserved when particles interact only with each other.


Definition 1 (Momentum) A particle of mass m > 0 moving along \vec x(t) has velocity \vec v = \dot{\vec x} and momentum \vec p = m\vec
v. A force \vec F(\vec x, \dot{\vec x}, t) acting on it determines its motion through Newton’s second law 
\frac{d\vec p}{dt} = \vec F ,
\tag{1} a second-order differential equation (Ordinary differential equations) whose solution is fixed by \vec x(0) and \dot{\vec x}(0). For several particles the forces they exert on each other come in equal and opposite pairs, \vec F_{12} = -\vec
F_{21} (third law).

NoteExamples





The simplest force is none at all. The second law then says that the momentum does not change, which is Newton’s first law: free particles move on straight lines at constant speed.

Example 1 (The free particle) With \vec F = 0, \dot{\vec p} = 0, so \vec p is constant and \vec x(t) = \vec x_0 + \vec v_0 t: uniform motion on a straight line. The first law is the special case of the second law with no force.

A constant force produces a constant acceleration, and the motion integrates in elementary functions. Near the surface of the Earth the gravitational force is -mg\,\vec e_z, and the second law gives the projectile’s parabola.

Example 2 (Uniform gravity) For \vec F = -mg\,\vec e_z, \dot{\vec p} = -mg\,\vec e_z integrates to \vec x(t) = \vec x_0 + \vec v_0 t - \tfrac12
gt^2\,\vec e_z, a parabola. The horizontal components of \vec p are conserved, because the force has no horizontal component, while p_z decreases at the rate mg (Exercise 1).

For two particles the third law makes the internal forces cancel in the total momentum. The centre of mass therefore moves like a free particle, whatever the particles do to each other.

Example 3 (Two interacting particles) If two particles exert forces \vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21} on each other and nothing else acts on them, the total momentum \vec P = \vec p_1 + \vec p_2 satisfies \dot{\vec P} = \vec F_{12} + \vec F_{21} = 0. The centre of mass \vec X = (m_1\vec x_1 + m_2\vec x_2)/(m_1 + m_2) moves uniformly, \vec X(t) = \vec X_0 + \vec Pt/(m_1 + m_2) (Exercise 3).










NoteExercises





The first exercise solves the projectile problem with Sage and asks which launch angle carries the projectile furthest. It is a direct application of the second law with a constant force.

Exercise 1 (The range of a projectile) Solve m\ddot x = 0, m\ddot z = -mg with Sage’s desolve for a launch at speed v_0 and angle \alpha from the origin, find the range (the distance at which z returns to 0), and the angle that maximises it.







NoteSolution





x = v_0t\cos\alpha and z = v_0t\sin\alpha - \tfrac12 gt^2; z = 0 again at t = 2v_0\sin\alpha/g, where x =
2v_0^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha/g = v_0^2\sin 2\alpha/g, maximal at \alpha = \pi/4 with range v_0^2/g:

t, g, v0, al = var("t g v0 alpha", domain="positive")
x, z = function("x")(t), function("z")(t)
xs = desolve(diff(x, t, 2) == 0, x, ics=[0, 0, v0 * cos(al)], ivar=t)
zs = desolve(diff(z, t, 2) == -g, z, ics=[0, 0, v0 * sin(al)], ivar=t)
print("x(t) =", xs, "; z(t) =", zs.expand())
tland = [s.rhs() for s in solve(zs == 0, t) if s.rhs() != 0][0]
R = xs.subs(t=tland).trig_reduce()
print("landing time:", tland, "; range:", R)
print("range maximal at alpha = pi/4:", bool(diff(R, al).subs({al: pi / 4}) == 0), "; maximal range:", R.subs({al: pi / 4}))
Output:
x(t) = t*v0*cos(alpha) ; z(t) = -1/2*g*t^2 + t*v0*sin(alpha)
landing time: 2*v0*sin(alpha)/g ; range: v0^2*sin(2*alpha)/g
range maximal at alpha = pi/4: True ; maximal range: v0^2/g




Forces that depend on the velocity are common in practice, and the second law handles them just as well. The second exercise treats linear air resistance, for which the momentum decays exponentially.

Exercise 2 (Linear drag) A particle moves on a line under the drag force F = -\gamma v, \gamma > 0. Solve the second law for v(t) with v(0) = v_0 and find the total distance travelled.







NoteSolution





m\dot v = -\gamma v gives v(t) = v_0e^{-\gamma t/m}, and x(t) - x(0) = \int_0^t v = \frac{mv_0}{\gamma}(1 -
e^{-\gamma t/m}), which tends to mv_0/\gamma: the particle stops after a finite distance, although never in a finite time. The momentum is not conserved, because the force does not vanish.



The two-body problem looks like a problem in six dimensions, but conservation of total momentum reduces it to the motion of a single fictitious particle. The third exercise performs the reduction, which is the first step in solving Kepler’s problem.

Exercise 3 (Reduction of the two-body problem) Two particles interact through \vec F_{12} = \vec f(\vec x_1 - \vec x_2) = -\vec F_{21} (the force on particle 1). Show that the relative coordinate \vec r = \vec x_1 - \vec x_2 satisfies \mu\ddot{\vec r} = \vec f(\vec r) with the reduced mass \mu = m_1m_2/(m_1 + m_2), and express \vec x_1, \vec x_2 through \vec X and \vec r.







NoteSolution





\ddot{\vec x}_1 = \vec f/m_1 and \ddot{\vec x}_2 = -\vec f/m_2, so \ddot{\vec r} = \vec f\,(1/m_1 + 1/m_2) = \vec
f/\mu. With M = m_1 + m_2, \vec x_1 = \vec X + \frac{m_2}{M}\vec r and \vec x_2 = \vec X - \frac{m_1}{M}\vec r, and \vec X moves uniformly (Example 3). For the Sun and a planet \mu is very close to the planet’s mass, and the Sun barely moves.









The work done by a force along a path changes the kinetic energy. For a large and important class of forces the work depends only on the endpoints, and then a potential energy can be defined whose sum with the kinetic energy is conserved.


Definition 2 (Conservative force) A force \vec F(\vec x) is conservative if \vec F = -\nabla V for a function V(\vec x), the potential energy. The kinetic energy is T = \tfrac12 m|\dot{\vec x}|^2; along any motion \frac{dT}{dt} = \vec F\cdot
\dot{\vec x}, and for a conservative force this is -\frac{dV}{dt}, so the energy E = T + V is conserved. On a simply connected region a force is conservative exactly when \nabla \times \vec F = 0.

NoteExamples





A spring that pulls towards the origin with a force proportional to the distance is the simplest conservative force. Its potential is quadratic, and energy conservation already shows that the motion is bounded.

Example 4 (Hooke’s law) \vec F = -k\vec x is -\nabla V with V = \tfrac12 k|\vec x|^2. The energy E = \tfrac12 m|\dot{\vec x}|^2 + \tfrac12
k|\vec x|^2 is conserved, so |\vec x| \le \sqrt{2E/k}; on a line the motion is the harmonic oscillator of Section 1.2, x = A\cos(\omega t + \delta) with \omega^2 = k/m.

Newtonian gravity is conservative with a potential inversely proportional to the distance. Energy conservation then answers a question that would otherwise require solving the equations of motion: how fast a body must be thrown to escape.

Example 5 (Newtonian gravity) A mass M at the origin attracts a particle with \vec F = -GMm\,\vec x/|\vec x|^3 = -\nabla V, V = -GMm/|\vec x|. A particle launched from radius R escapes to infinity exactly when E \ge 0, that is with speed at least v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/R} (Exercise 6).

Not every force derives from a potential. A force that circulates around the origin does work along a closed loop, which a gradient never does, and its curl detects the obstruction.

Example 6 (A non-conservative force) \vec F = (-y, x, 0) has \nabla\times\vec F = (0, 0, 2) \neq 0, so it is not a gradient; its work around the unit circle (\cos s, \sin s, 0) is \int_0^{2\pi}(\sin^2 s + \cos^2 s)\,ds = 2\pi \neq 0, while a gradient does no work around a closed loop. Velocity-dependent forces such as drag (Exercise 2) are not conservative either.










NoteExercises





The curl criterion is mechanical to apply, and Sage also finds the potential when it exists. The first exercise tests three forces and reconstructs two potentials.

Exercise 4 (Finding potentials) Compute the curl of \vec F_1 = (2xy, x^2, 0), \vec F_2 = (y, -x, 0) and \vec F_3 = -k\vec x/|\vec x|^3, and find a potential for those that are conservative.







NoteSolution





\nabla\times\vec F_1 = 0 with V_1 = -x^2y; \nabla\times\vec F_2 = (0, 0, -2), not conservative; \nabla\times\vec F_3 = 0 with V_3 = -k/|\vec x|. Sage checks the curls and that -\nabla V returns the force:

x, y, z, k = var("x y z k", domain="real")
X = vector([x, y, z]); r = sqrt(x**2 + y**2 + z**2)
def curl(F): return vector([diff(F[2], y) - diff(F[1], z), diff(F[0], z) - diff(F[2], x), diff(F[1], x) - diff(F[0], y)])
F1 = vector([2 * x * y, x**2, 0]); F2 = vector([y, -x, 0]); F3 = -k * X / r**3
for name, F in [("F1", F1), ("F2", F2), ("F3", F3)]:
    print("curl", name, "=", curl(F).simplify_full())
V1 = -x**2 * y; V3 = -k / r
print("-grad V1 == F1:", bool(-V1.gradient([x, y, z]) == F1), "; -grad V3 == F3:", bool((-V3.gradient([x, y, z]) - F3).simplify_full() == 0))
s = var("s")
print("work of F2 around the unit circle:", integrate(F2.subs(x=cos(s), y=sin(s)) * vector([-sin(s), cos(s), 0]), s, 0, 2 * pi))
Output:
curl F1 = (0, 0, 0)
curl F2 = (0, 0, -2)
curl F3 = (0, 0, 0)
-grad V1 == F1: True ; -grad V3 == F3: True
work of F2 around the unit circle: -2*pi




In one dimension energy conservation reduces the equation of motion to a single integration. The second exercise uses it to compute the period of the oscillator without solving the differential equation.

Exercise 5 (Motion in one dimension) Show that for m\ddot x = -V'(x) the time to go from x_1 to x_2 is \int_{x_1}^{x_2}dx/\sqrt{2(E - V(x))/m} while \dot x > 0, and use it to show that the period of the oscillator V = \tfrac12 kx^2 is 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} for every amplitude.







NoteSolution





From E = \tfrac12 m\dot x^2 + V, \dot x = \sqrt{2(E - V)/m}, so dt = dx/\sqrt{2(E - V)/m}. For the oscillator with amplitude A = \sqrt{2E/k}, \sqrt{2(E - V)/m} = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} with \omega = \sqrt{k/m}, and the time from -A to A is \frac1\omega\int_{-A}^{A}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}} = \frac{\pi}{\omega}. The period is twice this, 2\pi/\omega = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}, independent of A.



The escape speed is a statement about energies only. The third exercise evaluates it for the Earth, using the surface gravity g = GM/R^2 to avoid needing G and M separately.

Exercise 6 (Escape speed from the Earth) Derive v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/R} from energy conservation, write it as \sqrt{2gR}, and evaluate it for g = 9.
81\ \mathrm{m/s^2} and R = 6.371\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}.







NoteSolution





The particle reaches infinity, where V = 0, with non-negative kinetic energy exactly when E = \tfrac12 mv^2 -
GMm/R \ge 0, that is v \ge \sqrt{2GM/R}. Since g = GM/R^2, 2GM/R = 2gR, and \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 6.371
\times 10^6} \approx \sqrt{1.250\times10^8} \approx 1.12\times10^4\ \mathrm{m/s}, about 11.2 km/s.









A force that always points towards or away from a fixed centre exerts no torque about that centre. Its angular momentum is then conserved, the motion stays in a plane, and the radial motion becomes a one-dimensional problem in an effective potential.


Definition 3 (Central force) A central force is a force of the form \vec F = f(r)\,\vec x/r, r = |\vec x|; it is conservative, with V(r)
= -\int f\,dr. The angular momentum \vec L = \vec x \times \vec p is conserved, since \dot{\vec L} =
\dot{\vec x}\times m\dot{\vec x} + \vec x\times\vec F = 0, so the motion lies in the plane through the origin orthogonal to \vec L. In polar coordinates (r, \varphi) in that plane, L = mr^2\dot\varphi and 
E = \tfrac12 m\dot r^2 + U(r), \qquad U(r) = \frac{L^2}{2mr^2} + V(r) ,
\tag{2} with the effective potential U: the radial motion is one-dimensional.

NoteExamples





Conservation of angular momentum has a geometric meaning that Kepler found in the data before Newton explained it. The rate at which the radius vector sweeps area is proportional to the angular momentum, and hence constant.

Example 7 (Equal areas in equal times) In time dt the radius vector sweeps the triangle of area \tfrac12 r^2\,d\varphi, so \frac{dA}{dt} = \tfrac12
r^2\dot\varphi = \frac{L}{2m}, constant for every central force: Kepler’s second law, drawn in Figure 5 of Section 1.5.

For gravity the effective potential is the sum of a repulsive centrifugal barrier and the attractive Newtonian potential. Its minimum is a circular orbit, and its shape decides which orbits are bound.

Example 8 (The Kepler effective potential) For V = -k/r, U = \frac{L^2}{2mr^2} - \frac kr has its minimum at r_0 = L^2/(mk) with U(r_0) = -mk^2/(2L^2) (Figure 1, right). At E = U(r_0) the orbit is a circle; for U(r_0) < E < 0 the radius oscillates between two turning points; for E \ge 0 the particle comes in from infinity and returns to it.

The isotropic oscillator is the other central force whose bounded orbits all close. Here the orbits are ellipses centred at the origin rather than having the origin at a focus.

Example 9 (The isotropic oscillator) For V = \tfrac12 kr^2 every orbit is bounded, U = \frac{L^2}{2mr^2} + \tfrac12 kr^2 \to \infty at both ends. In Cartesian coordinates the motion is x = a\cos\omega t, y = b\cos(\omega t + \delta) with \omega^2 = k/m, an ellipse centred at the origin; Bertrand’s theorem says that -k/r and kr^2 are the only central potentials all of whose bounded orbits close.










NoteExercises





The difference between the two potentials appears in small oscillations about a circular orbit. The first exercise compares the radial and angular frequencies and finds why orbits close in both cases.

Exercise 7 (Radial oscillations about a circular orbit) For V = -k/r and V = \tfrac12 kr^2, find the radius r_0 of the circular orbit of angular momentum L, the frequency \omega_r of small radial oscillations (\omega_r^2 = U''(r_0)/m) and the angular frequency \omega_\varphi = L/(mr_0^2). Compare them.







NoteSolution





For Kepler r_0 = L^2/(mk) and \omega_r^2 = \omega_\varphi^2 = k/(mr_0^3): one radial oscillation per revolution, and the orbit closes (an ellipse with the centre at a focus). For the oscillator r_0^4 = L^2/(mk), \omega_r^2 =
4k/m and \omega_\varphi^2 = k/m: two radial oscillations per revolution, an ellipse centred at the origin.

r, m, k, L = var("r m k L", domain="positive")
for name, V in [("Kepler -k/r", -k / r), ("oscillator k r^2/2", k * r**2 / 2)]:
    U = L**2 / (2 * m * r**2) + V
    r0 = [s.rhs() for s in solve(diff(U, r) == 0, r) if bool(s.rhs().subs(m=1, k=1, L=1) == 1)][0]
    wr2 = (diff(U, r, 2).subs(r=r0) / m).simplify_full()
    wphi2 = ((L / (m * r0**2))**2).simplify_full()
    print(name, ": r0 =", r0, "; omega_r^2 =", wr2, "; omega_phi^2 =", wphi2, "; ratio omega_r/omega_phi =", sqrt(wr2 / wphi2).simplify_full())
Output:
Kepler -k/r : r0 = L^2/(k*m) ; omega_r^2 = k^4*m^2/L^6 ; omega_phi^2 = k^4*m^2/L^6 ; ratio omega_r/omega_phi = 1
oscillator k r^2/2 : r0 = sqrt(L)*(1/(k*m))^(1/4) ; omega_r^2 = 4*k/m ; omega_phi^2 = k/m ; ratio omega_r/omega_phi = 2




The orbit r(\varphi) satisfies a simpler equation than r(t) if one uses u = 1/r as the unknown. The second exercise derives this orbit equation, named after Binet, and solves it for gravity.

Exercise 8 (The orbit equation) Using \dot\varphi = L/(mr^2) to replace d/dt by d/d\varphi, show that u = 1/r satisfies u'' + u = -
\frac{m}{L^2u^2}f(1/u), and solve it for f = -k/r^2.







NoteSolution





\dot r = -\frac{\dot u}{u^2} = -\frac{u'\dot\varphi}{u^2} = -\frac{L}{m}u' and \ddot r = -\frac Lmu''\dot\varphi = -
\frac{L^2}{m^2}u^2u''. The radial equation m\ddot r - mr\dot\varphi^2 = f becomes -\frac{L^2}{m}u^2u'' -
\frac{L^2}{m}u^3 = f, that is u'' + u = -\frac{m}{L^2u^2}f(1/u). For f = -ku^2 the right side is the constant mk/L^2, so u = \frac{mk}{L^2}(1 + e\cos(\varphi - \varphi_0)): the conic of Proposition 1.



A circular orbit exists for any attractive force, but it need not be stable. The third exercise finds the power laws for which a slightly disturbed circular orbit stays close to the circle.

Exercise 9 (Stability of circular orbits) For the attractive power law f(r) = -kr^\alpha (k > 0), show that the circular orbit of angular momentum L is a minimum of U (stable) exactly when \alpha > -3.







NoteSolution





U'(r) = -\frac{L^2}{mr^3} - f(r), so a circular orbit has kr_0^\alpha = \frac{L^2}{mr_0^3}. Then U''(r_0) =
\frac{3L^2}{mr_0^4} - f'(r_0) = \frac{3L^2}{mr_0^4} + k\alpha r_0^{\alpha - 1} = (3 + \alpha)\frac{L^2}{mr_0^4}, which is positive exactly when \alpha > -3. Gravity (\alpha = -2) and the oscillator (\alpha = 1) are stable; an inverse-cube force is marginal, and steeper forces let the particle spiral in or out.









The attractive inverse-square force can be solved completely. Besides energy and angular momentum it conserves a third vector, the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector, which points to the closest approach and is the reason the orbits close.


Proposition 1 (Kepler orbits) For V = -k/r (k > 0) and angular momentum L \neq 0 the orbit is the conic 
r = \frac{p}{1 + e\cos(\varphi - \varphi_0)}, \qquad p = \frac{L^2}{mk}, \qquad E = \frac{k(e^2 - 1)}{2p} ,
\tag{3} an ellipse for E < 0 (0 \le e < 1), a parabola for E = 0 and a hyperbola branch for E > 0. The Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector \vec A = \vec p\times\vec L - mk\,\vec x/r is conserved, orthogonal to \vec L and of length |\vec A|^2 = m^2k^2 + 2mEL^2, that is |\vec A| = mke. A bound orbit with semi-major axis a =
p/(1 - e^2) has period T = 2\pi\sqrt{ma^3/k} (Kepler’s third law).

NoteExamples





The circle is the conic with e = 0. It is the orbit at the bottom of the effective potential, and its speed follows from balancing gravity against the centripetal acceleration.

Example 10 (Circular orbits) For e = 0, r = p and E = -k/(2p); the speed v satisfies mv^2/p = k/p^2, so v^2 = k/(mp) and the kinetic energy \tfrac12 mv^2 = k/(2p) is half the potential energy in absolute value, the virial theorem for 1/r potentials. The period is 2\pi p/v = 2\pi\sqrt{mp^3/k}, the third law with a = p.

Planetary orbits are ellipses of small eccentricity. The Earth’s orbit illustrates the formulas: the ratio of the closest to the furthest distance is close to one, and the period fixes the semi-major axis.

Example 11 (The Earth’s orbit) With e \approx 0.0167, perihelion and aphelion are r_\pm = p/(1 \pm e) = a(1 \mp e), in the ratio (1 - e)/(1 + e)
\approx 0.967. The third law T^2 = 4\pi^2ma^3/k, with k = GMm, gives T^2/a^3 = 4\pi^2/(GM), the same for all planets: in years and astronomical units, T^2 = a^3 (Exercise 12).

For positive energy the orbit is a hyperbola and the particle is deflected rather than captured. The asymptotes of the conic give the scattering angle, the classical starting point of Rutherford’s analysis.

Example 12 (Hyperbolic orbits and deflection) For e > 1, r \to \infty as \cos(\varphi - \varphi_0) \to -1/e, so the polar angle sweeps 2\arccos(-1/e) > \pi between the two asymptotes and the particle is deflected by \chi = 2\arccos(-1/e) - \pi, that is \sin(\chi/2) =
1/e (Figure 1, e = 1.4): fast or distant particles (e large) are deflected little.

The orbit can be read off from the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector without solving any differential equation. The first exercise performs this computation, checking the key identity with Sage.

Exercise 10 (The orbit from the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector) Show that \vec A\cdot\vec x = L^2 - mkr, and deduce Equation 3 with e = |\vec A|/(mk), \varphi measured from the direction of \vec A.







NoteSolution





\vec x\cdot(\vec p\times\vec L) = \vec L\cdot(\vec x\times\vec p) = L^2, so \vec A\cdot\vec x = L^2 - mkr. Writing \vec A\cdot\vec x = |\vec A|r\cos\varphi gives r(|\vec A|\cos\varphi + mk) = L^2, i.e. r = \frac{L^2/(mk)}{1 +
(|\vec A|/mk)\cos\varphi}. The vector \vec A points to the pericentre (\varphi = 0):

x, y, z, px, py, pz = var("x y z px py pz", domain="real")
m, k = var("m k", domain="positive")
X = vector([x, y, z]); P = vector([px, py, pz]); r = sqrt(X * X)
Lv = X.cross_product(P); A = P.cross_product(Lv) - m * k * X / r
print("A.x - (L^2 - m k r) =", (A * X - (Lv * Lv - m * k * r)).simplify_full())
# an example: pericentre at (1/(1+e), 0, 0) with p = 1 (m = k = L = 1); A points along +x with length e
e = var("e", domain="positive")
st = {x: 1 / (1 + e), y: 0, z: 0, px: 0, py: 1 + e, pz: 0, m: 1, k: 1}
print("A at the pericentre of the orbit with p = 1:", A.subs(st).simplify_full())
Output:
A.x - (L^2 - m k r) = 0
A at the pericentre of the orbit with p = 1: (e, 0, 0)




The third law can be derived from the second without integrating the radial equation. The second exercise divides the area of the ellipse by the constant areal velocity.

Exercise 11 (Kepler’s third law) Using the area \pi ab of the ellipse, b = a\sqrt{1 - e^2}, and dA/dt = L/(2m) (Example 7), show that T = 2\pi\sqrt{ma^3/k}.







NoteSolution





T = \pi ab\cdot 2m/L, and with L^2 = mkp = mka(1 - e^2) the dependence on e cancels: T^2 = 4\pi^2m^2a^4(1 -
e^2)/(mka(1 - e^2)) = 4\pi^2ma^3/k.

assume(e < 1)
b = a * sqrt(1 - e**2); L = sqrt(m * k * a * (1 - e**2))
T = pi * a * b * 2 * m / L
print("T =", T.simplify_full(), "; T == 2 pi sqrt(m a^3/k):", bool((T**2 - 4 * pi**2 * m * a**3 / k).simplify_full() == 0))

Comets move on very elongated ellipses, and the third law turns an observed period into the size of the orbit. The third exercise does this for Halley’s comet.

Exercise 12 (Halley’s comet) Halley’s comet has period T \approx 75.3 years and eccentricity e \approx 0.967. Find its semi-major axis, its perihelion and its aphelion distances in astronomical units.







NoteSolution





In years and astronomical units T^2 = a^3 (Example 11), so a = 75.3^{2/3} \approx 17.8. The perihelion is a(1 - e) \approx 17.8 \times 0.033 \approx 0.59 AU, inside the orbit of Venus, and the aphelion is a(1 + e) \approx 17.8 \times 1.967 \approx 35 AU, beyond Neptune.










Every theory in these lectures is defined by an action: a number assigned to each history of the system, whose stationary histories are the physical ones. The idea is simplest for a particle, where a history is a curve in configuration space and the action is an integral along it, and everything later, fields, gauge fields, gravity, is the same idea with the particle’s position replaced by a field. This section defines configuration spaces, Lagrangians, actions and the Euler-Lagrange equations, and works them on the oscillator, the pendulum and a particle on the sphere.
For more on this topic, see Godinho and Natário (2014, Ch. 5), Knauf (2018, Ch. 8), Kotkin and Serbo (2020, sec. 4, §9), Lee et al. (2018, Ch. 3, Ch. 4-5, Ch. 9) and Moretti (2023, Ch. 7-9, Ch. 5).


Newton’s laws are written in Cartesian coordinates, but a constrained system, such as a pendulum or a bead on a wire, has fewer degrees of freedom than its particles have Cartesian coordinates. The first step of the Lagrangian method is to describe the possible positions of the system by a manifold and any convenient coordinates on it.


Definition 4 (Configuration space) The configuration space of a mechanical system is the manifold Q (Definition 6 of Differential geometry) of its possible positions; coordinates q^i on Q are generalised coordinates, and the number of them, \dim Q, is the number of degrees of freedom. A history (or path) is a curve t \mapsto q(t) in Q, with velocity \dot q = dq/dt (Definition 16 of Differential geometry), a tangent vector.

NoteExamples





The configuration space of an unconstrained particle is ordinary space. Several particles have one copy of space for each, so the dimension grows with the number of particles.

Example 13 (A particle in space) A point particle in \mathbb{R}^3 has Q = \mathbb{R}^3 with Cartesian or spherical coordinates, three degrees of freedom; N particles have Q = \mathbb{R}^{3N}.

Constraints cut the configuration space down to a submanifold. A rigid rod of fixed length restricts a mass to a circle, and a mass tied to a fixed point by a string kept taut moves on a sphere.

Example 14 (Pendulum and particle on a sphere) A pendulum constrained to a circle has Q = S^1 with the angle q as coordinate; a particle constrained to the unit sphere has Q = S^2 with spherical coordinates (\theta, \varphi) (Exercise 28): the configuration spaces of constrained systems are the manifolds of Part I.

A rigid body is the standard example of a configuration space that is a group. Its positions with one point held fixed are the rotations that carry a reference orientation to the actual one.

Example 15 (A rigid body) The orientations of a rigid body with a fixed point form Q = SO(3), three degrees of freedom with the Euler angles as coordinates (The exponential map); a free rigid body has Q = \mathbb{R}^3 \times SO(3). Configuration spaces are often Lie groups or coset spaces.

A rigid body moving in a plane with constraints has a configuration space of small dimension, and its motion at each instant is a rotation about one point. The next example finds that point for a rod sliding along two walls.

Example 16 (A ladder sliding along two walls) A rod AB of length l moves with A on the x-axis and B on the y-axis: one degree of freedom, the angle \theta with A = (l\sin\theta, 0), B = (0, l\cos\theta), so Q is an interval. The velocities of A and B are horizontal and vertical, so the instantaneous centre of rotation, the point of the moving plane at rest at that instant, lies on the vertical through A and the horizontal through B: I =
(l\sin\theta, l\cos\theta). Its locus in space is the circle |I| = l about the corner, and its locus in the rod’s frame is the circle with diameter AB, of radius l/2: the motion is the rolling of the second circle inside the first (Sinha 2023, sec. 7.1.5).

NoteExercises





Counting degrees of freedom and recognising the manifold is a skill worth practising on a few systems. The first exercise asks for both on four mechanical systems.

Exercise 13 (Counting degrees of freedom) Find the configuration space and the number of degrees of freedom of: a double pendulum moving in a plane; a bead on a circular hoop; two particles in space joined by a rigid rod; a particle on the surface of a torus.







NoteSolution





The double pendulum has two angles, Q = S^1 \times S^1 = T^2, two degrees of freedom. The bead on a hoop has Q = S^1, one. The torus particle has Q = T^2, two. The rod is treated in Exercise 14: Q = \mathbb{R}^3 \times
S^2, five degrees of freedom (6 coordinates minus one constraint).



The rigid rod shows how a constraint and a good choice of coordinates go together. The second exercise separates the position of the rod from its direction.

Exercise 14 (The rigid rod) Two particles of masses m_1, m_2 at fixed distance d have positions \vec x_1, \vec x_2 with |\vec x_1 - \vec x_2| =
d. Show that (\vec X, \vec n), with \vec X the centre of mass and \vec n = (\vec x_1 - \vec x_2)/d, identify the configuration space with \mathbb{R}^3 \times S^2, and write the kinetic energy in these variables.







NoteSolution





With M = m_1 + m_2, \vec x_1 = \vec X + \frac{m_2d}{M}\vec n and \vec x_2 = \vec X - \frac{m_1d}{M}\vec n, so the pair (\vec X, \vec n) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \times S^2 determines the configuration and conversely. The kinetic energy is \tfrac12 m_1|\dot{\vec x}_1|^2 + \tfrac12 m_2|\dot{\vec x}_2|^2 = \tfrac12 M|\dot{\vec X}|^2 + \tfrac12\mu d^2|\dot{\vec
n}|^2, \mu = m_1m_2/M (the cross terms cancel): a free particle in \mathbb{R}^3 plus a particle on the sphere of radius d with the reduced mass.



The rigid body’s configuration space is the rotation group, and Euler angles are coordinates on it. The third exercise checks with Sage that the Euler-angle product of rotations is a rotation for every value of the angles.

Exercise 15 (Euler angles on SO(3)) With R_z(\alpha) and R_x(\alpha) the rotations about the z- and x-axes, show that R = R_z(\varphi)R_x(\theta)R_z(\psi) satisfies R^{\mathsf T}R = 1 and \det R = 1, and that R is the identity for \theta = 0, \varphi + \psi = 0: the chart degenerates there, as the spherical chart does at the poles.







NoteSolution





Each factor is orthogonal with determinant one, so the product is; at \theta = 0 the product is R_z(\varphi + \psi), which depends on the sum only:

ph, th, ps = var("phi theta psi", domain="real")
def Rz(a): return matrix([[cos(a), -sin(a), 0], [sin(a), cos(a), 0], [0, 0, 1]])
def Rx(a): return matrix([[1, 0, 0], [0, cos(a), -sin(a)], [0, sin(a), cos(a)]])
R = Rz(ph) * Rx(th) * Rz(ps)
print("R^T R = 1:", bool((R.transpose() * R).simplify_full() == identity_matrix(3)), "; det R = 1:", bool(R.det().simplify_full() == 1))
print("R at theta = 0 equals R_z(phi + psi):", bool((R.subs(theta=0) - Rz(ph + ps)).simplify_full() == 0))
print("R at theta = 0, psi = -phi is the identity:", bool(R.subs(theta=0, psi=-ph).simplify_full() == identity_matrix(3)))
Output:
R^T R = 1: True ; det R = 1: True
R at theta = 0 equals R_z(phi + psi): True
R at theta = 0, psi = -phi is the identity: True







Once the configuration space is chosen, the dynamics is encoded in a single function of positions and velocities. For the systems of these lectures it is the kinetic energy minus the potential energy, with the kinetic energy given by a metric on the configuration space.


Definition 5 (Lagrangian) A Lagrangian is a smooth function L(q, \dot q, t) of the generalised coordinates, the velocities and possibly time; for a particle of mass m in a potential V it is the kinetic energy minus the potential energy, L = \tfrac12 m\,g_{ij}(q)\dot q^i\dot q^j - V(q), with g_{ij} the metric (Definition 37 of Differential geometry) of the configuration space.

NoteExamples





The oscillator is the model for every system near a stable equilibrium. Its Lagrangian is the simplest non-trivial one: quadratic in both the position and the velocity.

Example 17 (The harmonic oscillator) L = \tfrac12 m\dot q^2 - \tfrac12 m\omega^2q^2 on Q = \mathbb{R}: kinetic energy minus the potential of a spring of frequency \omega (Exercise 27).

The pendulum keeps the quadratic kinetic energy but has a periodic potential. This makes its equation of motion nonlinear and its motion richer than the oscillator’s.

Example 18 (The pendulum) L = \tfrac12 ml^2\dot q^2 + mgl\cos q on Q = S^1, for a mass m at the end of a rod of length l in gravity g: the kinetic energy of a point moving on a circle of radius l and the potential -mgl\cos q of its height.

On a curved configuration space the kinetic energy involves the metric. A free particle on the sphere has no potential at all, and its whole dynamics comes from the geometry.

Example 19 (A free particle on the sphere) L = \tfrac12(\dot\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2), the kinetic energy built from the round metric Equation 22 of Differential geometry with m = 1 and no potential (Exercise 28): the Lagrangian of a free particle on a manifold is half the squared length of its velocity.

A rigid body swinging about a fixed horizontal axis has one degree of freedom, and its Lagrangian involves only its mass, the distance of its centre of mass from the axis, and its moment of inertia. The next example writes it down and finds the simple pendulum that moves in the same way.

Example 20 (The compound pendulum) Let a body of mass M turn about a horizontal axis through O, its centre of mass G at distance h from the axis, with moment of inertia I_O = Mk^2 about the axis (k is the radius of gyration). With \theta the angle of OG from the downward vertical, 
L = \tfrac12Mk^2\dot\theta^2 + Mgh\cos\theta ,
 which is the Lagrangian of a simple pendulum of length l = k^2/h times Mh/l: the two have the same motion. By the parallel axis theorem k^2 =
k_G^2 + h^2, so l = h + k_G^2/h > h; the point at distance l from O on OG is the centre of oscillation (Sinha 2023, sec. 2.4.1).

The equivalent length is a ratio of two integrals over the body. The next example evaluates it for a solid cone swinging about its vertex, where both integrals are elementary.

Example 21 (A cone swinging about its vertex) A solid homogeneous cone of height H and half-angle \alpha swings about a horizontal axis through its vertex, perpendicular to its axis. Its centre of mass is at h = \tfrac34H, and its moment of inertia about the axis is I = \tfrac35MH^2\bigl(1 + \tfrac14\tan^2\alpha\bigr), so the equivalent simple pendulum has length 
l = \frac{I}{Mh} = \frac H5\bigl(4 + \tan^2\alpha\bigr) .
