The simplest motion that involves all three angles is steady precession, in which the axis of a top turns uniformly about the vertical at a fixed inclination while the top spins about that axis. The first example evaluates the proposition for it.

Example 79 (Steady precession) For \theta = \theta_0, \varphi = \mu t and \psi = \nu t, Equation 13 gives \Omega = \mu\,e_3 + \nu\,(\sin
\theta_0\sin\mu t, -\sin\theta_0\cos\mu t, \cos\theta_0) = \mu\,e_3 + \nu\,Re_3, the precession about the vertical plus the spin about the moving axis Re_3 of the top (Exercise 81). In the body, \omega = (\mu\sin\theta_0\sin\nu t,
\mu\sin\theta_0\cos\nu t, \nu + \mu\cos\theta_0) turns about the third body axis, and |\omega|^2 = \mu^2 + \nu^2 +
2\mu\nu\cos\theta_0 is constant.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



The Euler chart degenerates at \theta = 0, and the kinematic equations show it. Books on rigid bodies often use a different convention for the middle rotation, and the second example also translates between the two.

Example 80 (The pole of the chart and the z-y-z convention) The matrix of coefficients of (\dot\theta, \dot\varphi, \dot\psi) in Equation 12 has determinant \sin\theta, so at \theta = 0 the rates cannot be recovered from \omega, and there \omega_3 = \dot\varphi + \dot\psi sees only the sum, as in Example 51 (Exercise 80). The z-y-z convention e^{\varphi'L_3}e^{\theta L_2}e^{\psi'
L_3} (Sinha 2023, sec. 1.1.29) describes the same rotation as ours with \varphi = \varphi' + \frac\pi2 and \psi
= \psi' - \frac\pi2, since e^{\theta L_2} = e^{\frac\pi2L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e^{-\frac\pi2L_3}; substituting, \omega_1 =
\dot\theta\sin\psi' - \dot\varphi'\sin\theta\cos\psi', \omega_2 = \dot\theta\cos\psi' + \dot\varphi'\sin\theta\sin\psi' and \omega_3 = \dot\psi' + \dot\varphi'\cos\theta, the form in which Sinha (2023, sec. 1.1.30) states them, with his \psi, \varphi in the roles of our \varphi', \psi'.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



The kinetic energy of a body turning about a fixed point is a quadratic form in its angular velocity in the body. For a body with equal moments of inertia it is the bi-invariant metric of the group, which gives the metric of the three-sphere a mechanical meaning.

Example 81 (The kinetic energy of a top) A body whose principal moments of inertia about its body axes are I_1 = I_2 and I_3 has kinetic energy \frac12I_1(\omega_1^2 + \omega_2^2) + \frac12I_3\omega_3^2 = \frac12I_1(\dot\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2) +
\frac12I_3(\dot\psi + \cos\theta\,\dot\varphi)^2, by the computation of Example 73. For a spherical top, I_1 = I_3 = I, it is \frac12I|\omega|^2, which is 2I times the metric Equation 25 of Differential geometry evaluated on the velocity: the free spherical top moves along the geodesics of the bi-invariant metric.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.












NoteExercises





The proposition can be checked by differentiating the product of three rotation matrices. The first exercise lets Sage do it, and derives the space components by hand from the addition rule.

Exercise 79 (Euler’s equations with Sage) With Sage, compute R^{-1}\dot R and \dot RR^{-1} for R(t) = e^{\varphi(t)L_3}e^{\theta(t)L_1}e^{\psi(t)L_3}, read off \omega and \Omega, and confirm Equation 12, Equation 13, \Omega = R\omega and the value of |\omega|^2. Derive Equation 13 by hand from Exercise 78.







NoteSolution





Applying \Omega = \Omega_1 + R_1\Omega_2 twice, \Omega = \dot\varphi\,e_3 + e^{\varphi L_3}\bigl(\dot\theta\,e_1 +
e^{\theta L_1}\dot\psi\,e_3\bigr) = \dot\varphi\,e_3 + \dot\theta\,(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi, 0) + \dot\psi\,
e^{\varphi L_3}(0, -\sin\theta, \cos\theta), and e^{\varphi L_3}(0, -\sin\theta, \cos\theta) = (\sin\theta\sin\varphi,
-\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta), which is Equation 13. The rule \omega = R_2^{-1}\omega_1 + \omega_2 gives Equation 12 the same way:

t = var("t")
th, ph, ps = [function(f)(t) for f in ("theta", "phi", "psi")]
L = [matrix(SR, [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]]), matrix(SR, [[0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [-1, 0, 0]]), matrix(SR, [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]])]
def rot(a, u): return identity_matrix(SR, 3) + sin(u) * L[a] + (1 - cos(u)) * L[a]^2
R = rot(2, ph) * rot(0, th) * rot(2, ps)
simp = lambda e: e.simplify_full().trig_reduce().simplify_full()
comp = lambda X: vector(SR, [simp(-(L[a] * X).trace() / 2) for a in range(3)])   # X = x_a L_a  ->  x_a
Rd = diff(R, t)
body, space = R.transpose() * Rd, Rd * R.transpose()
print("R^{-1} dR/dt and dR/dt R^{-1} antisymmetric:", bool((body + body.transpose()).apply_map(simp) == 0), bool((space + space.transpose()).apply_map(simp) == 0))
w, W = comp(body), comp(space)
dth, dph, dps = diff(th, t), diff(ph, t), diff(ps, t)
w_exp = vector(SR, [dth * cos(ps) + dph * sin(th) * sin(ps), -dth * sin(ps) + dph * sin(th) * cos(ps), dps + dph * cos(th)])
W_exp = vector(SR, [dth * cos(ph) + dps * sin(th) * sin(ph), dth * sin(ph) - dps * sin(th) * cos(ph), dph + dps * cos(th)])
print("body angular velocity omega =", w)
print("equals the left-invariant forms sigma^a(d/dt):", bool((w - w_exp).apply_map(simp) == 0))
print("space angular velocity Omega =", W)
print("equals the right-invariant forms:", bool((W - W_exp).apply_map(simp) == 0), "; Omega = R omega:", bool((W - R * w).apply_map(simp) == 0))
print("|omega|^2 = |Omega|^2 =", simp(w * w), ":", bool(simp(w * w - W * W) == 0))
Output:
R^{-1} dR/dt and dR/dt R^{-1} antisymmetric: True True
body angular velocity omega = (sin(psi(t))*sin(theta(t))*diff(phi(t), t) + cos(psi(t))*diff(theta(t), t), cos(psi(t))*sin(theta(t))*diff(phi(t), t) - sin(psi(t))*diff(theta(t), t), cos(theta(t))*diff(phi(t), t) + diff(psi(t), t))
equals the left-invariant forms sigma^a(d/dt): True
space angular velocity Omega = (sin(phi(t))*sin(theta(t))*diff(psi(t), t) + cos(phi(t))*diff(theta(t), t), -cos(phi(t))*sin(theta(t))*diff(psi(t), t) + sin(phi(t))*diff(theta(t), t), cos(theta(t))*diff(psi(t), t) + diff(phi(t), t))
equals the right-invariant forms: True ; Omega = R omega: True
|omega|^2 = |Omega|^2 = 2*cos(theta(t))*diff(phi(t), t)*diff(psi(t), t) + diff(phi(t), t)^2 + diff(psi(t), t)^2 + diff(theta(t), t)^2 : True










TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



Given the angular velocity, the Euler angles are found by integrating the kinematic equations. The second exercise solves them for the rates, wherever the chart allows.

Exercise 80 (Rates from the angular velocity) Solve Equation 12 for \dot\theta, \dot\varphi, \dot\psi when \sin\theta \neq 0, and compare the result with the dual frame of Example 75.







NoteSolution





\omega_1\cos\psi - \omega_2\sin\psi = \dot\theta and \omega_1\sin\psi + \omega_2\cos\psi = \dot\varphi\sin\theta, so \dot\varphi = (\omega_1\sin\psi + \omega_2\cos\psi)/\sin\theta and \dot\psi = \omega_3 - \cos\theta\,\dot\varphi. The velocity is then \dot\theta\,\partial_\theta + \dot\varphi\,\partial_\varphi + \dot\psi\,\partial_\psi = \omega_1\bigl(\cos
\psi\,\partial_\theta + \frac{\sin\psi}{\sin\theta}(\partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi)\bigr) + \omega_2\bigl(-\sin
\psi\,\partial_\theta + \frac{\cos\psi}{\sin\theta}(\partial_\varphi - \cos\theta\,\partial_\psi)\bigr) + \omega_3\,
\partial_\psi = \omega_a\xi_a, the dual frame: the velocity with body angular velocity \omega is \omega_a\xi_a.









TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



The axis of a top is its third body axis, the point Re_3 of the unit sphere. The third exercise follows that point and finds that the spin does not move it.

Exercise 81 (The motion of the axis) Show that Re_3 = (\sin\theta\sin\varphi, -\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta), so that its spherical angles are (\theta, \varphi - \frac\pi2), that \frac{d}{dt}(Re_3) = \Omega \times Re_3, and that its speed on the sphere is (\dot\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2)^{1/2}, independent of \dot\psi.







NoteSolution





e^{\psi L_3}e_3 = e_3, so Re_3 = e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e_3 = e^{\varphi L_3}(0, -\sin\theta, \cos\theta) =
(\sin\theta\sin\varphi, -\sin\theta\cos\varphi, \cos\theta). By Exercise 76 with x_0 = e_3, \frac{d}{dt}(Re_3) = \Omega \times Re_3, whose length is |R(\omega \times e_3)| = (\omega_1^2 + \omega_2^2)^{1/2} =
(\dot\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi^2)^{1/2} by Example 73. The spin \dot\psi turns the body about Re_3 and leaves the axis in place.









TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.
















NoteExercises





Three exercises that combine the four sections of this chapter: the double cover SU(2) \to SO(3) followed from the group to the Lie algebra and back, the affine group of the line taken through every construction of the chapter, and the Heisenberg group, a nilpotent counterpart of both.
The first integrative exercise builds the double cover on the whole group rather than on one subgroup. It uses the Euler angles, the adjoint representation, the Killing form and the exponential map together.

Exercise 82 (The double cover from end to end) For the Euler-angle element g(\theta, \varphi, \psi) of Equation 7 compute the matrix of \operatorname{Ad}_g in the basis T_a. Show that it is the rotation e^{\varphi L_3}e^{\theta L_1}e^{\psi L_3}, that it is orthogonal of determinant one, that \operatorname{Ad}_{-g} = \operatorname{Ad}_g, that its derivative is \operatorname{ad}_{T_a} = L_a with Killing form -2\delta_{ab}, and that (\theta, \varphi, \psi) = (0, 0, 2\pi) gives g = -1 and \operatorname{Ad}_g = 1.







NoteSolution





\operatorname{Ad} is a homomorphism, so \operatorname{Ad}_g = \operatorname{Ad}_{e^{\varphi T_3}}\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{\theta
T_1}}\operatorname{Ad}_{e^{\psi T_3}}, and each factor is \operatorname{Ad}_{e^{tT_a}} = e^{t\operatorname{ad}_{T_a}} =
e^{tL_a} (Exercise 51, Exercise 39). Orthogonality follows from the invariance of the Killing form -2\delta_{ab} (Exercise 32), and the determinant is one because \operatorname{Ad}_g is connected to the identity through \operatorname{Ad}_{g(t\theta, t\varphi, t\psi)}. Conjugation by -g equals conjugation by g, and g(0, 0, 2\pi) = e^{2\pi T_3} = -1 covers the identity rotation: the kernel \{\pm 1\} of the double cover is the centre of Exercise 8. Every rotation is an Euler-angle product, so \operatorname{Ad} is onto SO(3):

th, ph, ps = var("th ph ps", domain="real")
s = [matrix(SR, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]), matrix(SR, [[0, -I], [I, 0]]), matrix(SR, [[1, 0], [0, -1]])]
T = [-I / 2 * sa for sa in s]
L = [matrix(SR, [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]]), matrix(SR, [[0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [-1, 0, 0]]), matrix(SR, [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]])]
def expT(a, u): return cos(u/2) * identity_matrix(SR, 2) - I * sin(u/2) * s[a]
def rot(a, u): return identity_matrix(SR, 3) + sin(u) * L[a] + (1 - cos(u)) * L[a]^2
def simp(e): return e.exponentialize().simplify_full().trig_reduce().simplify_full()
g = expT(2, ph) * expT(0, th) * expT(2, ps); gi = g.conjugate_transpose()
Ad = matrix(SR, 3, 3, lambda a, b: simp(-2 * (T[a] * g * T[b] * gi).trace()))
R = rot(2, ph) * rot(0, th) * rot(2, ps)
print("Ad_g = e^{phi L_3} e^{theta L_1} e^{psi L_3}:", bool((Ad - R).apply_map(lambda e: e.trig_expand().simplify_full()) == 0))
print("Ad_g^T Ad_g = 1:", bool((Ad.transpose() * Ad).apply_map(lambda e: e.trig_expand().simplify_full()) == 1), "; det Ad_g =", Ad.det().trig_expand().simplify_full())
Adm = matrix(SR, 3, 3, lambda a, b: simp(-2 * (T[a] * (-g) * T[b] * (-gi)).trace()))
print("Ad_{-g} = Ad_g:", bool(Adm == Ad))
ad = [matrix(SR, 3, 3, lambda c, b: -2 * (T[c] * (T[a] * T[b] - T[b] * T[a])).trace()) for a in range(3)]
print("ad_{T_a} = L_a:", all(ad[a] == L[a] for a in range(3)), "; Killing form:", matrix(SR, 3, 3, lambda a, b: (ad[a] * ad[b]).trace()).list())
print("at (theta, phi, psi) = (0, 0, 2 pi): g =", g.subs(th=0, ph=0, ps=2 * pi).simplify_full().list(), ", Ad_g =", Ad.subs(th=0, ph=0, ps=2 * pi).list())
Output:
Ad_g = e^{phi L_3} e^{theta L_1} e^{psi L_3}: True
Ad_g^T Ad_g = 1: True ; det Ad_g = 1
Ad_{-g} = Ad_g: True
ad_{T_a} = L_a: True ; Killing form: [-2, 0, 0, 0, -2, 0, 0, 0, -2]
at (theta, phi, psi) = (0, 0, 2 pi): g = [-1, 0, 0, -1] , Ad_g = [1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1]




The second integrative exercise takes the affine group through every construction of the chapter. It is the smallest non-abelian example, and its Killing form shows what changes when the group is not semisimple.

Exercise 83 (The affine group throughout) For the affine group \{x \mapsto ax + b,\ a > 0\}: (a) build its Lie algebra in Sage’s LieAlgebra module and compute its Killing form; (b) compute the exponential map e^{xX + yY} and show that it is a bijection from \mathfrak{g} onto the group; (c) compute g^{-1}dg, check the Maurer-Cartan equation, and find the left-invariant volume form.







NoteSolution






[X, Y] = Y, and the Killing form is \kappa(X, X) = 1, all other components zero (Example 32): degenerate, so the algebra is not semisimple; it is solvable. (b) e^{xX + yY} = \begin{pmatrix} e^x & y(e^x - 1)/x \\ 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix} (Exercise 46). Given a > 0 and b, x = \log a is forced by the diagonal, and then y =
bx/(a - 1) (or y = b when a = 1), since (e^x - 1)/x > 0: the exponential map is a bijection, unlike that of SU(2) or SL(2, \mathbb{R}) (Example 50, Exercise 50). (c) g^{-1}dg = \sigma^XX + \sigma^YY with \sigma^X = da/a, \sigma^Y = db/a (Example 68), d\sigma^Y = -\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y (Exercise 71), and the left-invariant volume form is \sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y = da \wedge db/a^2 (Exercise 66):


aff = LieAlgebra(QQ, {("X", "Y"): {"Y": 1}}, names="X,Y")
Xg, Yg = aff.gens()
print("[X, Y] =", Xg.bracket(Yg), "; Killing form:", aff.killing_form_matrix().list(), "; semisimple:", aff.is_semisimple(), "; solvable:", aff.is_solvable())
x, y = var("x y", domain="real")
X = matrix(SR, [[1, 0], [0, 0]]); Y = matrix(SR, [[0, 1], [0, 0]])
E = (x * X + y * Y).exp().simplify_full()
print("exp(xX + yY) =", E.list())
a, b = var("a b", domain="real")
print("inverse of exp: given (a, b) with a > 0, x = log a, y = b log(a)/(a - 1):", bool(E.subs(x=log(a), y=b * log(a) / (a - 1)).simplify_full() == matrix(SR, [[a, b], [0, 1]])))
A = Manifold(2, "Aff"); C.<a, b> = A.chart("a:(0,+oo) b")
g = matrix(SR, [[a, b], [0, 1]])
print("g^-1 dg/da =", (g.inverse() * diff(g, a)).list(), "; g^-1 dg/db =", (g.inverse() * diff(g, b)).list())
sX = A.one_form(1 / a, 0); sY = A.one_form(0, 1 / a)
print("d sigma^X =", sX.exterior_derivative().display(), "; d sigma^Y + sigma^X ^ sigma^Y = 0:", sY.exterior_derivative() + sX.wedge(sY) == 0)
print("volume form sigma^X ^ sigma^Y =", sX.wedge(sY).display())
Output:
[X, Y] = Y ; Killing form: [1, 0, 0, 0] ; semisimple: False ; solvable: True
exp(xX + yY) = [e^x, y*(e^x - 1)/x, 0, 1]
inverse of exp: given (a, b) with a > 0, x = log a, y = b log(a)/(a - 1): True
g^-1 dg/da = [1/a, 0, 0, 0] ; g^-1 dg/db = [0, 1/a, 0, 0]
d sigma^X = 0 ; d sigma^Y + sigma^X ^ sigma^Y = 0: True
volume form sigma^X ^ sigma^Y = a^(-2) da∧db




The third integrative exercise repeats the analysis for the Heisenberg group, whose Lie algebra is nilpotent rather than solvable. Every construction of the chapter becomes polynomial.

Exercise 84 (The Heisenberg group throughout) For the Heisenberg group of Exercise 1: (a) show that its Lie algebra is \mathfrak{n}_3, with [X, Y] = Z central, and that the adjoint representation and the Killing form are as in Exercise 28; (b) compute e^N for N = xE_{12} + yE_{23} + zE_{13} and show that the exponential map is a diffeomorphism \mathfrak{n}_3 \to H; (c) verify that e^{X}e^{Y} = e^{X + Y + \frac12[X, Y]} exactly, and relate the Maurer-Cartan equation d\sigma^Z = -\sigma^X \wedge
\sigma^Y to the bracket.







NoteSolution






A curve h(x(t), y(t), z(t)) through the identity has velocity \dot x E_{12} + \dot yE_{23} + \dot zE_{13}, so the Lie algebra is \mathfrak{n}_3 (Exercise 20), with [E_{12}, E_{23}] = E_{13} central (Exercise 23); every \operatorname{ad} is nilpotent and \kappa = 0. (b) N^2 = xyE_{13} and N^3 = 0, so e^N = 1 + N + \tfrac12N^2 = h(x, y, z + \tfrac12xy); the inverse map h(x, y, z) \mapsto (x, y, z - \tfrac12xy) is polynomial, so \exp is a diffeomorphism. (c) e^{E_{12}}e^{E_{23}} = h(1, 0, 0)h(0, 1, 0) = h(1, 1, 1), while e^{E_{12} +
E_{23} + \frac12E_{13}} = h(1, 1, \tfrac12 + \tfrac12) = h(1, 1, 1): the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff series of Exercise 45 stops after the commutator because all higher brackets vanish. The Maurer-Cartan equation d\sigma^Z = -\sigma^X \wedge \sigma^Y of Exercise 64 is Equation 10 for the single structure constant f_{XY}{}^Z = 1, and d\sigma^X = d\sigma^Y = 0 because X and Y never appear as brackets.

title: Lie groups and Lie algebras
text:
A representation lets a Lie algebra act on a vector space by matrices, and the finite-dimensional representations of the compact Lie algebras are classified by a small amount of combinatorial data: weights, roots and highest weights. This chapter has three sections. Weights and the representations of \mathfrak{su}(2) introduces Cartan subalgebras and weights, builds the spin-j representations from ladder operators, exponentiates them to the rotation matrices of spin j and decomposes tensor products with the Clebsch-Gordan rule. Roots and \mathfrak{su}(3) runs the same programme in rank two, with the Gell-Mann basis, the hexagon of roots, highest weights, simple roots and the Cartan matrix. Branching rules restricts representations to subalgebras, works the branching of \mathfrak{su}(3) under \mathfrak{su}(2) \times \mathfrak{u}(1) and splits \mathfrak{so}(4) into two commuting copies of \mathfrak{su}(2). Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions, and many of the computations use Sage’s WeylCharacterRing and RootSystem.
For more on this topic, see Keski-Vakkuri et al. (2022, Ch. 6) and Mukunda and Chaturvedi (2022, Ch. 5).


The representations of \mathfrak{su}(2) are the spins of quantum mechanics, and they are classified by a single number because a diagonalisable generator, J_3, labels the states and two ladder operators move between them. The same mechanism, with a Cartan subalgebra in place of J_3 and roots in place of the ladder operators, classifies the representations of every compact Lie algebra, and Section 1.2.2 runs it for \mathfrak{su}(3).


To label the vectors of a representation by numbers we need operators that can be diagonalised simultaneously, and the largest commuting family inside the Lie algebra is the natural choice. The definition below names this family and its dimension, the single integer that organises everything else in the chapter.


Definition 19 (Cartan subalgebra) A Cartan subalgebra \mathfrak{h} of a Lie algebra \mathfrak{g} is a maximal abelian subalgebra whose elements act diagonalisably in every finite-dimensional representation (for compact Lie algebras, a maximal abelian subalgebra); its dimension is the rank of \mathfrak{g}.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





In \mathfrak{su}(2) any two independent generators fail to commute, so a Cartan subalgebra is a single line. The choice of that line is the choice of a quantisation axis in quantum mechanics.

Example 82 (\mathfrak{su}(2) has rank one) \mathfrak{h} = \operatorname{span}(T_3): no other generator commutes with T_3, since [T_3, T_1] = T_2 and [T_3, T_2] = -T_1. Every Cartan subalgebra of \mathfrak{su}(2) is the span of some n_aT_a, a choice of axis.

For the unitary algebras the diagonal matrices are the obvious commuting family. Tracelessness removes one dimension, which is why \mathfrak{su}(n) has rank one less than the size of its matrices.

Example 83 (\mathfrak{su}(3) has rank two) \mathfrak{h} = \operatorname{span}(\lambda_3, \lambda_8), the diagonal traceless matrices, which commute with each other (Section 1.2.2); \mathfrak{su}(n) has rank n - 1, its Cartan subalgebra being the diagonal traceless matrices.

At the other extreme every element of an abelian algebra commutes with every other. The rank then equals the dimension, and for a direct sum of algebras the ranks of the summands add.

Example 84 (Abelian algebras and \mathfrak{so}(4)) An abelian Lie algebra is its own Cartan subalgebra, with rank equal to its dimension; \mathfrak{u}(1) has rank one and the torus algebra \mathbb{R}^n rank n. \mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus
\mathfrak{su}(2) (Section 1.2.3) has rank 2, one T_3 from each factor.










NoteExercises





The first exercise checks by a direct computation that a Cartan subalgebra of \mathfrak{su}(2) cannot be enlarged, and that any axis serves as well as the third one. The cross product of vectors does all the work.

Exercise 85 (The commutant of an axis) Find all X = x_aT_a \in \mathfrak{su}(2) with [T_3, X] = 0, and more generally with [n_aT_a, X] = 0 for a unit vector n. Conclude that \operatorname{span}(n_aT_a) is a maximal abelian subalgebra.







NoteSolution





From [T_a, T_b] = \epsilon_{abc}T_c, [n_aT_a, x_bT_b] = \epsilon_{abc}n_ax_bT_c = (n \times x)_cT_c. This vanishes exactly when x is parallel to n, so the commutant of n_aT_a is the line it spans; for n = e_3 the condition reads x_1T_2 - x_2T_1 = 0, so x_1 = x_2 = 0. A line is abelian, and since nothing outside it commutes with n_aT_a it is maximal: the rank of \mathfrak{su}(2) is one, whichever axis is chosen.



For \mathfrak{su}(n) the second exercise shows that the diagonal traceless matrices cannot be enlarged either. A single diagonal matrix with distinct entries already forces every matrix commuting with it to be diagonal, which Sage confirms by solving the linear equations for n \leq 5.

Exercise 86 (The rank of \mathfrak{su}(n)) Show that the traceless matrices commuting with H = \operatorname{diag}(h_1, \dots, h_n), h_i distinct, are diagonal, so that the diagonal traceless matrices form a Cartan subalgebra of dimension n - 1. Check with Sage for n = 2, \dots, 5 by computing the dimension of the centraliser.







NoteSolution





[H, X]_{ij} = (h_i - h_j)X_{ij}, so [H, X] = 0 forces X_{ij} = 0 for i \neq j: X is diagonal. The diagonal traceless matrices commute among themselves and nothing else commutes with a generic one, so they form a maximal abelian subalgebra, of dimension n - 1 (the anti-Hermitian ones are i times real diagonal traceless matrices, with the same dimension over \mathbb{R}):

for n in [2, 3, 4, 5]:
    R = PolynomialRing(QQ, ["x%d_%d" % (i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n)])
    X = matrix(R, n, n, R.gens())
    H = diagonal_matrix(QQ, [k + 1 for k in range(n - 1)] + [-sum(range(1, n))])   # distinct eigenvalues, traceless
    eqs = (H * X - X * H).list() + [X.trace()]
    M = matrix(QQ, [[e.monomial_coefficient(g) for g in R.gens()] for e in eqs])
    dim_centraliser = n * n - M.rank()
    D = [diagonal_matrix(QQ, [1 if k == i else (-1 if k == i + 1 else 0) for k in range(n)]) for i in range(n - 1)]
    commute = all(A * B == B * A for A in D for B in D)

Once a Cartan subalgebra is fixed, its elements can be diagonalised together in any representation. The common eigenvalues are the labels we were looking for, and the definition below names them and counts their repetitions.


Definition 20 (Weight) In a representation V of \mathfrak{g} the simultaneous eigenvalues of the Cartan subalgebra are the weights of V: for a basis H_1, \dots, H_r of \mathfrak{h} a weight is the vector \mu = (\mu_1, \dots,

In quantum mechanics the same operators act on wave functions on the sphere. Their action on the spherical harmonics is the standard example of a ladder.

Exercise 93 (The Casimir operator) With J_a = iT_a, show that [J_a, J_b] = i\epsilon_{abc}J_c, that C = J_1^2 + J_2^2 + J_3^2 commutes with every J_a, and that C = J_-J_+ + J_3^2 + J_3. Evaluate C on a vector v with J_+v = 0, J_3v = jv.

Definition 22 (Spin-j representation) Starting from a highest weight vector v with J_+ v = 0 and J_3 v = jv and applying J_- repeatedly gives vectors of weights j, j - 1, j - 2, \dots; in a finite-dimensional representation the chain must end, and [J_+, J_-] = 2J_3 forces it to end at -j, so 2j is a non-negative integer. NoteExamples





The most famous instance combines two spin-\tfrac12 particles. Its four states split into the triplet and the singlet of atomic physics.

Example 97 (\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 = 1 \oplus 0) Two spinors have weights \pm\tfrac12 \pm \tfrac12 = 1, 0, 0, -1: a triplet (the symmetric combinations) and a singlet (the antisymmetric one): two spin-\tfrac12 particles combine to spin 1 or spin 0.

Two vectors give nine states, and the weights now have multiplicities up to three. Peeling off strings of weights produces three spins, which are the symmetric traceless, antisymmetric and trace parts of a two-index tensor.

Example 98 (1 \otimes 1 = 2 \oplus 1 \oplus 0) Two vectors have weights \{1, 0, -1\} + \{1, 0, -1\} with multiplicities 1, 2, 3, 2, 1 (Figure 5): spin 2 (the symmetric traceless tensors), spin 1 (the antisymmetric tensors, \mathbb{R}^3 \wedge \mathbb{R}^3
\cong \mathbb{R}^3, the adjoint again) and spin 0 (the trace), the decomposition 3 \otimes 3 = 5 \oplus 3 \oplus
1 of Example 78 of Group theory. In CSDR the scalars live in tensor products of this kind, and the Higgs potential is built from the invariant (spin 0) parts.

Combining an integer and a half-integer spin gives only half-integer spins, since every weight of the product is a half-integer. The orbital angular momentum 1 of an electron combined with its spin is the standard example.

Example 99 (1 \otimes \tfrac12 = \tfrac32 \oplus \tfrac12) Weights \{1, 0, -1\} + \{\pm\tfrac12\} = \tfrac32, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac32: the string of spin \tfrac32 leaves one copy of \pm\tfrac12 (Exercise 100); likewise \tfrac32 \otimes \tfrac12 = 2 \oplus 1.

With a Cartan subalgebra of rank two the weights become points in a plane, the roots a hexagon, and the whole Lie algebra is encoded in a 2 \times 2 integer matrix. \mathfrak{su}(3) is the gauge algebra of the strong interaction and the smallest simple Lie algebra of rank two, and this section works its roots, weights and Cartan matrix explicitly, with Sage’s root-system module alongside.


Computations in \mathfrak{su}(3) need a basis, and the standard one extends the Pauli matrices to three dimensions. The definition fixes the eight matrices and their normalisation, which the rest of the section uses throughout.


Definition 25 (Gell-Mann basis) \mathfrak{su}(3) is the eight-dimensional algebra of traceless anti-Hermitian 3 \times 3 matrices, with basis T_A = -\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_A built from the Gell-Mann matrices 
\begin{gathered}
\lambda_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&-i&0\\i&0&0\\0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&1\\0&0&0\\1&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \\
\lambda_5 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&-i\\0&0&0\\i&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_6 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&1&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_7 = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0\\0&0&-i\\0&i&0 \end{pmatrix}, \
\lambda_8 = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&-2 \end{pmatrix},
\end{gathered}
\tag{16} normalised by \operatorname{tr}(\lambda_A\lambda_B) = 2\delta_{AB}.

The first three Gell-Mann matrices are the Pauli matrices placed in the upper left corner. They therefore close into a copy of \mathfrak{su}(2), and two more copies sit in the other corners.

Example 103 (The \mathfrak{su}(2) subalgebra) \lambda_{1, 2, 3} are the Pauli matrices in the upper block and span an \mathfrak{su}(2) subalgebra, with [\lambda_1, \lambda_2] = 2i\lambda_3 and cyclic permutations (Proposition 11 of Section 1.2.3); \lambda_{4, 5} and \lambda_{6, 7} with the appropriate diagonal matrices span two further \mathfrak{su}(2)’s.

Two of the eight matrices are diagonal, and diagonal matrices commute. They form the Cartan subalgebra of Example 83 in the Gell-Mann normalisation.

Example 104 (The Cartan subalgebra) \lambda_3 and \lambda_8 are the diagonal traceless matrices, they commute, and no other generator commutes with both: the Cartan subalgebra is \operatorname{span}(\lambda_3, \lambda_8), rank 2 (Definition 19).

The brackets of the Gell-Mann matrices define structure constants, the analogue of \epsilon_{abc} for \mathfrak{su}(2). Only nine of them are independent and non-zero, and the example lists them.

Example 105 (Structure constants) [\lambda_A, \lambda_B] = 2if_{ABC}\lambda_C with totally antisymmetric f_{ABC}: f_{123} = 1, f_{147} = f_{246} =
f_{257} = f_{345} = \tfrac12, f_{156} = f_{367} = -\tfrac12, f_{458} = f_{678} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} (Exercise 108); f_{458} \neq 0 is what makes SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1) a non-symmetric coset (Reductive decompositions and isotropy).

The ladder operators of \mathfrak{su}(2) were eigenvectors of \operatorname{ad}_{J_3}. With a Cartan subalgebra of higher rank the same idea gives a family of simultaneous eigenvectors, and their eigenvalue vectors are the roots.


Definition 26 (Root) The roots of \mathfrak{g} are the non-zero weights of the adjoint representation: the eigenvalue vectors \alpha of \operatorname{ad}_{H_1}, \dots, \operatorname{ad}_{H_r} on common eigenvectors E_\alpha \in
\mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathbb{C}, the root vectors, with [H_i, E_\alpha] = \alpha_iE_\alpha. The roots come in pairs \pm\alpha, each of multiplicity one, and \mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathbb{C} = \mathfrak{h} \oplus
\bigoplus_\alpha \mathbb{C}E_\alpha (the root decomposition).

\mathbf{8} \oplus \mathbf{1} (Exercise 127).

In rank one the general theory reduces to the spin-j construction of the previous section. The example translates between the two languages, where a highest weight is a single number.

Example 111 (Spin j again) For \mathfrak{su}(2) the fundamental weight is \tfrac12, the highest weights are j = \tfrac12 n, and the highest-weight construction of Definition 22 is the rank-one case of the general theory.

Six roots are redundant: each is a combination of a few of them with integer coefficients. The definition below picks out a basis of the root system, as many roots as the rank, in terms of which all others are sums.


Definition 28 (Simple roots) The positive roots that are not sums of other positive roots are the simple roots \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_r, as many as the rank; every positive root is a non-negative integer combination of them.

The simple roots are determined up to rotation and scale by their lengths and the angles between them. The definition below records these in an integer matrix, which turns out to determine the whole Lie algebra.


Definition 29 (Cartan matrix) The Cartan matrix is A_{ij} = 2(\alpha_i \cdot \alpha_j)/(\alpha_j \cdot \alpha_j), with the inner product induced by the Killing form on \mathfrak{h}. Its diagonal entries are 2, its off-diagonal entries are non-positive integers, and it determines the Lie algebra up to isomorphism; its graph, with a node per simple root and A_{ij}A_{ji} lines between nodes i and j, is the Dynkin diagram.

For \mathfrak{su}(3) the two simple roots have equal length and meet at 120°. Their Cartan matrix is the simplest non-diagonal one.

Example 115 (The Cartan matrix of \mathfrak{su}(3)) All roots have length 2 and \alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2 = -2, so A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, the Cartan matrix of type A_2 (Proposition 10): two nodes joined by one line.

When simple roots are orthogonal the off-diagonal entries vanish. The Lie algebra then splits, as the example shows for \mathfrak{so}(4).

Example 116 (Type A_1 and A_1 \times A_1) \mathfrak{su}(2) has the 1 \times 1 Cartan matrix (2), a single node; \mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2)
\oplus \mathfrak{su}(2) has \operatorname{diag}(2, 2), two disconnected nodes, and a disconnected Dynkin diagram means a direct sum of Lie algebras.

The possible Cartan matrices are severely restricted, and their complete list is the classification of simple Lie algebras. The example names the families.

Example 117 (The classification) The Cartan matrices of the simple Lie algebras fall into the series A_n = \mathfrak{su}(n+1), B_n =
\mathfrak{so}(2n+1), C_n = \mathfrak{sp}(n), D_n = \mathfrak{so}(2n) and the exceptional G_2, F_4, E_6, E_7,
E_8; E_8 is the gauge algebra of the heterotic string and E_6 a candidate unification group of Part V.

Exercise 118 (The Cartan matrix of \mathfrak{so}(5)) The simple roots of B_2 = \mathfrak{so}(5) can be taken as \alpha_1 = (1, -1) and \alpha_2 = (0, 1). Compute the Cartan matrix, the angle between the roots, the ratio of their lengths, and the number of lines in the Dynkin diagram.







NoteSolution





\alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_1 = 2, \alpha_2 \cdot \alpha_2 = 1 and \alpha_1 \cdot \alpha_2 = -1, so A_{12} = 2(-1)/1 = -

The second exercise explains why so few Cartan matrices exist. The product A_{ij}A_{ji} is four times the squared cosine of the angle between two simple roots, and integrality leaves only four possible angles.

Exercise 119 (The allowed angles) Show that A_{ij}A_{ji} = 4\cos^2\theta_{ij}, deduce that A_{ij}A_{ji} \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} for i \neq j, and list the possible angles between simple roots and the possible ratios of their lengths.

The off-diagonal entries are non-positive (Definition 29; an acute angle would make \alpha_i - \alpha_j a root, which Exercise 116 excludes), so \theta_{ij} = 90°, 120°, 135° or 150°. NoteExamples





The symmetry of the hexagon is generated by reflections in lines perpendicular to the roots. The Cartan matrix describes how these reflections act on the simple roots.

Example 118 (Weyl reflections) The reflection in the line perpendicular to a root \alpha is s_\alpha(\mu) = \mu - \frac{2(\mu \cdot \alpha)}{\alpha
\cdot \alpha}\alpha. On simple roots s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha_i) = \alpha_i - A_{ij}\alpha_j, so s_{\alpha_1}(\alpha_2) =
\alpha_2 + \alpha_1 and s_{\alpha_1}(\alpha_1) = -\alpha_1. The three reflections and the rotations by \pm 120° form the Weyl group S_3 (Example 114), which permutes the weights of every representation preserving their multiplicities: it maps the triangle of \mathbf{3} to itself (Exercise 123).

The dimension of a Lie algebra is visible in its root diagram: one dimension for each root and the rank for the origin. The count recovers the familiar dimensions of the unitary algebras.

Example 119 (Dimension from the roots) By the root decomposition, \dim\mathfrak{g} = \text{rank} + \#\text{roots}: 2 + 6 = 8 for \mathfrak{su}(3), 1 + 2 =
3 for \mathfrak{su}(2), and (n - 1) + n(n - 1) = n^2 - 1 for \mathfrak{su}(n) (Exercise 111). The zero weight of the adjoint has multiplicity equal to the rank, 2 for \mathfrak{su}(3), as in Proposition 10.

Adding a root to another root repeatedly produces a string of roots, which breaks off after finitely many steps. The length of the string is fixed by the Cartan matrix, and for \mathfrak{su}(3) every string is short.

Example 120 (Root strings) The \alpha_1-string through \alpha_2 consists of the roots \alpha_2 + k\alpha_1: k = 0, 1 give roots, while \alpha_2 - \alpha_1 (Exercise 116) and \alpha_2 + 2\alpha_1 = (3, \sqrt3) are not roots. In general the string \beta - p\alpha, \dots, \beta + q\alpha has p - q = 2(\beta \cdot \alpha)/(\alpha \cdot \alpha); here p
= 0, q = 1 and A_{21} = -1. Since [E_\alpha, E_\beta] has root \alpha + \beta, the string says [E_{\alpha_1},
E_{\alpha_2}] \neq 0 but [E_{\alpha_1}, [E_{\alpha_1}, E_{\alpha_2}]] = 0.

Restricting a representation to a subalgebra breaks it into smaller pieces, and the list of pieces, the branching rule, is read off from the weights. Symmetry breaking in physics is governed by such rules: when a symmetry is reduced to a subgroup, the states of one multiplet split into multiplets of the subgroup with definite charges. This section defines restriction and branching, works the branchings of \mathfrak{su}(3) under \mathfrak{su}(2) \times
\mathfrak{u}(1) and under its maximal torus, and proves the isomorphism \mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2)
\oplus \mathfrak{su}(2) behind the isometries of the three-sphere.


A representation of a group is in particular a representation of each of its subgroups. The definition below names this operation; its interest lies in how an irreducible representation falls apart under it.


Definition 30 (Restriction of a representation) Restricting a representation \rho of G (or \mathfrak{g}) to a subgroup H (subalgebra \mathfrak{h}) gives a representation \rho|_H of H on the same space, usually reducible even when \rho is irreducible.

NoteExamples





The simplest case restricts the rotations of space to the rotations about one axis. The axis itself is fixed, and the plane perpendicular to it rotates.

Example 121 (The vector of SO(3) under SO(2)) Restricted to the rotations about the Z-axis, \mathbb{R}^3 splits into the fixed line \{(0, 0, z)\} (charge 0) and the plane \{(x, y, 0)\} on which SO(2) rotates (charges \pm 1 after complexification): \mathbf{3}
\to \mathbf{1}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_{1} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-1} (Example 68 of Group theory, Proposition 2 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles).

The fundamental representation of \mathfrak{su}(3) restricted to the \mathfrak{su}(2) of the upper left block splits by the block structure. The first two basis vectors form a doublet and the third is left alone.

Example 122 (The fundamental of \mathfrak{su}(3) under \mathfrak{su}(2)) Restricted to the \mathfrak{su}(2) of \lambda_{1, 2, 3}, \mathbb{C}^3 splits into the doublet (e_1, e_2) and the singlet e_3: \mathbf{3} \to \mathbf{2} \oplus \mathbf{1} (Exercise 127).

Restricting all the way down to a Cartan subalgebra leaves only one-dimensional pieces. The branching rule is then just the list of weights.

Example 123 (Spin j under \mathfrak{u}(1)) Restricted to \operatorname{span}(J_3), spin j splits into its 2j + 1 weight lines, the charges m = j, \dots, -
j of Definition 20: branching to a Cartan subalgebra is the weight decomposition.

The first exercise shows that the branching to \mathfrak{u}(1) does not depend on which axis is chosen. The reason is that any two axes are related by a rotation, and the rotation acts in the representation.

Restriction gives a reducible representation, and the next step is to decompose it into irreducibles of the subalgebra. The definition below names the result and explains how weights compute it.


Definition 31 (Branching rule) The decomposition of a restricted representation into irreducibles of H, written \rho \to \bigoplus_i
\rho_i, is the branching rule for G \supset H. It is computed from the weights: the weights of \rho|_H are the weights of \rho projected onto the Cartan subalgebra of H (plus the charges under any \mathfrak{u}(1) factors), and they are sorted into weight diagrams of irreducibles of H (Figure 7).

The neutral generators of the proposition form a subalgebra of their own, the set of all elements commuting with \lambda_8. It is a direct sum of \mathfrak{su}(2) and \mathfrak{u}(1).

Example 127 (The commutant of \lambda_8) \lambda_8 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2) has a repeated eigenvalue, and the matrices commuting with it are block diagonal with blocks of sizes 2 and 1. In \mathfrak{su}(3) these are spanned by \lambda_1,
\lambda_2, \lambda_3 and \lambda_8: the commutant is \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1) \cong \mathfrak{u}(2), exactly the neutral part \mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_0 of Equation 17.

The conjugate representation branches like the fundamental with the charges reversed. The example records it, because \mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}} is used to build the adjoint.

Example 128 (The branching of \bar{\mathbf{3}}) The weights of \bar{\mathbf{3}} are the negatives of those of \mathbf{3} (Exercise 90), so \bar{\mathbf{3}} \to \mathbf{2}_{-1/\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{2/\sqrt3}; the doublet \bar{\mathbf{2}} \cong
\mathbf{2} of \mathfrak{su}(2) is self-conjugate (Exercise 89), only the charges change sign.

In particle physics the \lambda_8-charge is rescaled to the hypercharge of the quark model. The example shows the familiar fractional values emerging from the branching rules.

Example 129 (Hypercharge) With Y = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\lambda_8 = \tfrac13\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2), the branching \mathbf{3} \to

Every branching found so far has charges that add up to zero. The second exercise explains why: \lambda_8 is a combination of commutators, and the trace of a commutator vanishes in any representation.

Exercise 131 (Charges add up to zero) Write \lambda_8 as a combination of [\lambda_1, \lambda_2] and [\lambda_4, \lambda_5] (Exercise 107), and deduce that the \lambda_8-charges of any finite-dimensional representation, counted with multiplicity, add up to zero. Check this on \mathbf{3}, \mathbf{8} and \mathbf{6}.







NoteSolution





[\lambda_1, \lambda_2] = 2i\lambda_3 and [\lambda_4, \lambda_5] = i(\lambda_3 + \sqrt3\lambda_8), so \lambda_8 =
\tfrac{1}{i\sqrt3}([\lambda_4, \lambda_5] - \tfrac12[\lambda_1, \lambda_2]). In a representation \rho, \operatorname{tr}\rho([X, Y]) = \operatorname{tr}[\rho(X), \rho(Y)] = 0, so \operatorname{tr}\rho(\lambda_8) = 0, which is the sum of the charges. Checks: \mathbf{3}: \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} - \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} = 0; \mathbf{8}: 2\sqrt3 - 2\sqrt3 = 0; \mathbf{6} (Exercise 129): 3 \cdot \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} - 2 \cdot
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} - \tfrac{4}{\sqrt3} = 0.

[H, X]_{ij} = (h_i - h_j)X_{ij}, so X commutes with H exactly when X_{ij} = 0 whenever h_i \neq h_j: the commutant is block diagonal, one block for each distinct eigenvalue, \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{u}(n_1) \oplus \dots) for eigenvalue multiplicities n_1, \dots. Under the \mathfrak{u}(1) of \lambda_3 the charges h_i - h_j give \mathbf{8} \to \mathbf{1}_{2} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-2} \oplus 2 \cdot

Some Lie algebras are built from smaller ones that do not interact at all. The definition below makes this precise, and the rest of the section shows that the rotations of four-dimensional space are of this kind.


Definition 32 (Direct sum of Lie algebras) The direct sum \mathfrak{g}_1 \oplus \mathfrak{g}_2 of two Lie algebras is their direct sum as vector spaces with [X_1 + X_2, Y_1 + Y_2] = [X_1, Y_1] + [X_2, Y_2]: elements of the two summands commute. A Lie algebra that is a direct sum of simple ones is semisimple, and its Dynkin diagram is disconnected (Example 116).

Example 131 (Self-dual and anti-self-dual rotations) With the generators M_{ij} of \mathfrak{so}(4) (Reductive decompositions and isotropy), the combinations 
J_a = -\tfrac12\left(\epsilon_{abc}M_{bc} + M_{a3}\right), \qquad K_a = -\tfrac12\left(\epsilon_{abc}M_{bc} - M_{a3}\right)
\tag{18} (with a, b, c \in \{1, 2, 3\} labelling the first three axes and 3 the fourth, axes numbered 0, 1, 2, 3 as in Exercise 137) satisfy [J_a, J_b] = \epsilon_{abc}J_c, [K_a, K_b] = \epsilon_{abc}K_c and [J_a, K_b] = 0 (Proposition 12): the six-dimensional \mathfrak{so}(4) is the direct sum of two commuting copies of \mathfrak{su}(2), the self-dual and anti-self-dual parts, so named because J and K are the \pm 1 eigenspaces of the Hodge star (Differential forms) on antisymmetric matrices.

The splitting of the Lie algebra has a counterpart for groups and for the geometry of the three-sphere. The three-sphere is itself the group SU(2), which can be multiplied from the left and from the right.

Example 132 (Isometries of the three-sphere) At the group level SO(4) \cong (SU(2) \times SU(2))/\mathbb{Z}_2: S^3 = SU(2) has isometry group SU(2) \times
SU(2) acting by left and right multiplication (Example 193 of Differential geometry), and the decomposition \mathfrak{so}(4) =
\mathfrak{so}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{k} of Reductive decompositions and isotropy is the diagonal \mathfrak{su}(2) plus its complement.










NoteExercises





The first exercise splits the unitary algebra \mathfrak{u}(2) into its trace part and its traceless part. It is the commutant of Example 127 seen on its own.

Exercise 133 (\mathfrak{u}(2) = \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)) Show that every anti-Hermitian 2 \times 2 matrix is uniquely X = X_0 + \tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}X)\mathbb{1} with X_0 \in \mathfrak{su}(2), and that this decomposition is a direct sum of Lie algebras. Is \mathfrak{u}(2) semisimple?







NoteSolution





X_0 = X - \tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}X)\mathbb{1} is traceless and anti-Hermitian (the trace of an anti-Hermitian matrix is imaginary, so \tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}X)\mathbb{1} is anti-Hermitian too), and the decomposition is unique since \mathfrak{su}(2) \cap i\mathbb{R}\mathbb{1} = 0. The identity commutes with everything, and [X, Y] = [X_0, Y_0] is traceless, so the brackets are those of \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1). It is not semisimple: the summand \mathfrak{u}(1) is abelian, not simple. Its centre i\mathbb{R}\mathbb{1} is the obstruction.



The second exercise describes the irreducible representations of a direct sum. They are tensor products of irreducible representations of the summands, and their dimensions multiply.

Exercise 134 (Representations of a direct sum) Given representations \rho_1 of \mathfrak{g}_1 on V_1 and \rho_2 of \mathfrak{g}_2 on V_2, show that \rho(X_1 +
X_2) = \rho_1(X_1) \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes \rho_2(X_2) is a representation of \mathfrak{g}_1 \oplus \mathfrak{g}_2. Find the dimensions and the weights, with respect to (J_3, K_3), of the representations (j, k) of \mathfrak{su}(2)
\oplus \mathfrak{su}(2).







NoteSolution





[\rho(X_1 + X_2), \rho(Y_1 + Y_2)] = [\rho_1(X_1), \rho_1(Y_1)] \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes [\rho_2(X_2), \rho_2(Y_2)], since the cross terms \rho_1(X_1) \otimes \rho_2(Y_2) appear twice with opposite signs; this is \rho([X_1, Y_1] + [X_2, Y_2]). The representation (j, k) has dimension (2j + 1)(2k + 1) and the weights (m, n) with |m| \leq j, |n| \leq k (steps of one), each once: a rectangle in the weight plane. For example (\tfrac12, \tfrac12) has the four weights (\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12) (Example 133).



The third exercise reads the direct-sum structure off the Cartan matrix and the Dynkin diagram, using Sage. The Cartan type D_2 of \mathfrak{so}(4) turns out to be A_1 \times A_1.

Exercise 135 (Disconnected Dynkin diagrams) With Sage, print the Cartan matrices of the types A_1 \times A_1, D_2 and A_2 \times A_1, check that their Dynkin diagrams are disconnected, and compute the dimensions of the representations (\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{2}) and (\mathbf{8}, \mathbf{3}) of \mathfrak{su}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2).







NoteSolution





The simple roots of the two summands are orthogonal, so the Cartan matrix is block diagonal; D_2 has the same matrix \operatorname{diag}(2, 2) as A_1 \times A_1, which is \mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus
\mathfrak{su}(2) at the level of root systems. The dimensions multiply (Exercise 134): 3 \cdot 2 = 6 and 8
\cdot 3 = 24:

for ct in ["A1xA1", ["D", 2], "A2xA1"]:
    T = CartanType(ct)
    print(T, "Cartan matrix:"); print(CartanMatrix(T))
    print("   Dynkin diagram connected:", T.dynkin_diagram().to_undirected().is_connected())
R = WeylCharacterRing("A2xA1", style="coroots")
print("irreducible (3, 2) of su(3) + su(2) has dimension", R(1, 0, 1).degree(), "= 3 * 2; (8, 3):", R(1, 1, 2).degree())
Output:
A1xA1 Cartan matrix:
[2 0]
[0 2]
   Dynkin diagram connected: False
['D', 2] Cartan matrix:
[2 0]
[0 2]
   Dynkin diagram connected: False
A2xA1 Cartan matrix:
[ 2 -1  0]
[-1  2  0]
[ 0  0  2]
   Dynkin diagram connected: False
irreducible (3, 2) of su(3) + su(2) has dimension 6 = 3 * 2; (8, 3): 24







The proposition states the splitting of Example 131 as a list of matrix identities. Each of them can be checked entry by entry on 4 \times 4 matrices.


Proposition 12 (\mathfrak{so}(4) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)) The matrices Equation 18 satisfy the \mathfrak{so}(3) relations separately and commute with each other.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. KaluzaKlein.Representations.so4_splits_brackets, KaluzaKlein.Representations.so4_splits_commute and KaluzaKlein.Representations.JK_of_M4, entry by entry, with the axes numbered 0, 1, 2, 3.

/-- `J` and `K` commute: `[J_a, K_b] = 0` for all `a, b`, so `so(4) ≅ su(2) ⊕ su(2)`. -/
theorem so4_splits_commute (a b : Fin 3) : ⁅J a, K b⁆ = 0
KaluzaKlein.Representations.so4_splits_commute in KaluzaKlein/Groups/Representations.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.Representations

Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The defining representation of \mathfrak{so}(4) on \mathbb{C}^4 has four weights. Under the splitting they form the representation (\tfrac12, \tfrac12), a doublet of each \mathfrak{su}(2).

Example 133 (The vector of \mathfrak{so}(4) is (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)) Take the Cartan generators J_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23}) and K_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} - M_{23}) of Exercise 136. iM_{01} has eigenvalues \pm 1 on the plane (x_0, x_1) and 0 on (x_2, x_3), and iM_{23} the reverse. So (iJ_3, iK_3) has the weights \mp(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) on the first plane and \mp(\tfrac12, -\tfrac12) on the second: the four weights (\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12) of (\tfrac12, \tfrac12), of dimension 2 \cdot 2 = 4 (Exercise 137).

The adjoint representation of a direct sum is the sum of the adjoints of the summands. For \mathfrak{so}(4) this splits the six generators into the two triples.

Example 134 (The adjoint of \mathfrak{so}(4)) The J_a span a triplet of the first \mathfrak{su}(2) on which the second acts trivially, and the K_a the reverse: the adjoint is (1, 0) \oplus (0, 1), of dimension 3 + 3 = 6. In the language of forms, the antisymmetric matrices, or two-forms on \mathbb{R}^4, split into self-dual and anti-self-dual parts (Example 131).

The rotations of the first three axes form a subalgebra \mathfrak{so}(3) \subset \mathfrak{so}(4). In terms of the splitting it is the diagonal \mathfrak{su}(2), and the branchings follow from Clebsch-Gordan.

Example 135 (The diagonal \mathfrak{so}(3)) From Equation 18, J_a + K_a involves only the M_{bc} with b, c among the first three axes: the diagonal \mathfrak{su}(2) is the \mathfrak{so}(3) fixing the fourth axis. Restricted to it, (\tfrac12, \tfrac12) \to
\tfrac12 \otimes \tfrac12 = 1 \oplus 0, which is \mathbb{R}^4 = \mathbb{R}^3 \oplus \mathbb{R}, and (1, 0) \oplus
(0, 1) \to 1 \oplus 1, which is \mathfrak{so}(4) = \mathfrak{so}(3) \oplus \mathfrak{k} with \mathfrak{k} spanned by the M_{a3} (Exercise 126).










NoteExercises





The first exercise checks two of the brackets of the proposition by hand. It uses the general bracket formula of the rotation generators.

Exercise 136 (Checking the splitting by hand) Verify [J_3, K_3] = 0 and [J_1, J_2] = J_3 from the brackets of the M_{ij} computed in Exercise 31 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles.







NoteSolution





J_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23}) and K_3 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} - M_{23}) (in the labels of Reductive decompositions and isotropy, where the axes are 0, 1, 2, 3), and [M_{01}, M_{23}] = 0 since the pairs share no index, so [J_3, K_3] =
\tfrac14([M_{01}, -M_{23}] + [M_{23}, M_{01}]) = 0. For [J_1, J_2] expand the four brackets with [M_{ij}, M_{kl}] = \delta_{jk}M_{il} - \delta_{ik}M_{jl} - \delta_{jl}M_{ik} + \delta_{il}M_{jk} and collect: the result is -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23}) = J_3.









TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. The bracket [J_1, J_2] = J_3 is part of the theorem KaluzaKlein.Representations.so4_splits_brackets.
Sage. Pending.



The second exercise repeats the whole computation in Sage with explicit 4 \times 4 matrices, with the axes numbered 0, 1, 2, 3. It also computes the weights of Example 133.

Exercise 137 (The splitting with explicit matrices) With (M_{ij})_{kl} = \delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} - \delta_{il}\delta_{jk} on axes 0, 1, 2, 3, define J_a = -\tfrac12(M_{bc} +
M_{a3}) and K_a = -\tfrac12(M_{bc} - M_{a3}) for (a, b, c) a cyclic permutation of (0, 1, 2). Check all brackets of Proposition 12, write J_0 in terms of the M_{ij}, and find the simultaneous eigenvalues of (iJ_2, iK_2) on \mathbb{C}^4.







NoteSolution





In these labels J_2 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23}) is the J_3 of Exercise 136. All brackets hold, J_0 = -\tfrac12(M_{12} +
M_{03}), and the weights are (\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12):

def M(i, j):
    return matrix(QQ, 4, 4, lambda k, l: (1 if (k, l) == (i, j) else 0) - (1 if (k, l) == (j, i) else 0))
cyc = [(0, 1, 2), (1, 2, 0), (2, 0, 1)]
J = [-(M(b, c) + M(a, 3)) / 2 for a, b, c in cyc]
K = [-(M(b, c) - M(a, 3)) / 2 for a, b, c in cyc]
br = lambda A, B: A * B - B * A
print("[J_a, J_b] = J_c (cyclic):", all(br(J[a], J[b]) == J[c] for a, b, c in cyc))
print("[K_a, K_b] = K_c (cyclic):", all(br(K[a], K[b]) == K[c] for a, b, c in cyc))
print("[J_a, K_b] = 0 for all a, b:", all(br(X, Y) == 0 for X in J for Y in K))
print("J_0 = Lean's J 0:", J[0] == matrix(QQ, [[0,0,0,-1/2],[0,0,-1/2,0],[0,1/2,0,0],[1/2,0,0,0]]))
P = (I * J[2]).change_ring(QQbar); Q = (I * K[2]).change_ring(QQbar)
V = (QQbar^4)
ws = []
for ev, vecs, m in P.eigenvectors_right():
    sub = matrix(QQbar, vecs).transpose()
    Qr = sub.solve_right(Q * sub)                 # i K_2 restricted to the i J_2 eigenspace (they commute)
    ws += [(QQ(ev), QQ(e)) for e in Qr.eigenvalues()]
print("weights (i J_2, i K_2) of R^4 (x) C:", sorted(ws))
Output:
[J_a, J_b] = J_c (cyclic): True
[K_a, K_b] = K_c (cyclic): True
[J_a, K_b] = 0 for all a, b: True
J_0 = Lean's J 0: True
weights (i J_2, i K_2) of R^4 (x) C: [(-1/2, -1/2), (-1/2, 1/2), (1/2, -1/2), (1/2, 1/2)]










TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. The labels and matrices are those of the Lean file: J_0 is the matrix of KaluzaKlein.Representations.JK_of_M4.
Sage. The computation in the solution above.



The third exercise justifies the names self-dual and anti-self-dual. The Hodge star acts on antisymmetric 4 \times 4 matrices, and the J_a and K_a are its eigenvectors.

Exercise 138 (Self-dual and anti-self-dual) Define (\star M)_{ij} = \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijkl}M_{kl} with \epsilon_{0123} = 1. Show that \star M_{01} = M_{23}, \star M_{12} = M_{03}, \star M_{02} = -M_{13} and \star^2 = 1, and deduce that, in the labels of Exercise 137, \star J_a = J_a and \star K_a = -K_a.







NoteSolution





(\star M_{01})_{ij} = \tfrac12(\epsilon_{ij01} - \epsilon_{ij10}) = \epsilon_{ij01}, non-zero only for \{i, j\} = \{2,
3\}, with \epsilon_{2301} = 1 (the permutation (02)(13) is even): \star M_{01} = M_{23}. Likewise \epsilon_{0312}
= 1 (a 3-cycle) gives \star M_{12} = M_{03}, and \epsilon_{1302} = -1 (a 4-cycle) gives \star M_{02} =
-M_{13}. Applying the same computation to the images shows \star^2 = 1. Then J_2 = -\tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{23}) and J_0 = -\tfrac12(M_{12} + M_{03}) are fixed by \star, and J_1 = -\tfrac12(M_{20} + M_{13}) = -\tfrac12(-M_{02} +
M_{13}) is mapped to -\tfrac12(M_{13} - M_{02}) = J_1; the K_a, with the opposite relative sign, change sign.
















NoteExercises





Three exercises that combine the three sections of this chapter: the octet of \mathfrak{su}(3) seen through weights, roots and branching at once, the full root-system analysis of \mathfrak{so}(4), and the decuplet with its weights, highest weight and branching.
The first integrative exercise builds the adjoint of \mathfrak{su}(3) from the fundamental in three independent ways. The final check is that restriction commutes with tensor products, so the branching of the octet follows from that of the triplet.

Exercise 139 (The octet three ways)  

Check with the Weyl character ring that \mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}} = \mathbf{8} \oplus \mathbf{1}. (b) Using Exercise 89, show that the weights of \mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}} are the six roots and the zero weight three times. (c) Using the branchings of \mathbf{3} and \bar{\mathbf{3}} (Exercise 128,


and Equation 15, branch \mathbf{3} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{3}} under \mathfrak{su}(2)
\times \mathfrak{u}(1) and recover Equation 17.








NoteSolution






is a one-line computation in Sage. (b) The weights are w_a - w_b; for a = b this is 0 three times, and for a
\neq b the differences of the corners of the triangle, which are the six roots (also checked in figures/su3_weights.sage). Removing one zero weight for the singlet leaves the weights of the adjoint (Example 87). (c) (\mathbf{2}_{1/\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{1}_{-2/\sqrt3}) \otimes (\mathbf{2}_{-1/\sqrt3} \oplus
\mathbf{1}_{2/\sqrt3}): charges add and spins combine by Clebsch-Gordan, giving \mathbf{2} \otimes \mathbf{2} =
\mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{1}_0, \mathbf{2}_{1/\sqrt3} \otimes \mathbf{1}_{2/\sqrt3} = \mathbf{2}_{\sqrt3}, \mathbf{1}_{-2/\sqrt3} \otimes \mathbf{2}_{-1/\sqrt3} = \mathbf{2}_{-\sqrt3} and \mathbf{1}_0. Removing the singlet \mathbf{1}_0 of (a) leaves Equation 17:


A2 = WeylCharacterRing("A2", style="coroots"); A1 = WeylCharacterRing("A1", style="coroots")
print("(1) 3 x 3bar = 8 + 1:", A2(1, 0) * A2(0, 1) == A2(1, 1) + A2(0, 0))
w3 = [(1, 1/sqrt(3)), (-1, 1/sqrt(3)), (0, -2/sqrt(3))]
diffs = [((a[0] - b[0]), (a[1] - b[1]).simplify_full()) for a in w3 for b in w3]
zero = sum(1 for d in diffs if d == (0, 0))
print("(2) weights of 3 x 3bar: the zero weight", zero, "times and the roots", sorted(set(d for d in diffs if d != (0, 0))))
# (3) su(2) x u(1) content: pairs (spin, charge); tensor product = Clebsch-Gordan in spin, sum of charges
three = [(QQ(1)/2, 1/sqrt(3)), (0, -2/sqrt(3))]
threebar = [(QQ(1)/2, -1/sqrt(3)), (0, 2/sqrt(3))]
out = []
for j1, q1 in three:
    for j2, q2 in threebar:
        for k in range(int(min(2 * j1, 2 * j2)) + 1):
            out.append((j1 + j2 - k, (q1 + q2).simplify_full()))
print("(3) (3 x 3bar) under su(2) x u(1), as (spin, lambda_8-charge):", sorted(out, key=lambda t: (float(t[1]), t[0])))
eight = [(1, 0), (0, 0), (QQ(1)/2, sqrt(3)), (QQ(1)/2, -sqrt(3))]
print("    equals 8 -> 3_0 + 1_0 + 2_{sqrt3} + 2_{-sqrt3} plus a singlet 1_0:", sorted(map(str, out)) == sorted(map(str, eight + [(0, 0)])))
print("    Sage levi branching of 8 + 1:", (A2(1, 1) + A2(0, 0)).branch(A1, rule="levi"))
Output:
(1) 3 x 3bar = 8 + 1: True
(2) weights of 3 x 3bar: the zero weight 3 times and the roots [(-2, 0), (-1, -sqrt(3)), (-1, sqrt(3)), (1, -sqrt(3)), (1, sqrt(3)), (2, 0)]
(3) (3 x 3bar) under su(2) x u(1), as (spin, lambda_8-charge): [(1/2, -sqrt(3)), (0, 0), (0, 0), (1, 0), (1/2, sqrt(3))]
    equals 8 -> 3_0 + 1_0 + 2_{sqrt3} + 2_{-sqrt3} plus a singlet 1_0: True
    Sage levi branching of 8 + 1: 2*A1(0) + 2*A1(1) + A1(2)




The second integrative exercise treats \mathfrak{so}(4) as a rank-two algebra in its own right. Its Cartan subalgebra, roots and Cartan matrix are computed from the splitting, and the result is compared with the hexagon of \mathfrak{su}(3).

Exercise 140 (The root system of \mathfrak{so}(4)) Using Proposition 12: (a) show that \operatorname{span}(J_3, K_3) is a Cartan subalgebra; (b) find the roots with respect to (iJ_3, iK_3), with root vectors built from the ladder operators of the two copies of \mathfrak{su}(2); (c) choose simple roots and compute the Cartan matrix; (d) compare the number of roots and the dimension with \mathfrak{su}(3), which also has rank two.







NoteSolution






J_3 and K_3 commute by Proposition 12, and an element \sum_a(x_aJ_a + y_aK_a) commuting with both has x
\parallel e_3 and y \parallel e_3 by Exercise 85 applied to each summand: the span is maximal abelian, rank 2 (Example 84). (b) The ladder operators J_\pm of the first copy commute with K_3 and have iJ_3-weights \pm 1 (Example 89), so their roots are (\pm 1, 0); those of the second copy give (0, \pm 1). Four roots and rank two make \dim = 6, as it should. (c) With a direction such as \ell(\mu) = \mu_1 + 2\mu_2 the positive roots are (1, 0) and (0, 1), both simple and orthogonal, so A = \operatorname{diag}(2, 2), the disconnected diagram of type A_1 \times A_1 = D_2 (Example 116, Exercise 135). (d) \mathfrak{su}(3) has six roots forming a hexagon, at angles of 60°, and dimension 8; the four roots of \mathfrak{so}(4) form a square whose simple roots meet at 90°, the case A_{12}A_{21} = 0 of Exercise 119.




The third integrative exercise studies the decuplet \mathbf{10}, which appears in \mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} \otimes
\mathbf{3}. Its weights form a large triangle, shown in the interactive version of Figure 6, and its branching is a tower of spins.

Exercise 141 (The decuplet)  

Decompose \mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} with Sage. (b) List the weights of \mathbf{10} =
\operatorname{Sym}^3\mathbf{3} in the (\lambda_3, \lambda_8) plane (Exercise 122) and check that the highest weight is 3\omega_1. (c) Branch \mathbf{10} under \mathfrak{su}(2) \times \mathfrak{u}(1) with \lambda_8-charges, and check that the charges add up to zero (Exercise 131).








NoteSolution






\mathbf{3} \otimes \mathbf{3} = \mathbf{6} \oplus \bar{\mathbf{3}} (Exercise 113), and then \mathbf{6} \otimes
\mathbf{3} = \mathbf{10} \oplus \mathbf{8}, \bar{\mathbf{3}} \otimes \mathbf{3} = \mathbf{8} \oplus \mathbf{1}: 27 =
10 + 8 + 8 + 1. (b) The weights are w_a + w_b + w_c, a \leq b \leq c, ten points of multiplicity one on a triangle with corners 3w_u = (3, \sqrt3), 3w_d = (-3, \sqrt3) and 3w_s = (0, -2\sqrt3); the highest is 3w_u = 3\omega_1.
Grouping by the number of s quarks, the charges are \sqrt3, 0, -\sqrt3, -2\sqrt3 with \lambda_3-strings of lengths 4, 3, 2, 1: \mathbf{10} \to \mathbf{4}_{\sqrt3} \oplus \mathbf{3}_0 \oplus \mathbf{2}_{-\sqrt3} \oplus
\mathbf{1}_{-2\sqrt3}, the \Delta, \Sigma^*, \Xi^* and \Omega^- of the baryon decuplet. The charges sum to 4\sqrt3 + 0 - 2\sqrt3 - 2\sqrt3 = 0:


A2 = WeylCharacterRing("A2", style="coroots"); A1 = WeylCharacterRing("A1", style="coroots")
print("3 x 3 x 3 =", A2(1, 0)^3, " (A2(3,0) = 10, A2(1,1) = 8, A2(0,0) = 1)")
def plane(w):                                   # ambient weight (w1, w2, w3) -> (lambda_3, lambda_8) eigenvalues
    return (w[0] - w[1], ((w[0] + w[1] - 2 * w[2]) / sqrt(3)).simplify_full())
W10 = A2(3, 0).weight_multiplicities()
pts = sorted((plane(w.to_vector()) for w in W10), key=lambda p: (-float(p[1]), -float(p[0])))
print("weights of 10 (each multiplicity", set(W10.values()), "):", pts)
hw = max(pts, key=lambda p: float(p[1]) + 1e-3 * float(p[0]))
print("highest weight", hw, "= 3 omega_1 = 3 (1, 1/sqrt3):", bool(vector(hw) == 3 * vector([1, 1/sqrt(3)])))
rows = {}
for l3, l8 in pts:
    rows.setdefault(l8, []).append(l3)
for q in sorted(rows, key=lambda q: -float(q)):
    print(f"  lambda_8 = {q}: lambda_3 weights {rows[q]} -> spin {QQ(len(rows[q]) - 1)/2}")
print("Sage levi branching of 10:", A2(3, 0).branch(A1, rule="levi"))
Output:
3 x 3 x 3 = A2(0,0) + 2*A2(1,1) + A2(3,0)  (A2(3,0) = 10, A2(1,1) = 8, A2(0,0) = 1)
weights of 10 (each multiplicity {1} ): [(3, sqrt(3)), (1, sqrt(3)), (-1, sqrt(3)), (-3, sqrt(3)), (2, 0), (0, 0), (-2, 0), (1, -sqrt(3)), (-1, -sqrt(3)), (0, -2*sqrt(3))]
highest weight (3, sqrt(3)) = 3 omega_1 = 3 (1, 1/sqrt3): True
  lambda_8 = sqrt(3): lambda_3 weights [3, 1, -1, -3] -> spin 3/2
  lambda_8 = 0: lambda_3 weights [2, 0, -2] -> spin 1
  lambda_8 = -sqrt(3): lambda_3 weights [1, -1] -> spin 1/2
  lambda_8 = -2*sqrt(3): lambda_3 weights [0] -> spin 0
Sage levi branching of 10: A1(0) + A1(1) + A1(2) + A1(3)

title: Differential geometry
text:
Differential geometry is calculus on curved spaces. A manifold is a space covered by charts, open pieces that look like open sets of \mathbb{R}^n; on it one defines tangent vectors and vector fields, one-forms, tensors and differential forms; a metric then measures lengths, angles and volumes; a connection differentiates vectors along curves, and its failure to commute is the curvature; and the flows of vector fields describe motions of the manifold, the Killing vectors being those that preserve the metric. The chapter follows this order in five parts: charts and manifolds, vector fields and tensors, metrics, connections and curvature, flows and Killing vectors. The sphere, the torus, the plane in polar coordinates and the group SU(2) are the running examples throughout.


A manifold is a space that looks locally like \mathbb{R}^n: around every point one can lay down coordinates, but no single coordinate system need cover the whole space. This chapter builds that idea in three sections. Charts and atlases introduces the local coordinate systems, the charts, the collections of them that cover a space, the atlases, and the transition maps that convert one set of coordinates into another on the overlaps, with the circle and the sphere as running examples and the stereographic projection as the central construction. Manifolds turns a space with a smooth atlas into a smooth manifold and defines, chart by chart, the smooth functions, maps and curves on it, and the product of two manifolds, with the torus and the group SU(2), which is the three-sphere, as the new examples. Embeddings and Gram matrices realises manifolds as surfaces in Euclidean space through parametrisations, studies the velocities of the coordinate curves, singles out the parametrisations that are embeddings, and collects the inner products of the coordinate velocities in the Gram matrix, the first encounter with a metric. Every statement is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions; the computations are carried out with SageManifolds, and the algebraic identities behind the stereographic atlas, the SU(2) determinant and the two Gram matrices are stated as propositions. The reader who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the conventions for indices are those of Prerequisites and conventions.
For more on this topic, see Gadea et al. (2013, Ch. 1), Godinho and Natário (2014, Ch. 1, Ch. 3), Lee (2013, Ch. 1-3), Rudolph and Schmidt (2013, Ch. 1) and Castillo (2020, Ch. 1, Ch. 5-6).


A sphere cannot be covered by a single coordinate system without singular points, and on a circle any angle coordinate necessarily jumps somewhere. The way out is to use several coordinate systems, each valid on a piece, and to record how they are related on the overlaps. This section defines charts, coordinate curves, atlases, transition maps and smooth atlases, with the circle and the sphere as running examples, and ends with the proposition that makes the stereographic atlas of the sphere rigorous.


The first question is what a coordinate system is when the space is not \mathbb{R}^n itself. The answer is a labelling of the points of a piece of the space by n numbers, one label per point and every label in an open region used; the picture to keep is a map of a region of the Earth, flat paper labelling points of a curved surface.


Definition 1 (Chart) A chart on a set M is a bijection x : U \to V from a subset U \subseteq M, the chart’s domain, onto an open subset V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n. It assigns to every point p \in U its n coordinates x^i(p), i = 1, \dots, n, and the inverse x^{-1} : V \to U parametrises the domain by coordinates.

NoteExamples





The simplest curved space is the circle, and its natural coordinate is the angle. The first example shows that the angle is a chart only after one point is removed, because a full turn would label that point twice; this one missing point is the whole reason atlases are needed.

Example 1 (The angle chart on the circle) On the unit circle S^1 = \{(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : X^2 + Y^2 = 1\} the angle \varphi \in (0, 2\pi) is a chart with inverse 
\varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi),
\tag{1} whose domain is the circle minus the point (1, 0). The coordinate \varphi is periodic: \varphi and \varphi + 2\pi would label the same point, which is why the chart stops short of a full turn. This periodicity is what quantises charge in Part III.

One dimension up, the sphere has the familiar latitude and longitude. The second example records them as a chart and locates exactly where they fail: a half-meridian is missing for the same reason as the point of the circle, and the two poles are missing for a new reason, that longitude has no value there.

Example 2 (Spherical coordinates on the sphere) On the unit sphere S^2 = \{(X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1\} the spherical coordinates (\theta, \varphi) \in (0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi) form a chart with inverse 
(\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),
\tag{2} shown in Figure 1. Its domain misses the two poles Z = \pm 1, where \theta = 0, \pi and \varphi is undefined, and the half-meridian \varphi = 0. At the poles the map Equation 2 is still defined but ceases to be a chart: all values of \varphi give the same point.







Figure 1: The spherical chart on S^2: parallels \theta = \text{const} (black), meridians \varphi = \text{const} (grey), the two poles where the chart degenerates (red), and the point (\theta, \varphi) = (\pi/3, \pi/4) with the two coordinate curves that lead to it from the pole and from the meridian \varphi = 0 (green). Generated by figures/s2_chart.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.
A different chart on the same sphere misses a single point instead of a half-meridian and two poles. The third example is the stereographic projection, a construction from a straight line through a pole, whose domain is the whole sphere minus that pole and whose image is the whole plane; it is the chart on which the rest of the section is built.

Example 3 (Stereographic coordinates on the sphere) The stereographic projection from the north pole N = (0, 0, 1) sends a point p of the sphere to the point (u, v) where the line through N and p meets the plane Z = 0 (Figure 2): (u, v) = (X, Y)/(1 - Z). Solving for the point with given (u, v) gives the inverse chart 
(u, v) \mapsto \left( \frac{2u}{1 + u^2 + v^2},\ \frac{2v}{1 + u^2 + v^2},\ \frac{u^2 + v^2 - 1}{1 + u^2 + v^2} \right),
\qquad (u, v) \in \mathbb{R}^2 ,
\tag{3} whose domain is the sphere minus N: as u^2 + v^2 \to \infty the point approaches N. That the right-hand side lies on the sphere is Proposition 1.

The definition asks for a bijection onto an open set, and the first exercise checks both halves of that condition on the circle by hand. Reading off the angle of a few given points is the computational part; the argument that no point is labelled twice and every point of the domain is labelled is the conceptual one.

Exercise 1 (Reading the angle chart) Find the coordinate \varphi \in (0, 2\pi) of the points (0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1) and (\tfrac12, -
\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}) of the circle, and show that the angle chart of Example 1 is a bijection from S^1 \setminus \{(1, 0)\} onto the open interval (0, 2\pi).







NoteSolution





\varphi = \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2 and 5\pi/3 respectively, since \cos(5\pi/3) = \tfrac12 and \sin(5\pi/3)
= -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}. Every unit vector is (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) for exactly one \varphi \in [0, 2\pi), because \cos\varphi fixes \varphi up to sign and \sin\varphi fixes the sign; the value \varphi = 0 gives the excluded point (1, 0), so \varphi \mapsto (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) is a bijection from (0, 2\pi) onto S^1 \setminus \{(1, 0)\}, and its inverse is the chart.



Charts need not be angles. The second exercise uses the two Cartesian coordinates X, Y themselves as a chart on the upper hemisphere, where the third coordinate is recovered by a square root, and compares the result with the stereographic chart from the south pole, which also covers the hemisphere, with Sage doing the algebra.

Exercise 2 (The hemispherical chart) Show that (X, Y) is a chart on the upper hemisphere Z > 0 of S^2 with image the open unit disc, write down its inverse, and compute the south stereographic coordinates (u', v') = (X, Y)/(1 + Z) of its points. Check with Sage that the hemisphere is sent into the open unit disc u'^2 + v'^2 < 1 and compute the Jacobian determinant of (X, Y) \mapsto (u', v').







NoteSolution





On Z > 0 the point is recovered from (X, Y) as (X, Y, \sqrt{1 - X^2 - Y^2}), so the map is injective, and the image is the open disc X^2 + Y^2 < 1 (the equator Z = 0 would give the boundary circle, which is excluded). Substituting, u'^2 + v'^2 = (1 - Z)/(1 + Z) < 1, with equality only at Z = 0; the Jacobian determinant is 1/(Z(1 + Z)^2), finite and positive on the hemisphere:

X, Y = var("X Y", domain="real")
assume(X**2 + Y**2 < 1)
Z = sqrt(1 - X**2 - Y**2)
print("the inverse chart lands on the sphere, X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1:", bool((X**2 + Y**2 + Z**2).simplify_full() == 1))
up = X/(1 + Z); vp = Y/(1 + Z)                      # south stereographic coordinates (X, Y)/(1 + Z)
rho2 = (up**2 + vp**2).simplify_full()
print("u'^2 + v'^2 = (1 - Z)/(1 + Z):", bool((rho2 - (1 - Z)/(1 + Z)).simplify_full() == 0))
print("1 - (u'^2 + v'^2) =", (1 - rho2).simplify_full().factor(), " which is positive for Z > 0: the image is inside the unit disc")
J = jacobian((up, vp), (X, Y))
d = J.det().simplify_full()
print("Jacobian determinant of (X, Y) -> (u', v') is 1/(Z (1 + Z)^2):", bool((d - 1/(Z*(1 + Z)**2)).simplify_full() == 0), " (non-zero on the hemisphere)")
print("the centre (X, Y) = (0, 0), the north pole, goes to (u', v') =", (up.subs(X=0, Y=0), vp.subs(X=0, Y=0)))
print("the point (X, Y) = (3/5, 0) with Z = 4/5 goes to (u', v') =", (up.subs(X=3/5, Y=0), vp.subs(X=3/5, Y=0)))
Output:
the inverse chart lands on the sphere, X^2 + Y^2 + Z^2 = 1: True
u'^2 + v'^2 = (1 - Z)/(1 + Z): True
1 - (u'^2 + v'^2) = 2*(X^4 + 2*X^2*Y^2 + Y^4 - 3*sqrt(-X^2 - Y^2 + 1)*X^2 - 3*sqrt(-X^2 - Y^2 + 1)*Y^2 - 5*X^2 - 5*Y^2 + 4*sqrt(-X^2 - Y^2 + 1) + 4)/(X^4 + 2*X^2*Y^2 + Y^4 - 4*sqrt(-X^2 - Y^2 + 1)*X^2 - 4*sqrt(-X^2 - Y^2 + 1)*Y^2 - 8*X^2 - 8*Y^2 + 8*sqrt(-X^2 - Y^2 + 1) + 8)  which is positive for Z > 0: the image is inside the unit disc
Jacobian determinant of (X, Y) -> (u', v') is 1/(Z (1 + Z)^2): True  (non-zero on the hemisphere)
the centre (X, Y) = (0, 0), the north pole, goes to (u', v') = (0, 0)
the point (X, Y) = (3/5, 0) with Z = 4/5 goes to (u', v') = (1/3, 0)




Polar coordinates on the plane are a chart too, and the third exercise asks where. The point of the exercise is that the origin can never be included, whatever intervals are chosen for r and \varphi, and that the same obstruction reappears for spherical coordinates on space along a whole axis.

Exercise 3 (Polar and spherical coordinates as charts) Polar coordinates (r, \varphi) \in (0, \infty) \times (0, 2\pi) have inverse (r\cos\varphi, r\sin\varphi). Find the domain of this chart on the plane, explain why no choice of intervals makes the origin part of the domain of a polar chart, and determine on which subset of \mathbb{R}^3 the spherical coordinates (\rho, \theta,
\varphi) \in (0, \infty) \times (0, \pi) \times (0, 2\pi), with inverse \rho times Equation 2, form a chart.







NoteSolution





The image of (0, \infty) \times (0, 2\pi) is the plane minus the closed half-line \{Y = 0, X \geq 0\}, which is the domain. At the origin every value of \varphi gives the same point (0, 0), so a map including r = 0 is not injective, and no interval for \varphi can repair this; the origin is for polar coordinates what the poles are for spherical ones. In space, \rho times Equation 2 is injective on the stated box with image \mathbb{R}^3 minus the closed half-plane \{Y = 0, X \geq 0\}, which contains the whole Z-axis (where \theta = 0, \pi) and the half-plane \varphi = 0; that complement is the domain of the chart.









A chart does more than label points: it draws a grid on its domain. The next definition names the lines of that grid, obtained by letting one coordinate vary while the others are frozen; on a map of the Earth they are the parallels and meridians, and their velocities will become the basic tangent vectors in Section 1.2.1.


Definition 2 (Coordinate curve) The i-th coordinate curve through a point of a chart domain is the curve along which only the coordinate x^i varies, the others being held fixed: t \mapsto x^{-1}(x^1, \dots, x^i + t, \dots, x^n).
