Casimir on 3 cos^2(theta) - 1: True (eigenvalue -6 = -l(l+1), l = 2)







The plane and the sphere both have three Killing fields in two dimensions, and the exercise on \mathbb{R}^n found n(n + 1)/2. The next definition makes this number an upper bound for every metric and names the metrics that attain it.


Definition 79 (Maximally symmetric space) A metric on an n-dimensional manifold has at most n(n+1)/2 linearly independent Killing fields (n “translations” and n(n-1)/2 “rotations” at a point); a space attaining this maximum is maximally symmetric, and it has constant sectional curvature.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The two running examples of dimension two both attain the bound. They differ in curvature, zero for the plane and positive for the sphere, and in whether the “translations” commute.

Example 340 (Plane and sphere) The plane with its three Killing fields and the sphere with its three are maximally symmetric for n = 2; the sphere’s isometry group is SO(3), and in Part IV the metric on M_4 \times S^2 is deformed by g_{\mu m} =
A^a_\mu(x) K_a^m(y), one four-dimensional vector field per Killing vector, and Equation 56 become the structure constants of the gauge group.

Being flat is not enough for maximal symmetry, since the global shape of a manifold can rule out symmetries that hold locally. The circle and the two tori of Exercise 350 illustrate the different possibilities.

Example 341 (Circle and torus) The circle has one Killing field, the maximum n(n+1)/2 = 1 for n = 1; the flat torus has two, \partial_a and \partial_b, fewer than the maximum 3 (it is flat but its global shape breaks the rotation); the embedded torus has only \partial_b, since g_{bb} depends on a.

The bound applies to metrics of any signature. In four dimensions it is ten, attained by the flat spacetime of special relativity and by the de Sitter spacetime of cosmology.

Example 342 (Minkowski space and de Sitter space) Minkowski space has 4 + 6 = 10 Killing fields, the translations and Lorentz transformations of the Poincaré group; de Sitter space (The Einstein equations) also has 10, forming \mathfrak{so}(4, 1): both are maximally symmetric, the second with constant positive curvature.










NoteExercises





The first exercise is a count. It tabulates the bound in low dimensions and matches it against the isometry groups of Euclidean spaces, spheres and Minkowski spaces.

Exercise 354 (Counting symmetries) Compute n(n + 1)/2 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and check it against the dimensions of the Euclidean group E(n), of SO(n + 1) (the isometries of S^n) and of the Poincaré group in n dimensions. How many Killing fields does S^2 \times S^1 have, and is it maximally symmetric?







NoteSolution





The values are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. E(n) has n translations and \dim SO(n) = n(n - 1)/2 rotations, in total n(n + 1)/2; \dim SO(n + 1) = (n + 1)n/2, the same number; the Poincaré group in n dimensions has n translations and \dim SO(1, n - 1) = n(n - 1)/2 Lorentz transformations, again n(n + 1)/2 (10 for n = 4). The product S^2
\times S^1 has the 3 Killing fields of S^2 and the 1 of S^1, 4 < 6: it is homogeneous (every point can be moved to every other) but not maximally symmetric, since no isometry rotates a sphere direction into the circle direction.



A maximally symmetric surface of negative curvature completes the picture. The second exercise verifies with SageManifolds that the hyperbolic plane has three Killing fields and finds their Lie algebra, which is neither the Euclidean algebra nor \mathfrak{so}(3).

Exercise 355 (The hyperbolic plane) On the upper half-plane y > 0 with g = (dx^2 + dy^2)/y^2, check with SageManifolds that P = \partial_x, D =
x\,\partial_x + y\,\partial_y and S = (x^2 - y^2)\,\partial_x + 2xy\,\partial_y are Killing, compute their brackets and the scalar curvature, and check whether the Euclidean rotation -y\,\partial_x + x\,\partial_y is Killing.







NoteSolution





All three are Killing, with [P, D] = P, [P, S] = 2D, [D, S] = S: the algebra \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R}) of the isometry group PSL(2, \mathbb{R}) acting by Möbius transformations z \mapsto (az + b)/(cz + d). The scalar curvature is -2, so the Gauss curvature (Definition 66) is the constant -1. The dilation D, conformal for the Euclidean metric, is an isometry here because the factor 1/y^2 compensates it, while the Euclidean rotation does not preserve the half-plane and is not Killing:

M = Manifold(2, "H2", structure="Riemannian"); C = M.chart("x y:(0,+oo)"); x, y = C[:]
g = M.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = 1 / y ** 2; g[1, 1] = 1 / y ** 2
P = M.vector_field(1, 0, name="P"); D = M.vector_field(x, y, name="D"); S = M.vector_field(x ** 2 - y ** 2, 2 * x * y, name="S")
for name, V in [("P", P), ("D", D), ("S", S)]:
    print(f"L_{name} g =", g.lie_derivative(V).display(), " -> Killing:", g.lie_derivative(V) == 0)
print("[P, D] = P:", P.bracket(D) == P, ";  [P, S] = 2 D:", P.bracket(S) == 2 * D, ";  [D, S] = S:", D.bracket(S) == S)
print("scalar curvature R =", g.ricci_scalar().expr(), " (Gauss curvature R/2 = -1)")
print("the Euclidean rotation -y d/dx + x d/dy is Killing here:", g.lie_derivative(M.vector_field(-y, x)) == 0)
Output:
L_P g = 0  -> Killing: True
L_D g = 0  -> Killing: True
L_S g = 0  -> Killing: True
[P, D] = P: True ;  [P, S] = 2 D: True ;  [D, S] = S: True
scalar curvature R = -2  (Gauss curvature R/2 = -1)
the Euclidean rotation -y d/dx + x d/dy is Killing here: False




The bound n(n + 1)/2 was stated without proof in the definition. The third exercise derives it from the fact that a Killing field is determined by its value and its first derivatives at a single point.

Exercise 356 (Why n(n + 1)/2 is the maximum) Using the identity \nabla_i\nabla_jK_k = R_{lijk}K^l (with a suitable sign convention for the lowered Riemann tensor), valid for every Killing field, show that K is determined on a connected manifold by K_k(p) and \nabla_jK_k(p) at one point p, and deduce the bound n(n + 1)/2.







NoteSolution





Along any curve \gamma from p, set u_k = K_k(\gamma(s)) and v_{jk} = \nabla_jK_k(\gamma(s)). Differentiating along \dot\gamma gives \dot u_k = \dot\gamma^j v_{jk} (plus connection terms linear in u) and, by the identity, \dot v_{jk} = \dot\gamma^i R_{lijk}u^l (plus terms linear in v): a linear system of ordinary differential equations for (u, v), whose solution is fixed by the initial values at p. So the map K \mapsto (K(p),
\nabla K(p)) is injective on Killing fields. Killing’s equation makes \nabla_jK_k antisymmetric, so the initial data lie in a space of dimension n + n(n - 1)/2 = n(n + 1)/2, and the Killing fields form a vector space of at most this dimension. Equality requires every initial value to extend, which forces the curvature to be the same in every plane at every point: constant sectional curvature.
















NoteExercises





Three exercises that combine the two sections of this chapter: the flow of a Killing field of the sphere followed until it is seen to be a group of isometries, the full symmetry analysis of the Minkowski plane, and the conserved quantities that Killing fields give along geodesics.
The first integrative exercise integrates a Killing field of the sphere and checks the defining property of an isometry on the flow itself, not just at t = 0. It contrasts the result with the flow of the conformal field of the second section.

Exercise 357 (The flow of K_1 is a group of isometries) Let \Phi_t = R_X(t) \circ E, with E the embedding of the sphere and R_X(t) the rotation about the X-axis. With SageManifolds, show that \frac{d}{dt}\big|_0\Phi_t = J K_1, that the rotations satisfy the group law, and that the pullback of the Euclidean metric by \Phi_t is the round metric for every t. Then pull the round metric back by the flow of -\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta (Exercise 329) and compare.







NoteSolution





The generator of the rotations about X is the ambient field \xi_1 = (0, -z, y), which is JK_1 by Exercise 345, so the flow of K_1 is \Phi_t read in the chart (Definition 74). Since R_X(t) is orthogonal, \Phi_t^*\delta = E^*R_X(t)^*\delta = E^*\delta = g for every t (Exercise 335): each map of the flow is an isometry, the integrated form of \mathcal{L}_{K_1}g = 0 (Proposition 30). The meridian flow gives a pullback whose \theta\theta component is g_{\theta\theta} times a factor e^{2t}/(1 + (e^{2t} -
1)\cos^2(\theta/2))^2 that depends on \theta: conformal, not isometric, as Example 332 predicts.

t, s = var("t s", domain="real")
S2 = Manifold(2, "S2", structure="Riemannian"); C = S2.chart(r"th:(0,pi):\theta ph:(0,2*pi):\varphi"); th, ph = C[:]
g = S2.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = 1; g[1, 1] = sin(th) ** 2
R3 = EuclideanSpace(3, "R3"); cart = R3.cartesian_coordinates(); delta = R3.metric()
E = vector([sin(th) * cos(ph), sin(th) * sin(ph), cos(th)])
RX = lambda a: matrix([[1, 0, 0], [0, cos(a), -sin(a)], [0, sin(a), cos(a)]])
Phi = lambda a: RX(a) * E
K1 = vector([-sin(ph), -cos(th) / sin(th) * cos(ph)])
gen = diff(Phi(t), t).subs(t=0); JK1 = jacobian(E, (th, ph)) * K1
print("generator d/dt|0 Phi_t = J K_1 (the ambient field xi_1 = (0, -z, y)):", bool(all((a - b).simplify_full() == 0 for a, b in zip(gen, JK1))))
print("group law Phi_s o Phi_t = Phi_{s+t} (R_X(s) R_X(t) = R_X(s+t)):", bool(all((a - b).simplify_trig() == 0 for a, b in zip((RX(s) * RX(t)).list(), RX(s + t).list()))))
F = S2.diff_map(R3, list(Phi(t)), name="Phi_t")
h = F.pullback(delta); h.apply_map(lambda e: e.simplify_full())
print("Phi_t^* delta =", h.display(), " = g for every t:", h == g)
# the flow of the conformal field X = -sin(th) d/dth: theta -> 2 arctan(tan(theta/2) e^{-t}), phi fixed
G = S2.diff_map(S2, [2 * arctan(tan(th / 2) * exp(-t)), ph], name="Psi_t")
k = G.pullback(g); k.apply_map(lambda e: e.simplify_full())
print("conformal flow: Psi_t^* g == g:", k == g, ";  ratio of the theta-theta components:", (k[0, 0] / g[0, 0]).expr().simplify_full().factor())
Output:
generator d/dt|0 Phi_t = J K_1 (the ambient field xi_1 = (0, -z, y)): True
group law Phi_s o Phi_t = Phi_{s+t} (R_X(s) R_X(t) = R_X(s+t)): True
Phi_t^* delta = Phi_t^*(g) = dth⊗dth + sin(th)^2 dph⊗dph  = g for every t: True
conformal flow: Psi_t^* g == g: False ;  ratio of the theta-theta components: e^(2*t)/(cos(1/2*th)^2*e^(2*t) - cos(1/2*th)^2 + 1)^2




The second integrative exercise collects everything this chapter says about the Minkowski plane: its flows, the pullbacks they induce, its Killing fields and their algebra. It is a Lorentzian counterpart of the Euclidean plane treated throughout.

Exercise 358 (The Minkowski plane: flows, Killing fields and algebra) For ds^2 = dt^2 - dx^2: (a) write the flows of P_t = \partial_t, P_x = \partial_x and B = x\,\partial_t +
t\,\partial_x and show that each pulls \eta back to itself; (b) use Exercise 344, adapted to \eta, to show that these are all the Killing fields; (c) compute the brackets and compare them with the Euclidean algebra of Example 334.







NoteSolution






The translations (t + s, x) and (t, x + s) have identity Jacobian, so they pull \eta back to itself. The boost flow \Lambda_w = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh w & \sinh w \\ \sinh w & \cosh w \end{pmatrix} (Exercise 343) satisfies \Lambda_w^{\mathsf{T}}\eta\Lambda_w = \eta because \cosh^2w - \sinh^2w = 1; so \Lambda_w^*\eta = \eta, and t^2 - x^2 is preserved. (b) With K_\mu = \eta_{\mu\nu}K^\nu, Killing’s equation for constant \eta is \partial_\mu
K_\nu + \partial_\nu K_\mu = 0, and the argument of Exercise 344 goes through unchanged: K_\mu = a_\mu +
\omega_{\mu\nu}x^\nu with \omega antisymmetric, 2 + 1 = 3 parameters, so the plane is maximally symmetric. With \omega_{tx} = -\omega_{xt} = 1: K_t = x, K_x = -t, so K^t = x, K^x = t, the boost. (c) [P_t, P_x] = 0, [B, P_t] = -\partial_t(x, t) = -P_x and [B, P_x] = -\partial_x(x, t) = -P_t. In the Euclidean algebra [J, P_1] = -
P_2 but [J, P_2] = +P_1; the change of one sign is the change of signature, and it makes \operatorname{ad}_B diagonalisable with real eigenvalues \pm 1 on the light-cone translations P_t \pm P_x, where \operatorname{ad}_J has eigenvalues \pm i.




The third integrative exercise uses a Killing field to find a quantity conserved along geodesics of the previous chapter. On the sphere the three conserved quantities turn out to be the components of the angular momentum.

Exercise 359 (Conserved quantities along geodesics) Show that for a geodesic \gamma (Definition 61) and a Killing field K, Q = g(K, \dot\gamma) is constant, by proving \frac{dQ}{ds} = \tfrac12(\mathcal{L}_Kg)(\dot\gamma, \dot\gamma) with the geodesic equation Equation 39. Check with SageManifolds that \frac{dQ_a}{ds} = 0 for the three Killing fields of the sphere, that Q_a = (x \times
\dot x)_a for any curve on the sphere, and evaluate Q on a tilted great circle.







NoteSolution





\frac{d}{ds}(g_{ij}K^i\dot\gamma^j) = \partial_kg_{ij}\dot\gamma^kK^i\dot\gamma^j + g_{ij}\partial_kK^i\dot\gamma^k
\dot\gamma^j + g_{ij}K^i\ddot\gamma^j, and substituting \ddot\gamma^j = -\Gamma^j_{kl}\dot\gamma^k\dot\gamma^l with Equation 34, the first and last terms combine to \tfrac12K^m\partial_mg_{kl}\dot\gamma^k\dot\gamma^l, so that \frac{dQ}{ds} = \tfrac12(\mathcal{L}_Kg)_{kl}\dot\gamma^k\dot\gamma^l by Equation 52, which vanishes for a Killing field. For K_3 = \partial_\varphi, Q_3 = \sin^2\theta\,\dot\varphi is Clairaut’s relation. Since JK_a = \xi_a and \xi_a\cdot\dot x = \epsilon_{abc}x^b\dot x^c, the three quantities form the angular momentum x \times \dot x, which for a great circle is the unit normal of its plane:

S2 = Manifold(2, "S2", structure="Riemannian"); C = S2.chart(r"th:(0,pi):\theta ph:(0,2*pi):\varphi"); thc, phc = C[:]
g = S2.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = 1; g[1, 1] = sin(thc) ** 2
Gam = g.christoffel_symbols()
sv = var("s", domain="real")
th = function("th")(sv); ph = function("ph")(sv)
sub = {thc: th, phc: ph}
q = [th, ph]; qd = [diff(th, sv), diff(ph, sv)]
acc = [-sum(Gam[k, i, j].expr().subs(sub) * qd[i] * qd[j] for i in range(2) for j in range(2)) for k in range(2)]
Kc = [[-sin(phc), -cos(thc) / sin(thc) * cos(phc)], [cos(phc), -cos(thc) / sin(thc) * sin(phc)], [0, 1]]
for a in range(3):
    Q = sum(g[i, j].expr().subs(sub) * Kc[a][i].subs(sub) * qd[j] for i in range(2) for j in range(2))
    dQ = diff(Q, sv).subs({diff(th, sv, 2): acc[0], diff(ph, sv, 2): acc[1]})
    print(f"Q_{a+1} = {Q.simplify_full()};  dQ_{a+1}/ds on geodesics = {dQ.simplify_full()}")
X = vector([sin(th) * cos(ph), sin(th) * sin(ph), cos(th)]); Xd = diff(X, sv)
Qs = [sum(g[i, j].expr().subs(sub) * Kc[a][i].subs(sub) * qd[j] for i in range(2) for j in range(2)) for a in range(3)]
print("Q_a = (x cross x')_a for any curve:", bool(all((Qs[a] - X.cross_product(Xd)[a]).simplify_full() == 0 for a in range(3))))
# a concrete geodesic: the great circle in the plane spanned by e1 and (0, cos(al), sin(al)), unit speed
al = pi / 3
Y = vector([cos(sv), sin(sv) * cos(al), sin(sv) * sin(al)]); Yd = diff(Y, sv)
print("great circle with tilt pi/3: Q =", [e.simplify_full() for e in Y.cross_product(Yd)], "(constant, normal to its plane)")
Output:
Q_1 = -cos(ph(s))*cos(th(s))*sin(th(s))*diff(ph(s), s) - sin(ph(s))*diff(th(s), s);  dQ_1/ds on geodesics = 0
Q_2 = -cos(th(s))*sin(ph(s))*sin(th(s))*diff(ph(s), s) + cos(ph(s))*diff(th(s), s);  dQ_2/ds on geodesics = 0
Q_3 = sin(th(s))^2*diff(ph(s), s);  dQ_3/ds on geodesics = 0
Q_a = (x cross x')_a for any curve: True
great circle with tilt pi/3: Q = [0, -1/2*sqrt(3), 1/2] (constant, normal to its plane)

title: Functional analysis
text:
Functional analysis studies vector spaces of functions and sequences together with a notion of size, and the linear maps between them. It is the language of quantum mechanics, of partial differential equations and of the renormalisation of field theories, and it supplies the Fredholm index that counts the zero modes of the Dirac operator in the reductions of the later parts. This chapter develops the subject from normed spaces to operator algebras, on explicit examples. Normed and Banach spaces defines norms and completeness, with the sequence spaces \ell^p, the function spaces L^p and C(K), bounded linear maps and dual spaces. The four principles proves the Hahn-Banach, uniform-boundedness, open-mapping and closed-graph theorems and shows by counterexamples why each hypothesis is needed. Weak topologies and reflexivity treats weak and weak-* convergence and the Banach-Alaoglu theorem. Inner product and Hilbert spaces, Bounded operators and Spectral theory specialise to the inner-product case, where geometry and the spectral theorem are available. Compact and Fredholm operators proves the Fredholm alternative and defines the index. Unbounded operators and the Laplacian, Sobolev spaces and Traces, determinants and heat kernels treat the differential operators of physics and their spectra. Banach and C*-algebras ends with the spectrum of an element of an algebra and the continuous functional calculus. Every statement is followed by at least three examples of increasing complexity and at least three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions. The sequence spaces, the Pauli matrices, the exponentials e^{inx} on the circle, the spherical harmonics and the Gaussian are the running examples.


A norm measures the size of a vector and turns a vector space into a metric space in which limits, series and continuity make sense. This part defines norms and complete normed spaces, introduces the three families of spaces that the rest of the chapter works in, the sequence spaces \ell^p, the function spaces L^p and the continuous functions C(K), and then studies the linear maps between normed spaces and the dual space of continuous linear functionals. The line of argument follows the lecture notes of Arcozzi (2025, Ch. 1 and 3), with the Hilbert-space special cases of Rainer Picard and Waurick (2020, App. B) as examples.
For more on this topic, see Cheung (2024, sec. 4.2).


On \mathbb{R}^n the Euclidean length is one way among many to measure a vector: the largest coordinate or the sum of the absolute values of the coordinates serve as well. The figure draws the unit balls of several such measures in the plane, and the definition below names the three properties that all of them share.






Figure 1: Unit balls \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \|x\|_p \leq 1\} of the norms \|x\|_p = (|x_1|^p + |x_2|^p)^{1/p} for p =
1, \tfrac32, 2, 4 and \|x\|_\infty = \max(|x_1|, |x_2|). Each ball is convex and symmetric under x \mapsto -x; the balls grow with p, and only the disc p = 2 comes from an inner product. Generated by figures/fa2-unit-balls.sage.





Definition 1 (Norm) A norm on a real or complex vector space X (Definition 1 of Linear algebra) is a map \|\cdot\| : X \to [0, \infty) that is definite, \|x\| = 0 only for x = 0, homogeneous, \|\lambda x\| = |\lambda|\,\|x\| for scalars \lambda, and satisfies the triangle inequality \|x + y\| \leq \|x\| + \|y\|. The pair (X, \|\cdot\|) is a normed space; it is a metric space with the distance d(x, y) = \|x - y\|, so that a sequence converges to x when \|x_n - x\| \to 0. Two norms \|\cdot\|_a, \|\cdot\|_b on X are equivalent if c\|x\|_a \leq
\|x\|_b \leq C\|x\|_a for constants 0 < c \leq C and all x; equivalent norms have the same convergent sequences.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The first examples live in \mathbb{R}^n, where every coordinate gives a way of measuring. The three norms below are the ones drawn in the figure for n = 2, and the example compares them with explicit constants.

Example 1 (Three norms on \mathbb{R}^n) \|x\|_1 = \sum_k|x_k|, \|x\|_2 = (\sum_k|x_k|^2)^{1/2} and \|x\|_\infty = \max_k|x_k| are norms on \mathbb{R}^n and \mathbb{C}^n. For x = (3, -4) they give 7, 5 and 4. They are equivalent: \|x\|_\infty
\leq \|x\|_2 \leq \|x\|_1 \leq n\|x\|_\infty, and the constants are attained, the first two by x = (1, 0, \dots,
0) and the last by x = (1, 1, \dots, 1).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



On a space of functions the same three ideas give the supremum norm and the integral norms. The second example shows that on the continuous functions they are no longer equivalent, because a function can be large on a small set.

Example 2 (Supremum and integral norms) On the continuous functions on [0, 1], \|f\|_\infty = \max_x|f(x)| and \|f\|_1 = \int_0^1|f(x)|\,dx are norms Arcozzi (2025, sec. 1.1.1). For f_n(x) = x^n one finds \|f_n\|_\infty = 1 and \|f_n\|_1 = 1/(n + 1) \to 0, so f_n \to 0 in \|\cdot\|_1 but not in \|\cdot\|_\infty, and no inequality \|f\|_\infty \leq C\|f\|_1 can hold. The inequality \|f\|_1 \leq \|f\|_\infty does hold, so the supremum norm is the stronger of the two.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



Inner products are the source of the most important norms, and the parallelogram law tells which norms come from one. The third example states the criterion and applies it to the norms of the figure.

Example 3 (Norms from inner products) An inner product (Definition 12) gives the norm \|u\| = \langle u, u\rangle^{1/2}; the triangle inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz, which Rainer Picard and Waurick (2020, Lemma B.1.5) derives from the non-negativity of the Gram determinant \langle u, u\rangle\langle v, v\rangle - |\langle u, v\rangle|^2. Such a norm satisfies the parallelogram law \|u + v\|^2 + \|u - v\|^2 = 2\|u\|^2 + 2\|v\|^2, and conversely a norm satisfying it comes from an inner product Rainer Picard and Waurick (2020, Lemma B.1.7 and the remark after it). For u = (1, 0), v = (0, 1) the law reads 2\cdot 2^{2/p} = 4 in \|\cdot\|_p, true only for p = 2.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.












NoteExercises





The checks that a proposed norm is one are short, but the triangle inequality is the delicate part, as the first exercise shows by an example where it fails. The exercise also shows why the exponents p < 1 are excluded from the family drawn in the figure.

Exercise 1 (When the triangle inequality fails) Show that \|\cdot\|_1 and \|\cdot\|_\infty are norms on \mathbb{C}^n. Then show that N(x) = (\sqrt{|x_1|} +
\sqrt{|x_2|})^2 on \mathbb{R}^2 is definite and homogeneous but violates the triangle inequality, by evaluating it on (1, 0), (0, 1) and their sum.







NoteSolution





Definiteness and homogeneity are clear, and |x_k + y_k| \leq |x_k| + |y_k| summed (or maximised) over k gives the triangle inequality for \|\cdot\|_1 (or \|\cdot\|_\infty). For N: N(\lambda x) = (\sqrt{|\lambda|}
(\sqrt{|x_1|} + \sqrt{|x_2|}))^2 = |\lambda|N(x), and N(x) = 0 forces x = 0. But N(1, 0) = N(0, 1) = 1 while N(1, 1) = 4 > 2. The unit “ball” \{N \leq 1\} is the region inside the astroid-like curve \sqrt{|x_1|} +
\sqrt{|x_2|} = 1, which is not convex; a norm always has a convex unit ball.
A check of the three norms with Sage, including the triangle inequality of the two genuine norms on random complex vectors:

N = lambda x: (sqrt(abs(x[0])) + sqrt(abs(x[1])))^2
print("N(1,0) =", N((1, 0)), " N(0,1) =", N((0, 1)), " N(1,1) =", N((1, 1)), " > N(1,0) + N(0,1):", N((1, 1)) > 2)
print("homogeneity N(-3 x) = 3 N(x) at x = (2, 5):", bool(N((-6, -15)) == 3 * N((2, 5))))
set_random_seed(1)
vs = [vector(CC, [CC.random_element() for _ in range(4)]) for _ in range(200)]
print("triangle inequality for the 1-norm and the sup-norm on 100 random pairs in C^4:",
      all(((u + v).norm(1) <= u.norm(1) + v.norm(1) + 1e-12) and ((u + v).norm(Infinity) <= u.norm(Infinity) + v.norm(Infinity) + 1e-12) for u, v in zip(vs[::2], vs[1::2])))
print("midpoint of (1,0) and (0,1) has N =", N((1 / 2, 1 / 2)), "> 1: the set N <= 1 is not convex")
Output:
N(1,0) = 1  N(0,1) = 1  N(1,1) = 4  > N(1,0) + N(0,1): True
homogeneity N(-3 x) = 3 N(x) at x = (2, 5): True
triangle inequality for the 1-norm and the sup-norm on 100 random pairs in C^4: True
midpoint of (1,0) and (0,1) has N = 2 > 1: the set N <= 1 is not convex










TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.

The parallelogram law is a computable test, and the second exercise applies it numerically to the whole family \|\cdot\|_p on \mathbb{R}^2. Its result is that the Euclidean norm is the only member of the family with an inner product behind it.

Four theorems carry most of the weight of functional analysis on Banach spaces. The Hahn-Banach theorem supplies enough continuous functionals to separate points; the Baire category theorem turns completeness into a statement about the size of sets; the uniform boundedness principle and the open mapping theorem, both consequences of Baire’s, turn pointwise information into uniform estimates. This part states each theorem, proves the shorter ones in the exercises, and shows by counterexamples why each hypothesis, completeness above all, is needed. The proofs follow Arcozzi (2025, secs. 3.2, 3.5 and 3.6); closed operators follow Rainer Picard and Waurick (2020, sec. B.4) and Waterstraat (2016, sec. 1.2).
For more on this topic, see Gasiński and Papageorgiou (2014, Ch. 5).


A functional defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole space without increasing its norm. In a Hilbert space this is an orthogonal projection followed by the Riesz representation, but in a general normed space there is no projection, and the extension needs an argument by induction on dimensions closed off by Zorn’s lemma.


Theorem 6 (Hahn-Banach theorem) Let X be a real vector space, p : X \to \mathbb{R} sublinear (p(x + y) \leq p(x) + p(y) and p(tx) = tp(x) for t \geq 0), Y \subset X a subspace and \ell : Y \to \mathbb{R} linear with \ell \leq p on Y. Then \ell has a linear extension L to X with L \leq p on X; over \mathbb{C} the same holds with |\ell| \leq p Arcozzi (2025, Thms. 3.4 and 3.5). Consequences for a normed space X: every \lambda \in Y^* extends to some L \in
X^* with \|L\| = \|\lambda\|; for every x \in X there is \varphi \in X^* with \|\varphi\| = 1 and \varphi(x)
= \|x\|; the canonical map x \mapsto \hat x of X into X^{**} is an isometry; and for a subspace Z and y at distance d(y, Z) > 0 there is \varphi \in X^* with \|\varphi\| = 1, \varphi|_Z = 0 and \varphi(y) = d(y, Z) Arcozzi (2025, Cors. 3.1-3.3, Thm. 3.7). In geometric form, two disjoint convex sets, one of them open, are separated by a closed real hyperplane Ramesh (2020, Thm. 2.15).

In infinite dimensions the closed unit ball is never compact in norm, so bounded sequences need not have convergent subsequences. Weakening the notion of convergence restores compactness: a sequence converges weakly when every continuous functional converges along it. This part defines weak and weak-* convergence on the examples of oscillating, travelling and concentrating bumps, proves that the dual unit ball is weak-* compact (the Banach-Alaoglu theorem), and characterises the reflexive spaces, in which bounded sequences always have weakly convergent subsequences. The exposition follows Ramesh (2020) and Arcozzi (2025, sec. 3.4).

An inner product assigns a complex number to two vectors and gives a vector space lengths, angles and orthogonality. This section defines inner products and orthonormal systems, introduces completeness and the two model Hilbert spaces \ell^2 and L^2, defines orthonormal bases with Parseval’s identity, and quotes the Riesz representation theorem; the Gram-Schmidt process and the orthogonal projection are then carried out on explicit vectors and functions.
For more on this topic, see Axler (2024, Ch. 6, Ch. 7) and Dereziński and Gérard (2022, Ch. 1-2).


A bilinear form (Definition 11 of Linear algebra) assigns a number to two vectors, and on a real space a positive definite symmetric one gives lengths and angles. On a complex space the form must be adjusted so that \langle u, u\rangle stays real and positive, and the definition below fixes the convention used throughout: the inner product is antilinear in its first slot and linear in its second, which is the convention of quantum mechanics.


Definition 12 (Inner product) An inner product on a complex vector space V (Definition 1 of Linear algebra) is a map \langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle : V
\times V \to \mathbb{C} that is linear in the second slot, \langle u, \alpha v + \beta w\rangle =
\alpha\langle u, v\rangle + \beta\langle u, w\rangle, conjugate symmetric, \langle v, u\rangle =
\overline{\langle u, v\rangle}, and positive definite, \langle u, u\rangle > 0 for u \neq 0. The two rules together make it antilinear in the first slot, \langle \alpha u, v\rangle = \bar\alpha\langle u,
v\rangle. The norm is \|u\| = \sqrt{\langle u, u\rangle}; it satisfies the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality |\langle u, v\rangle| \leq \|u\|\,\|v\| and the triangle inequality \|u + v\| \leq \|u\| + \|v\|. A vector space with an inner product is an inner product space, and on a real vector space the same definition with real scalars recovers a positive definite symmetric bilinear form.

NoteExamples





The first instance is the complex version of the dot product, in which the conjugation on the first vector is exactly what makes \langle u, u\rangle a sum of squared moduli. It also shows why the conjugate is needed at all: without it the “length” of (1, i) would be zero.

Example 66 (\mathbb{C}^n) \langle u, v\rangle = \sum_k \bar u_k v_k is an inner product on \mathbb{C}^n, with \|u\|^2 = \sum |u_k|^2. For u = (1, i) this gives \|u\|^2 = 1 + 1 = 2, whereas the unconjugated sum \sum u_k u_k = 1 + i^2 = 0 would not be a norm; \langle (1, i), (i, 1)\rangle = \bar 1\cdot i + \bar i\cdot 1 = i - i = 0, so the two vectors are orthogonal.

Matrices form a vector space, and the trace supplies an inner product on it that will reappear as the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product of operators. The example computes it on the Pauli matrices, which turn out to be orthogonal to each other and to the identity.

Example 67 (Matrices with the trace form) \langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(A^\dagger B), with A^\dagger = \bar A^{\mathsf{T}} the conjugate transpose, is an inner product on the n \times n complex matrices: \langle A, A\rangle = \sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2. The identity and the three Pauli matrices \sigma_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \sigma_2 =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix}, \sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix} satisfy \langle\sigma_a, \sigma_b\rangle = 2\delta_{ab} and \langle 1, \sigma_a\rangle = \operatorname{tr}\sigma_a = 0 (Exercise 76): they are an orthogonal basis of the 2 \times 2 matrices.

Functions on an interval form an infinite-dimensional vector space, and the integral replaces the sum of the previous examples. The third example is the inner product that the rest of the chapter uses, and it shows a first orthogonality relation between exponentials.

Example 68 (Continuous functions on an interval) On the continuous complex functions on [0, 2\pi], \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}\overline{f(x)}g(x)\,dx is an inner product (the Riemann integral of The Riemann integral), and positive definiteness holds because a continuous |f|^2 with zero integral vanishes identically. For e_n(x) = e^{inx} one finds \langle e_m,
e_n\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(n - m)x}dx = 2\pi\delta_{mn}, the orthogonality of modes of Fourier series.

Two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product vanishes, and a family of mutually orthogonal unit vectors is the right-angled coordinate frame of an inner product space. The figure shows the Gram-Schmidt process turning two vectors of the plane into such a frame, and the orthogonal projection onto a line; the definition below names the frame, the process and the projection.

Definition 13 (Orthonormal system) Vectors u, v are orthogonal, u \perp v, if \langle u, v\rangle = 0. A family (e_k) is an orthonormal system if \langle e_j, e_k\rangle = \delta_{jk}. The Gram-Schmidt process turns linearly independent vectors v_1, v_2, \dots into an orthonormal system spanning the same subspaces: e_1 = v_1/\|v_1\|, and e_k = w_k/\|w_k\| with w_k = v_k - \sum_{j < k}\langle e_j, v_k\rangle e_j. For a finite orthonormal system e_1, \dots, e_n the orthogonal projection onto their span is Pu = \sum_k \langle e_k, u\rangle
e_k; u - Pu is orthogonal to the span, Pu is the point of the span closest to u, and \|Pu\|^2 = \sum_k
|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2 \leq \|u\|^2 (Bessel’s inequality).

Exercise 78 (Bessel’s inequality and best approximation) For an orthonormal system e_1, \dots, e_n and Pu = \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k, show that u - Pu \perp

\langle e_j, u - Pu\rangle = \langle e_j, u\rangle - \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle\delta_{jk} = 0. For w in the span, u - w = (u - Pu) + (Pu - w) with Pu - w in the span and so orthogonal to u - Pu; hence \|u - w\|^2 =
\|u - Pu\|^2 + \|Pu - w\|^2 \geq \|u - Pu\|^2, with equality only for w = Pu.

An inner product space in which Cauchy sequences (Definition 3 of Real analysis) need not converge is like the rationals inside the reals: limits that “should” exist are missing. The definition below adds completeness, and the result is the class of spaces in which infinite expansions in orthonormal systems make sense.


Definition 14 (Hilbert space) A Hilbert space is an inner product space H that is complete: every Cauchy sequence, \|u_m - u_n\| \to
0 as m, n \to \infty, converges to some u \in H in the norm, \|u_n - u\| \to 0. A subspace that is closed in the norm is again a Hilbert space. Every inner product space has a completion, a Hilbert space containing it as a dense subspace, obtained as for \mathbb{R} from \mathbb{Q} by adjoining limits of Cauchy sequences.

Finite-dimensional inner product spaces are automatically complete, because convergence in norm is convergence of each coordinate. The first example records this, so that the real content of completeness lies in infinite dimensions.

Example 72 (\mathbb{C}^n is complete) In \mathbb{C}^n with the standard inner product, |u_k - v_k| \leq \|u - v\| for each coordinate, so a Cauchy sequence of vectors has Cauchy, hence convergent, coordinates, and converges to the vector of the limits. Every finite-dimensional inner product space is a Hilbert space, and so is the space of n \times n matrices with the trace inner product.

The first infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is the space of square-summable sequences, the natural home for coefficient sequences (\langle e_k, u\rangle)_k. The example defines it and sketches why it is complete, with the details in Exercise 80.

Example 73 (The sequence space \ell^2) \ell^2 = \{(a_n)_{n \geq 1} : \sum_n |a_n|^2 < \infty\} with \langle a, b\rangle = \sum_n \bar a_n b_n is a Hilbert space; the series converges absolutely by Cauchy-Schwarz on partial sums. Completeness: a Cauchy sequence a^{(m)} has Cauchy coordinates a^{(m)}_n \to a_n, and the limit sequence a is in \ell^2 with a^{(m)} \to
a (Exercise 80). The sequence a_n = 1/n is in \ell^2 (\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6, Series), while a_n = 1/\sqrt n is not.

The continuous functions with the integral inner product of Example 68 are the standard example of an incomplete space: a Cauchy sequence of continuous functions can converge in norm towards a jump. The third example exhibits such a sequence, and the completion is the space L^2 defined next.

Example 74 (Continuous functions are not complete in the L^2 norm) On [-1, 1] let f_n(x) = \max(-1, \min(1, nx)), continuous and equal to the sign function outside [-1/n, 1/n]. Then \|f_m - f_n\|^2 \leq \int_{-1/n}^{1/n} 4\,dx = 8/n for m > n, a Cauchy sequence, but the only candidate limit is the discontinuous \operatorname{sign}(x), which is not in the space: the norm limit is missing. The completion is L^2(-1, 1) (Definition 15), in which \operatorname{sign} is an element.

The completion of the continuous functions in the integral norm is the space of square-integrable functions, and describing it requires an integral more general than Riemann’s. The definition below introduces the Lebesgue integral informally, as the integral that handles limits of integrable functions, together with the identification of functions that differ only on a negligible set.


Definition 15 (L^2 space) Let X be an interval, a region of \mathbb{R}^n or a surface with its volume element d\mu. The Lebesgue integral \int_X f\,d\mu extends the Riemann integral (Definition 11 of Real analysis) to a larger class of functions with the property that limits can be exchanged with the integral under mild conditions; every Riemann integrable function is Lebesgue integrable with the same integral. A set is null (of measure zero) if it can be covered by intervals of arbitrarily small total length, and functions that agree outside a null set are identified. The space L^2(X) consists of the (classes of) measurable functions with \int_X|f|^2d\mu <
\infty, with the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_X\bar f g\,d\mu; it is a Hilbert space (the  Riesz-Fischer theorem**), and the continuous functions are dense in it.

A finite orthonormal system spans a subspace; the question is when an infinite one spans, in the sense of limits, the whole Hilbert space. The definition below answers it with the notion of an orthonormal basis and records Parseval’s identity, the infinite-dimensional Pythagorean theorem, which turns Bessel’s inequality into an equality.


Definition 16 (Orthonormal basis) An orthonormal system (e_k) in a Hilbert space H is an orthonormal basis if it is complete: the only vector orthogonal to every e_k is 0. Equivalently, every u \in H is the norm-convergent sum of its expansion u = \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k, and equivalently again Parseval’s identity \|u\|^2 =
\sum_k|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2 holds for all u; then also \langle u, v\rangle = \sum_k\overline{\langle e_k,
u\rangle}\langle e_k, v\rangle. A Hilbert space with a countable orthonormal basis is separable, and the map u \mapsto (\langle e_k, u\rangle)_k is then an isomorphism of H onto \ell^2 preserving inner products. An orthonormal basis of an infinite-dimensional space is not a basis in the sense of Definition 5 of Linear algebra, since infinite sums are allowed.

The last exercise constructs the isomorphism and shows why the plane waves cannot be an orthonormal system in L^2(\mathbb{R}).

U is linear and preserves inner products by Parseval’s identity in its polarised form, hence is injective; it is surjective because for a \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}) the sum \sum a_ne_n converges in L^2 (its partial sums are Cauchy) to an f with Uf = a. For the plane waves: they are not in L^2(\mathbb{R}) at all (Example 76), and an orthonormal system in a separable space is countable, since the balls of radius 1/2 around its members are disjoint and a countable dense set must meet each; \mathbb{R} is uncountable. The plane waves are instead a “continuous basis” in the sense of the Fourier transform (The Fourier transform) and of distributions (Distributions).









A linear functional (Definition 8 of Linear algebra) on a Hilbert space is a linear map to the scalars, and taking the inner product with a fixed vector is one. The theorem below, quoted without proof, says that in a Hilbert space there are no others among the continuous ones: the dual space (Definition 9 of Linear algebra) is the space itself, which is why bra vectors and ket vectors can be identified.


Theorem 11 (Riesz representation theorem) Let H be a Hilbert space and \varphi : H \to \mathbb{C} a linear functional that is bounded: |\varphi(u)|
\leq C\|u\| for some constant C and all u. Then there is a unique v \in H with \varphi(u) = \langle v,
u\rangle for all u, and the smallest constant C equals \|v\|. Conversely every u \mapsto \langle v,
u\rangle is bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz. The proof takes v in the orthogonal complement of the kernel of \varphi, which is a closed subspace of codimension one; the statement is quoted here and the outline is Exercise 90.

The evaluation f \mapsto f(x_0) is the most important linear functional on functions, and the third example explains why it is not represented by any vector of L^2: the would-be representing function is the delta function. This is where the Riesz theorem hands over to the theory of distributions.

Example 83 (Evaluation is not bounded on L^2) On L^2(-1, 1) the functional f \mapsto f(0) is not even well defined, since f(0) depends on the representative (Exercise 84); on continuous functions it is defined but not bounded in the L^2 norm: f_n(x) = \max(0, 1 - n|x|) has f_n(0) = 1 and \|f_n\|^2 = 2/(3n) \to 0. So there is no g \in L^2 with f(0) = \int\bar gf\,dx; the “function” \delta(x) that would do it is a distribution (Distributions). The theorem does apply to f \mapsto \int_{-1}^0f\,dx, represented by the indicator function of [-1, 0].

The computations of this section, Gram-Schmidt on monomials, the orthogonal projection in the plane and in L^2(-1, 1), and Parseval’s identity for f(x) = x, are collected in one proposition. Each of them is a finite computation with exact integrals and exact arithmetic.


Proposition 1 (Orthonormalisation and projection) Gram-Schmidt on 1, x, x^2, x^3 in L^2(-1, 1) gives P_0, P_1, \tfrac23P_2, \tfrac25P_3; the projection of (1, 2) onto the line spanned by (2, 1) is (\tfrac85, \tfrac45) with residual (-\tfrac35, \tfrac65) orthogonal to the line; the L^2(-1, 1) projection of e^x onto polynomials of degree \leq 2 has a smaller error than the Taylor polynomial of degree 2; the partial Parseval sums of f(x) = x on (-\pi, \pi) increase towards \|f\|^2 = 2\pi^3/3 and equal 4\pi\sum_{n \leq N}1/n^2; and Cauchy-Schwarz holds with its sharp constant for (1, i, 0), (1, 1, 1).

A bounded operator is a linear map of a Hilbert space to itself that stretches no vector by more than a fixed factor; in finite dimensions every linear map is one. This section defines the operator norm, the adjoint and the three classes of operators that quantum mechanics and spectral theory use constantly, self-adjoint, unitary and projection operators, and ends with the commutator; the figure shows how an operator deforms the unit circle, and the proposition checks the identities in Sage.
For more on this topic, see Scott (2023, Ch. 4).


A linear map (Definition 7 of Linear algebra) between inner product spaces may stretch different vectors by different factors, and the largest stretching factor measures its size. The figure shows the image of the unit circle under three operators, an ellipse, a circle and a segment, whose longest radius is this factor; the definition below names it.






Figure 13: The unit circle of \mathbb{R}^2 and its images under a general matrix A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 &
1\end{pmatrix} (an ellipse whose semi-axes are the singular values \sigma_1 = \|A\| \approx 2.29 and \sigma_2
\approx 0.87, with \sigma_1\sigma_2 = |\det A| = 2), under a rotation U (the circle itself, \|U\| = 1) and under the orthogonal projection P onto the diagonal (a segment, \|P\| = 1). Generated by figures/operator_norm_ellipse.sage.





Definition 17 (Bounded operator) A linear map A : H \to H on a Hilbert space is a bounded operator if its operator norm \|A\| =
\sup_{u \neq 0}\|Au\|/\|u\| = \sup_{\|u\| = 1}\|Au\| is finite, so that \|Au\| \leq \|A\|\,\|u\| for all u; a linear map is bounded exactly when it is continuous. The bounded operators form a vector space \mathcal{B}(H) with \|A + B\| \leq \|A\| + \|B\|, \|\alpha A\| = |\alpha|\|A\|, and the composition satisfies \|AB\| \leq
\|A\|\,\|B\|. In finite dimensions every linear map is bounded and \|A\| is the largest singular value of A, the square root of the largest eigenvalue of A^\dagger A, with A^\dagger = \bar A^{\mathsf{T}}.

0. The differentiation operator, by contrast, is not bounded on any natural domain in L^2 (Exercise 97), which is why Section 1.8 is needed.

Moving an operator from one slot of the inner product to the other produces, in general, a different operator; for matrices this is the conjugate transpose already used above. The definition below introduces it for bounded operators, where the Riesz representation theorem guarantees its existence.


Definition 18 (Adjoint operator) The adjoint of a bounded operator A is the unique bounded operator A^\dagger with \langle Au, v\rangle =
\langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle for all u, v \in H; it exists because for fixed v the functional u \mapsto
\langle v, Au\rangle is bounded and so, by Theorem 11, equals \langle A^\dagger v, u\rangle for a unique vector A^\dagger v. The adjoint satisfies (A^\dagger)^\dagger = A, (AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger
A^\dagger, (\alpha A + B)^\dagger = \bar\alpha A^\dagger + B^\dagger, \|A^\dagger\| = \|A\| and \|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2. For a matrix in an orthonormal basis, A^\dagger = \bar A^{\mathsf{T}}, the conjugate transpose. In Dirac’s notation the operator |u\rangle\langle v| : w \mapsto \langle v, w\rangle u has adjoint |v\rangle\langle u|.

The conjugate transpose is the adjoint because the standard inner product on \mathbb{C}^n conjugates the first vector. The first example verifies the defining identity on a matrix with a complex entry, where the conjugation matters.

Example 90 (The conjugate transpose) For A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}, A^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -i & 2\end{pmatrix}. With u = (1, 0) and v = (0, 1): Au = (1, 0), \langle Au, v\rangle = 0, and A^\dagger v = (0, 2), \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle = 0; with u = (0, 1), v = (1, 0): \langle Au, v\rangle = \overline{i}\cdot1 = -
i and \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle = \overline{1}\cdot(-i) = -i. Without the conjugation the second pair would give i \neq -i (Exercise 99).

The adjoint of the shift is the backward shift, and the two compositions S^\dagger S and SS^\dagger differ, which is impossible for square matrices. The second example is the first sign that infinite dimensions change the algebra of operators.

Example 91 (The adjoint of the shift) \langle Sa, b\rangle = \sum_{n \geq 2}\bar a_{n-1}b_n = \sum_{n \geq 1}\bar a_nb_{n+1} = \langle a, S^*b\rangle with S^*b = (b_2, b_3, \dots): the adjoint S^\dagger is the backward shift. S^\dagger S = 1, but SS^\dagger
a = (0, a_2, a_3, \dots), so SS^\dagger = 1 - P_1 with P_1 the projection onto the first coordinate: a one-sided inverse that is not two-sided (Exercise 114).

For multiplication and integral operators the adjoint is found by rewriting an integral, and the answer is to conjugate the multiplier or to conjugate and transpose the kernel. The third example gives both rules, which cover most operators met in practice.

Example 92 (Multiplication and integral operators) \langle M_gf, h\rangle = \int\overline{gf}\,h = \int\bar f(\bar gh) = \langle f, M_{\bar g}h\rangle, so M_g^\dagger = M_{\bar g}. For an integral operator (Kf)(x) = \int k(x, y)f(y)\,dy with a square-integrable kernel, exchanging the order of integration gives K^\dagger with kernel k^\dagger(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)} (Exercise 100), the continuous analogue of the conjugate transpose.

The algebraic rules for adjoints follow from the uniqueness in the definition, and the norm identities from Cauchy-Schwarz. The first exercise asks for the three rules that are used most often.

Exercise 98 (Rules for adjoints) Prove (AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger A^\dagger, (A^\dagger)^\dagger = A and \|A^\dagger\| = \|A\|, and deduce \|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2.







NoteSolution





\langle ABu, v\rangle = \langle Bu, A^\dagger v\rangle = \langle u, B^\dagger A^\dagger v\rangle, and uniqueness gives the first rule. Conjugating \langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle gives \langle v,
Au\rangle = \langle A^\dagger v, u\rangle, which says (A^\dagger)^\dagger = A. Then \|A^\dagger v\|^2 =
\langle A^\dagger v, A^\dagger v\rangle = \langle AA^\dagger v, v\rangle \leq \|A\|\|A^\dagger v\|\|v\|, so \|A^\dagger v\| \leq \|A\|\|v\| and \|A^\dagger\| \leq \|A\|; by symmetry equality holds. Finally \|A^\dagger A\| \leq \|A\|^2 by submultiplicativity, and \|Au\|^2 = \langle u, A^\dagger Au\rangle \leq
\|A^\dagger A\|\|u\|^2 gives the reverse inequality.

Integral operators are the infinite-dimensional matrices, with the kernel k(x, y) playing the role of the entry A_{xy}, and the rule for their adjoint follows from Fubini’s theorem. The last exercise derives it and identifies the self-adjoint kernels.

Exercise 100 (The adjoint kernel) For (Kf)(x) = \int_0^1k(x, y)f(y)\,dy on L^2(0, 1) with continuous k, show that K^\dagger has kernel \overline{k(y, x)}, and conclude that K is self-adjoint exactly when k(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)}. Which of k = xy, k = x - y, k = i(x - y), k = e^{i(x - y)} give self-adjoint operators?







NoteSolution





\langle Kf, g\rangle = \int\overline{\int k(x, y)f(y)dy}\,g(x)dx = \int\bar f(y)\left(\int\overline{k(x, y)}
g(x)dx\right)dy = \langle f, K'g\rangle with (K'g)(y) = \int\overline{k(x, y)}g(x)dx, so K^\dagger has kernel (y, x) \mapsto \overline{k(x, y)}, that is, k^\dagger(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)}. Self-adjointness means k(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)}: true for xy (real symmetric), false for x - y (antisymmetric), true for i(x -
y) (since \overline{i(y - x)} = i(x - y)), and true for e^{i(x - y)} (since \overline{e^{i(y - x)}} =
e^{i(x - y)}).









Operators equal to their own adjoint are the infinite-dimensional Hermitian matrices, and they are the operators whose expectation values \langle u, Au\rangle are real. The definition below fixes the term and records the two properties, reality and the decomposition of an arbitrary operator into self-adjoint parts, that make them central.


Definition 19 (Self-adjoint operator) A bounded operator is self-adjoint (or Hermitian) if A^\dagger = A, that is, \langle Au, v\rangle =
\langle u, Av\rangle for all u, v. Then \langle u, Au\rangle = \overline{\langle Au, u\rangle} =
\overline{\langle u, Au\rangle} is real for every u, and on a complex Hilbert space the converse holds (Exercise 101). A self-adjoint A is positive, A \geq 0, if \langle u, Au\rangle \geq 0 for all u. Every bounded operator is uniquely A = B + iC with B = \tfrac12(A + A^\dagger) and C =
\tfrac{1}{2i}(A - A^\dagger) self-adjoint, the analogue of real and imaginary parts.

NoteExamples





The Pauli matrices are the basic Hermitian 2 \times 2 matrices, and together with the identity they span all of them with real coefficients. The first example records this, which is the reason they parametrise the observables of a two-level system.

Example 93 (Hermitian 2 \times 2 matrices) \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3 are Hermitian: \sigma_2^\dagger = \overline{\sigma_2}^{\mathsf{T}} =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & i \\ -i & 0\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}} = \sigma_2. A matrix a_0 1 + \sum_a a_a\sigma_a is Hermitian exactly when all a_\mu are real (Exercise 76 gave a = (2, 2, 1, -1) for a Hermitian example), and \sigma_a^2 = 1 makes each \sigma_a a Hermitian matrix whose square is positive.

A multiplication operator is self-adjoint exactly when its multiplier is real, and positive when the multiplier is non-negative. The second example applies this to the position operator and to the potential-energy operators of quantum mechanics, which are all of this type.

Example 94 (Real multiplication operators) M_g^\dagger = M_{\bar g} (Example 92), so M_g is self-adjoint exactly when g is real, and then \langle f, M_gf\rangle = \int g|f|^2 is real, positive if g \geq 0. The position operator on L^2(0, 1) is positive; multiplication by \cos x on L^2(0, 2\pi) is self-adjoint but not positive; multiplication by e^{ix} is not self-adjoint, and its decomposition B + iC is M_{\cos x} + iM_{\sin x}.

The operator -i\,d/dx on smooth periodic functions is formally self-adjoint: integration by parts moves the derivative across and the boundary terms cancel. The third example performs this computation, which is the model for all differential operators in Section 1.8, and shows that the eigenvalues it produces are real.

Example 95 (-i\,d/dx on periodic functions) On smooth 2\pi-periodic f, g, \langle -if', g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}\overline{(-if')}g\,dx =
i\int\bar f'g\,dx = i[\bar fg]_0^{2\pi} - i\int\bar fg'\,dx = \langle f, -ig'\rangle, the boundary term vanishing by periodicity. The operator is symmetric, and its eigenfunctions e^{inx} have real eigenvalues n; it is not bounded (Exercise 97), so the full definition of self-adjointness for it is deferred to Definition 29.

Reality of all expectation values characterises self-adjoint operators on complex spaces, and the proof is a polarisation argument. The first exercise asks for it and for the counterexample showing that the statement fails on real spaces.

Exercise 101 (Real expectation values) Show that a bounded operator on a complex Hilbert space with \langle u, Au\rangle \in \mathbb{R} for all u is self-adjoint, and that on \mathbb{R}^2 the rotation by 90^\circ has \langle u, Au\rangle = 0 for all u without being symmetric.







NoteSolution





Let B = A - A^\dagger; then \langle u, Bu\rangle = \langle u, Au\rangle - \overline{\langle u, Au\rangle} = 0 for all u. Polarising, \langle u, Bv\rangle = \tfrac14\sum_k i^{-k}\langle u + i^kv, B(u + i^kv)\rangle = 0 for all u, v (the identity of Exercise 75 holds for the form \langle u, Bv\rangle by the same expansion), so B = 0. On \mathbb{R}^2 the rotation J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} has \langle u,
Ju\rangle = -u_1u_2 + u_2u_1 = 0 but J^{\mathsf{T}} = -J \neq J; complex scalars are needed for the polarisation step.



The decomposition into self-adjoint parts is unique and behaves like real and imaginary parts, but the two parts need not commute. The second exercise computes the decomposition for a matrix and shows that A is determined by expectation values alone in the complex case.

Exercise 102 (Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts) Decompose A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} as B + iC with B, C Hermitian, compute [B, C], and show that two bounded operators on a complex Hilbert space with the same expectation values \langle u,
Au\rangle = \langle u, A'u\rangle for all u are equal.







NoteSolution





B = \tfrac12(A + A^{\mathsf{T}}) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} and C = \tfrac{1}{2i}(A -
A^{\mathsf{T}}) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix} = \sigma_2, both Hermitian; [B, C] = BC - CB =
\begin{pmatrix} i & -i \\ i & -i\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} -i & -i \\ i & i\end{pmatrix} = 2i\sigma_3 \neq
0. If \langle u, (A - A')u\rangle = 0 for all u, the polarisation identity of the previous solution gives \langle u, (A - A')v\rangle = 0 for all u, v, hence A = A'.

Operators that preserve all inner products, hence all lengths and angles, are the symmetries of a Hilbert space, and they generalise rotations. The definition below gives the algebraic characterisation through the adjoint and separates it from the weaker notion of an isometry, which in infinite dimensions is genuinely different.


Definition 20 (Unitary operator) A bounded operator U is unitary if U^\dagger U = UU^\dagger = 1, that is, U is invertible with U^{-1}
= U^\dagger. Equivalently, U is surjective and preserves inner products, \langle Uu, Uv\rangle = \langle u,
v\rangle, or surjective and preserves norms, \|Uu\| = \|u\| (Exercise 104). An operator with U^\dagger U
= 1 alone is an isometry; in finite dimensions every isometry is unitary. A unitary has \|U\| = 1, maps orthonormal bases to orthonormal bases, and the unitaries of H form a group under composition, U(n) for H =
\mathbb{C}^n.

Rotations of the plane and the diagonal phase matrices are the unitaries one can draw, and the exponential of i times a Pauli matrix produces both. The first example records these, with the Lie groups of Lie groups in the background.

Example 96 (Rotations and phases) R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix} satisfies R_\theta^{\mathsf{T}}R_\theta = 1: it is unitary (orthogonal) and maps the unit circle to itself (Figure 13). The diagonal matrix e^{i\theta\sigma_3} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta},
e^{-i\theta}) is unitary with \det = 1, an element of SU(2) \subset U(2), and e^{i\theta\sigma_2} =
\cos\theta + i\sin\theta\,\sigma_2 = R_\theta (Exercise 105).

On function spaces the basic unitaries are multiplication by a phase and translation, and the Fourier transform itself. The second example lists them; the unitarity of the Fourier transform is Plancherel’s theorem of The Fourier transform.

Example 97 (Phases, translations and the Fourier transform) Multiplication by e^{i\alpha(x)} with real \alpha is unitary on L^2(X), since M_{e^{i\alpha}}^\dagger =
M_{e^{-i\alpha}} is its inverse. Translation (T_af)(x) = f(x - a) is unitary on L^2(\mathbb{R}), as \int|f(x - a)|^2dx = \int|f|^2dx and T_a^{-1} = T_{-a}. The Fourier transform \hat f(k) = (2\pi)^{-1/2}\int
f(x)e^{-ikx}dx is unitary on L^2(\mathbb{R}): \|\hat f\| = \|f\| is Plancherel’s theorem (The Fourier transform), and it turns T_a into multiplication by e^{-ika}.

The shift is an isometry that is not unitary, since its range misses the first coordinate, while the two-sided shift on \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}) is unitary. The third example contrasts the two and identifies the bilateral shift with a multiplication operator through the Fourier isomorphism.

Example 98 (Isometries that are not unitary) The shift S on \ell^2 has S^\dagger S = 1 but SS^\dagger = 1 - P_1 \neq 1 (Example 91): an isometry whose range is the proper closed subspace \{a_1 = 0\}, so not unitary. The bilateral shift (Va)_n =

The projection onto a subspace was defined in Definition 13 through an orthonormal basis of the subspace; as an operator it is characterised by two equations. The definition below gives this characterisation and the Dirac notation for rank-one projections, which is the notation of quantum mechanics.


Definition 21 (Orthogonal projection) An orthogonal projection is a bounded operator P with P^2 = P and P^\dagger = P. Its range K = PH is a closed subspace, Pu is the point of K closest to u, and 1 - P is the projection onto the orthogonal complement K^\perp = \{v : \langle v, k\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } k \in K\}, so that H = K \oplus K^\perp. Conversely every closed subspace is the range of exactly one orthogonal projection. If e_1, e_2, \dots is an orthonormal basis of K then P = \sum_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|, where |e\rangle\langle e| : u \mapsto \langle
e, u\rangle e is the projection onto the line \mathbb{C}e for a unit vector e; \|P\| = 1 unless P = 0.

The projection onto a line in \mathbb{C}^2 is a 2 \times 2 matrix of rank one, and for the eigenvectors of a Pauli matrix it is a simple combination of that Pauli matrix and the identity. The first example computes it and checks the two defining equations.

Example 99 (Projection onto a line in \mathbb{C}^2) For e = (1, i)/\sqrt2, P = |e\rangle\langle e| has entries P_{jk} = e_j\bar e_k: P = \tfrac12
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \\ i & 1\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac12(1 + \sigma_2). Then P^\dagger = P and P^2 = \tfrac14(1 +
2\sigma_2 + \sigma_2^2) = \tfrac12(1 + \sigma_2) = P; the complementary projection 1 - P = \tfrac12(1 -
\sigma_2) projects onto (1, -i)/\sqrt2, and \sigma_2 = P - (1 - P).

For each Pauli matrix the two projections onto its eigenvectors add up to the identity and multiply to zero, and the matrix itself is their difference weighted by its eigenvalues. The second example writes this out for \sigma_3; it is the spectral decomposition of Section 1.6 in its smallest case.

Example 100 (Complementary projections and \sigma_3) P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma_3) are \operatorname{diag}(1, 0) and \operatorname{diag}(0, 1), the projections onto the eigenvectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) of \sigma_3. They satisfy P_+ + P_- = 1, P_+P_- = 0, P_\pm^2 =

Truncating a Fourier series is an orthogonal projection, and letting the truncation grow gives a sequence of projections converging to the identity vector by vector but not in norm. The third example states this distinction, which is typical of infinite dimensions.

Example 101 (Fourier truncation) P_N = \sum_{|n| \leq N}|e_n\rangle\langle e_n| on L^2(-\pi, \pi) is the projection onto the trigonometric polynomials of degree \leq N (Example 71). Two operators may be applied in either order, and the difference between the two orders measures how far they are from commuting. The definition below names this difference and lists its algebraic rules; its importance is that commuting self-adjoint operators can be diagonalised simultaneously, while non-commuting ones cannot.


Definition 22 (Commutator) The commutator of two bounded operators is [A, B] = AB - BA, and A, B commute if [A, B] = 0. It is bilinear and antisymmetric, satisfies the Jacobi identity [A, [B, C]] + [B, [C, A]] + [C, [A, B]] = 0 and the Leibniz rule [A, BC] = [A, B]C + B[A, C], and [A, B]^\dagger = [B^\dagger, A^\dagger]; for self-adjoint A, B the commutator is anti-self-adjoint and i[A, B] is self-adjoint. In finite dimensions \operatorname{tr}[A, B] = 0. The anticommutator is \{A, B\} = AB + BA.

The ellipse in the figure is determined by the singular value decomposition of A: its axes point along the images of the eigenvectors of A^{\mathsf{T}}A. The first example reads the geometry of the left panel from the computation.

Example 105 (The ellipse of a matrix) A^{\mathsf{T}}A has eigenvectors v_\pm for the eigenvalues 3 \pm \sqrt5, and Av_\pm are orthogonal with lengths \sigma_\pm = \sqrt{3 \pm \sqrt5} \approx 2.288, 0.874: the unit circle is mapped to the ellipse with these semi-axes, and the area scales by \sigma_+\sigma_- = \sqrt{9 - 5} = 2 = |\det A|. A unitary maps the unit sphere onto itself, and in two real dimensions the only such maps are rotations and reflections. The second example contrasts this with a non-unitary matrix of norm 1, whose image of the circle touches the circle only at the stretched direction.

Example 106 (Circles onto circles) R_\theta maps the unit circle onto itself and \|R_\theta u\| = \|u\| for every u, since R_\theta^{\mathsf{T}}R_\theta = 1. The matrix \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/2\end{pmatrix} also has norm 1 but is not unitary: its ellipse has semi-axes 1 and \tfrac12 and meets the unit circle only at (\pm1, 0). The vanishing trace of a commutator is the obstruction to realising [x, p] = i with matrices, and it holds identically for general 3 \times 3 matrices with symbolic entries. The third example records the computation and its consequence for the operators of Section 1.8.

The spectrum of an operator is the set of numbers \lambda for which A - \lambda fails to be invertible; for a matrix these are the eigenvalues, and for operators on infinite-dimensional spaces the set may also contain a continuous part without eigenvectors. This section defines eigenvalues and the spectrum, proves the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, quotes it for compact self-adjoint operators, and builds the functional calculus that defines f(A), in particular the unitary e^{iA}; the figure shows the eigenvectors and the exponential of a symmetric matrix.
For more on this topic, see Scott (2023, Ch. 6).


A vector that an operator merely rescales is the simplest thing an operator can do, and the rescaling factor is the number attached to it. The definition below fixes the terms, including the multiplicity of an eigenvalue and the eigenspace, in a form that applies equally to matrices and to operators on function spaces.


Definition 23 (Eigenvalue of an operator) A number \lambda \in \mathbb{C} is an eigenvalue of an operator A if Au = \lambda u for some non-zero eigenvector u; the eigenspace \ker(A - \lambda) is the set of all such u together with 0, and its dimension is the multiplicity of \lambda. For a self-adjoint operator every eigenvalue is real and eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal; for a unitary operator every eigenvalue has modulus 1 (Exercise 117). An n \times n matrix has at least one and at most n eigenvalues, the roots of its characteristic polynomial \det(A - \lambda); an operator on an infinite-dimensional space may have none at all.

Multiplication by x on L^2(0, 1) is bounded and self-adjoint but has no eigenvalue whatsoever, since an eigenfunction would have to be concentrated at a single point. The third example proves this and introduces the approximate eigenvectors that replace eigenvectors in the next definition.

[0, 1] there are nonetheless approximate eigenvectors, f_n = \sqrt n\,\mathbf{1}_{[\lambda, \lambda + 1/n]} with \|f_n\| = 1 and \|(x - \lambda)f_n\|^2 = n\int_\lambda^{\lambda + 1/n}(x - \lambda)^2dx = 1/(3n^2) \to 0 (Example 112).

Definition 24 (Spectrum) The spectrum \sigma(A) of a bounded operator is the set of \lambda \in \mathbb{C} for which A - \lambda has no bounded inverse; its complement is the resolvent set, on which the resolvent R(\lambda) = (A -

A Hermitian matrix can be diagonalised by a unitary change of basis, and this is the single most used fact of linear algebra in quantum mechanics. The figure shows what it means geometrically for a symmetric 2 \times 2 matrix, and the theorem below states and proves it, with the decomposition into eigenprojections as the form that generalises.






Figure 14: Left: the symmetric matrix A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix} maps the unit circle to an ellipse whose axes lie along the orthonormal eigenvectors (1, 1)/\sqrt2 and (1, -1)/\sqrt2 and have lengths equal to the eigenvalues 3 and 1. Right: the eigenvalues 3 and 1 on the real line and the eigenvalues e^{3i} and e^{i} of the unitary e^{iA} on the unit circle; the dotted arcs trace e^{3it} and e^{it} for 0 \leq t \leq
1. Generated by figures/hermitian_spectrum.sage.





Theorem 12 (Spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices) A Hermitian n \times n matrix A has real eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n (with multiplicity) and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors e_1, \dots, e_n. Equivalently A = UDU^\dagger with U the unitary matrix whose columns are the e_k and D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_k), or A = \sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda with P_\lambda the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace of \lambda, where \sum_\lambda P_\lambda = 1 and P_\lambda P_\mu = 0 for \lambda \neq \mu (the spectral decomposition). Proof. By induction on n. The characteristic polynomial has a root \lambda_1 \in \mathbb{C}, real by Exercise 117, with a unit eigenvector e_1. The orthogonal complement K = e_1^\perp is invariant under A: for v \perp e_1, \langle e_1, Av\rangle = \langle Ae_1, v\rangle = \lambda_1\langle e_1, v\rangle = 0. The restriction of A to K is Hermitian on an (n - 1)-dimensional space, so by induction K has an orthonormal eigenbasis e_2, \dots,
e_n, and e_1, \dots, e_n is the required basis. The matrix forms follow by writing u = \sum_k\langle e_k,
u\rangle e_k and applying A. The same statement holds for normal matrices (AA^\dagger = A^\dagger A), in particular for unitary matrices, with complex eigenvalues (Exercise 124).

Two Hermitian matrices can be diagonalised in the same basis exactly when they commute, which is the mathematical content of “compatible observables”. The second exercise asks for the proof, through the invariance of eigenspaces.

Exercise 123 (Simultaneous diagonalisation) Show that Hermitian matrices A, B with [A, B] = 0 have a common orthonormal eigenbasis, and that conversely matrices with a common eigenbasis commute. Find a common eigenbasis of \sigma_3 and \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\
0 & 5\end{pmatrix}, and explain why \sigma_1 and \sigma_3 have none.







NoteSolution





If Au = \lambda u then A(Bu) = BAu = \lambda Bu, so B maps each eigenspace E_\lambda of A into itself; B restricted to E_\lambda is Hermitian and has an orthonormal eigenbasis by the theorem, and the union over \lambda of these bases is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of both A and B. Conversely, if A = UDU^\dagger and B = UD'U^\dagger then AB = UDD'U^\dagger = BA since diagonal matrices commute. \sigma_3 and \operatorname{diag}(1, 5) are both diagonal in the standard basis. [\sigma_1, \sigma_3] = -2i\sigma_2 \neq 0, so no common eigenbasis exists; indeed the eigenvectors (1, \pm1)/\sqrt2 of \sigma_1 are not eigenvectors of \sigma_3.



The theorem for normal matrices reduces to the Hermitian case by splitting A into commuting Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts. The last exercise asks for this reduction and applies it to unitaries.

A unitary is normal (U^\dagger U = 1 = UU^\dagger), so U = \sum_k\lambda_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k| with |\lambda_k| = 1, that is, \lambda_k = e^{i\theta_k}.









Operators on infinite-dimensional spaces that behave most like matrices are those that squeeze bounded sets into sets with compact closure (Definition 19 of Sets, relations and topology). The definition below introduces them, with the finite-rank operators and their norm limits as the examples that cover every case met in this chapter.


Definition 25 (Compact operator) A bounded operator A on H is compact if the image of the unit ball has compact closure, equivalently if every bounded sequence u_n has a subsequence along which Au_n converges in norm. Operators of finite rank (finite-dimensional range) are compact, norm limits of compact operators are compact, and on a Hilbert space every compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. An operator with \sum_k\|Ae_k\|^2 < \infty for an orthonormal basis (e_k) is Hilbert-Schmidt, and Hilbert-Schmidt operators are compact; an integral operator with kernel k \in L^2(X \times X) is Hilbert-Schmidt with \sum_k\|Ae_k\|^2 = \int\int|k(x, y)|^2dx\,dy. The identity on an infinite-dimensional space is not compact.

Compact self-adjoint operators are the operators for which the matrix spectral theorem survives word for word, with countably many eigenvalues tending to zero. The theorem below, quoted without proof, states this; the proof mimics the matrix case, using compactness to produce the first eigenvector as a maximiser of |\langle u,
Au\rangle|.


Theorem 13 (Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators) Let A be a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space H. Then H has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A; the non-zero eigenvalues are real, each of finite multiplicity, and form a finite set or a sequence \lambda_k \to 0; \|A\| = \max_k|\lambda_k| is attained; and A = \sum_k\lambda_k|e_k\rangle\langle
e_k| with convergence in operator norm. For an integral operator with Hermitian kernel k \in L^2(X \times X) the kernel itself expands as k(x, y) = \sum_k\lambda_ke_k(x)\overline{e_k(y)} in L^2(X \times X) (the Hilbert-Schmidt theorem). The theorem is quoted; the first eigenvalue is characterised in Exercise 129.

Example 122 (Discrete spectra from compact inverses) If an operator L (such as -d^2/dx^2 with Dirichlet conditions, or -\Delta on a compact surface restricted to functions of mean zero) has a compact self-adjoint inverse G, then Ge_k = \mu_ke_k with \mu_k \to 0 gives Le_k = \mu_k^{-1}e_k: L has an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues \lambda_k = 1/\mu_k \to \infty, each of finite multiplicity. This is how the Sturm-Liouville theorem (Theorem 2 of Differential equations, Exercise 130) and the discreteness of the Laplacian’s spectrum on compact spaces (Theorem 18) are proved.

Once an operator is diagonal, any function can be applied to it by applying the function to the diagonal. The definition below turns this into the functional calculus, whose most important instance is the unitary e^{itA} generated by a self-adjoint A, and quotes Stone’s theorem, which says that all one-parameter unitary groups arise this way.


Definition 26 (Functional calculus) For a self-adjoint operator with spectral decomposition A = \sum_k\lambda_kP_k (a Hermitian matrix or a compact self-adjoint operator) and a function f on the spectrum, f(A) = \sum_kf(\lambda_k)P_k. This functional calculus agrees with the algebraic definition for polynomials, satisfies (fg)(A) = f(A)g(A), f(A)^\dagger =
\bar f(A), \|f(A)\| = \max_k|f(\lambda_k)|, and \sigma(f(A)) = f(\sigma(A)) (the spectral mapping theorem); for a multiplication operator, f(M_g) = M_{f \circ g}. In particular e^{itA} is unitary for real t with e^{itA}e^{isA} = e^{i(t + s)A}, and \sqrt A = \sum\sqrt{\lambda_k}P_k is the positive square root of a positive A. For a general bounded self-adjoint operator the same calculus exists with the sum replaced by an integral over the spectrum (the general spectral theorem, quoted); Stone’s theorem (quoted) states that every strongly continuous family of unitaries with U(t)U(s) = U(t + s) is U(t) = e^{itA} for a unique self-adjoint, possibly unbounded, A.

A symmetric operator has D(A) \subseteq D(A^\dagger) and is self-adjoint only when its domain is large enough. Eigenvectors are required to lie in the domain, and the spectrum is defined as in Definition 24. For self-adjoint A the spectrum is real, the spectral theorem and the functional calculus extend (quoted), and e^{itA} is a unitary group on all of H.

The example introduces the Sobolev space on which that version lives.

Example 150 (-i\,d/dx on L^2(\mathbb{R})) p = -i\,d/dx with domain C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}) (smooth, zero outside a bounded set) is symmetric by integration by parts, the boundary terms vanishing at infinity, and unbounded (Exercise 97). It is not self-adjoint on this domain: D(p^\dagger) is the much larger Sobolev space H^1(\mathbb{R}) =
\{f \in L^2 : f' \in L^2\} with f' in the sense of distributions (Distributions). Extending p to H^1(\mathbb{R}) makes it self-adjoint, with spectrum \mathbb{R} and no eigenvalues (Exercise 162).

Multiplication by x on L^2(\mathbb{R}) is unbounded because the line is infinite, and its natural domain is the set of functions for which xf is still square-integrable. The second example checks membership for a Gaussian and for a slowly decaying function, and notes that this operator is self-adjoint without further ado.

Example 151 (The position operator on L^2(\mathbb{R})) (xf)(x) = xf(x) with the maximal domain D(x) = \{f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) : xf \in L^2(\mathbb{R})\} is self-adjoint (Exercise 160), unbounded, with spectrum \mathbb{R} and no eigenvalues (Example 110 with (0, 1) replaced by \mathbb{R}). The Gaussian e^{-x^2/2} is in the domain; f = 1/(1 + |x|) is in L^2 but not in D(x), since |xf|^2 \to 1 at infinity is not integrable. In the Fourier picture (The Fourier transform), x becomes i\,d/dk and p becomes multiplication by k.

The second derivative on periodic functions is the Laplacian of the circle, and its domain question is settled by the Fourier isomorphism, under which it becomes multiplication by n^2 on sequences. The third example describes this, which is the pattern for all Laplacians on compact spaces.

Example 152 (-d^2/dx^2 on the circle) On L^2(S^1) = L^2(-\pi, \pi) with periodic functions, -d^2/dx^2 on smooth periodic functions is symmetric and positive, since \langle f, -g''\rangle = \int\bar f'g'\,dx after one integration by parts without boundary terms. Under U : f \mapsto (\langle e_n, f\rangle)_n of Exercise 106 it becomes the multiplication operator (a_n) \mapsto (n^2a_n) on \ell^2(\mathbb{Z}), self-adjoint on the domain \{a : \sum n^4|a_n|^2 <
\infty\}, which pulls back to the periodic Sobolev space H^2(S^1) (Exercise 158). Its spectrum is \{n^2\}, discrete, with the eigenfunctions e^{inx} as an orthonormal basis.

An everywhere-defined symmetric operator is automatically bounded, which is why unbounded symmetric operators must have restricted domains; and a symmetric operator always sits inside its adjoint. The second exercise asks for the second statement and for the proof that a bounded symmetric operator is self-adjoint.

Exercise 159 (Symmetric operators and their adjoints) Show that for a symmetric operator D(A) \subseteq D(A^\dagger) with A^\dagger = A on D(A), and that a bounded symmetric operator defined on all of H is self-adjoint. Explain, using Example 95, why -i\,d/dx on smooth periodic functions is symmetric but has a strictly larger adjoint domain.







NoteSolution





For v \in D(A) the functional u \mapsto \langle v, Au\rangle = \langle Av, u\rangle is bounded by \|Av\|\|u\|, so v \in D(A^\dagger) and A^\dagger v = Av by uniqueness in the Riesz theorem. If A is bounded on H, then D(A^\dagger) = H = D(A), since every u \mapsto \langle v, Au\rangle is bounded, and A^\dagger = A there. For -i\,d/dx on smooth periodic functions, any v \in H^1(S^1) (for example a continuous piecewise linear periodic function) makes u \mapsto \langle v, -iu'\rangle = \langle -iv', u\rangle bounded, so v \in
D(A^\dagger) without being smooth; the self-adjoint version is the extension to H^1(S^1).



The position operator with its maximal domain is self-adjoint, and the proof is a direct computation of the adjoint’s domain. The last exercise asks for it, which is the simplest instance of showing D(A^\dagger) = D(A).

Exercise 160 (Self-adjointness of the position operator) Let x act on D(x) = \{f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) : xf \in L^2(\mathbb{R})\}. Show that x is symmetric and that D(x^\dagger) = D(x), so that x is self-adjoint.







NoteSolution





Symmetry: \langle xf, g\rangle = \int\overline{xf}g = \int\bar f(xg) = \langle f, xg\rangle since x is real. If v \in D(x^\dagger), there is w = x^\dagger v \in L^2 with \int\bar v\,xu = \int\bar w\,u for all u \in
D(x); taking u supported in a bounded set (where D(x) contains all of L^2) gives xv = w on every bounded set, hence xv = w \in L^2 and v \in D(x). Together with D(x) \subseteq D(x^\dagger) (Exercise 159) this gives equality of domains, and x^\dagger = x.









Position and momentum on the line are the pair of unbounded self-adjoint operators whose commutator is the identity, the relation that Example 104 showed to be impossible for matrices. The definition below fixes the operators, their common domain and the relation, with \hbar = 1.


Definition 30 (Canonical commutation relation) On the Schwartz space \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}) \subset L^2(\mathbb{R}) of smooth functions decaying, with all their derivatives, faster than any power, the position operator (xf)(x) = xf(x) and the momentum operator (pf)(x) = -if'(x) (units with \hbar = 1) are symmetric, map \mathcal{S} into itself, and satisfy the canonical commutation relation [x, p] = i on \mathcal{S}: (xp - px)f = -ixf' + i(xf)' = if. Both extend to self-adjoint operators on L^2(\mathbb{R}) with spectrum \mathbb{R} and no eigenvalues, and the Fourier transform \mathcal{F} exchanges them, \mathcal{F}p\mathcal{F}^{-1} is multiplication by k. For a unit vector \psi, \langle x\rangle = \langle\psi, x\psi\rangle is the expectation value and (\Delta x)^2 = \langle (x -
\langle x\rangle)^2\rangle the variance, and the relation implies the uncertainty inequality \Delta x\,
\Delta p \geq \tfrac12 (Exercise 239).
