The relation itself is a one-line computation with the product rule, valid for every differentiable function. The first example records it and the related commutators with functions of x.

Example 153 ([x, p\rbrack f = if) For f \in \mathcal{S}: (px)f = -i(xf)' = -if - ixf' and (xp)f = -ixf', so [x, p]f = -ixf' + if + ixf' =
if (Proposition 4). More generally [g(x), p] = ig'(x) for smooth g, by the same product rule, and [x, p^2] = 2ip by the Leibniz rule of Definition 22; these are the identities behind Ehrenfest’s theorem in quantum mechanics.

Gaussians are the states for which the uncertainty inequality is an equality, and the variances are computed by two integrals. The second example computes them for a Gaussian of width s, showing that narrow position means wide momentum.

Example 154 (Gaussian wave packets) For \psi_s(x) = (2\pi s^2)^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/4s^2}, a unit vector with \langle x\rangle = \langle p\rangle = 0: (\Delta x)^2 = \int x^2|\psi_s|^2dx = s^2 and (\Delta p)^2 = \int|\psi_s'|^2dx = 1/(4s^2), so \Delta x\,
\Delta p = \tfrac12 exactly (Proposition 4): Gaussians saturate the uncertainty inequality, and shrinking s trades position spread for momentum spread. The Fourier transform of \psi_s is a Gaussian of width 1/(2s) in k (The Fourier transform), which is the same statement.

The combinations a = (x + ip)/\sqrt2 and a^\dagger = (x - ip)/\sqrt2 turn the canonical commutation relation into [a, a^\dagger] = 1, and they generate the eigenfunctions of x^2 + p^2 from the Gaussian. The third example introduces them; the full theory is in The harmonic oscillator.

Example 155 (Ladder operators) a = (x + ip)/\sqrt2 and a^\dagger = (x - ip)/\sqrt2 satisfy [a, a^\dagger] = \tfrac12[x + ip, x - ip] =
\tfrac12(-i[x, p] + i[p, x]) = -i\cdot i = 1, and \tfrac12(x^2 + p^2) = a^\dagger a + \tfrac12. The Gaussian \psi_0 = \pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2} satisfies a\psi_0 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(x\psi_0 + \psi_0') = 0, and \psi_n \propto
(a^\dagger)^n\psi_0 are eigenfunctions of \tfrac12(x^2 + p^2) with eigenvalues n + \tfrac12 (Exercise 161): the Hermite functions, an orthonormal basis of L^2(\mathbb{R}) (Boundary value and Sturm-Liouville problems). The truncated matrices of Exercise 115 are these operators in the basis \psi_n, cut off at n = N - 1.

The Fourier transform turns p into multiplication by k, which identifies its spectrum, and the plane waves are approximate eigenvectors made square-integrable by a Gaussian envelope. The second exercise asks for both.

Exercise 162 (The spectrum of the momentum operator) Using \widehat{f'}(k) = ik\hat f(k) (The Fourier transform), show that \mathcal{F}p\mathcal{F}^{-1} is multiplication by k on L^2(\mathbb{R}, dk), so \sigma(p) = \mathbb{R} with no eigenvalues. Then show directly that \psi_L(x) = e^{ikx}e^{-x^2/2L^2} satisfies \|(p - k)\psi_L\|/\|\psi_L\| = 1/(L\sqrt2), so k is an approximate eigenvalue.







NoteSolution





\widehat{pf} = -i\cdot ik\hat f = k\hat f, so under the unitary \mathcal{F} the operator p becomes M_k, whose spectrum is the range \mathbb{R} of k and which has no eigenvalues (Example 112); the “eigenfunctions” e^{ikx} are not in L^2 (Example 76). Directly, (p - k)\psi_L = -i\psi_L' - k\psi_L =
(ix/L^2)\psi_L, so \|(p - k)\psi_L\|^2 = L^{-4}\int x^2e^{-x^2/L^2}dx = L^{-4}\cdot\tfrac{L^3\sqrt\pi}{2} and \|\psi_L\|^2 = L\sqrt\pi, whose ratio is 1/(2L^2); the ratio of norms is 1/(L\sqrt2) \to 0 as L \to
\infty.

A symmetric operator on a small domain can often be enlarged to a self-adjoint operator in several ways, each with its own spectrum; for differential operators on an interval these ways are boundary conditions. The definition below introduces the notion and quotes von Neumann’s criterion for existence and uniqueness.


Definition 31 (Self-adjoint extension) A self-adjoint extension of a symmetric operator A is a self-adjoint operator B with D(B) \supseteq D(A) and B = A on D(A). A symmetric operator may have none, exactly one or infinitely many; it is essentially self-adjoint if its closure is self-adjoint, equivalently if the extension is unique. Von Neumann’s criterion (quoted): with the deficiency indices n_\pm = \dim\ker(A^\dagger \mp i), self-adjoint extensions exist iff n_+ = n_-, the extension is unique iff n_+ = n_- = 0, and for n_+ = n_- = n > 0 the extensions are parametrised by the unitary group U(n). For a differential operator on an interval the extensions are the self-adjoint boundary conditions, and different conditions give different spectra.

The momentum operator on a bounded interval has a circle’s worth of self-adjoint extensions, one for each phase relating the values at the two ends. The first example describes them with their eigenfunctions, and the periodic one is the operator of Example 95.

Example 156 (Twisted periodic conditions) -i\,d/dx on C_c^\infty(0, 2\pi) has n_+ = n_- = 1: \ker(A^\dagger \mp i) is spanned by e^{\pm x}. Its self-adjoint extensions are indexed by \alpha \in [0, 2\pi), with domain \{f \in H^1(0, 2\pi) : f(2\pi) =
e^{i\alpha}f(0)\}; the boundary term -i[\bar fg]_0^{2\pi} vanishes on it (Exercise 166). The eigenfunctions are e^{i(n + \alpha/2\pi)x} with eigenvalues n + \alpha/2\pi, n \in \mathbb{Z} (Exercise 164): the spectrum is the integers shifted by \alpha/2\pi, and \alpha = 0 is the periodic case.

On a half-line the two deficiency indices differ, so the momentum operator has no self-adjoint extension at all, while the position operator is unproblematic. The second example records this, the standard illustration that not every symmetric operator is an observable.

Example 157 (No momentum on the half-line) -i\,d/dx on C_c^\infty(0, \infty) \subset L^2(0, \infty) is symmetric, and \ker(A^\dagger - i) is spanned by e^{-x} (square-integrable) while \ker(A^\dagger + i) would be spanned by e^{x}, which is not: n_+ = 1, n_-
= 0, and no self-adjoint extension exists. The position operator on L^2(0, \infty), by contrast, is self-adjoint on its maximal domain exactly as in Exercise 160; and -d^2/dx^2 on the half-line has a one-parameter family of extensions, the conditions f'(0) = \kappa f(0).

The Laplacian on an interval has a four-parameter family of extensions, and the familiar boundary conditions are special members whose spectra differ already in the lowest eigenvalue. The third example lists Dirichlet, Neumann and periodic conditions with their spectra.

Example 158 (Boundary conditions for -d^2/dx^2 on (0, \pi)) -d^2/dx^2 on C_c^\infty(0, \pi) has n_+ = n_- = 2 (\ker(A^\dagger \mp i) is spanned by e^{\pm\sqrt{\mp
i}\,x}, two solutions each), so the extensions form a four-parameter family. Dirichlet f(0) = f(\pi) = 0: eigenfunctions \sin nx, eigenvalues n^2, n \geq 1. Neumann f'(0) = f'(\pi) = 0: \cos nx, eigenvalues n^2, n \geq 0, including 0. Periodic f(0) = f(\pi), f'(0) = f'(\pi): e^{2inx}, eigenvalues 4n^2 with multiplicity 2 for n \neq 0. The same symbol -d^2/dx^2 thus names three different self-adjoint operators (Exercise 165, Boundary value and Sturm-Liouville problems).

Dirichlet, Neumann and Robin conditions all make -d^2/dx^2 symmetric, and the proof is to check that the boundary terms of the two integrations by parts cancel. The second exercise asks for this and for the eigenvalues under Robin conditions in a special case.

Exercise 165 (Symmetric boundary conditions) Show that -d^2/dx^2 is symmetric on smooth functions on [0, \pi] satisfying Dirichlet, Neumann or Robin conditions f'(0) = \kappa f(0), f'(\pi) = -\kappa f(\pi) with real \kappa, and that for Dirichlet conditions the eigenvalues are exactly n^2, n \geq 1.







NoteSolution





Two integrations by parts give \langle -f'', g\rangle - \langle f, -g''\rangle = [-\bar f'g + \bar fg']_0^\pi. Under Dirichlet conditions both f, g vanish at the ends; under Neumann both derivatives vanish; under Robin conditions -\bar f'g + \bar fg' = -\kappa\bar fg + \kappa\bar fg = 0 at 0 and similarly at \pi (real \kappa is essential). For Dirichlet eigenfunctions, -f'' = \lambda f has solutions A\sin\sqrt\lambda x +
B\cos\sqrt\lambda x; f(0) = 0 forces B = 0 and f(\pi) = 0 forces \sin\sqrt\lambda\pi = 0, so \lambda =

The three examples share a feature that holds on every compact space: the eigenvalues form a sequence tending to infinity with finite multiplicities, and the eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis. The theorem below, quoted without proof, states this; the mechanism is that the inverse of -\Delta is a compact operator, so that Theorem 13 applies as in Example 122.


Theorem 18 (Discrete spectrum of the Laplacian on a compact manifold) Let M be a compact connected Riemannian manifold without boundary. The operator -\Delta, extended from smooth functions to its natural domain in L^2(M), is self-adjoint and non-negative, and its spectrum is discrete: the eigenvalues form a sequence 0 = \lambda_0 < \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots \to \infty, each of finite multiplicity, with \lambda_0 = 0 belonging to the constants. The eigenfunctions \varphi_k can be chosen to form an orthonormal basis of L^2(M), so that every f \in L^2(M) has the mode expansion f = \sum_k\langle
\varphi_k, f\rangle\varphi_k, and Weyl’s law gives the growth: the number N(\lambda) of eigenvalues \leq \lambda satisfies N(\lambda) \sim \frac{\operatorname{Vol}(M)}{(4\pi)^{d/2}\Gamma(d/2 + 1)}\lambda^{d/2} for d = \dim M. The theorem is quoted; its proof applies Theorem 13 to the Green’s operator of -\Delta on the complement of the constants, which is compact by Rellich’s theorem.

Example 162 (Weyl’s law on the circle) For S^1_R, N(\lambda) = \#\{n \in \mathbb{Z} : n^2 \leq R^2\lambda\} = 2\lfloor R\sqrt\lambda\rfloor + 1 \sim
2R\sqrt\lambda. Weyl’s law with d = 1, \operatorname{Vol} = 2\pi R, \Gamma(3/2) = \sqrt\pi/2 gives \frac{2\pi R}{\sqrt{4\pi}\cdot\sqrt\pi/2}\lambda^{1/2} = 2R\sqrt\lambda, in agreement. The mode expansion is the Fourier series, and the finite multiplicities are the pairs \pm n.

On the sphere the eigenvalues l(l + 1) have multiplicities 2l + 1, so counting them is a sum of odd numbers, a perfect square. The second example verifies Weyl’s law for the sphere and records the mode expansion in spherical harmonics.

Example 163 (Weyl’s law on the sphere) For the unit sphere, N(\lambda) = \sum_{l(l + 1) \leq \lambda}(2l + 1) = (L + 1)^2 with L the largest l allowed, and L(L + 1) \leq \lambda gives (L + 1)^2 \sim \lambda. Weyl’s law with d = 2, \operatorname{Vol} =
4\pi, \Gamma(2) = 1 gives \frac{4\pi}{4\pi}\lambda = \lambda. The mode expansion f(\theta, \varphi) =
\sum_{l, m}\langle Y_{lm}, f\rangle Y_{lm} is the expansion in spherical harmonics of Harmonic analysis on the sphere and on compact groups, and on the torus it is the double Fourier series (Exercise 170).

The practical content of the theorem is that a function of time and of a point on a compact space can be expanded in the modes, turning a partial differential equation into countably many ordinary ones with discrete frequencies. The third example carries this out for the wave equation on \mathbb{R} \times M.

Example 164 (Fields on a compact space decompose into modes) Let \phi(t, y) on \mathbb{R} \times M satisfy the wave equation \partial_t^2\phi = \Delta_M\phi (Partial differential equations). Expanding \phi(t, \cdot) = \sum_kc_k(t)\varphi_k in the eigenbasis gives \ddot c_k = -\lambda_kc_k, so c_k(t) = a_ke^{i\sqrt{\lambda_k}t} + b_ke^{-i\sqrt{\lambda_k}t}: the field is a sum of independent oscillators with the discrete frequencies \omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k}, one for each eigenfunction (counted with multiplicity). On the circle \omega_n = |n|/R, on the sphere \omega_l = \sqrt{l(l + 1)}/R; the zero mode k =
0 has \ddot c_0 = 0. Compactness of M is what makes the frequencies discrete, and the heat equation separates the same way with c_k(t) = c_k(0)e^{-\lambda_kt} (Exercise 172).

The three bar charts of the figure are three growth patterns for the same kind of spectrum: quadratic eigenvalues with constant multiplicity, quadratic eigenvalues with linearly growing multiplicity, and all sums of two squares with arithmetic multiplicities. The first example reads them against Weyl’s law.

Example 165 (Reading the spectra) On the circle the eigenvalues n^2 thin out (N(\lambda) \sim 2\sqrt\lambda) but each has multiplicity 2; on the sphere l(l + 1) also thins out, but the multiplicity 2l + 1 grows so that N(\lambda) \sim \lambda; on the torus every sum of two squares occurs, with N(\lambda) \sim \pi\lambda. In two dimensions N(\lambda) grows linearly in both cases, with slope \operatorname{Vol}/4\pi: 1 for the unit sphere, \pi for the square torus of area 4\pi^2, exactly as Weyl’s law predicts.

All eigenvalues scale as 1/R^2 with the size of the space, so a small compact space has a large gap between the zero mode and the first excited mode. The second example records this scaling and the gaps, which is the quantitative form of “compactness makes frequencies discrete”.

Example 166 (Scaling with the radius) Since \Delta_R = R^{-2}\Delta_1, the spectrum of -\Delta on S^1_R is \{n^2/R^2\}, on S^2_R it is \{l(l + 1)/R^2\} and on the torus \{m^2/R_1^2 + n^2/R_2^2\} (Exercise 173): the spectral gap \lambda_1 is 1/R^2, 2/R^2 and \min(R_1, R_2)^{-2} respectively, and the frequencies \omega_k =
\sqrt{\lambda_k} of Example 164 scale as 1/R. The zero mode is the only one that survives as R \to 0 at fixed frequency, while all others become arbitrarily stiff.

The multiplicities on the circle and the sphere are the dimensions of the irreducible representations of their isometry groups, because the Laplacian commutes with isometries and so acts on each irreducible piece by a scalar. The third example states this connection to Representations and Schur’s lemma and contrasts the torus.

Example 167 (Multiplicities as dimensions of representations) The isometries of S^2 form SO(3) and commute with \Delta, so each eigenspace is a representation of SO(3); the eigenspace of l(l + 1) is the irreducible spin-l representation of dimension 2l + 1 (Weights and the representations of su(2), Harmonic analysis on the sphere and on compact groups). On the circle the isometry group SO(2) has one-dimensional irreducibles e^{\pm
in\theta}, and the multiplicity 2 comes from the reflection \theta \mapsto -\theta pairing n with -n. On the torus the group U(1)^2 is abelian, all irreducibles are one-dimensional, and the multiplicities r_2(N) are accidental coincidences of eigenvalues rather than dimensions of irreducibles.

Exercise 194 (Heat flow smooths) For t > 0 let e^{t\Delta} act on L^2(T^1) by c_k \mapsto e^{-tk^2}c_k. Show \|e^{t\Delta}\|_{L^2 \to H^s} = \sup_k(1 +
k^2)^{s/2}e^{-tk^2}, bound it by e^t(s/(2et))^{s/2} for t \leq s/2, and conclude that e^{t\Delta}f is smooth.







NoteSolution





The operator is diagonal from the L^2 to the H^s coordinates with entries (1 + k^2)^{s/2}e^{-tk^2}, so its norm is their supremum. With y = 1 + k^2, y^{s/2}e^{-t(y - 1)} \leq e^ty^{s/2}e^{-ty}, maximal at y = s/(2t), giving e^t(s/(2et))^{s/2} (the maximiser y = s/(2t) is admissible because t \leq s/2). Every H^s norm being finite, e^{t\Delta}f is C^\infty by Theorem 19.
Sage compares the supremum over k with the bound for a few values of s and t:

    bound = exp(t) * (s / (2 * e * t))^(s / 2) if t <= s / 2 else None
    print("s = %2d, t = %.2f: norm %.4f, bound %s" % (s, t, RDF(sup), "%.4f" % RDF(bound) if bound else "(t > s/2)"))

Rellich’s theorem in one dimension can be proved with Arzelà-Ascoli, since H^1 functions are uniformly Hölder. The second integrative exercise does so, with values in C(T^1) rather than L^2.

Exercise 195 (Rellich by Arzelà-Ascoli) Use Example 175 and Exercise 181 to show that the unit ball of H^1(T^1) is bounded and equicontinuous in C(T^1), and conclude that H^1(T^1) \to C(T^1) is compact.







NoteSolution





\|f\|_\infty \leq 0.71\|f\|_{H^1} \leq 0.71 and |f(x) - f(y)| \leq |x - y|^{1/2} on the unit ball, so the ball is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous; by Arzelà-Ascoli its image has compact closure in C(T^1). This is stronger than compactness into L^2, since \|f\|_2 \leq \sqrt{2\pi}\|f\|_\infty.

Weak solutions of Poisson’s equation exist by the Riesz representation theorem in a Sobolev space. The third integrative exercise carries this out on the circle.

Exercise 196 (Weak solutions by Riesz) On \dot H^1 = \{u \in H^1(T^1) : \int u = 0\} use the inner product (u, v) = \int\bar u'v'. Show that it is equivalent to the H^1 inner product (by Exercise 192), and that for f \in L^2 with \int f = 0 there is a unique u \in \dot H^1 with (\varphi,
u) = \int\bar\varphi f for all \varphi \in \dot H^1. Show that u solves -u'' = f and lies in H^2.







NoteSolution

The trace of a matrix is the sum of its eigenvalues, and for an operator on an infinite-dimensional space the sum may or may not converge; when it does for e^{-t(-\Delta)}, the resulting function of t encodes the spectrum of the Laplacian and, through its small-t behaviour, the geometry of the space. This section defines trace-class operators and determinants, the heat kernel and heat trace, quotes the small-t asymptotics, and introduces zeta regularisation with the Casimir energy as its application in outline; the figure shows the heat trace of the circle against its leading asymptotics.
For more on this topic, see Buchbinder and Shapiro (2021, sec. 13.4).


Summing the diagonal entries of an infinite matrix may give a different answer in a different basis, or no answer at all, unless the entries decay fast enough. The definition below isolates the operators for which the trace is well defined and basis independent, with the eigenvalue sum as the formula that matters.


Definition 36 (Trace class) For a positive operator A \geq 0 the trace \operatorname{tr}A = \sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle \in [0,
\infty] is independent of the orthonormal basis (e_k) (Exercise 198). A bounded operator A is  trace class** if \|A\|_1 = \operatorname{tr}|A| < \infty with |A| = \sqrt{A^\dagger A}; then \operatorname{tr}A = \sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle converges absolutely, is basis independent, and satisfies |\operatorname{tr}A| \leq \|A\|_1 and \operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA) for bounded B. Trace-class operators are Hilbert-Schmidt, hence compact; a compact self-adjoint operator is trace class iff \sum_k|\lambda_k| < \infty, and then \operatorname{tr}A = \sum_k\lambda_k. An integral operator on a compact space with a continuous kernel that is trace class has \operatorname{tr}K = \int k(x, x)\,dx.

NoteExamples





For matrices the trace is the sum of the diagonal entries and of the eigenvalues, and its cyclic property is the reason it is basis independent. The first example records these facts and the trace of a projection.

Example 187 (Traces of matrices) For an n \times n matrix, \operatorname{tr}A = \sum_jA_{jj} = \sum_k\lambda_k (from A = UDU^\dagger and \operatorname{tr}(UDU^\dagger) = \operatorname{tr}(DU^\dagger U) = \operatorname{tr}D), and \operatorname{tr}
(AB) = \sum_{jk}A_{jk}B_{kj} = \operatorname{tr}(BA). The trace of an orthogonal projection is the dimension of its range (eigenvalues 1 and 0), \operatorname{tr}\sigma_a = 0, and \operatorname{tr}e^{iA} = \sum
e^{i\lambda_k} as in Example 128 (Exercise 197).

A diagonal operator is trace class exactly when its diagonal is absolutely summable, and the Green’s operator of Example 119 is an example whose trace can be computed in two ways. The second example compares the eigenvalue sum with the integral of the kernel along the diagonal.

Example 188 (Diagonal operators and the Green’s operator) De_n = \lambda_ne_n is trace class iff \sum|\lambda_n| < \infty: \lambda_n = 1/n^2 gives \operatorname{tr}D = \pi^2/6, while \lambda_n = 1/n is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class (the harmonic series diverges, Series). The Green’s operator G with kernel g(x, y) = \min(x, y) - xy has eigenvalues 1/(n\pi)^2 and \operatorname{tr}G = \sum_n1/(n\pi)^2 = 1/6, which equals \int_0^1g(x, x)\,dx = \int_0^1(x -
x^2)\,dx = 1/6 (Exercise 197): the trace formula for kernels.

The heat operator on the circle is trace class for every positive time, with a trace given by a rapidly convergent series, but at time zero it degenerates to the identity. The third example introduces this trace, the main object of the rest of the section.

Example 189 (The heat operator on the circle) e^{t\Delta} on L^2(S^1) has eigenvalues e^{-tn^2} on e^{in\theta} (Definition 26 extended to the unbounded \Delta), and \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}e^{-tn^2} < \infty for t > 0: the operator is trace class with \operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} = \sum_ne^{-tn^2} = 1 + 2e^{-t} + 2e^{-4t} + \dots, the heat trace. At t = 0 the operator is the identity, not trace class, and the trace diverges as t \to 0 like \sqrt{\pi/t} (Theorem 22, Figure 21).

Basis independence of the trace of a positive operator is proved by inserting a second orthonormal basis and exchanging the order of two non-negative sums. The second exercise asks for this proof through the square root of A.

Exercise 198 (Basis independence of the trace) For A \geq 0 with square root \sqrt A, show that \sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle = \sum_k\|\sqrt Ae_k\|^2 =
\sum_j\|\sqrt Af_j\|^2 for any two orthonormal bases (e_k), (f_j), and deduce that \operatorname{tr}A is basis independent and that \operatorname{tr}(U^\dagger AU) = \operatorname{tr}A for unitary U.







NoteSolution





\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle = \langle\sqrt Ae_k, \sqrt Ae_k\rangle = \|\sqrt Ae_k\|^2. By Parseval in the basis (f_j), \|\sqrt Ae_k\|^2 = \sum_j|\langle f_j, \sqrt Ae_k\rangle|^2 = \sum_j|\langle\sqrt Af_j, e_k\rangle|^2 (self-adjointness of \sqrt A), and summing over k and exchanging the sums of non-negative terms gives \sum_j\|\sqrt Af_j\|^2 by Parseval in the basis (e_k). Hence the trace is basis independent; U^\dagger AU has the diagonal entries \langle Ue_k, AUe_k\rangle, which is the trace of A in the orthonormal basis (Ue_k).



Trace class is strictly stronger than Hilbert-Schmidt, and absolute convergence of the diagonal sum is what makes the trace well defined. The last exercise asks for the inclusion and for the absolute convergence through the polar decomposition.

Exercise 199 (Trace class versus Hilbert-Schmidt) Show that a compact self-adjoint operator with \sum|\lambda_k| < \infty has \sum\lambda_k^2 < \infty, that the diagonal operator with \lambda_n = 1/n is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, and that for trace-class A =
U|A| (polar decomposition) the series \sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle converges absolutely with |\operatorname{tr}A| \leq \operatorname{tr}|A|.







NoteSolution





\sum\lambda_k^2 \leq (\max|\lambda_k|)\sum|\lambda_k| < \infty. For \lambda_n = 1/n, \sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6 but \sum 1/n = \infty. With A = U|A|, \langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle = \langle|A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k, |A|^{1/2}
e_k\rangle, so |\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle| \leq \||A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k\|\,\||A|^{1/2}e_k\| and by Cauchy-Schwarz over k, \sum_k|\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle| \leq (\sum_k\||A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k\|^2)^{1/2}
(\sum_k\||A|^{1/2}e_k\|^2)^{1/2} \leq \operatorname{tr}|A|, using \sum_k\||A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k\|^2 =
\operatorname{tr}(U|A|U^\dagger) \leq \operatorname{tr}|A| (the trace of U|A|U^\dagger equals that of |A| when U is unitary, and is bounded by it for a partial isometry).









The determinant of a matrix is the product of its eigenvalues, and for an operator of the form 1 + A with A trace class the infinite product converges. The definition below introduces this Fredholm determinant and the formula \det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A} that ties it to the trace.


Definition 37 (Fredholm determinant) For a trace-class operator A with eigenvalues \lambda_k (with multiplicity), the Fredholm determinant is \det(1 + A) = \prod_k(1 + \lambda_k), absolutely convergent because \sum|\lambda_k| < \infty (Exercise 201). It satisfies \det((1 + A)(1 + B)) = \det(1 + A)\det(1 + B), \det(1 + A) \neq 0 iff 1 + A is invertible, \det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}, and for \|A\| < 1 the expansion \log\det(1 + zA)
= \sum_{m \geq 1}\frac{(-1)^{m + 1}}{m}z^m\operatorname{tr}(A^m), so that \operatorname{tr}A is the derivative of \det(1 + zA) at z = 0. For a compact self-adjoint A of trace class, z \mapsto \det(1 - zA) = \prod_k(1 -
z\lambda_k) is an entire function whose zeros are the reciprocals of the eigenvalues.

NoteExamples





For a matrix the Fredholm determinant is the ordinary one, and the identity \det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A} follows from triangularisation. The first example records it on an explicit matrix and gives the expansion of the determinant in traces.

Example 190 (Determinants of matrices) For A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}, \det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A} = e^5 although e^A itself has transcendental entries (Exercise 200); in general e^A = Ue^TU^{-1} with T upper triangular gives \det e^A = \prod e^{T_{kk}} = e^{\sum T_{kk}}. For 2 \times 2 matrices \det(1 + zA) = 1 +
z\operatorname{tr}A + z^2\det A, and the series \log\det(1 + zA) = z\operatorname{tr}A - \tfrac{z^2}{2}
\operatorname{tr}A^2 + \dots reproduces \det A = \tfrac12((\operatorname{tr}A)^2 - \operatorname{tr}A^2).

The Fredholm determinant of the Green’s operator is Euler’s product for the sine, and its zeros are the eigenvalues of the Dirichlet Laplacian. The second example states this identity, the model for the determinants of differential operators defined by zeta regularisation below.

Example 191 (The sine as a Fredholm determinant) For the Green’s operator G with eigenvalues 1/(n\pi)^2 (Example 119), \det(1 - zG) =
\prod_{n \geq 1}\left(1 - \frac{z}{n^2\pi^2}\right) = \frac{\sin\sqrt z}{\sqrt z}, Euler’s product for the sine (Analytic continuation and special functions), an entire function of z with zeros at z = n^2\pi^2, the eigenvalues of -d^2/dx^2 with Dirichlet conditions on (0, 1). The coefficient of z is -\operatorname{tr}G = -1/6, which is the Taylor coefficient of \sin\sqrt z/\sqrt z = 1 - z/6 + z^2/120 - \dots (Exercise 202).

The determinant of -\Delta itself cannot be a Fredholm determinant, since the eigenvalues grow; the way out is to define it through the derivative of the spectral zeta function, as in Definition 39. The third example previews this by rewriting \log\det as a trace of a logarithm.

Example 192 (\log\det = \operatorname{tr}\log) For a positive matrix, \log\det A = \sum_k\log\lambda_k = \operatorname{tr}\log A, and formally \sum_k\log
\lambda_k = -\frac{d}{ds}\sum_k\lambda_k^{-s}\big|_{s = 0}. For -\Delta on a compact space the sum \sum\log
\lambda_k diverges, but \zeta_\Delta(s) = \sum\lambda_k^{-s} converges for large \operatorname{Re}s and continues analytically to s = 0, which is how \det{}_\zeta(-\Delta) = e^{-\zeta_\Delta'(0)} is defined; for the Dirichlet operator on (0, \pi) this gives \det{}_\zeta = 2\pi (Example 200).

An infinite product \prod(1 + \lambda_k) converges absolutely exactly when \sum|\lambda_k| does, which is why the Fredholm determinant needs trace class and not merely Hilbert-Schmidt. The second exercise asks for this and for the regularised determinant that works for Hilbert-Schmidt operators.

Exercise 201 (Convergence of the product) Show that for \lambda_k \to 0 the product \prod_k(1 + \lambda_k) converges absolutely (that is, \sum|\log(1 +

NoteSolution





For |\lambda| \leq \tfrac12, \tfrac12|\lambda| \leq |\log(1 + \lambda)| \leq \tfrac32|\lambda|, so the two series converge or diverge together. \prod_{n \leq N}(1 + 1/n) = \prod_{n \leq N}\tfrac{n + 1}{n} = N + 1 \to

The functional calculus applied to the Laplacian with the function e^{-t\lambda} gives the solution operator of the heat equation, and this operator has a kernel built from the eigenfunctions. The definition below introduces the heat kernel and the heat trace, which the figure plots for the circle.






Figure 21: Left: the heat trace Z(t) = \operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}e^{-tn^2} of the unit circle against its small-t asymptotics \sqrt{\pi/t} and its large-t limit 1 (the zero mode). Right: the difference Z(t) - \sqrt{\pi/t} on a logarithmic scale against the first correction 2\sqrt{\pi/t}\,e^{-\pi^2/t} from the Poisson summation formula; the asymptotics is exponentially accurate. Definition 38 (Heat kernel) Let -\Delta on a compact manifold M have the orthonormal eigenbasis \varphi_k with eigenvalues \lambda_k (Theorem 18). The heat operator e^{t\Delta} = \sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k}|\varphi_k\rangle
\langle\varphi_k|, t > 0, solves the heat equation: u(t) = e^{t\Delta}f satisfies \partial_tu = \Delta u, u(0) = f (Definition 21 of Differential equations). It is the integral operator with the heat kernel K_t(x, y) =
\sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k}\varphi_k(x)\overline{\varphi_k(y)}, a smooth function for t > 0 with K_t(x, \cdot) \to
\delta_x as t \to 0 and the semigroup property \int_MK_t(x, z)K_s(z, y)\,dz = K_{t + s}(x, y). The heat trace is Z(t) = \operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} = \sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k} = \int_MK_t(x, x)\,dx, finite for every t > 0 by Weyl’s law, so e^{t\Delta} is trace class.

NoteExamples





On the real line, which is not compact, the heat kernel is the Gaussian and the heat operator is not trace class, since the integral of the kernel along the diagonal diverges. The first example records this, the continuous spectrum showing up as an infinite trace.

Example 193 (The line: the Gaussian kernel) On L^2(\mathbb{R}), K_t(x, y) = (4\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-(x - y)^2/4t} solves \partial_tK = \partial_x^2K with K_t \to \delta (Partial differential equations), and e^{t\partial_x^2} is multiplication by e^{-tk^2} in the Fourier picture, with continuous spectrum (0, 1]. It is not trace class: K_t(x, x) = (4\pi t)^{-1/2} is constant and \int_{\mathbb{R}}
K_t(x, x)\,dx = \infty. Compactness of the space is what makes the heat trace finite.

On the circle the heat kernel is a Fourier series, and the Poisson summation formula rewrites it as a sum over images of the Gaussian kernel of the line. The second example gives both forms, which produce the two regimes of the figure.

Example 194 (The circle: Fourier and image sums) On S^1 with \varphi_n = e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi}, K_t(\theta, \theta') = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n \in
\mathbb{Z}}e^{-tn^2}e^{in(\theta - \theta')}, and by the Poisson summation formula (Exercise 205) K_t(\theta, \theta') = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}(4\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-(\theta - \theta' - 2\pi k)^2/4t}: the kernel of the line summed over the images \theta' + 2\pi k. The heat trace is Z(t) = \sum_ne^{-tn^2} = \sqrt{\pi/t}\sum_k

As t \to 0 the heat kernel concentrates near the diagonal and only sees the local geometry, so the heat trace has an expansion in powers of t whose coefficients are integrals of curvature invariants. The theorem below, quoted, states the first two coefficients; they determine the dimension, the volume and the total scalar curvature of the space.


Theorem 22 (Heat trace asymptotics) On a compact Riemannian manifold M of dimension d without boundary, the heat trace of -\Delta has the asymptotic expansion Z(t) = \operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} \sim (4\pi t)^{-d/2}\left(a_0 + a_1t + a_2t^2 +

For flat M all a_k with k \geq 1 vanish and the corrections are exponentially small. Weyl’s law of Theorem 18 follows from the leading term by a Tauberian argument (Exercise 207).

Sums over the spectrum such as \sum_k\lambda_k or \sum_k\log\lambda_k diverge, but the function \sum_k
\lambda_k^{-s} converges for large s and continues analytically to the values of s at which the divergent sums would sit. The definition below assigns values to such sums in this way and connects the procedure to the heat trace.


Definition 39 (Zeta regularisation) For an operator with discrete spectrum 0 < \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots (zero modes excluded) satisfying Weyl’s law in dimension d, the spectral zeta function \zeta_A(s) = \sum_k\lambda_k^{-s} converges for \operatorname{Re}s > d/2 and extends to a meromorphic function of s, regular at s = 0 and at the negative integers, through the Mellin transform \zeta_A(s) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(s)}\int_0^\infty t^{s - 1}(Z(t) - \dim\ker
A)\,dt and the heat trace asymptotics (Exercise 210). The zeta-regularised sum of the eigenvalues is \sum_k\lambda_k := \zeta_A(-1), and the zeta-regularised determinant is \det{}_\zeta A := e^{-\zeta_A'(0)}, formalising \sum\log\lambda_k = -\zeta_A'(0). For \lambda_k = k the spectral zeta function is Riemann’s \zeta(s) (Definition 20 of Complex analysis), and \zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}, \zeta(0) = -\tfrac12, \zeta(-3) =
\tfrac{1}{120}, \zeta'(0) = -\tfrac12\log 2\pi.

The regularised value of 1 + 2 + 3 + \dots is -1/12, and a cutoff shows what this means: the divergence is a pure power of the cutoff and the finite remainder is -1/12. The first example makes this comparison, which is the form in which the value is used in physics.

Example 199 (1 + 2 + 3 + \dots = -1/12) \zeta(-1) = -1/12 is the analytic continuation of \sum n^{-s} to s = -1 (Sage returns it exactly from Bernoulli numbers, \zeta(-n) = -B_{n + 1}/(n + 1), Exercise 217). With an exponential cutoff, \sum_{n \geq
1}ne^{-\varepsilon n} = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)^2} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2} - \frac{1}{12} +
\frac{\varepsilon^2}{240} + \dots (Proposition 6): the divergent part 1/\varepsilon^2 depends on the cutoff and the finite part is -1/12. Likewise \sum_{n \geq 1}e^{-\varepsilon n} = \frac1\varepsilon - \frac12 +
\dots has finite part \zeta(0) = -\tfrac12 (Exercise 211).

The Dirichlet Laplacian on an interval has spectral zeta function \zeta(2s), and its regularised determinant is a pure number. The second example computes it, the simplest determinant of a differential operator.

Example 200 (The determinant of -d^2/dx^2 on (0, \pi)) With Dirichlet conditions the eigenvalues are n^2 (Example 158), so \zeta_A(s) = \sum n^{-2s} =

\zeta(2s), and \det{}_\zeta = e^{-2\log(L/\pi)\zeta(0) - 2\zeta'(0)} = (L/\pi)\cdot 2\pi = 2L: the determinant scales with the length, as \zeta_A(0) = \zeta(0) = -\tfrac12 dictates.

On the circle the zero mode is removed and each non-zero eigenvalue is doubled; the regularised sums of even powers vanish and the determinant is 4\pi^2. The third example records these values and the regularised sum of |n|, which is the Casimir energy of the circle.

Example 201 (The circle) For -\Delta on the unit circle with the zero mode removed, \zeta_\Delta(s) = \sum_{n \neq 0}(n^2)^{-s} =
2\zeta(2s). Then \det{}_\zeta(-\Delta') = e^{-4\zeta'(0)} = (2\pi)^2 = 4\pi^2; the regularised sum of the eigenvalues is 2\zeta(-2) = 0, as \zeta vanishes at the negative even integers; and for the frequencies \omega_n = |n| = \sqrt{\lambda_n}, \sum_{n \neq 0}|n| = 2\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac16, the value that enters the Casimir energy of a periodic field (Exercise 241).

A quantised field confined to a finite region has a zero-point energy \tfrac12\sum\omega_k over its modes, which diverges; zeta regularisation extracts a finite part that depends on the size of the region and produces a measurable force. The proposition below states the result for an interval and quotes it for parallel plates, as an outline of how the regularised sums of this section enter physics.


Proposition 5 (Casimir energy) For a massless scalar field on an interval of length L with Dirichlet conditions at both ends, the modes have frequencies \omega_n = n\pi/L (Example 158, \omega_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n} as in Example 164), and the zero-point energy E = \tfrac12\sum_n\omega_n has the zeta-regularised value E(L) = \frac{\pi}{2L}\zeta(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{24L} (units \hbar = c = 1), giving the attractive Casimir force F = -\frac{dE}{dL} = -\frac{\pi}{24L^2} between the ends. With a cutoff, E_\varepsilon = \frac{L}{2\pi
\varepsilon^2} - \frac{\pi}{24L} + O(\varepsilon^2): the divergent part is proportional to L, a bulk energy density independent of the boundaries, and only the finite part gives an L-dependent force. For the electromagnetic field between parallel conducting plates at separation a the same method gives E/A = -
\frac{\pi^2\hbar c}{720a^3} and F/A = -\frac{\pi^2\hbar c}{240a^4} (Casimir, quoted; Exercise 214). The statement is an outline: the field quantisation that produces \tfrac12\sum\omega_n is the subject of Quantum field theory.

The functional equation of the theta function converts large-t information into small-t information and vice versa, and it fixes the asymptotics in both directions. The second exercise asks for these consequences and for the modular reading of the identity.

Exercise 216 (Two regimes from one identity) From \theta(t) = \sqrt{\pi/t}\,\theta(\pi^2/t) and the definition of \theta, derive \theta(t) \to 1 as t \to

NoteSolution





From the definition, \theta(t) = 1 + 2\sum_{n \geq 1}e^{-tn^2} \to 1 as t \to \infty, the terms decaying exponentially. Applying the identity, \theta(t) = \sqrt{\pi/t}(1 + 2e^{-\pi^2/t} + 2e^{-4\pi^2/t} + \dots), so \theta(t) - \sqrt{\pi/t} = 2\sqrt{\pi/t}e^{-\pi^2/t}(1 + e^{-3\pi^2/t} + \dots). Multiplying the identity by t^{1/4}: t^{1/4}\theta(t) = \pi^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\theta(\pi^2/t) = (\pi^2/t)^{1/4}\theta(\pi^2/t), invariant. For small t the series \sum e^{-tn^2} converges slowly (about 1/\sqrt t terms matter), while the dual series needs one term: the identity exchanges the two regimes, which is the content of modular invariance.

Bounded operators can be added, multiplied and normed, and many of their properties depend only on these operations. A Banach algebra abstracts them; a C*-algebra adds the adjoint and the identity \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 that holds for operators on a Hilbert space. This part defines both, proves that every element of a Banach algebra has a non-empty compact spectrum whose radius is \lim\|a^n\|^{1/n}, and constructs the continuous functional calculus of self-adjoint elements, which is how functions of observables are defined in quantum mechanics. The outline follows Arcozzi (2025, sec. 6.1) and Landsman (1998, secs. 2.1–2.5 and 2.8), with numerical examples from Izaac and Wang (2018, Ch. 7).
For more on this topic, see Dereziński and Gérard (2022, Ch. 4-6) and Tornetta (2022, Ch. 1).

The circle has appeared in every section: the exponentials are an orthonormal basis, multiplication by e^{ix} is a unitary shift, the Laplacian has spectrum n^2, the heat trace is a theta function and the spectral zeta function is 2\zeta(2s). The last exercise assembles these into one computation ending with the Casimir energy of a periodic field.

Exercise 241 (The circle from orthonormal basis to Casimir energy) On L^2(S^1) with e_n = e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}: (a) check orthonormality and Parseval for f(x) = x on (-\pi,
\pi) in Sage, recovering \zeta(2); (b) verify -\Delta e_n = n^2e_n and compute the heat trace by Poisson summation at t = 0.1; (c) write \zeta_\Delta(s) = 2\zeta(2s) for the non-zero modes and compute \det{}_\zeta(-\Delta') = 4\pi^2, \sum_{n \neq 0}n^2 = 2\zeta(-2) = 0 and \sum_{n \neq 0}|n| = 2\zeta(-1) = -
\tfrac16; (d) deduce that a massless field on a circle of circumference L, with \omega_n = 2\pi|n|/L, has the regularised zero-point energy E = -\pi/(6L).







NoteSolution






is Example 79; (b) is Example 159 and Example 194; (c) \zeta_\Delta(s) = \sum_{n \neq 0} |
n|^{-2s} = 2\zeta(2s), \zeta_\Delta'(0) = 4\zeta'(0) = -2\log 2\pi, so \det{}_\zeta = (2\pi)^2, and the regularised sums follow from \zeta(-2) = 0, \zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}; (d) E = \tfrac12\sum_{n \neq 0}
\omega_n = \frac{\pi}{L}\sum_{n \neq 0}|n| = \frac{\pi}{L}\cdot 2\zeta(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{6L}, the periodic Casimir energy of Example 203, with force -\pi/(6L^2):


x = var("x", domain="real")
e = lambda n: exp(I * n * x) / sqrt(2 * pi)
print("Gram matrix of e_{-1}, e_0, e_1:", matrix(SR, 3, 3, lambda j, k: integrate(conjugate(e(j - 1)) * e(k - 1), x, -pi, pi)).list())
n = var("n", domain="integer")
print("Parseval for x: ||x||^2 / (4 pi) =", integrate(x ** 2, x, -pi, pi) / (4 * pi), "= zeta(2) =", zeta(2))
print("-e_n'' = n^2 e_n for n = -3..3:", all(bool(-diff(e(k), x, 2) == k ** 2 * e(k)) for k in range(-3, 4)))
RF = RealField(80); t = RF(1) / 10
print("heat trace at t = 0.1: %.15f  Poisson: %.15f" % (sum(exp(-t * k ** 2) for k in range(-60, 61)), sqrt(RF(pi) / t) * sum(exp(-RF(pi) ** 2 * k ** 2 / t) for k in range(-5, 6))))
s = var("s")
zD = 2 * zeta(2 * s)
print("det_zeta(-Delta') = exp(-zeta_Delta'(0)) =", exp(-diff(zD, s).subs(s=0)).n(digits=15), "; 4 pi^2 =", (4 * pi ** 2).n(digits=15))
print("regularised sum n^2 = 2 zeta(-2) =", 2 * zeta(-2), "; sum |n| = 2 zeta(-1) =", 2 * zeta(-1))
L = var("L", domain="positive")
print("Casimir energy E = (pi/L) 2 zeta(-1) =", pi / L * 2 * zeta(-1))
Output:
Gram matrix of e_{-1}, e_0, e_1: [1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1]
Parseval for x: ||x||^2 / (4 pi) = 1/6*pi^2 = zeta(2) = 1/6*pi^2
-e_n'' = n^2 e_n for n = -3..3: True
heat trace at t = 0.1: 5.604991216397929  Poisson: 5.604991216397929
det_zeta(-Delta') = exp(-zeta_Delta'(0)) = 39.4784176043574 ; 4 pi^2 = 39.4784176043574
regularised sum n^2 = 2 zeta(-2) = 0 ; sum |n| = 2 zeta(-1) = -1/6
Casimir energy E = (pi/L) 2 zeta(-1) = -1/6*pi/L

title: Functional analysis
text:
A norm measures the size of a vector and turns a vector space into a metric space in which limits, series and continuity make sense. This part defines norms and complete normed spaces, introduces the three families of spaces that the rest of the chapter works in, the sequence spaces \ell^p, the function spaces L^p and the continuous functions C(K), and then studies the linear maps between normed spaces and the dual space of continuous linear functionals. The line of argument follows the lecture notes of Arcozzi (2025, Ch. 1 and 3), with the Hilbert-space special cases of Rainer Picard and Waurick (2020, App. B) as examples.
For more on this topic, see Cheung (2024, sec. 4.2).


On \mathbb{R}^n the Euclidean length is one way among many to measure a vector: the largest coordinate or the sum of the absolute values of the coordinates serve as well. The figure draws the unit balls of several such measures in the plane, and the definition below names the three properties that all of them share.






Figure 1: Unit balls \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \|x\|_p \leq 1\} of the norms \|x\|_p = (|x_1|^p + |x_2|^p)^{1/p} for p =
1, \tfrac32, 2, 4 and \|x\|_\infty = \max(|x_1|, |x_2|). Each ball is convex and symmetric under x \mapsto -x; the balls grow with p, and only the disc p = 2 comes from an inner product. Generated by figures/fa2-unit-balls.sage.





Definition 1 (Norm) A norm on a real or complex vector space X (Definition 1 of Linear algebra) is a map \|\cdot\| : X \to [0, \infty) that is definite, \|x\| = 0 only for x = 0, homogeneous, \|\lambda x\| = |\lambda|\,\|x\| for scalars \lambda, and satisfies the triangle inequality \|x + y\| \leq \|x\| + \|y\|. The pair (X, \|\cdot\|) is a normed space; it is a metric space with the distance d(x, y) = \|x - y\|, so that a sequence converges to x when \|x_n - x\| \to 0. Two norms \|\cdot\|_a, \|\cdot\|_b on X are equivalent if c\|x\|_a \leq
\|x\|_b \leq C\|x\|_a for constants 0 < c \leq C and all x; equivalent norms have the same convergent sequences.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The first examples live in \mathbb{R}^n, where every coordinate gives a way of measuring. The three norms below are the ones drawn in the figure for n = 2, and the example compares them with explicit constants.

Example 1 (Three norms on \mathbb{R}^n) \|x\|_1 = \sum_k|x_k|, \|x\|_2 = (\sum_k|x_k|^2)^{1/2} and \|x\|_\infty = \max_k|x_k| are norms on \mathbb{R}^n and \mathbb{C}^n. For x = (3, -4) they give 7, 5 and 4. They are equivalent: \|x\|_\infty
\leq \|x\|_2 \leq \|x\|_1 \leq n\|x\|_\infty, and the constants are attained, the first two by x = (1, 0, \dots,
0) and the last by x = (1, 1, \dots, 1).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



On a space of functions the same three ideas give the supremum norm and the integral norms. The second example shows that on the continuous functions they are no longer equivalent, because a function can be large on a small set.

Example 2 (Supremum and integral norms) On the continuous functions on [0, 1], \|f\|_\infty = \max_x|f(x)| and \|f\|_1 = \int_0^1|f(x)|\,dx are norms Arcozzi (2025, sec. 1.1.1). For f_n(x) = x^n one finds \|f_n\|_\infty = 1 and \|f_n\|_1 = 1/(n + 1) \to 0, so f_n \to 0 in \|\cdot\|_1 but not in \|\cdot\|_\infty, and no inequality \|f\|_\infty \leq C\|f\|_1 can hold. The inequality \|f\|_1 \leq \|f\|_\infty does hold, so the supremum norm is the stronger of the two.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



Inner products are the source of the most important norms, and the parallelogram law tells which norms come from one. The third example states the criterion and applies it to the norms of the figure.

Example 3 (Norms from inner products) An inner product (Definition 12) gives the norm \|u\| = \langle u, u\rangle^{1/2}; the triangle inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz, which Rainer Picard and Waurick (2020, Lemma B.1.5) derives from the non-negativity of the Gram determinant \langle u, u\rangle\langle v, v\rangle - |\langle u, v\rangle|^2. Such a norm satisfies the parallelogram law \|u + v\|^2 + \|u - v\|^2 = 2\|u\|^2 + 2\|v\|^2, and conversely a norm satisfying it comes from an inner product Rainer Picard and Waurick (2020, Lemma B.1.7 and the remark after it). For u = (1, 0), v = (0, 1) the law reads 2\cdot 2^{2/p} = 4 in \|\cdot\|_p, true only for p = 2.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.












NoteExercises





The checks that a proposed norm is one are short, but the triangle inequality is the delicate part, as the first exercise shows by an example where it fails. The exercise also shows why the exponents p < 1 are excluded from the family drawn in the figure.

Exercise 1 (When the triangle inequality fails) Show that \|\cdot\|_1 and \|\cdot\|_\infty are norms on \mathbb{C}^n. Then show that N(x) = (\sqrt{|x_1|} +
\sqrt{|x_2|})^2 on \mathbb{R}^2 is definite and homogeneous but violates the triangle inequality, by evaluating it on (1, 0), (0, 1) and their sum.







NoteSolution





Definiteness and homogeneity are clear, and |x_k + y_k| \leq |x_k| + |y_k| summed (or maximised) over k gives the triangle inequality for \|\cdot\|_1 (or \|\cdot\|_\infty). For N: N(\lambda x) = (\sqrt{|\lambda|}
(\sqrt{|x_1|} + \sqrt{|x_2|}))^2 = |\lambda|N(x), and N(x) = 0 forces x = 0. But N(1, 0) = N(0, 1) = 1 while N(1, 1) = 4 > 2. The unit “ball” \{N \leq 1\} is the region inside the astroid-like curve \sqrt{|x_1|} +
\sqrt{|x_2|} = 1, which is not convex; a norm always has a convex unit ball.
A check of the three norms with Sage, including the triangle inequality of the two genuine norms on random complex vectors:

N = lambda x: (sqrt(abs(x[0])) + sqrt(abs(x[1])))^2
print("N(1,0) =", N((1, 0)), " N(0,1) =", N((0, 1)), " N(1,1) =", N((1, 1)), " > N(1,0) + N(0,1):", N((1, 1)) > 2)
print("homogeneity N(-3 x) = 3 N(x) at x = (2, 5):", bool(N((-6, -15)) == 3 * N((2, 5))))
set_random_seed(1)
vs = [vector(CC, [CC.random_element() for _ in range(4)]) for _ in range(200)]
print("triangle inequality for the 1-norm and the sup-norm on 100 random pairs in C^4:",
      all(((u + v).norm(1) <= u.norm(1) + v.norm(1) + 1e-12) and ((u + v).norm(Infinity) <= u.norm(Infinity) + v.norm(Infinity) + 1e-12) for u, v in zip(vs[::2], vs[1::2])))
print("midpoint of (1,0) and (0,1) has N =", N((1 / 2, 1 / 2)), "> 1: the set N <= 1 is not convex")
Output:
N(1,0) = 1  N(0,1) = 1  N(1,1) = 4  > N(1,0) + N(0,1): True
homogeneity N(-3 x) = 3 N(x) at x = (2, 5): True
triangle inequality for the 1-norm and the sup-norm on 100 random pairs in C^4: True
midpoint of (1,0) and (0,1) has N = 2 > 1: the set N <= 1 is not convex










TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



The parallelogram law is a computable test, and the second exercise applies it numerically to the whole family \|\cdot\|_p on \mathbb{R}^2. Its result is that the Euclidean norm is the only member of the family with an inner product behind it.

Exercise 2 (The parallelogram law for \|\cdot\|_p) Compute D(p) = \|u + v\|_p^2 + \|u - v\|_p^2 - 2\|u\|_p^2 - 2\|v\|_p^2 for u = (1, 0), v = (0, 1) and for u = (1, 1), v = (1, -1), as a function of p \geq 1, and find where it vanishes. What is D for \|\cdot\|_\infty?







NoteSolution





For the first pair D(p) = 2\cdot 4^{1/p} - 4, which vanishes only at p = 2 and is positive for p < 2; for the second pair the roles are exchanged, D(p) = 8 - 4\cdot 4^{1/p}, negative for p < 2. For \|\cdot\|_\infty the first pair gives D = -2. So no \|\cdot\|_p with p \neq 2 satisfies the law, and by the converse of Example 3 none of them comes from an inner product.
Sage computes D(p) symbolically for both pairs and finds the zeros:

p = var('p'); assume(p >= 1)
nrm = lambda x, p: (sum(abs(t)^p for t in x))^(1 / p)
def D(u, v):
    w1 = [a + b for a, b in zip(u, v)]; w2 = [a - b for a, b in zip(u, v)]
    return (nrm(w1, p)^2 + nrm(w2, p)^2 - 2 * nrm(u, p)^2 - 2 * nrm(v, p)^2).simplify_full()
D1 = D((1, 0), (0, 1)); D2 = D((1, 1), (1, -1))
print("u = (1,0), v = (0,1): D(p) =", D1, " zero at", solve(D1 == 0, p))
print("u = (1,1), v = (1,-1): D(p) =", D2, " zero at", solve(D2 == 0, p))
print("D at p = 1, 2, 3, 10:", [(D1.subs(p=q), D2.subs(p=q)) for q in (1, 2, 3, 10)])
sup = lambda x: max(abs(t) for t in x)
print("sup norm, first pair:", sup((1, 1))^2 + sup((1, -1))^2 - 2 * sup((1, 0))^2 - 2 * sup((0, 1))^2)
Output:
u = (1,0), v = (0,1): D(p) = 2^(2/p + 1) - 4  zero at [
p == 2
]
u = (1,1), v = (1,-1): D(p) = -2^(2/p + 2) + 8  zero at [
p == 2
]
D at p = 1, 2, 3, 10: [(4, -8), (0, 0), (2*2^(2/3) - 4, -4*2^(2/3) + 8), (2*2^(1/5) - 4, -4*2^(1/5) + 8)]
sup norm, first pair: -2










TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



A norm gives a translation-invariant, homogeneous distance, and the third exercise shows the converse, following an exercise of Arcozzi (2025). It explains why normed spaces are exactly the metric vector spaces whose metric respects the linear structure.

Exercise 3 (Metrics that come from norms) Let d be a metric on a vector space X with d(x + a, y + a) = d(x, y) and d(\lambda x, \lambda y) =
|\lambda|d(x, y). Show that \|x\| = d(x, 0) is a norm and that d(x, y) = \|x - y\| Arcozzi (2025, Exercise 1.1). Give a translation-invariant metric on \mathbb{R} that does not come from a norm.







NoteSolution





Translation invariance gives d(x, y) = d(x - y, 0) = \|x - y\|. Definiteness is that of d; homogeneity is d(\lambda x, 0) = d(\lambda x, \lambda 0) = |\lambda|d(x, 0); and \|x + y\| = d(x + y, 0) \leq d(x + y, y) + d(y,
0) = d(x, 0) + d(y, 0). The metric d(x, y) = \min(|x - y|, 1) is translation invariant but not homogeneous: d(2,
0) = 1 \neq 2d(1, 0) = 2.









TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.






In finite dimensions all norms measure convergence in the same way, which is why \mathbb{R}^n has one topology. The theorem below states this; its proof uses the compactness of the unit sphere of \|\cdot\|_1, and it fails in every infinite-dimensional space, as Example 2 already showed on C[0, 1].


Theorem 1 (Equivalence of norms in finite dimension) On a finite-dimensional vector space any two norms are equivalent. Consequently every finite-dimensional normed space is complete, every linear subspace of finite dimension of a normed space is closed, and a set in a finite-dimensional normed space is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. On every infinite-dimensional normed space there are norms that are not equivalent to the given one.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The best constants between the norms of \mathbb{R}^n grow with the dimension, which is the first sign of the infinite-dimensional failure. The first example records the constants between \|\cdot\|_1 and \|\cdot\|_2.

Example 4 (Constants that grow with the dimension) On \mathbb{R}^n, \|x\|_2 \leq \|x\|_1 \leq \sqrt n\,\|x\|_2: the second inequality is Cauchy-Schwarz applied to (|x_1|, \dots, |x_n|) and (1, \dots, 1), with equality at x = (1, \dots, 1). The constant \sqrt n is finite for each n, as the theorem says, but unbounded in n; on the finitely supported sequences, the union of all the \mathbb{R}^n, the two norms are therefore not equivalent.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



Polynomials of a fixed degree form a finite-dimensional space of functions, so the supremum and integral norms of Example 2 become equivalent on it. The second example finds how the constant depends on the degree.

Example 5 (Polynomials of bounded degree) On the polynomials of degree at most n on [0, 1], the theorem gives \|p\|_\infty \leq C_n\|p\|_1. The polynomial p(x) = (1 - x)^n has \|p\|_\infty = 1 and \|p\|_1 = 1/(n + 1), so C_n \geq n + 1: the norms are equivalent in each degree, but no single constant works for all polynomials, in agreement with the failure on C[0,
1].







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



An infinite-dimensional space has a norm inequivalent to any given one, and on the sequences the construction is explicit. The third example gives it for the finitely supported sequences.

Example 6 (Inequivalent norms on sequences) On the space c_{00} of finitely supported sequences, \|a\|_\infty and \|a\|_w = \sum_n|a_n| are norms with \|a\|_\infty \leq \|a\|_w, but a^{(N)} = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots) (N ones) has \|a^{(N)}\|_w = N\|a^{(N)}\|_
\infty. The sequence a^{(N)}/N tends to 0 in \|\cdot\|_\infty and has norm 1 in \|\cdot\|_w for every N.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.












NoteExercises





The first exercise asks for the proof of the theorem. The argument is the standard one and shows exactly where finite dimension enters, namely in the compactness of a sphere.

Exercise 4 (Proof of the equivalence theorem) Let \|\cdot\| be any norm on \mathbb{R}^n. Show that \|x\| \leq M\|x\|_1 with M = \max_k\|e_k\|, deduce that \|\cdot\| is continuous for \|\cdot\|_1, and use the compactness of \{\|x\|_1 = 1\} to find m > 0 with \|x\| \geq m\|x\|_1. Conclude that any two norms on \mathbb{R}^n are equivalent.







NoteSolution





\|x\| = \|\sum_kx_ke_k\| \leq \sum_k|x_k|\,\|e_k\| \leq M\|x\|_1, and |\|x\| - \|y\|| \leq \|x - y\| \leq M\|x -
y\|_1 makes \|\cdot\| continuous. On the compact set S = \{\|x\|_1 = 1\} (closed and bounded in \mathbb{R}^n) it attains a minimum m, and m > 0 because 0 \notin S. By homogeneity \|x\| \geq m\|x\|_1 for all x. Two norms are each equivalent to \|\cdot\|_1, hence to each other.









TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



The constants between the p-norms can be computed exactly, and the extremal vectors are the simplest ones. The second exercise finds the best constants between \|\cdot\|_p and \|\cdot\|_q.

Exercise 5 (Best constants between p-norms) For 1 \leq p < q \leq \infty show \|x\|_q \leq \|x\|_p \leq n^{1/p - 1/q}\|x\|_q on \mathbb{R}^n, with both constants attained. Evaluate the constant n^{1/p - 1/q} for n = 3 with p = 1, q = 2 and with p = 2, q =
\infty, and check it on (1, 1, 1).







NoteSolution





If \|x\|_p = 1 then |x_k| \leq 1, so |x_k|^q \leq |x_k|^p and \|x\|_q \leq 1; homogeneity gives the first inequality, with equality at e_1. The second is Hölder’s inequality (Theorem 3) with exponents q/p and its conjugate applied to \sum_k|x_k|^p\cdot 1, with equality at (1, \dots, 1). For n = 3 both constants are 3^{1/2}: \|(1, 1, 1)\|_1 = 3 = \sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3 = \sqrt3\,\|(1, 1, 1)\|_2 and \|(1, 1, 1)\|_2 = \sqrt3 =
\sqrt3\,\|(1, 1, 1)\|_\infty.
Sage evaluates the constants and tests both inequalities on random vectors:

n = 3
for p, q in [(1, 2), (2, oo)]:
    c = n^(1 / p - (0 if q == oo else 1 / q))
    x = vector([1, 1, 1])
    print("p = %s, q = %s: constant %s; |x|_p = %s, c |x|_q = %s" % (p, q, c, x.norm(p), c * x.norm(q if q != oo else Infinity)))
set_random_seed(2)
ok = True
for _ in range(500):
    x = vector(RDF, [RDF.random_element(-1, 1) for _ in range(n)])
    for p, q in [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (1.5, 2.5)]:
        ok = ok and x.norm(q) <= x.norm(p) + 1e-12 and x.norm(p) <= n^(1 / p - 1 / q) * x.norm(q) + 1e-12
print("both inequalities on 500 random vectors and four pairs (p, q):", ok)
Output:
p = 1, q = 2: constant sqrt(3); |x|_p = 3, c |x|_q = 3
p = 2, q = +Infinity: constant sqrt(3); |x|_p = sqrt(3), c |x|_q = sqrt(3)
both inequalities on 500 random vectors and four pairs (p, q): True










TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



Since a finite-dimensional subspace is complete, it is closed, and this fact has a quick but instructive proof. The third exercise asks for it and for a counterexample when the dimension is infinite.

Exercise 6 (Finite-dimensional subspaces are closed) Use the theorem to show that a finite-dimensional subspace F of a normed space X is complete, hence closed in X. Then show that the polynomials are a subspace of (C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty) that is not closed.







NoteSolution





Choose a basis of F; the norm of X restricted to F is equivalent to the coordinate norm \|\cdot\|_1, in which a Cauchy sequence has Cauchy coordinates, which converge in \mathbb{R} or \mathbb{C}. So F is complete, and a complete subset of a metric space is closed. The Taylor polynomials of e^x converge uniformly on [0, 1] to e^x, which is not a polynomial (all its derivatives are e^x \neq 0), so the polynomials are not closed; by Theorem 4 their closure is all of C[0, 1].









TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.









A normed space can have Cauchy sequences without limits, just as the rationals do. The figure shows such a sequence among the continuous functions with the integral norm: the ramps converge in the norm towards a jump, which is not a continuous function, and the definition below names the spaces in which this cannot happen.






Figure 2: Left: the continuous ramps f_n, equal to 0 on [0, \tfrac12 - \tfrac1n], to 1 on [\tfrac12, 1] and linear in between, for n = 2, 4, 8, 16. They form a Cauchy sequence in \|f\|_1 = \int_0^1|f| since \|f_m - f_n\|_1 \leq
\tfrac1{2\min(m, n)}, and converge in this norm to the step function, which is not continuous. Right: the distances \|f_n - f_{2n}\|_1 and \|f_n - f_{2n}\|_\infty; the second stays at \tfrac12, so in the supremum norm the sequence is not Cauchy. Generated by figures/fa2-incomplete-ramps.sage.





Definition 2 (Banach space) A sequence (x_n) in a normed space is a Cauchy sequence if \|x_n - x_m\| \to 0 as m, n \to \infty (Definition 3 of Real analysis). A normed space is complete, or a Banach space, if every Cauchy sequence in it converges to an element of the space. Every normed space X has a completion: a Banach space \tilde X with a linear isometry i : X \to \tilde X whose range is dense, unique up to a unique linear isometry, built from the classes of Cauchy sequences of X that are at distance zero from each other Arcozzi (2025, Thm. 1.1 and Prop. 1.1).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





Every finite-dimensional normed space is a Banach space, and the argument is the coordinate argument of Michele Cini and Rotondi (2023, sec. 2.8). The first example records it.

Example 7 (Finite dimensions) In \mathbb{C}^n with \|\cdot\|_2, a Cauchy sequence x^{(m)} has |x^{(m)}_k - x^{(l)}_k| \leq \|x^{(m)} -
x^{(l)}\|_2, so each coordinate is a Cauchy sequence of complex numbers with a limit x_k, and \|x^{(m)} - x\|_2^2
= \sum_k|x^{(m)}_k - x_k|^2 \to 0 as a finite sum of null sequences Michele Cini and Rotondi (2023, sec. 2.8). By Theorem 1 the same holds for any norm on a finite-dimensional space.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



The bounded sequences with the supremum norm are a Banach space by a uniform version of the same argument. The second example gives it, together with the closed subspaces of convergent and null sequences that recur in the duality theory.

Example 8 (Bounded and null sequences) \ell^\infty = \{a : \sup_n|a_n| < \infty\} with \|a\|_\infty = \sup_n|a_n| is a Banach space: a Cauchy sequence a^{(m)} converges coordinatewise to some a, and letting l \to \infty in |a^{(m)}_n - a^{(l)}_n| \leq
\varepsilon gives \|a^{(m)} - a\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon for large m. The convergent sequences c and the null sequences c_0 = \{a : a_n \to 0\} are closed subspaces, hence Banach spaces too.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.



The continuous functions with the integral norm are the standard incomplete space, and the third example works out the sequence of the figure. Its completion is the space L^1 of the next section.

Example 9 (The ramps of the figure) For the ramps f_n of the figure and m > n, f_m - f_n vanishes outside [\tfrac12 - \tfrac1n, \tfrac12] and has modulus at most 1 there, so \|f_m - f_n\|_1 \leq \tfrac1n: the sequence is Cauchy in \|\cdot\|_1. If it had a continuous limit f, then f = 0 on [0, \tfrac12) and f = 1 on [\tfrac12, 1], which is impossible. So (C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1) is not a Banach space.
