Equations without closed-form solutions, such as the pendulum of Example 6, are solved by stepping forward in small time steps \tau. For the oscillator each step is a linear map of the phase plane, a two-by-two matrix, and the eigenvalue criteria of this section decide whether the computed motion stays bounded. The proposition compares the simplest step with a one-line modification of it (Foulaadvand 2023, secs. 3.2–3.3).


Proposition 3 (Euler and Euler-Cromer steps for the oscillator) For \ddot x = -\omega^2x with time step \tau and (x_n, v_n) approximating (x, \dot x) at t = n\tau:

the Euler step x_{n + 1} = x_n + \tau v_n, v_{n + 1} = v_n - \tau\omega^2x_n is (x, v)_{n + 1} = E(x, v)_n with E = \begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau \\ -\omega^2\tau & 1\end{pmatrix}, and it multiplies the energy \mathcal E = \tfrac12(v^2 +
\omega^2x^2) by exactly 1 + \omega^2\tau^2 at every step, so the amplitude grows like (1 + \omega^2\tau^2)^{n/2} \approx
e^{\omega^2\tau t/2} for every \tau > 0;
the Euler-Cromer step v_{n + 1} = v_n - \tau\omega^2x_n, x_{n + 1} = x_n + \tau v_{n + 1} is given by C = \begin{pmatrix}1 - \omega^2\tau^2 & \tau \\ -\omega^2\tau & 1\end{pmatrix} with \det C = 1 and \operatorname{tr}C =
2 - \omega^2\tau^2. For \omega\tau < 2 its eigenvalues are e^{\pm i\theta} with \cos\theta = 1 - \omega^2\tau^2/2, the quadratic form v^2 + \omega^2x^2 - \omega^2\tau xv is conserved, and the computed motion is bounded, with frequency \theta/\tau = \frac2\tau\arcsin\frac{\omega\tau}2 = \omega\bigl(1 + \frac{\omega^2\tau^2}{24} + \dots\bigr).

Proof. (a) (v - \tau\omega^2x)^2 + \omega^2(x + \tau v)^2 = (1 + \omega^2\tau^2)(v^2 + \omega^2x^2), the cross terms cancelling. (b) Substituting v_{n + 1} into the position update gives x_{n + 1} = (1 - \omega^2\tau^2)x_n + \tau v_n, hence C; its determinant is 1 - \omega^2\tau^2 + \omega^2\tau^2 = 1. The eigenvalues solve \lambda^2 - (2 -
\omega^2\tau^2)\lambda + 1 = 0; their product is 1, and for |2 - \omega^2\tau^2| < 2 they are complex conjugate, hence e^{\pm i\theta}. Expanding Q(C(x, v)) for Q = v^2 + \omega^2x^2 - \omega^2\tau xv returns Q(x, v) (a direct computation, done in Sage in Exercise 44). Q is positive definite for \omega\tau < 2, its discriminant being \omega^4\tau^2 - 4\omega^2 < 0, so its level ellipses confine the iterates.

Exercise 46 (The stability limit \omega\tau < 2) Show that for \omega\tau > 2 the matrix C of Proposition 3 has a real eigenvalue of modulus larger than 1, and that the computed motion then grows like |\lambda|^n with alternating sign. For a chain of masses whose highest normal frequency is \omega_{\max}, what does this imply for the step?







NoteSolution





For \omega\tau > 2, \operatorname{tr}C = 2 - \omega^2\tau^2 < -2, so the roots of \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}C)\lambda +
1 = 0 are real, negative and have product 1; one of them has |\lambda| > 1. A generic initial value has a component along its eigenvector, and (x_n, v_n) then alternates in sign and grows like |\lambda|^n. At \omega\tau = 2 the eigenvalue -1 is double and the growth is linear. Since the same step treats every normal mode separately (for a linear chain the modes decouple), the step must satisfy \omega_{\max}\tau < 2: the fastest mode limits \tau even when only the slow motion is of interest.

title: Differential equations
text:
Replacing the initial conditions at one point by conditions at the two ends of an interval changes the character of a linear equation: a solution may fail to exist or fail to be unique, and the values of a parameter for which non-zero solutions exist, the eigenvalues, carry the physics of vibrating strings, drums and quantum systems. This section defines boundary value problems and the Sturm-Liouville form, the weighted inner product under which the eigenfunctions are orthogonal, quotes the Sturm-Liouville theorem, and introduces the Legendre polynomials and Bessel functions, the eigenfunctions that appear when the Laplacian is separated in spherical and cylindrical coordinates. The proposition at the end collects the identities of these functions used later.
For more on this topic, see Magnus (2023, Ch. 7).




Definition 12 (Boundary value problem) A boundary value problem for a second-order equation on an interval [a, b] is the equation together with one condition at each end, boundary conditions: Dirichlet conditions prescribe u(a) and u(b), Neumann conditions prescribe u'(a) and u'(b), and mixed (or Robin) conditions prescribe combinations \alpha u(a) + \beta u'(a) and \gamma u(b) + \delta u'(b). The conditions are homogeneous if the prescribed values are zero.

NoteExamples





The first example is the simplest Dirichlet problem, a loaded string with fixed ends. Its solution exists and is unique, and can be written by two integrations.

Example 49 (A loaded string) -u'' = f(x) on [0, 1] with u(0) = u(1) = 0 describes the shape of a string fixed at both ends under the transverse load f. For f = 1, integrating twice gives u = -x^2/2 + C_1x + C_2, and the two conditions give C_2 = 0, C_1 = 1/2: u = x(1 - x)/2, a parabola (Proposition 9).

The second example shows that a homogeneous boundary value problem can have non-zero solutions for special values of a parameter. That is the eigenvalue problem which the rest of the section is about.

Example 50 (A homogeneous problem with non-zero solutions) u'' + \lambda u = 0 on [0, \pi] with u(0) = u(\pi) = 0 has the solution u = 0 for every \lambda; but for \lambda = n^2, n = 1, 2, \dots, it also has u = \sin nx, since \sin n\pi = 0. For every other \lambda the zero solution is the only one (Exercise 51).

The third example shows a problem with no solution at all. Boundary value problems do not enjoy the automatic existence that Theorem 1 gives initial value problems.

Example 51 (A problem without a solution) u'' + u = 0 with u(0) = 0 and u(\pi) = 1 has no solution: u(0) = 0 forces u = C\sin x, and then u(\pi)

Exercise 50 (A Dirichlet problem with Sage) Solve -u'' = \sin\pi x on [0, 1] with u(0) = u(1) = 0 using desolve with boundary conditions, and check the answer u = \sin(\pi x)/\pi^2.

Exercise 51 (Dirichlet eigenvalues) Show that u'' + \lambda u = 0, u(0) = u(\pi) = 0 has a non-zero solution exactly for \lambda = n^2, n =
1, 2, \dots, treating the cases \lambda < 0, \lambda = 0 and \lambda > 0 separately.







NoteSolution





For \lambda = -\mu^2 < 0, u = C_1e^{\mu x} + C_2e^{-\mu x}; u(0) = 0 gives C_2 = -C_1 and u(\pi) =
2C_1\sinh\mu\pi = 0 forces C_1 = 0. For \lambda = 0, u = C_1 + C_2x and both conditions force C_1 = C_2 =
0. For \lambda = k^2 > 0, u = C_1\cos kx + C_2\sin kx; u(0) = 0 gives C_1 = 0 and u(\pi) = C_2\sin k\pi =
0 allows C_2 \neq 0 exactly when k is an integer n \geq 1. So the eigenvalues are n^2 with eigenfunctions \sin nx.

The third exercise establishes the alternative between existence for all data and uniqueness. It generalises the third example to an arbitrary right-hand side.

Exercise 52 (Existence versus uniqueness) For the problem u'' + \lambda u = f on [0, \pi] with u(0) = u(\pi) = 0, show that if \lambda is not an eigenvalue then a solution exists for every continuous f and is unique, and that if \lambda = n^2 then a solution exists only when \int_0^\pi f(x)\sin nx\,dx = 0, and is then not unique.







NoteSolution





Uniqueness: the difference of two solutions solves the homogeneous problem, which has only the zero solution when \lambda is not an eigenvalue. Existence: with the Green’s function of Definition 26 (constructed in Exercise 113 for \lambda = 0 and analogously for other non-eigenvalues) u = \int G f is a solution. If \lambda = n^2, multiply the equation by \sin nx and integrate by parts twice: \int(u'' + n^2u)\sin nx\,dx =
\int u(\sin nx)'' + n^2u\sin nx\,dx = 0 because the boundary terms vanish, so \int f\sin nx\,dx = 0 is necessary; when it holds, any solution plus C\sin nx is another.

The eigenvalue problem of the examples is a special case of a form that covers every separated Laplacian. The definition isolates that form and its boundary conditions.


Definition 13 (Sturm-Liouville problem) A Sturm-Liouville problem on [a, b] is the eigenvalue equation -\frac{d}{dx}\Big(p(x)\frac{du}{dx}\Big) + q(x)\,u = \lambda\,w(x)\,u with p, p', q, w continuous, together with homogeneous separated boundary conditions at a and b. A number \lambda for which a non-zero solution exists is an eigenvalue and the solution an eigenfunction; w > 0 is the weight. The problem is regular if p > 0 and w > 0 on the closed interval, and singular if p or w vanishes at an endpoint or the interval is infinite, in which case the boundary condition there is replaced by the requirement that u stay bounded.

The third exercise proves that the eigenvalues of a regular problem with q \geq 0 are non-negative. It uses the integration by parts that recurs throughout the theory.

Exercise 55 (Non-negative eigenvalues) For a regular Sturm-Liouville problem with q \geq 0 and Dirichlet conditions, multiply the equation by u and integrate by parts to show \lambda\int_a^b wu^2\,dx = \int_a^b (p u'^2 + qu^2)\,dx, and deduce \lambda \geq 0, with \lambda = 0 only if u is constant and q = 0.







NoteSolution





\int_a^b -(pu')'u\,dx = -[pu'u]_a^b + \int_a^b pu'^2\,dx = \int_a^b pu'^2\,dx, the boundary term vanishing because u(a) = u(b) = 0. Adding \int qu^2 gives the identity. The right side is non-negative, and the left side has \int wu^2 > 0 for u \neq 0, so \lambda \geq 0. If \lambda = 0 then \int pu'^2 = 0 with p > 0 forces u' = 0, and \int qu^2 = 0 forces q = 0 where u \neq 0; but a constant with u(a) = 0 is zero, so in fact \lambda > 0 for Dirichlet conditions, consistent with Exercise 51.

Definition 14 (Orthogonal functions) For a weight w > 0 on [a, b], the weighted inner product of two real functions is \langle f, g\rangle_w =

Orthogonality of the sines and the Legendre polynomials is no coincidence: both are eigenfunctions of Sturm-Liouville problems. The theorem states this and adds the completeness that makes eigenfunction expansions possible.


Theorem 2 (Sturm-Liouville theorem) For a regular Sturm-Liouville problem: the eigenvalues are real, simple, and form an increasing sequence \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \dots \to \infty; eigenfunctions of distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal for the weight w; the n-th eigenfunction has exactly n - 1 zeros inside (a, b); and the eigenfunctions are complete: every function f with \|f\|_w < \infty is the limit in the norm \|\cdot\|_w of its expansion \sum_n
c_n\varphi_n with c_n = \langle f, \varphi_n\rangle_w/\|\varphi_n\|_w^2. Reality and orthogonality are proved in Exercise 59 and Exercise 60; the rest is quoted without proof, and the same conclusions hold for the singular Legendre and Bessel problems.

Exercise 59 (Orthogonality of eigenfunctions) Let u, v be eigenfunctions with eigenvalues \lambda \neq \mu of a regular problem with Dirichlet conditions. Show that (\lambda - \mu)\int_a^b uvw\,dx = [p(uv' - u'v)]_a^b = 0.

As \lambda \neq \mu, \int uvw = 0.

Legendre’s and Bessel’s equations, met in Example 53 and Example 54, have coefficients that blow up at the ends of the interval, and their solutions are found as power series. Whether a series solution exists near a point depends on how badly the coefficients blow up there, and the definition sorts the points accordingly (Michele Cini and Rotondi 2023, sec. 7.1.1).


Definition 15 (Regular singular point) Write a linear second-order equation as y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = 0. A point x_0 is ordinary if P and Q are analytic at x_0 (given by convergent power series in x - x_0), and singular otherwise. A singular point is regular if (x - x_0)P(x) and (x - x_0)^2Q(x) are analytic at x_0, and irregular otherwise. The point at infinity is classified by the substitution z = 1/x and the resulting equation at z = 0.

Example 61 (The singular points of Legendre’s equation) Dividing (1 - x^2)y'' - 2xy' + l(l + 1)y = 0 by 1 - x^2 gives P = -2x/(1 - x^2) and Q = l(l + 1)/(1 - x^2), analytic except at x = \pm1. Definition 16 (Legendre polynomial) The Legendre polynomial P_n is the polynomial solution of degree n of Legendre’s equation (1 - x^2)u'' -
2xu' + n(n + 1)u = 0 normalised by P_n(1) = 1. Equivalently (Rodrigues’ formula), P_n(x) =
\frac{1}{2^nn!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2 - 1)^n; the first few are P_0 = 1, P_1 = x, P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1), P_3 = \tfrac12(5x^3 - 3x), and they satisfy \int_{-1}^1P_mP_n\,dx = \frac{2}{2n + 1}\delta_{mn}.

Definition 17 (Bessel function) The Bessel function of order n = 0, 1, 2, \dots is the solution of Bessel’s equation x^2u'' + xu' + (x^2 -

The second example links J_1 to J_0 by differentiation. The derivative relations are the Bessel analogue of the Legendre recurrence.

Example 71 (J_0' = -J_1) Differentiating the series of J_0 term by term gives -\sum_{k \geq 1}\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!\,k!}(x/2)^{2k-1}
= -J_1(x). More generally J_{n-1} - J_{n+1} = 2J_n' and J_{n-1} + J_{n+1} = \frac{2n}xJ_n (Exercise 73), so every J_n is obtained from J_0 and J_1.

Exercise 71 (The series in the equation) Substitute the series of J_n truncated at k = K into Bessel’s equation with Sage for n = 0, 1, 2 and K =
6, and show that the residual is the single term \frac{(-1)^K}{K!\,(K + n)!}\frac{x^{2K+n+2}}{2^{2K+n}}.







NoteSolution





Every term of the series cancels against its neighbour except the last, whose partner would be the k = K + 1 term; the leftover is its x^2 contribution:

x = var("x")
K = 6
for n in range(3):
    J = sum((-1) ** k / (factorial(k) * factorial(k + n)) * (x / 2) ** (2 * k + n) for k in range(K + 1))
    res = (x ** 2 * diff(J, x, 2) + x * diff(J, x) + (x ** 2 - n ** 2) * J).expand()
    predicted = (-1) ** K / (factorial(K) * factorial(K + n)) * x ** (2 * K + n + 2) / 2 ** (2 * K + n)
    print("n =", n, ": residual =", res, "| equals the predicted monomial:", bool((res - predicted).expand() == 0))

The third exercise derives the recurrence relations from the series. They are the tools for every manipulation of Bessel functions.

Exercise 73 (The recurrence relations) Show from the series that \frac{d}{dx}[x^nJ_n(x)] = x^nJ_{n-1}(x) and \frac{d}{dx}[x^{-n}J_n(x)] = -

NoteSolution





x^nJ_n = \sum_k\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(k + n)!}\frac{x^{2k+2n}}{2^{2k+n}}, and differentiating gives \sum_k\frac{(-1)^k(2k + 2n)}{k!(k + n)!}\frac{x^{2k+2n-1}}{2^{2k+n}} = x^n\sum_k\frac{(-1)^k}{k!(k + n -
1)!}\frac{x^{2k+n-1}}{2^{2k+n-1}} = x^nJ_{n-1}; the second identity is the same computation with the k = 0 term dropping out and the index shifted. Expanding the derivatives, J_n' + \frac nxJ_n = J_{n-1} and J_n' - \frac
nxJ_n = -J_{n+1}; adding and subtracting gives the two relations.

The first exercise computes a Legendre norm by hand to see where 2/(2n + 1) comes from. The integral is of a polynomial and short.

Exercise 74 (The norm of P_2) Compute \int_{-1}^1P_2^2\,dx by hand and check it against 2/(2n + 1); then show that \int_{-1}^1P_0P_2\,dx =
0 and \int_{-1}^1 xP_2\,dx = 0.







NoteSolution





P_2^2 = \tfrac14(9x^4 - 6x^2 + 1), whose integral over [-1, 1] is \tfrac14(\tfrac{18}5 - 4 + 2) = \tfrac14
\cdot\tfrac85 = \tfrac25 = \tfrac{2}{2\cdot2 + 1}. \int_{-1}^1\tfrac12(3x^2 - 1)\,dx = \tfrac12(2 - 2) = 0, and \int_{-1}^1xP_2\,dx = 0 because the integrand is odd.

The third exercise derives the Bessel orthogonality relation with weight x from the Sturm-Liouville form. It is the orthogonality of Exercise 59 in a singular case.

Exercise 76 (Orthogonality of the drum modes) Show that u_k(x) = J_0(j_{0,k}x) satisfies -(xu_k')' = j_{0,k}^2xu_k, and deduce from Lagrange’s identity that \int_0^1J_0(j_{0,k}x)J_0(j_{0,l}x)\,x\,dx = 0 for k \neq l.







NoteSolution





With y = j_{0,k}x, Bessel’s equation for n = 0 reads y^2J_0'' + yJ_0' + y^2J_0 = 0, that is, (yJ_0')' = -
yJ_0. Since u_k' = j_{0,k}J_0'(y), xu_k' = yJ_0'(y), and by the chain rule (xu_k')' = j_{0,k}\frac{d}{dy}
(yJ_0') = -j_{0,k}yJ_0 = -j_{0,k}^2xu_k. Lagrange’s identity for u_k, u_l with p = x gives (j_{0,k}^2 -
j_{0,l}^2)\int_0^1u_ku_lx\,dx = [x(u_ku_l' - u_k'u_l)]_0^1; at x = 1 both u_k, u_l vanish, and at x = 0 the factor x kills the term. Hence the integral vanishes for k \neq l.

/-- If `F` satisfies Bessel's equation of order `0`, `y²F'' + yF' + y²F = 0`, then `u(x) = F(jx)` has

Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions with weight `x`. -/
theorem drum_mode (j x : ℝ) (F F' F'' : ℝ → ℝ) (hF : ∀ y, HasDerivAt F (F' y) y) (hF' : ∀ y, HasDerivAt F' (F'' y) y)

    HasDerivAt (fun s => F (j * s)) (j * F' (j * x)) x ∧
      HasDerivAt (fun s => j * F' (j * s)) (j ^ 2 * F'' (j * x)) x ∧
      x ^ 2 * (j ^ 2 * F'' (j * x)) + x * (j * F' (j * x)) + j ^ 2 * x ^ 2 * F (j * x) = 0

title: Differential equations
text:
A field depends on several variables, and its equation of motion involves partial derivatives with respect to all of them. This section defines partial differential equations and the classification of the linear second-order ones into hyperbolic, parabolic and elliptic types, then treats the representative of each type: the wave equation, solved by d’Alembert’s formula, the heat equation, solved by its kernel, and Laplace’s equation, whose solutions are the harmonic functions. Separation of variables, which reduces all three to the Sturm-Liouville problems of Section 1.3, closes the section, and the proposition collects the solutions, each of which satisfies its equation by substitution. The d’Alembertian is \Box = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2 in the signature (+, -, -, -) of Prerequisites and conventions.
For more on this topic, see Borodzik et al. (2019, Ch. 3, Ch. 4).




Definition 18 (Partial differential equation) A partial differential equation (PDE) for an unknown function u(x^1, \dots, x^n) of several variables is a relation between u, the variables and the partial derivatives of u (Definition 14 of Real analysis) up to some order, the order of the equation. It is linear if it has the form Lu = f with L a linear combination of derivatives with coefficients depending on the variables, and homogeneous if f = 0; the solutions of a homogeneous linear equation form a vector space, so solutions can be superposed.







TipVerification

Lean.

/-- The solutions of a homogeneous linear equation `Lu = 0` form a vector space: combinations of solutions are
solutions. -/
theorem pde_superposition {V W : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℝ V] [AddCommGroup W] [Module ℝ W] (L : V →ₗ[ℝ] W)
    (u₁ u₂ : V) (α β : ℝ) (h₁ : L u₁ = 0) (h₂ : L u₂ = 0) : L (α • u₁ + β • u₂) = 0

/-- … and `u₁ + u₂` solves `Lu = f₁ + f₂` when `uᵢ` solves `Lu = fᵢ`. -/
theorem superposition_sources {V W : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℝ V] [AddCommGroup W] [Module ℝ W]
    (L : V →ₗ[ℝ] W) (u₁ u₂ : V) (f₁ f₂ : W) (h₁ : L u₁ = f₁) (h₂ : L u₂ = f₂) : L (u₁ + u₂) = f₁ + f₂

NoteExamples





The first example is the wave equation in one space dimension, the equation of a vibrating string. It is linear, second order and homogeneous.

Example 76 (The wave equation) u_{tt} - c^2u_{xx} = 0, with subscripts for partial derivatives, governs the transverse displacement u(t, x) of a string with wave speed c. In three space dimensions it reads \Box u = u_{tt} - \nabla^2u = 0 with c = 1, and the Klein-Gordon equation (\Box + m^2)u = 0 adds a mass term.







TipVerification

Lean.

/-- The wave (and Klein-Gordon) operator is linear: superposition in the jet variables `(u_tt, u_xx, u)`. -/
theorem wave_linear (c m a b p q r p' q' r' : ℝ) :

The three examples behave very differently: waves propagate, heat spreads, and equilibrium is attained. The next definition sorts linear second-order equations into the three types by an algebraic criterion.


Definition 19 (Classification of second-order equations) A linear second-order equation in two variables, Au_{xx} + 2Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + (\text{lower order}) = 0, is hyperbolic where B^2 - AC > 0, parabolic where B^2 - AC = 0 and elliptic where B^2 - AC < 0. Exercise 83 (Heat conduction with a relaxation time) Fourier’s law q = -\kappa u_x for the heat flux, with the balance \mu u_t + q_x = 0 (\mu the heat capacity per length), gives the heat equation. The Maxwell-Cattaneo-Vernotte law \tau q_t + q = -\kappa u_x, with a relaxation time \tau > 0, gives instead \tau\mu u_{tt} + \mu u_t - \kappa u_{xx} = 0. Derive this, classify it by Definition 19, find its characteristic speed, and find the decay rates of the modes e^{ikx}. What happens as \tau \to 0?







NoteSolution





Applying \tau\partial_t + 1 to the balance and substituting (\tau\partial_t + 1)q_x = -\kappa u_{xx} gives \tau\mu u_{tt} +
\mu u_t - \kappa u_{xx} = 0, the telegraph equation. In the variables (t, x) the coefficients are A = \tau\mu, B = 0, C = -\kappa, so B^2 - AC = \tau\mu\kappa > 0: hyperbolic, with characteristics x \pm ct, c =
\sqrt{\kappa/(\tau\mu)}, so that heat now travels at a finite speed. For u = e^{ikx + st}, \tau\mu s^2 + \mu s + \kappa k^2 =
0, so s = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4\tau\kappa k^2/\mu}}{2\tau}: long waves decay like e^{-\kappa k^2t/\mu}, as for the heat equation, while waves with k^2 > \mu/(4\tau\kappa) oscillate and decay at the fixed rate 1/(2\tau). As \tau \to 0 the speed c diverges, the second root s \approx -1/\tau decays instantly, and the parabolic heat equation \mu u_t =
\kappa u_{xx} (Definition 21, \kappa/\mu the diffusivity) remains.

Exercise 88 (The similarity solution) Show that u(t, x) = t^{-1/2}F(x/\sqrt{4\kappa t}) solves the heat equation exactly when F'' + 2\xi F' + 2F =

The elliptic representative has no initial data; its solutions are determined by boundary values. The definition names them and states their two basic properties.


Definition 22 (Laplace’s equation) Laplace’s equation is \nabla^2u = 0, and its twice differentiable solutions are the harmonic functions. The Dirichlet problem asks for a harmonic function in a bounded region with prescribed values on the boundary; its solution is unique, because a harmonic function satisfies the mean value property (its value at a point is the average over any sphere around the point inside the region) and hence the maximum principle (its maximum and minimum over the closed region are attained on the boundary).

Most equations met in physics have no solution formula on the domains of interest, and they are solved on a grid: derivatives become differences of grid values and the equation becomes an update rule. As for the oscillator in Proposition 3, the rule may amplify errors, and the test is to follow a single Fourier mode e^{ikx} through one step. The proposition applies this test to the three model equations of this section (Foulaadvand 2023, secs. 5.3, 6.2 and 6.4).


Proposition 6 (Stability of finite-difference schemes) Let u^n_j approximate u(n\tau, j\,\Delta x), and call a scheme stable if no grid mode u^n_j = g^ne^{ikj\Delta x} has |g| > 1, so that errors are not amplified. Write s = \sin\frac{k\Delta x}2.

For u_t = \kappa u_{xx} the forward-time centred-space (FTCS) scheme u^{n + 1}_j = u^n_j + r(u^n_{j + 1} - 2u^n_j +
u^n_{j - 1}), r = \kappa\tau/\Delta x^2, has g = 1 - 4rs^2 and is stable if and only if r \leq \tfrac12.
For u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} the leapfrog scheme u^{n + 1}_j = 2u^n_j - u^{n - 1}_j + C^2(u^n_{j + 1} - 2u^n_j + u^n_{j - 1}), with the Courant number C = c\tau/\Delta x, has the two amplification factors with g + g^{-1} = 2 - 4C^2s^2; both lie on the unit circle for every k if C \leq 1, and for C > 1 some mode has |g| > 1.
For u_t + cu_x = 0 the FTCS scheme u^{n + 1}_j = u^n_j - \frac C2(u^n_{j + 1} - u^n_{j - 1}) has |g|^2 = 1 + C^2\sin^2k\Delta x and is unstable for every \tau, while the Lax scheme u^{n + 1}_j = \frac12(u^n_{j + 1} + u^n_{j - 1}) - \frac C2(u^n_{j + 1} -
u^n_{j - 1}) has |g|^2 = 1 - (1 - C^2)\sin^2k\Delta x and is stable if and only if |C| \leq 1, the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition.

Proof. Inserting the mode and dividing by g^ne^{ikj\Delta x} uses e^{ik\Delta x} - 2 + e^{-ik\Delta x} = -4s^2 and e^{ik\Delta x} -
e^{-ik\Delta x} = 2i\sin k\Delta x. (a) g = 1 - 4rs^2 lies in [1 - 4r, 1], and g \geq -1 for all s exactly when r \leq
\tfrac12. (b) g^2 - (2 - 4C^2s^2)g + 1 = 0 has roots with product 1; they are complex conjugate on the unit circle when |2 - 4C^2s^2| \leq 2, that is C^2s^2 \leq 1, which holds for all s iff C \leq 1; for C > 1 and s near 1 the roots are real with product 1, one of modulus above 1. (c) FTCS gives g = 1 - iC\sin k\Delta x, and Lax gives g =
\cos k\Delta x - iC\sin k\Delta x; their moduli are as stated.

Laplace’s equation has no time variable to step, and on a grid it becomes one large linear system. The proposition shows that the system always has exactly one solution and that the simplest iteration, which replaces each value by the average of its neighbours, converges to it, slowly (Foulaadvand 2023, secs. 7.2–7.3).


Proposition 7 (The discrete Dirichlet problem and Jacobi relaxation) On the grid x_i = i\,h, y_j = j\,h, 0 \leq i, j \leq N, of the unit square, let \Delta_h\Phi_{ij} = (\Phi_{i + 1, j} + \Phi_{i - 1, j} + \Phi_{i,
j + 1} + \Phi_{i, j - 1} - 4\Phi_{ij})/h^2.

A grid function with \Delta_h\Phi = 0 at the interior points equals at each of them the average of its four neighbours, and it attains its maximum and its minimum on the boundary (discrete maximum principle).
Hence the discrete Dirichlet problem, \Delta_h\Phi = 0 inside with given boundary values, has exactly one solution.
The Jacobi iteration \Phi^{(m + 1)}_{ij} = \frac14(\Phi^{(m)}_{i + 1, j} + \Phi^{(m)}_{i - 1, j} + \Phi^{(m)}_{i, j + 1} + \Phi^{(m)}_{i, j - 1}) inside, with the boundary values kept fixed, converges to it from any starting values; the error is a sum of modes \sin\frac{p\pi i}N\sin\frac{q\pi j}N, 1 \leq p, q < N, each multiplied per sweep by \frac12(\cos\frac{p\pi}N + \cos\frac{q\pi}N), so the slowest decays by \rho = \cos\frac\pi N \approx 1 - \frac{\pi^2}{2N^2} per sweep.

Proof. (a) \Delta_h\Phi_{ij} = 0 is the averaging property. If the maximum M were attained at an interior point and not on the boundary, the four neighbours, whose average is M and which are at most M, would all equal M; repeating the argument along a row reaches the boundary, a contradiction. The same applies to -\Phi. (b) The difference of two solutions has zero boundary values, so by (a) its maximum and minimum are 0. The problem is a square linear system for the interior values, and a square system with trivial kernel has exactly one solution. (c) The error e = \Phi^{(m)} - \Phi obeys the iteration with zero boundary values. By \sin\frac{p\pi(i + 1)}N + \sin\frac{p\pi(i - 1)}N = 2\cos\frac{p\pi}N\sin\frac{p\pi
i}N the products of sines are eigenvectors with the stated eigenvalues; there are (N - 1)^2 of them, independent by the discrete orthogonality of sines, so they form a basis, and all eigenvalues have modulus at most \cos\frac\pi N < 1.

\mathbf k|^2, so the equation holds exactly when this vanishes: the residual is this polynomial times the wave, and it vanishes at \omega = \sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2 + m^2}.

title: Differential equations
text:
A linear differential operator L can be inverted: if G solves LG = \delta with a point source, then u =
\int G f solves Lu = f for any source f, by superposition. This section defines the delta function as far as this use requires, the fundamental solution and the Green’s function with boundary conditions, and computes the Green’s functions of the Laplacian and of the static Klein-Gordon operator; for the wave operator, where LG =
\delta has several solutions, it describes the retarded and the Feynman prescriptions in outline. The proposition collects the properties of -1/(4\pi r) and of the Yukawa function, and the figure shows the radial Green’s functions and the Green’s function of a string.
For more on this topic, see Aliev and Lara (2024, Ch. 1).




Definition 24 (Dirac delta) The Dirac delta \delta(x) is the rule that assigns to every continuous function its value at the origin, written as an integral: \int_{-\infty}^\infty\delta(x)f(x)\,dx = f(0), and \delta(x - a) picks out f(a). It is not a function but the limit of a sequence of functions of unit integral concentrating at 0, such as the heat kernel K(t, x) as t \to 0^+; it is the derivative of the step function \theta(x) (0 for x < 0, 1 for x > 0) in the sense that \int\theta'f = -\int\theta f' = f(0); and in n dimensions \delta^n(\mathbf
x) = \delta(x^1)\cdots\delta(x^n) picks out the value at the origin of \mathbb{R}^n.

Definition 26 (Green’s function) The Green’s function of a linear operator L on a region \Omega with homogeneous boundary conditions is the function G(\mathbf x, \mathbf y) that, for each source point \mathbf y \in \Omega, satisfies L_{\mathbf

x. Then u(\mathbf x) = \int_\Omega G(\mathbf x, \mathbf y)f(\mathbf y)\,d^ny solves Lu = f with the boundary conditions; for a self-adjoint L (such as a Sturm-Liouville operator or the Laplacian with Dirichlet conditions) G is symmetric, G(\mathbf x, \mathbf y) = G(\mathbf y, \mathbf x).

The second exercise proves the symmetry of the Green’s function for a Sturm-Liouville operator. It is Lagrange’s identity applied to two Green’s functions.

Exercise 114 (Symmetry of the Green’s function) For L = -(pu')' + qu with Dirichlet conditions on [a, b], show that G(x, \xi) = G(\xi, x) by applying Lagrange’s identity (Exercise 59) to u = G(\cdot, \xi) and v = G(\cdot, \eta).

\int_a^b(vLu - uLv)\,dx = [p(uv' - u'v)]_a^b = 0 by the boundary conditions. With Lu = \delta(x - \xi) and Lv = \delta(x - \eta) the left side is v(\xi) - u(\eta) = G(\xi, \eta) - G(\eta, \xi), which therefore vanishes. Physically: the response at \xi to a unit source at \eta equals the response at \eta to a unit source at \xi (reciprocity).

The Laplacian has one fundamental solution that vanishes at infinity. The wave operator has several, because solutions of the homogeneous wave equation can be added; the physical choice is the one that respects causality.


Definition 27 (Retarded Green’s function) The retarded Green’s function of the wave operator \Box = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2 is the fundamental solution G_{\mathrm{ret}}(t, \mathbf x) that vanishes for t < 0: \Box G_{\mathrm{ret}} =
\delta(t)\delta^3(\mathbf x) and G_{\mathrm{ret}} = 0 before the source acts. In three dimensions it is G_{\mathrm{ret}} = \frac{\delta(t - r)}{4\pi r}, a spherical shell expanding at the speed of light, and the solution of \Box u = f that is zero before the source switches on is the retarded potential u(t, \mathbf x)
= \int\frac{f(t - |\mathbf x - \mathbf y|, \mathbf y)}{4\pi|\mathbf x - \mathbf y|}d^3y. The advanced Green’s function \delta(t + r)/(4\pi r) vanishes for t > 0 instead; the two differ by a solution of the homogeneous equation.

Exercise 121 (Wick rotation of the k_0 integral) Compute \int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dk_4}{2\pi}\frac{e^{ik_4\tau}}{k_4^2 + \omega^2} =

The Euclidean propagator decays exponentially in Euclidean time with rate \omega, the energy of the mode; continuing \tau \to it turns e^{-\omega|\tau|} into e^{-i\omega|t|}, and the Jacobian dk_0 = i\,dk_4 supplies the factor i of \frac{i}{2\omega}e^{-i\omega|t|}. The rotation is legitimate because the Feynman poles lie in the second and fourth quadrants, which the rotating contour never crosses (Contour integration).

Exercise 124 (Deriving the Yukawa function) Solve -\frac1{r^2}(r^2G')' + m^2G = 0 for r > 0 by the substitution G = v/r, select the solution decaying at infinity, and fix its normalisation by the flux condition at r \to 0.

    Tendsto (fun m => Real.exp (-m * r) / (4 * Real.pi * r)) (𝓝 0) (𝓝 (1 / (4 * Real.pi * r)))

/-- With `G = v/r`: `(1/r²)(r²G')' = v''/r` (from `r²G' = rv' - v`, whose derivative is `rv''`). -/
theorem yukawa_substitution (r v v' v'' : ℝ) (hr : r ≠ 0) : 1 / r ^ 2 * (r * v'' + v' - v') = v'' / r

    HasDerivAt (fun s => v s / s) ((r * v' - v r) / r ^ 2) r

/-- `v = Ae^{-mr} + Be^{mr}` solves `v'' = m²v`. -/
theorem yukawa_radial_general (A B m : ℝ) (v : ℝ → ℝ) (hv : v = fun s => A * Real.exp (-m * s) + B * Real.exp (m * s))
    (r : ℝ) : deriv (deriv v) r = m ^ 2 * v r

/-- Decay at infinity forces `B = 0`: `e^{-mr} → 0` while `e^{mr} → ∞` (`m > 0`). -/
theorem yukawa_decay (A B m : ℝ) (hm : 0 < m) (hB : B ≠ 0) :
    ¬ Tendsto (fun r => A * Real.exp (-m * r) + B * Real.exp (m * r)) atTop (𝓝 0)

theorem yukawa_normalisation (r : ℝ) (hr : r ≠ 0) :
    -deriv (fun s => 1 / (4 * Real.pi) / s) r * (4 * Real.pi * r ^ 2) = 1

title: Differential equations
text:
NoteExercises





Three exercises combine the sections of this chapter. The first takes the pendulum from its phase portrait to the matrix exponential of its linearisation, the second takes the string from its Sturm-Liouville modes through the wave equation to its Green’s function, and the third takes the Klein-Gordon equation from plane waves to the Yukawa potential. The first exercise asks for the linear approximation of a non-linear system near each equilibrium and a quantitative comparison with the exact flow. It uses the Jacobian of Section 1.1, the classification of Section 1.2 and Sage’s matrix exponential.

Exercise 125 (The damped pendulum near its equilibria) Linearise the damped pendulum (\theta, \omega)' = (\omega, -\sin\theta - \gamma\omega) with \gamma = 0.3 at (0, 0) and at (\pi, 0), classify the two equilibria by Definition 9, compute e^{tA} for the linearisation at (0, 0) with Sage, and compare the linear solution starting at (0.1, 0) with the numerical solution of the full system over 0 \le t \le 10.







NoteSolution





The Jacobian is \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -\cos\theta & -\gamma \end{pmatrix}: at (0, 0) it has trace -0.3 and determinant 1, a spiral sink with eigenvalues -0.15 \pm 0.989i (underdamped, \omega_d = \sqrt{1 - 0.0225}); at (\pi, 0) the determinant is -1, a saddle. The linear and the non-linear solutions from (0.1, 0) agree to about 10^{-4}, the error being of order \theta^3/6 from \sin\theta:

th, om, t = var("th om t")
gam = QQ(3) / 10
F = vector([om, -sin(th) - gam * om])
Jac = jacobian(F, [th, om])
for pt in [(0, 0), (pi, 0)]:
    A = Jac.subs(th=pt[0], om=pt[1])
    print("Jacobian at", pt, ":", A.list(), "| trace", A.trace(), "det", A.det(), "| eigenvalues", [numerical_approx(e) for e in A.change_ring(SR).eigenvalues()])
A0 = Jac.subs(th=0, om=0).change_ring(SR)
alpha, beta = -gam / 2, sqrt(1 - gam ** 2 / 4)                     # eigenvalues alpha +- i beta
E = exp(alpha * t) * (cos(beta * t) * identity_matrix(SR, 2) + sin(beta * t) / beta * (A0 - alpha * identity_matrix(SR, 2)))
print("exp(tA) at (0, 0) (closed form e^(alpha t)[cos(beta t) + sin(beta t)/beta (A - alpha)]):")
print(E)
print("d/dt exp(tA) = A exp(tA) and exp(0) = 1 (which identifies the exponential):", bool((E.derivative(t) - A0 * E).apply_map(lambda e: e.simplify_full()) == 0), bool(E.subs(t=0) == identity_matrix(2)))
raw = (t * A0).exp().apply_map(lambda e: e.rectform().simplify_full())
print("Sage's exp(tA) agrees with the closed form numerically at t = 1:", bool(abs(numerical_approx(raw.subs(t=1)[0, 0]) - numerical_approx(E.subs(t=1)[0, 0])) < 1e-12))
lin = E * vector([QQ(1) / 10, 0])
times = srange(0, 10.01, 0.5)
num = desolve_odeint([om, -sin(th) - gam * om], [0.1, 0], times, [th, om])
err = max(abs(float(lin[0].subs(t=tt)) - num[i][0]) for i, tt in enumerate(times))
print("largest difference in theta between the linear and the full solution over [0, 10]:", "%.2e" % err)
print("below 1e-3 (the cubic error of sin theta for theta = 0.1):", err < 1e-3)
Output:
Jacobian at (0, 0) : [0, 1, -1, -3/10] | trace -3/10 det 1 | eigenvalues [-0.150000000000000 - 0.988685996664259*I, -0.150000000000000 + 0.988685996664259*I]
Jacobian at (pi, 0) : [0, 1, 1, -3/10] | trace -3/10 det -1 | eigenvalues [-1.16118742080783, 0.861187420807834]
exp(tA) at (0, 0) (closed form e^(alpha t)[cos(beta t) + sin(beta t)/beta (A - alpha)]):
[ 1/391*(3*sqrt(391)*sin(1/20*sqrt(391)*t) + 391*cos(1/20*sqrt(391)*t))*e^(-3/20*t)                                 20/391*sqrt(391)*e^(-3/20*t)*sin(1/20*sqrt(391)*t)]
[                               -20/391*sqrt(391)*e^(-3/20*t)*sin(1/20*sqrt(391)*t) -1/391*(3*sqrt(391)*sin(1/20*sqrt(391)*t) - 391*cos(1/20*sqrt(391)*t))*e^(-3/20*t)]
d/dt exp(tA) = A exp(tA) and exp(0) = 1 (which identifies the exponential): True True
Sage's exp(tA) agrees with the closed form numerically at t = 1: True
largest difference in theta between the linear and the full solution over [0, 10]: 9.15e-05
below 1e-3 (the cubic error of sin theta for theta = 0.1): True










TipVerification

Lean.

/-- The Jacobian's entry `∂_θ(-sin θ - γω) = -cos θ`. -/
theorem pendulum_jacobian (θ ω γ : ℝ) : deriv (fun s => -Real.sin s - γ * ω) θ = -Real.cos θ
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_jacobian in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- At `(0, 0)` (with `γ = 0.3`): trace `-0.3` … -/
theorem pendulum_trace : Matrix.trace !![(0 : ℝ), 1; -Real.cos 0, -0.3] = -0.3
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_trace in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- … determinant `1`: a spiral sink … -/
theorem pendulum_det : Matrix.det !![(0 : ℝ), 1; -Real.cos 0, -0.3] = 1
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_det in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- … with eigenvalues `-0.15 ± i√0.9775` (`0.15 = 3/20`, `0.9775 = 391/400`, `γ = 0.3 = 3/10`). -/
theorem pendulum_eigenvalues (i s : ℂ) (hi : i ^ 2 = -1) (hs : s ^ 2 = 391 / 400) :
    (-3 / 20 + i * s) ^ 2 + 3 / 10 * (-3 / 20 + i * s) + 1 = 0
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_eigenvalues in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- `ω_d = √(1 - 0.0225) ≈ 0.989`. -/
theorem pendulum_damped_frequency : |Real.sqrt (1 - 9 / 400) - 989 / 1000| < (1 / 2000 : ℝ)
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_damped_frequency in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- At `(π, 0)` the determinant is `-1`: a saddle. -/
theorem pendulum_upright_det : Matrix.det !![(0 : ℝ), 1; -Real.cos Real.pi, -0.3] = -1
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_upright_det in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- `e^{tA}` by the spiral formula: `B = A + 0.15` has `B² = -0.9775`. -/
theorem pendulum_spiral_B :
    !![(3 / 20 : ℝ), 1; -1, -3 / 20] * !![(3 / 20 : ℝ), 1; -1, -3 / 20] = !![-391 / 400, 0; 0, -391 / 400]
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_spiral_B in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- The linearisation error: `θ - θ³/6 < sin θ ≤ θ` for `θ > 0`, an error of order `θ³/6`. -/
theorem pendulum_sine_error (θ : ℝ) (h0 : 0 < θ) : θ - θ ^ 3 / 6 < Real.sin θ ∧ Real.sin θ ≤ θ
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.pendulum_sine_error in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- Every spiral: if `B² = -β²` (`β ≠ 0`), then `e^{t(α + B)} = e^{αt}[cos βt + (sin βt/β) B]`
(the closed form behind the rotation and the spiral sink). -/
theorem exp_spiral {n : ℕ} (B : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (α β : ℝ) (hβ : β ≠ 0)
    (hB : B * B = -(β ^ 2) • (1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ)) (t : ℝ) :
    NormedSpace.exp (t • (α • (1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) + B)) =
      Real.exp (α * t) • (Real.cos (β * t) • (1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) + (Real.sin (β * t) / β) • B)
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.MatrixExponential.exp_spiral in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/LinearSystems.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.MatrixExponential


/-- The pendulum force is Lipschitz with constant `1`: `|sin a - sin b| ≤ |a - b|`, the hypothesis of
Picard-Lindelöf for the pendulum. -/
theorem pendulum_lipschitz (a b : ℝ) : |Real.sin a - Real.sin b| ≤ |a - b|
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.InitialValueProblems.pendulum_lipschitz in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/OrdinaryDifferentialEquations.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.InitialValueProblems

Sage. Sage differentiates every derivative in the statement and confirms the identity. Sage evaluates the matrix identity, determinant or trace exactly. Sage writes the difference of the two sides as a combination of the hypotheses (Gröbner cofactors), or expands it to zero. Sage confirms the identity exactly (or the bound in interval arithmetic) before the rewrite. Test instances: θ - θ³/6 < sin θ ≤ θ in interval arithmetic at θ = 1/100 (edge, small angle), 1/2, 3. Test instances: e^{t(α + B)} = e^{αt}[cos βt + (sin βt/β)B] for B² = -β² by Sage: (B, α, β) = (J, 0, 1), (A2 + 1, -1, 1), (2J, 3, 2), at t = 1 (and t = 0, edge). Test instances: |sin a - sin b| ≤ |a - b| in interval arithmetic at (0, 0) (edge), (1, 2), (-3, 1/2).



The second exercise follows one physical system, the string with fixed ends, through three sections. Its modes are Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions, its motion is a solution of the wave equation, and its static response is given by a Green’s function that the modes also express as a series.

Exercise 126 (The string: modes, waves and Green’s function) For the string on [0, \pi] with fixed ends: (a) show that the Green’s function of -d^2/dx^2 is G(x, \xi) =
x_<(\pi - x_>)/\pi and that it equals the eigenfunction series \frac2\pi\sum_n\frac{\sin nx\sin n\xi}{n^2}, by checking the sine coefficients with Sage; (b) use it to find the static shape under the load f = 1; (c) release the string from that shape and write the motion as a standing-wave series; (d) check that the energy of Exercise 85 is constant for the partial sums.







NoteSolution






The one-sided solutions are x and \pi - x with W = -\pi, giving the tent function; its sine coefficients in x at fixed \xi are \frac{2}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\sin n\xi}{n^2}, which are the coefficients of the series. (b) u = \int_0^\pi G(x, \xi)\,d\xi = x(\pi - x)/2. (c) With u(0, x) = x(\pi - x)/2 and u_t(0, x) =
0, u = \sum_{n\ \mathrm{odd}}\frac{4}{\pi n^3}\sin nx\cos nt (half the coefficients of Exercise 95). (d) For a partial sum the energy is \frac\pi4\sum_nn^2b_n^2, independent of t, since the cross terms integrate to zero and \cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1:


x, xi, t = var("x xi t")
assume(xi > 0, xi < pi, x > 0, x < pi)
Ga, Gb = x * (pi - xi) / pi, xi * (pi - x) / pi
print("(a) slope jump at x = xi:", (diff(Gb, x) - diff(Ga, x)).subs(x=xi).simplify_full(), "| continuity:", bool((Ga - Gb).subs(x=xi) == 0))
coef = lambda n: (2 / pi * (integrate(Ga * sin(n * x), x, 0, xi) + integrate(Gb * sin(n * x), x, xi, pi))).simplify_full()   # x < xi on [0, xi], x > xi on [xi, pi]
print("    sine coefficients of G(., xi) for n = 1, 2, 3:", [coef(n) for n in range(1, 4)], "| equal 2 sin(n xi)/(pi n^2):", all(bool((coef(n) - 2 * sin(n * xi) / (pi * n ** 2)).simplify_full() == 0) for n in range(1, 4)))
u0 = (integrate(Gb, xi, 0, x) + integrate(Ga, xi, x, pi)).simplify_full()   # int_0^pi G(x, xi) * 1 dxi: xi < x uses Gb, xi > x uses Ga
print("(b) static shape under f = 1:", u0, "| -u'' = 1 and u(0) = u(pi) = 0:", bool(-diff(u0, x, 2) == 1), bool(u0.subs(x=0) == 0), bool(u0.subs(x=pi) == 0))
b = lambda n: (2 / pi * integrate(u0 * sin(n * x), x, 0, pi)).simplify_full()
N = 5
u = sum(b(n) * sin(n * x) * cos(n * t) for n in range(1, N + 1))
print("(c) b_1..b_5:", [b(n) for n in range(1, 6)], "| u_tt = u_xx:", bool((diff(u, t, 2) - diff(u, x, 2)).simplify_full() == 0), "| u_t(0, x) = 0:", bool(diff(u, t).subs(t=0) == 0))
energy = (integrate(diff(u, t) ** 2 + diff(u, x) ** 2, x, 0, pi) / 2).simplify_full()
print("(d) energy of the partial sum:", energy, "| constant in t:", bool(diff(energy, t) == 0), "| equals (pi/4) sum n^2 b_n^2:", bool((energy - pi / 4 * sum(n ** 2 * b(n) ** 2 for n in range(1, N + 1))).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
(a) slope jump at x = xi: -1 | continuity: True
    sine coefficients of G(., xi) for n = 1, 2, 3: [2*sin(xi)/pi, cos(xi)*sin(xi)/pi, 2/9*(4*cos(xi)^2 - 1)*sin(xi)/pi] | equal 2 sin(n xi)/(pi n^2): True
(b) static shape under f = 1: 1/2*pi*x - 1/2*x^2 | -u'' = 1 and u(0) = u(pi) = 0: True True True
(c) b_1..b_5: [4/pi, 0, 4/27/pi, 0, 4/125/pi] | u_tt = u_xx: True | u_t(0, x) = 0: True
(d) energy of the partial sum: 205324/50625/pi | constant in t: True | equals (pi/4) sum n^2 b_n^2: True

/-- (a) On `[0, π]`: `u_a = x`, `u_b = π - x`, `W = x·(-1) - 1·(π - x) = -π`. -/
theorem string_wronskian (x : ℝ) : x * (-1) - 1 * (Real.pi - x) = -Real.pi

/-- The sine coefficients of `G(·, ξ) = x_<(π - x_>)/π`, `n = 1`: `∫₀^ξ x(π - ξ)/π sin x dx` … -/
theorem string_coeff1_left (ξ : ℝ) :
    ∫ x in (0 : ℝ)..ξ, x * (Real.pi - ξ) / Real.pi * Real.sin (1 * x) =
      (Real.pi - ξ) / Real.pi * (Real.sin (1 * ξ) / 1 ^ 2 - ξ * Real.cos (1 * ξ) / 1)

    ∫ x in ξ..Real.pi, ξ * (Real.pi - x) / Real.pi * Real.sin (1 * x) =
      ξ / Real.pi * ((Real.pi - ξ) * Real.cos (1 * ξ) / 1 + Real.sin (1 * ξ) / 1 ^ 2)
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.string_coeff1_right in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- `n = 2`: `∫₀^ξ x(π - ξ)/π sin 2x dx` … -/
theorem string_coeff2_left (ξ : ℝ) :
    ∫ x in (0 : ℝ)..ξ, x * (Real.pi - ξ) / Real.pi * Real.sin (2 * x) =
      (Real.pi - ξ) / Real.pi * (Real.sin (2 * ξ) / 2 ^ 2 - ξ * Real.cos (2 * ξ) / 2)
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.string_coeff2_left in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- … `∫_ξ^π ξ(π - x)/π sin 2x dx` … -/
theorem string_coeff2_right (ξ : ℝ) :
    ∫ x in ξ..Real.pi, ξ * (Real.pi - x) / Real.pi * Real.sin (2 * x) =
      ξ / Real.pi * ((Real.pi - ξ) * Real.cos (2 * ξ) / 2 + Real.sin (2 * ξ) / 2 ^ 2)
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.string_coeff2_right in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- … and the two pieces add to `sin nξ/n²`, so `(2/π)∫₀^π G sin nx = (2/π) sin nξ/n²`, the coefficient of the
eigenfunction series `(2/π)Σ sin nx sin nξ/n²`. -/
theorem string_coeff_sum (n ξ : ℝ) (hn : n ≠ 0) :
    (Real.pi - ξ) / Real.pi * (Real.sin (n * ξ) / n ^ 2 - ξ * Real.cos (n * ξ) / n) +
      ξ / Real.pi * ((Real.pi - ξ) * Real.cos (n * ξ) / n + Real.sin (n * ξ) / n ^ 2) = Real.sin (n * ξ) / n ^ 2
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.string_coeff_sum in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- (b) The static shape under `f = 1`: `∫₀ˣ ξ(π - x)/π dξ + ∫ₓ^π x(π - ξ)/π dξ = x(π - x)/2`; the first piece … -/
theorem string_static_left (x : ℝ) : ∫ ξ in (0 : ℝ)..x, ξ * (Real.pi - x) / Real.pi = x ^ 2 * (Real.pi - x) / (2 * Real.pi)
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.string_static_left in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- … the second piece … -/
theorem string_static_right (x : ℝ) :
    ∫ ξ in x..Real.pi, x * (Real.pi - ξ) / Real.pi = x * (Real.pi - x) ^ 2 / (2 * Real.pi)
KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises.string_static_right in KaluzaKlein/PartI/DifferentialEquations/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.DifferentialEquations.Exercises


/-- … and their sum. -/
theorem string_static_sum (x : ℝ) :

Exercise 127 (The Klein-Gordon equation from plane waves to the Yukawa potential) For (\Box + m^2)u = 0 with \Box = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2: (a) show that u = e^{-i\omega t}v(\mathbf x) reduces the equation to -\nabla^2v = (\omega^2 - m^2)v, a Helmholtz equation, and that for \omega < m the spherically symmetric solution decaying at infinity is the Yukawa function with mass \sqrt{m^2 - \omega^2}; (b) in a box [0, \pi]^3 with Dirichlet conditions, find the allowed frequencies from the separated modes and show that the lowest is \sqrt{3 + m^2}; (c) derive the one-dimensional retarded Green’s function of \partial_t^2 -
\partial_x^2 + m^2 in the form G = \tfrac12\theta(t - |x|)J_0(m\sqrt{t^2 - x^2}) by checking with Sage that J_0(m\sqrt{t^2 - x^2}) solves the homogeneous equation inside the light cone, and explain how the value \tfrac12 on the cone reproduces Example 115 for m = 0.

\partial_t^2u = -\omega^2u, so (-\omega^2 - \nabla^2 + m^2)v = 0; for \omega < m this is (-\nabla^2 +

title: Real analysis
text:
Real analysis is the theory behind calculus: what a limit is, when an infinite sum has a value, what it means for a function to be continuous, differentiable or integrable, and how these notions extend to functions of several variables. This chapter develops it in six sections, each on explicit examples. Real numbers, sequences and limits fixes the completeness of the real line and the vocabulary of limits, Cauchy sequences and monotone convergence. Series treats infinite sums, absolute convergence, the convergence tests and power series with their radius of convergence. Continuity and differentiability defines limits of functions, continuity, the derivative, and the mean value and Taylor theorems. The Riemann integral defines the integral as a limit of sums, proves the fundamental theorem of calculus and treats improper integrals, with the Gaussian integral as the central example. Calculus on \mathbb{R}^n extends derivatives to several variables, with the Jacobian matrix, the chain rule and the inverse function theorem. Multiple integrals and convergence of functions ends with the change of variables formula, uniform convergence and differentiation under the integral sign. Every statement is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions. The reader who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the sequences 1/n, (1 + 1/n)^n, the geometric and harmonic series, the exponential function and the Gaussian e^{-x^2} are the running examples.


The real numbers are the complete ordered field: every bounded set has a least upper bound. Everything else in analysis, limits, sums, derivatives and integrals, rests on this one property. This section defines suprema, the limit of a sequence and Cauchy sequences, proves the monotone convergence theorem, and checks the limits of the running examples in Sage.
For more on this topic, see Radożycki (2020, Ch. 3-5).


Before limits can be discussed at all one needs to know which numbers exist, and the answer is encoded in a single property of the real line. The definition below introduces the least upper bound of a set and states the completeness axiom, the promise that every bounded set has one.


Definition 1 (Supremum) A number M is an upper bound of a set S \subseteq \mathbb{R} if s \leq M for every s \in S; the set is bounded above if it has an upper bound. The supremum \sup S is the least upper bound: an upper bound M such that no M' < M is an upper bound. The completeness axiom of the real numbers states that every non-empty set bounded above has a supremum. The infimum \inf S, the greatest lower bound, is defined the same way with the inequalities reversed, and \inf S = -\sup(-S).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Test (kernel-checked, 4 instances); script ra-completeness-test.sage; Test (kernel-checked, 4 instances); script ra-sinf-eq-neg-ssup-neg-test.sage.
Lean.

/-- The completeness axiom: a non-empty set of reals bounded above has a least upper bound. -/
theorem completeness (S : Set ℝ) (hne : S.Nonempty) (hb : BddAbove S) : ∃ M, IsLUB S M

/-- The infimum is the negated supremum of the negated set: `inf S = -sup(-S)`. -/
theorem sInf_eq_neg_sSup_neg (S : Set ℝ) : sInf S = -sSup (-S)
KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences.sInf_eq_neg_sSup_neg in KaluzaKlein/PartI/RealAnalysis/Sequences.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Sequences

Sage. a least upper bound exists: Sage computes the supremum of each set, Lean checks it is the least upper bound; inf S = -sup(-S) on intervals, both sides computed exactly.










NoteExamples





The first thing to see is that a least upper bound may or may not belong to the set, and that an unbounded set has none at all. Sets with finitely many elements and intervals already show all three behaviours.

Example 1 (Finite sets and intervals) \sup\{1, 4, 2\} = 4, a maximum; \sup [0, 1) = 1, which is not an element of the set: a supremum need not be attained. \inf (0, \infty) = 0 and the set (0, \infty) has no supremum, being unbounded above.

The next example is the set of values of a sequence, where the supremum is approached but never reached. Verifying it requires the \varepsilon-argument that will reappear in the definition of a limit: nothing smaller than 1 can be an upper bound.

Example 2 (The set \{1 - 1/n\}) S = \{1 - 1/n : n = 1, 2, \dots\} = \{0, \tfrac12, \tfrac23, \dots\} has \sup S = 1: every element is below 1, and for every \varepsilon > 0 the element with n > 1/\varepsilon exceeds 1 - \varepsilon, so nothing smaller than 1 is an upper bound (Exercise 3). This is the typical way a supremum is a limit.

/-- `sup {1 - 1/n} = 1` in the `ε` form: every element is below `1`, and for `n > 1/ε` the element `1 - 1/n`
exceeds `1 - ε`. -/
theorem one_sub_inv_sup (ε : ℝ) (hε : 0 < ε) :
    (∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → 1 - 1 / (n : ℝ) < 1) ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 / ε < n → 1 - ε < 1 - 1 / (n : ℝ)

Why should completeness be an axiom rather than a theorem? The third example answers by exhibiting a bounded set of rationals with no rational least upper bound, so the property genuinely separates \mathbb{R} from \mathbb{Q}.

Example 3 (Why completeness is an axiom) The set \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q^2 < 2\} is bounded above in \mathbb{Q} but has no least upper bound in \mathbb{Q}, since \sqrt2 is irrational: the rationals are not complete. In \mathbb{R} its supremum is \sqrt2, and the completeness axiom is exactly what guarantees that such numbers exist.

The property that singled out 1 as the supremum of \{1 - 1/n\} is in fact a characterisation of the supremum, and it is the form in which completeness is used in proofs. The second exercise asks for both directions of the equivalence.

Exercise 2 (The \varepsilon-characterisation) Prove that M is the supremum of a non-empty set S if and only if M is an upper bound and for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an s \in S with s > M - \varepsilon.







NoteSolution





If M = \sup S and some \varepsilon > 0 had no s > M - \varepsilon, then M - \varepsilon would be an upper bound smaller than M, contradicting leastness. Conversely, if M is an upper bound with the \varepsilon property, any M' < M fails to be an upper bound: take \varepsilon = M - M' and the corresponding s > M'. So M is the least upper bound.

A sequence converges when its terms eventually stay as close to a number as one demands; the figure shows three sequences entering a band of half-width \varepsilon around their limits and never leaving it. The definition below makes “eventually” and “as close as demanded” precise with the two quantifiers \varepsilon and N, and records the rules for combining limits.






Figure 1: Three sequences and their limits: 1/n and (-1)^n/n converge to 0, (1 + 1/n)^n converges to e; the shaded bands have half-width \varepsilon = 0.3, and from n = 4 on every term lies inside its band. Generated by figures/sequence_limits.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


Definition 2 (Limit of a sequence) A sequence is a map n \mapsto a_n from the positive integers to \mathbb{R}. It converges to the limit L, written a_n \to L or \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L, if for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N such that |a_n - L| < \varepsilon for all n \geq N. A sequence with no limit diverges; a_n \to \infty means that for every M there is an N with a_n > M for n \geq N. Limits are unique, and a_n \to L, b_n \to M imply a_n + b_n \to L + M, a_n b_n \to LM and a_n / b_n \to L/M when M \neq 0 (the limit rules).

The definition of a limit requires knowing the limit in advance, which is often exactly what one does not know. The notion below tests convergence from the terms alone, by asking that they eventually cluster together, and completeness guarantees that this is enough.


Definition 3 (Cauchy sequence) A sequence is a Cauchy sequence if its terms eventually stay close to each other: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N such that |a_m - a_n| < \varepsilon for all m, n \geq N. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, and in \mathbb{R} every Cauchy sequence converges (the Cauchy criterion, equivalent to the completeness axiom): convergence can be tested without knowing the limit.

Theorem 1 (Monotone convergence theorem) An increasing sequence that is bounded above converges, to the supremum of its set of values; a decreasing sequence bounded below converges to the infimum. The two estimates behind the convergence of (1 + 1/n)^n are both binomial expansions, and the second exercise works them out in full. The same computation yields the bound e \leq 3.

Exercise 11 ((1 + 1/n)^n is increasing and bounded) Prove that a_n = (1 + 1/n)^n is increasing and that a_n < 3 for all n, and conclude that it converges.







NoteSolution





By the binomial theorem a_n = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} n^{-k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \tfrac{1}{k!}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1 -
j/n). Each product increases with n and a_{n+1} has one more positive term, so a_{n+1} > a_n. Each product is at most 1, so a_n \leq \sum_{k=0}^n 1/k! \leq 1 + \sum_{k=1}^n 2^{1-k} < 3. By the monotone convergence theorem a_n converges, and the limit is by definition e; the same bound shows e \leq 3.

A series is a sequence of partial sums; it converges when they do. This section defines series and absolute convergence, states the comparison and ratio tests, introduces power series and their radius of convergence, and evaluates the running series exactly in Sage: the geometric series, \sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6, the exponential series and the alternating harmonic series.
For more on this topic, see Radożycki (2020, Ch. 13 and 15).


An infinite sum has no meaning until one says which sequence is supposed to converge; the figure shows the partial sums of three series, two settling down and one drifting off like \log n. Definition 4 (Series) The series \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k with terms a_k is the sequence of partial sums s_n = a_1 + \dots +
a_n. It converges to the sum S if s_n \to S, and diverges otherwise. If the series converges then a_n = s_n - s_{n-1} \to 0; the converse fails.

Most series met in practice are not telescoping, and their convergence is decided by comparing them with a series that is already understood. The theorem below gives the two workhorses, comparison with a dominating series and the ratio test, whose proof reduces to a geometric comparison.


Theorem 2 (Comparison and ratio tests) Comparison test: if 0 \leq a_k \leq b_k and \sum b_k converges, then \sum a_k converges; if \sum a_k diverges, so does \sum b_k. A power series converges on an interval centred at x_0, and the half-length of that interval is determined by the coefficients alone. The definition below names it and gives two formulas for computing it.


Definition 7 (Radius of convergence) The radius of convergence R \in [0, \infty] of \sum c_k (x - x_0)^k is the number such that the series converges absolutely for |x - x_0| < R and diverges for |x - x_0| > R; it is given by R = 1/\limsup |c_k|^{1/k}, and by R = \lim |c_k / c_{k+1}| when this limit exists. At the endpoints |x - x_0| = R anything can happen.

Limits of functions are limits of sequences of values; continuity says the limit is the value, differentiability that the function is linear to first order. This section defines both, states the mean value theorem and Taylor’s theorem, and checks derivatives, Taylor polynomials and remainders in Sage, with \sin x and e^x as the running examples.
For more on this topic, see Cheung (2024, Ch. 2, Ch. 4) and Radożycki (2020, Ch. 7-8, Ch. 9-12).


What a function approaches near a point concerns the values nearby, not the value at the point itself. The definition below is the \varepsilon-\delta version, its reformulation through sequences, and the one-sided and infinite variants.


Definition 8 (Limit of a function) For f defined near a (not necessarily at a), \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L means: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is a \delta > 0 such that |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon whenever 0 < |x - a| < \delta. Equivalently, f(x_n)

Continuity at a point means that the limit equals the value, and continuity on an interval has strong consequences. The definition below records the algebraic rules and the two theorems on closed bounded intervals.


Definition 9 (Continuous function) f is continuous at a if \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a), and continuous on a set if it is continuous at every point of it. Sums, products, quotients with non-zero denominator and compositions of continuous functions are continuous; polynomials, \exp, \sin, \cos are continuous on \mathbb{R}, \log on (0, \infty). A continuous function on a closed bounded interval [a, b] is bounded, attains its maximum and minimum (extreme value theorem) and takes every value between f(a) and f(b) (intermediate value theorem).

Two facts about continuous functions, composition and the fixed-point property on [0, 1], are proved from the sequential characterisation and the intermediate value theorem. The second exercise asks for both.

Exercise 38 (Composition and the intermediate value theorem) Prove that the composition of continuous functions is continuous, and that a continuous f : [0, 1] \to [0, 1] has a fixed point.







NoteSolution





If x_n \to a then f(x_n) \to f(a) by continuity of f, and then g(f(x_n)) \to g(f(a)) by continuity of g at f(a): the sequential characterisation gives continuity of g \circ f. Definition 10 (Derivative) f is differentiable at a if the difference quotient (f(a + h) - f(a))/h has a limit as h \to 0; the limit is the derivative f'(a) = \frac{df}{dx}(a), the slope of the tangent line, and f(a + h) = f(a) + f'(a)h +
o(h). A differentiable function is continuous. The derivative obeys the sum, product, quotient and chain rules: (fg)' = f'g + fg', (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g^2, (g \circ f)' = (g' \circ f)\,f', and (f^{-1})'(y) =
1/f'(x) at y = f(x) when f'(x) \neq 0.

The derivative at a point controls the function near it; the theorem below makes this global, relating the increment over an interval to the derivative at some interior point. It is proved from the extreme value theorem through Rolle’s theorem, and its consequences are the ones used throughout the book.


Theorem 3 (Mean value theorem) If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there is a c \in (a, b) with f(b) - f(a) =
f'(c)(b - a). Proof. The function g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}(x - a) vanishes at a and b; by the extreme value theorem it attains a maximum or minimum at an interior point c (unless it is constant, when any c works), and there g'(c) = 0 (Rolle’s theorem), which is the claim. Consequences: f' = 0 on an interval forces f constant, f' > 0 forces f increasing, and |f'| \leq M gives |f(x) - f(y)| \leq M|x - y|.

The tangent line is the first-order approximation; higher-order approximations by polynomials come with an explicit remainder. The theorem below gives the Taylor polynomial and the Lagrange form of the error, which is what makes the approximation usable.


Theorem 4 (Taylor’s theorem) If f has n + 1 continuous derivatives near a, then f(a + h) = T_n(h) + R_n(h) with the Taylor polynomial T_n(h) = \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!} h^k and the Lagrange remainder R_n(h) =
\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!} h^{n+1} for some c between a and a + h; in particular |R_n(h)| \leq
\frac{M}{(n+1)!}|h|^{n+1} if |f^{(n+1)}| \leq M on the interval. Proof. Apply the mean value theorem (in Cauchy’s form) to f - T_n and h^{n+1} repeatedly, n + 1 times.

The integral measures the area under a graph as a limit of sums of rectangles; the fundamental theorem of calculus turns it into the inverse of differentiation. This section defines the Riemann integral and antiderivatives, proves the fundamental theorem, treats improper integrals, and computes the Gaussian integral \int e^{-x^2}dx =
\sqrt\pi, the integral behind every Gaussian probability and every free field theory.
For more on this topic, see Radożycki (2020, Ch. 14).


The area under a graph is approximated from below and from above by rectangles, and the figure shows both approximations for x^2 on [0, 1] closing in as the subintervals shrink. The definition below makes this the definition of the integral, and lists the functions for which the two approximations meet and the basic properties of the result.






Figure 4: Lower (blue) and upper (red) Riemann sums of x^2 on [0, 1] with n = 4 and n = 16 subintervals; both converge to the integral \tfrac13, and their difference is 1/n. Generated by figures/riemann_sums.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


Definition 11 (Riemann integral) For f bounded on [a, b] and a partition a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b, the lower and upper sums are L = \sum_k m_k (x_k - x_{k-1}) and U = \sum_k M_k (x_k - x_{k-1}) with m_k, M_k the infimum and supremum of f on [x_{k-1}, x_k]. f is Riemann integrable if \sup L = \inf U over all partitions, and the common value is the integral \int_a^b f(x)\,dx. Continuous functions, and bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities, are integrable; the integral is linear, monotone (f \leq g implies \int f \leq \int g) and additive over intervals, and \int_a^b f = -\int_b^a f.

The definition’s claim that functions with finitely many discontinuities are integrable rests on enclosing each jump in a small subinterval. The last exercise proves this for step functions and for a single jump.

The two halves of the section, the integral as a limit of sums and the antiderivative, are connected by the fundamental theorem, which is why both are called integration. The theorem below states both directions and proves them from continuity and the mean value theorem.


Theorem 5 (Fundamental theorem of calculus) If f is continuous on [a, b], then F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt is differentiable with F' = f (every continuous function has an antiderivative), and for any antiderivative G of f, \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = G(b) - G(a). Proof. F(x + h) - F(x) = \int_x^{x+h} f(t)\,dt lies between h\min f and h\max f over [x, x + h], and both bounds tend to h f(x) by continuity, so F'(x) = f(x). Then G - F is constant (Example 44), and G(b) - G(a) =
F(b) - F(a) = F(b).

When both limits of an integral depend on x the chain rule enters; when the integrand does too, more care is needed. The second exercise has one case of each, the latter being a solution formula for y'' = f.

Exercise 59 (Differentiating with variable limits) Compute \frac{d}{dx}\int_{x}^{x^2} e^{-t^2}dt and \frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x (x - t) f(t)\,dt.







NoteSolution





By the fundamental theorem and the chain rule, \frac{d}{dx}\int_{u(x)}^{v(x)} g(t)\,dt = g(v)v' - g(u)u': here 2x e^{-x^4} - e^{-x^2}. For the second, expand \int_0^x (x - t)f(t)\,dt = x\int_0^x f - \int_0^x t f(t)\,dt; differentiating gives \int_0^x f(t)\,dt + x f(x) - x f(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt, and differentiating again gives f(x): this integral is the solution of y'' = f with y(0) = y'(0) = 0 (Ordinary differential equations).

The Riemann integral is defined for bounded functions on bounded intervals, and many important integrals, the Gaussian among them, are neither. The definition below extends the integral by a limit and gives the comparison test and the p-integrals as benchmarks.


Definition 13 (Improper integral) An improper integral extends the Riemann integral to unbounded intervals or unbounded integrands by a limit: \int_a^\infty f = \lim_{b \to \infty}\int_a^b f and \int_a^b f = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\int_{a+\varepsilon}^b
f when f is unbounded near a; the integral converges if the limit exists. The comparison test holds: 0
\leq f \leq g with \int g convergent forces \int f convergent, and \int_1^\infty dx/x^p converges exactly for p > 1, \int_0^1 dx/x^p exactly for p < 1.

Functions of several variables are differentiated one variable at a time, and the partial derivatives assemble into the Jacobian matrix, the linear map that approximates the function near a point. This section collects the notions that differential geometry transports to manifolds through charts: partial derivatives, smooth maps, the Jacobian, the chain rule and diffeomorphisms, with the polar map of the plane as running example. Freezing all variables but one turns a function of several variables into a function of one, which can be differentiated as in Definition 10. The partial derivatives obtained this way are the building blocks of everything that follows.


Definition 14 (Partial derivative) For f : U \to \mathbb{R} on an open set U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n, the partial derivative with respect to x^i at p is the derivative of f along the i-th coordinate line, \partial_i f(p) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(p + h e_i) - f(p)}{h}, when the limit exists. The row (\partial_1 f, \dots, \partial_n f) is the gradient \nabla f.

The partial derivatives of a map with m components in n variables fill an m \times n matrix, which is the matrix of the best linear approximation of the map. Composing two maps multiplies their linear approximations, which is the chain rule in matrix form. It is the single most used theorem of this chapter: every change of coordinates on a manifold is an instance.

Definition 19 (Uniform convergence) A sequence of functions f_n converges pointwise to f on a set S if f_n(x) \to f(x) for every x \in S, and uniformly if \sup_{x \in S}|f_n(x) - f(x)| \to 0: one N works for all x at once. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, and uniform convergence on [a, b] allows the exchange \lim \int_a^b f_n =

An integral depending on a parameter can be differentiated by differentiating the integrand, under a mild condition; the rule generates families of integrals from one and is Feynman’s favourite trick. The theorem below states it, and the Gaussian moments are its first application.


Theorem 8 (Differentiation under the integral sign) If f(x, a) and \partial_a f(x, a) are continuous on [c, d] \times I, then F(a) = \int_c^d f(x, a)\,dx is differentiable on I with F'(a) = \int_c^d \partial_a f(x, a)\,dx (the Leibniz rule). theorem wallis_product (k : ℕ) :
    ((2 : ℝ) * k + 1) / (2 * k + 2) * (π / 2) ≤ Real.Wallis.W k ∧ Real.Wallis.W k ≤ π / 2
KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Exercises.wallis_product in KaluzaKlein/PartI/RealAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.RealAnalysis.Exercises
