title: Linear algebra
text:
A multilinear map takes several vectors and covectors and returns a number, linearly in each; equivalently it is an array of components that transforms in a fixed way under a change of basis. This section defines tensors on a single vector space V: multilinear maps, the tensor product space, elementary tensors, tensors of mixed type, their components and their contractions, with a closing proposition on the dimension of a tensor product.
For more on this topic, see Axler (2024).


Linear functionals take one vector and bilinear forms take two; the next step is to allow any number of arguments. The definition requires linearity in each slot separately, and the determinant is the picture to keep in mind.


Definition 15 (Multilinear map) A map T : V_1 \times \dots \times V_k \to \mathbb{R} is multilinear (k-linear) if it is linear in each argument when the others are held fixed. Bilinear forms (Definition 11) are the case k = 2, linear functionals the case k = 1.







TipVerification

/-- The determinant is linear in each row (here: the first row of a `3 × 3` matrix). -/
theorem det_linear_first_row (a b c a' b' c' t d e f g h i : ℝ) :
    Matrix.det !![a + t * a', b + t * b', c + t * c'; d, e, f; g, h, i] =
      Matrix.det !![a, b, c; d, e, f; g, h, i] + t * Matrix.det !![a', b', c'; d, e, f; g, h, i]

/-- The determinant as mathlib's alternating multilinear map of the rows. -/
theorem det_is_alternating {n : ℕ} (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) :
    Matrix.detRowAlternating (fun i => A i) = A.det

Seen as a function of its n columns, \det is multilinear and alternating. The example records both properties and names it as the volume form of Differential forms.

Example 58 (The determinant) (v_1, \dots, v_n) \mapsto \det(v_1 | \dots | v_n) on \mathbb{R}^n is n-linear, and alternating: it changes sign when two arguments are swapped. It is the volume form of Differential forms.

Multiplying the values of several covectors gives a multilinear map, one factor per argument. The example gives the trilinear case, which is an elementary tensor of covectors in disguise.

Example 59 (Products of functionals) For covectors \alpha, \beta, \gamma, (u, v, w) \mapsto \alpha(u)\beta(v)\gamma(w) is trilinear; its value is a product of three linear functions, one of each argument.

    (α ⬝ᵥ (u + t • u')) * (β ⬝ᵥ v) * (γ ⬝ᵥ w) =
      (α ⬝ᵥ u) * (β ⬝ᵥ v) * (γ ⬝ᵥ w) + t * ((α ⬝ᵥ u') * (β ⬝ᵥ v) * (γ ⬝ᵥ w))

The Riemann tensor is a four-linear map at each point, with one covector slot and three vector slots. The example also shows a function of two vectors, sectional curvature, that is not multilinear, to mark the boundary of the notion.

Example 60 (Curvature) The Riemann tensor at a point (The Riemann tensor) is a 4-linear map R(\alpha, u, v, w) = \alpha(R(v, w) u) taking one covector and three vectors; the quantity “the sectional curvature of the plane of v and w” is a function of two vector arguments that is not bilinear but a ratio of multilinear expressions.

Trilinearity on \mathbb{R}^3 is tested slot by slot. The exercise presents three expressions built from dot and cross products and asks which are trilinear, naming the slot that fails.

Exercise 58 (Which maps are trilinear?) Decide which of the following maps \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} are trilinear: (u, v, w) \mapsto u \cdot (v \times w); (u, v, w) \mapsto |u|\,(v \cdot w); (u, v, w) \mapsto (u
\cdot v)(v \cdot w).







NoteSolution





The triple product u \cdot (v \times w) = \det(u | v | w) is trilinear. |u|\,(v \cdot w) is not linear in u (|{-u}| = |u|, not -|u|). (u \cdot v)(v \cdot w) is quadratic in v: replacing v by 2v multiplies it by 4, not 2.

A trilinear map on \mathbb{R}^3 has 27 components, most of which may vanish. The exercise computes them for a simple instance, counts them, and evaluates the map by contracting components with arguments, in SageManifolds.

Exercise 59 (Components of a trilinear map) For T(u, v, w) = u^1 v^2 w^3 - u^2 v^1 w^3 on \mathbb{R}^3, find the components T_{ijk} = T(e_i, e_j, e_k), count how many components a trilinear map on \mathbb{R}^3 has, and evaluate T on u = (1, 2, 3), v = (0, 1, -
1), w = (2, 0, 1).







NoteSolution





T_{123} = 1, T_{213} = -1, all other 25 of the 3^3 = 27 components vanish; T(u, v, w) = T_{ijk} u^i v^j
w^k = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 0 \cdot 1 = 1. In SageManifolds’ free-module tensors:

T = V.tensor((0, 3), name="T")
T[0, 1, 2] = 1; T[1, 0, 2] = -1

When two arguments of an alternating map coincide its value is zero, and conversely a form that vanishes on the diagonal is antisymmetric. The exercise asks for both proofs and connects them to singular matrices with repeated columns.

Exercise 60 (Alternating maps vanish on repeated arguments) Show that an alternating bilinear or multilinear map vanishes whenever two of its arguments coincide, and conversely that a bilinear form with B(v, v) = 0 for all v is antisymmetric.







NoteSolution





Swapping two equal arguments changes nothing but, by the alternating property, changes the sign: T(\dots, v,
\dots, v, \dots) = -T(\dots, v, \dots, v, \dots), so the value is 0. Conversely, 0 = B(v + w, v + w) = B(v, v) +
B(v, w) + B(w, v) + B(w, w) = B(v, w) + B(w, v). For the determinant this says that a matrix with two equal columns is singular.

Bilinear maps on pairs of covectors form a vector space, and this is the tensor product. The definition gives its basis and its dimension, the product of the two dimensions; the figure above shows its elements as arrays.


Definition 16 (Tensor product space) The tensor product V \otimes W of two finite-dimensional vector spaces is the vector space of bilinear maps V^* \times W^* \to \mathbb{R}. If e_i is a basis of V and f_a a basis of W, the bilinear maps e_i \otimes
f_a defined by (e_i \otimes f_a)(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha(e_i)\beta(f_a) form a basis of V \otimes W, so \dim (V \otimes W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W.

The tensor product of two vectors is the simplest element of the tensor product space. The definition gives its components, the products v^i w^a, and names the tensors of this form elementary; a general tensor is a sum of elementary ones.


Definition 17 (Elementary tensor) The tensor product of vectors v \in V, w \in W is the element v \otimes w \in V \otimes W with (v \otimes w)(\alpha, \beta) = \alpha(v)\beta(w); it is bilinear in (v, w), and its components are the products v^i w^a. Tensors of the form v \otimes w are elementary (or decomposable); a general tensor is a sum of them.

A sum of two elementary tensors is elementary only under a proportionality condition. The exercise asks for the proof and for a counterexample, and identifies the rank of the component matrix with the minimal number of elementary terms.

Exercise 66 (When is a sum of two elementary tensors elementary?) Show that u \otimes v + w \otimes z is elementary if w is a multiple of u or z a multiple of v, and that e_1 \otimes e_1 + e_2 \otimes e_2 is not elementary.







NoteSolution





If w = \lambda u, bilinearity gives u \otimes v + \lambda u \otimes z = u \otimes (v + \lambda z); similarly for z = \mu v. The component matrix of e_1 \otimes e_1 + e_2 \otimes e_2 is \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, 0) of rank 2, while an elementary tensor has rank at most 1 (Exercise 64), so it is not elementary. The rank of the component matrix is the smallest number of elementary terms needed.

A tensor’s components are its values on dual-basis and basis vectors, one index per slot. The definition gives the formula and the transformation rule: upper indices transform with A^{-1}, lower ones with A.


Definition 19 (Components of a tensor) The components of a type (r, s) tensor T in a basis e_i with dual basis e^j are the numbers T^{i_1 \dots i_r}{}_{j_1 \dots j_s} = T(e^{i_1}, \dots, e^{i_r}, e_{j_1}, \dots, e_{j_s}), so that T =
T^{i_1 \dots i_r}{}_{j_1 \dots j_s}\, e_{i_1} \otimes \dots \otimes e^{j_s}. Under a change of basis e'_i = A^j{}_i e_j, each upper index transforms with A^{-1} and each lower index with A.

The invariance of the trace follows from the cyclic property \mathrm{tr}(XY) = \mathrm{tr}(YX). The exercise asks for the proof and for its consequence for type (1, 1) tensors.

Exercise 73 (The trace does not depend on the basis) Prove that \mathrm{tr}(A^{-1} T A) = \mathrm{tr}\, T for every invertible A, and conclude that the contraction of a type (1, 1) tensor does not depend on the basis.

A type (2, 2) tensor admits four single contractions and two full ones. The exercise asks for the count and for the specific contraction of an elementary tensor that gives \alpha(u)\beta(v).

Exercise 74 (How many contractions?) How many distinct contractions does a tensor of type (2, 2) admit, and what are their types? Which contraction of T^{ij}{}_{kl} = u^i v^j \alpha_k \beta_l gives \alpha(u)\,\beta(v)?







NoteSolution





One contraction pairs one of the two upper indices with one of the two lower ones: 2 \cdot 2 = 4 contractions, each of type (1, 1); contracting again gives two full contractions of type (0, 0). For the elementary tensor, contracting i with k and j with l gives u^i\alpha_i\, v^j\beta_j = \alpha(u)\beta(v); contracting i with l and j with k gives \beta(u)\alpha(v) instead.

SageManifolds’ trace and contract methods implement contractions. The exercise computes the trace of the running type (1, 1) tensor, a partial contraction of a type (2, 1) tensor, and a(u).

Exercise 75 (Contractions in Sage) With a free module of rank 3, compute the trace of the type (1, 1) tensor of Example 73, contract a type (2, 1) tensor S^{ij}{}_k over i and k, and recover a(u) as a contraction.







NoteSolution





trace() contracts the two indices of a type (1, 1) tensor; trace(0, 2) contracts the first and third index positions of S, leaving a vector; a.contract(u) is a_i u^i:

V = FiniteRankFreeModule(QQ, 3, name="V")
e = V.basis("e")
T = V.tensor((1, 1), name="T"); T[:] = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 3, 1], [0, 0, 5]]
print("trace of T (type (1, 1)):", T.trace(), "= 1 + 3 + 5")
S = V.tensor((2, 1), name="S")
S[0, 0, 0] = 1; S[1, 0, 1] = 2; S[2, 1, 2] = 3; S[0, 2, 0] = 4
c = S.trace(0, 2)   # contract the first (upper) index with the third (lower) one
print("S^{ij}_k contracted over i = k gives the vector with components", c.comp(e)[:], "of type", c.tensor_type())
a = V.linear_form(name="a"); a[:] = [1, 0, -1]; u = V([1, 2, 3], basis=e, name="u")
print("the pairing a_i u^i as a contraction:", a.contract(u), "= a(u) =", a(u))
Output:
trace of T (type (1, 1)): 9 = 1 + 3 + 5
S^{ij}_k contracted over i = k gives the vector with components [3, 3, 4] of type (1, 0)
the pairing a_i u^i as a contraction: -2 = a(u) = -2

Example 76 (Counting the basis) The e_i \otimes e_j with i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\} are nine tensors; they are independent because the component array of \sum c^{ij} e_i \otimes e_j is (c^{ij}), and they span because every bilinear map on V^* \times V^* is determined by its nine values on pairs of dual basis vectors.

A tensor product of spaces of different dimensions has rectangular component arrays. The exercise asks for the dimension of \mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3, its basis, and the shape of its arrays.

Exercise 76 (A rectangular tensor product) Find \dim(\mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3) and list its basis; what shape do the component arrays have?







NoteSolution





2 \cdot 3 = 6, with basis e_i \otimes f_a for i = 1, 2 and a = 1, 2, 3; the components T^{ia} form a 2 \times 3 matrix, and \mathbb{R}^2 \otimes \mathbb{R}^3 is the space of such matrices (equivalently of linear maps (\mathbb{R}^3)^* \to \mathbb{R}^2).

The proposition is stated for \mathbb{R}^3, but the same two facts prove the general case. The exercise asks for that proof and for its meaning in terms of matrices.

Exercise 77 (The dimension of V^* \otimes V) Prove that \dim(V^* \otimes V) = (\dim V)^2 for every finite-dimensional V, and explain the count in terms of the matrices of linear maps V \to V.







NoteSolution





The product formula gives \dim(V^* \otimes V) = \dim V^* \cdot \dim V, and \dim V^* = \dim V (Definition 9) turns it into (\dim V)^2. In a basis, V^* \otimes V is the space of linear maps V \to V (Example 63), whose matrices have n \cdot n = n^2 entries.

Inside V \otimes V the symmetric tensors and the antisymmetric ones have dimensions n(n+1)/2 and n(n-1)/2, as matrices do. The exercise asks for these counts for n = 2, 3, 4 and checks in Sage that they add up to n^2.

Exercise 78 (Symmetric and antisymmetric tensors) Find the dimensions of the symmetric (T^{ij} = T^{ji}) and antisymmetric (T^{ij} = -T^{ji}) tensors in V \otimes V for \dim V = 2, 3, 4, and check that they add up to n^2.







NoteSolution





n(n + 1)/2 and n(n - 1)/2, as for matrices (Exercise 17): 3 + 1 = 4, 6 + 3 = 9, 10 + 6 = 16:

for n in [2, 3, 4]:
    M = MatrixSpace(QQ, n, n)
    sym = span([vector(QQ, (m + m.transpose()).list()) for m in M.basis()], QQ)
    anti = span([vector(QQ, (m - m.transpose()).list()) for m in M.basis()], QQ)
    print("n =", n, ": symmetric", sym.dimension(), "= n(n+1)/2:", sym.dimension() == n * (n + 1) / 2, "; antisymmetric", anti.dimension(), "= n(n-1)/2:", anti.dimension() == n * (n - 1) / 2, "; sum", sym.dimension() + anti.dimension(), "= n^2")

n = 3 : symmetric 6 = n(n+1)/2: True ; antisymmetric 3 = n(n-1)/2: True ; sum 9 = n^2
n = 4 : symmetric 10 = n(n+1)/2: True ; antisymmetric 6 = n(n-1)/2: True ; sum 16 = n^2

title: Linear algebra
text:
NoteExercises





Three exercises that combine the sections of this chapter: a bilinear form seen through a non-standard basis, a linear map seen as a mixed tensor, and an antisymmetric tensor on Minkowski space.
The first integrative exercise looks at the dot product through the skewed basis f. Its Gram matrix, its signature and the lowering and raising of an index all appear, and the invariant v_i v^i must come out equal to the standard |v|^2.

Exercise 79 (The dot product in the basis f) Compute the Gram matrix G_{ij} = f_i \cdot f_j of the basis f = ((2, 1), (1, 2)), its signature, lower the index of the vector with f-coordinates (2, 1) and raise it back, and check that v_i v^i equals the standard |v|^2 of v = (5, 4).







NoteSolution





G = A^{\mathsf{T}} A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} (Exercise 45), positive definite with signature (2, 0, 0) and \det G = 9 = (\det A)^2. Lowering: v_i = G_{ij} v^j = (14, 13); raising with G^{-1} returns (2, 1); v_i v^i = 28 + 13 = 41 = 5^2 + 4^2:

A = matrix(QQ, [[2, 1], [1, 2]]).transpose()
G = A.transpose() * A
print("Gram matrix G_ij = f_i . f_j =", G.rows(), "; symmetric:", G.is_symmetric(), "; det =", G.det(), "; signature:", QuadraticForm(QQ, 2 * G).signature_vector())
c = vector(QQ, [2, 1])             # f-coordinates of v = (5, 4)
low = G * c
print("v^i = (2, 1) lowered: v_i = G_ij v^j =", low, "; raised again with G^-1:", G.inverse() * low)
v = A * c
print("|v|^2 = v_i v^i =", low * c, "= standard |v|^2 =", v * v)
Output:
Gram matrix G_ij = f_i . f_j = [(5, 4), (4, 5)] ; symmetric: True ; det = 9 ; signature: (2, 0, 0)
v^i = (2, 1) lowered: v_i = G_ij v^j = (14, 13) ; raised again with G^-1: (2, 1)
|v|^2 = v_i v^i = 41 = standard |v|^2 = 41










TipVerification

title: Complex analysis
text:
Complex analysis is the calculus of functions of a complex variable that are differentiable in the complex sense. Such functions are far more rigid than differentiable functions of two real variables: once they are differentiable they are infinitely differentiable, equal to their Taylor series, determined on a whole domain by their values on any small piece of it, and their integrals around closed curves are computed by adding up a few numbers, the residues, attached to the points where the function fails to be defined. This chapter develops that rigidity in five sections. Complex numbers and functions sets up the field \mathbb{C}, modulus and argument, the exponential and the many-valued logarithm with its branches and branch cuts. Holomorphic functions defines the complex derivative, derives the Cauchy-Riemann equations and their consequences for harmonic functions and angle-preserving maps. Contour integration defines integrals along curves and proves the two theorems of Cauchy that drive everything else, with Liouville’s theorem as a first consequence. Series and residues treats Taylor and Laurent expansions, classifies isolated singularities and states the residue theorem, the tool that evaluates the real integrals of physics (Fourier transforms, propagators, dispersion relations) in a few lines. Analytic continuation and special functions extends functions beyond their original domain of definition, introduces the Gamma, Beta and zeta functions that appear in every dimensional regularisation and every loop integral, and explains Wick rotation as a deformation of a contour of integration. Each definition is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions; each section closes with a proposition that collects its explicit computations, and the quoted theorems (Cauchy, Liouville, the residue theorem) are stated with their hypotheses and argued in the text. The reader who knows this material can skim the definitions and try the exercises; the conventions for the signature and for indices are fixed in Prerequisites and conventions, and the real analysis assumed here (limits, series, the Riemann integral, partial derivatives) is that of Real numbers, sequences and limits, Series, The Riemann integral and Calculus on \mathbb{R}^n.


The field \mathbb{C}, modulus and argument, the exponential and the logarithm, branches and branch cuts. The six notions of this section are the vocabulary of the chapter; the single proposition at its end, on the roots of unity, exercises all of them on explicit numbers.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 1-2, Ch. 4).






Figure 1: The complex plane. Left: z = 2 + i, its conjugate \bar z = 2 - i, its modulus |z| = \sqrt 5, its argument, and the six sixth roots of unity on the unit circle. Right: the imaginary part of the principal logarithm, \operatorname{Arg} z \in (-\pi, \pi], which jumps by 2\pi across the branch cut along the negative real axis. Generated by figures/complex_plane.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.




Definition 1 (Complex number) A complex number is a pair of real numbers written z = x + iy, with x = \operatorname{Re} z the real part, y = \operatorname{Im} z the imaginary part and i a symbol with i^2 = -1. Complex numbers are added componentwise and multiplied by expanding and using i^2 = -1: (x + iy)(u + iv) = (xu - yv) + i(xv + yu). With these operations the set \mathbb{C} of complex numbers is a field: every z \neq 0 has an inverse. The complex conjugate of z is \bar z = x - iy; conjugation respects sums and products, \overline{z + w} = \bar
z + \bar w and \overline{zw} = \bar z \bar w. As a real vector space (Vector spaces) \mathbb{C} is \mathbb{R}^2 with basis 1, i, and z is the point (x, y) of the complex plane (Figure 1).

Having the arithmetic, we need a notion of size. The modulus measures the distance of a point from the origin and turns the complex plane into the metric space on which limits, continuity and open sets make sense.


Definition 2 (Modulus) The modulus (or absolute value) of z = x + iy is |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{z \bar z}, the Euclidean length of the vector (x, y). It is multiplicative, |zw| = |z||w|, and satisfies the triangle inequality |z + w| \leq |z| + |w|; |z - w| is the distance between the points z and w, so \mathbb{C} is a metric space with the open discs D(z_0, r) = \{z : |z - z_0| < r\} as basic open sets (the topology of Topological spaces). A set is open, closed, compact or connected in \mathbb{C} exactly when it is so in \mathbb{R}^2; a domain is a non-empty open connected set.

The modulus is only half of the polar description of a complex number. The other half is the angle, and the subtlety that it is defined only up to multiples of 2\pi is the seed of every branch cut in this chapter.


Definition 3 (Argument) An argument of z \neq 0 is any real \theta with z = |z|(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta); the arguments of z form the set \arg z = \{\theta_0 + 2\pi k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}, and the one in (-\pi, \pi] is the principal argument \operatorname{Arg} z. The expression z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) with r = |z| is the polar form; multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments, \arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w as sets modulo 2\pi, which for the principal value holds only up to a multiple of 2\pi. The argument of 0 is undefined.

The exponential is the most important function of the chapter. Defined by its power series, it ties the polar form to the arithmetic of \mathbb{C} through Euler’s formula and makes trigonometry a chapter of complex analysis.


Definition 4 (Complex exponential) The complex exponential is e^z = \exp z = \sum_{n \geq 0} z^n/n!, a series that converges absolutely for every z (compare the ratio test of Series); equivalently, by multiplying the series, e^{x + iy} = e^x(\cos
y + i\sin y) (Euler’s formula). It satisfies e^{z + w} = e^z e^w, never vanishes, has |e^{x + iy}| = e^x and \arg e^{x + iy} \ni y, and is periodic with period 2\pi i. The polar form becomes z = r e^{i\theta}. The trigonometric and hyperbolic functions are defined from it: \cos z = \tfrac12(e^{iz} + e^{-iz}), \sin z =
\tfrac1{2i}(e^{iz} - e^{-iz}), \cosh z = \tfrac12(e^z + e^{-z}), \sinh z = \tfrac12(e^z - e^{-z}).

The third example evaluates cosine and sine at imaginary arguments. The result is that bounded real functions become unbounded in the plane, a fact Liouville’s theorem will later explain.

The second exercise derives the addition formulas of trigonometry from the exponential. Nothing about the argument requires z and w to be real, which is the point.

Exercise 11 (Addition formulas from the exponential) Derive \cos(z + w) = \cos z\cos w - \sin z\sin w and \cos^2 z + \sin^2 z = 1 for complex z, w from the definitions in Definition 4 and e^{z + w} = e^z e^w.

Inverting the exponential is the first place where many-valuedness becomes unavoidable. The logarithm is defined as a set of values, and a principal choice is made so that formulas have a definite meaning.


Definition 5 (Complex logarithm) A logarithm of z \neq 0 is any w with e^w = z; the logarithms of z form the set \log z = \ln|z| +
i\arg z = \{\ln|z| + i(\operatorname{Arg} z + 2\pi k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}. The principal logarithm is \operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + i\operatorname{Arg} z, with imaginary part in (-\pi, \pi]. Complex powers are defined through the logarithm, z^a = e^{a\log z} (many-valued in general), with the principal power e^{a
\operatorname{Log} z}; for integer a all values agree, for a = 1/n there are n values, the n-th roots.

The repeated appearance of a choice among many values deserves a name. A branch is a continuous selection of one value, and a branch cut is the price paid for it.


Definition 6 (Branch) Let F be a many-valued function such as \log or z^{1/n}. A branch of F on a domain D is a continuous function f : D \to \mathbb{C} with f(z) \in F(z) for every z \in D. A branch point is a point around which no branch exists on any punctured neighbourhood (circling it once changes the value), and a branch cut is a curve removed from the plane so that a branch exists on the remainder; the principal branch of \log and of z^a uses the cut (-\infty, 0], with branch point 0. The branch of \sqrt z on \mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty, 0] with \sqrt 1 = 1 is the principal square root.

The second exercise generalises the vanishing sum to arbitrary powers of the roots. The result is the discrete orthogonality relation behind the discrete Fourier transform.

Exercise 20 (Sums of powers of the roots) Prove that for n \geq 2 and \omega = e^{2\pi i/n}, \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega^{km} equals n if n divides m and 0 otherwise.







NoteSolution





If n \mid m then \omega^m = 1 and every term is 1. Otherwise \omega^m \neq 1 and the geometric sum is (1 - \omega^{mn})/(1 - \omega^m) = 0 since \omega^{mn} = (\omega^n)^m = 1. This orthogonality of the discrete exponentials is the finite version of \int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(m - n)\theta}\,d\theta = 2\pi\delta_{mn} in Exercise 57.

The complex derivative, the Cauchy-Riemann equations, harmonic functions and conformal maps. A function of a complex variable is differentiable when its difference quotient has a limit that does not depend on the direction of approach; this single requirement, written out in real and imaginary parts, is the pair of Cauchy-Riemann equations, and it forces the real and imaginary parts to be harmonic and the map to preserve angles.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 4).

Right: the image of the Cartesian grid under z \mapsto z^2; the image curves still meet at right angles, since the map is conformal away from z = 0. Generated by figures/domain_colouring.sage.

Definition 7 (Complex derivative) A function f : D \to \mathbb{C} on an open set D is complex differentiable at z_0 \in D if the limit f'(z_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)}{h}, \qquad h \in \mathbb{C}, exists; f'(z_0) is the complex derivative. The limit is over complex h, so the quotient must approach the same value along every direction. The sum, product, quotient and chain rules hold with the same proofs as in Continuity and differentiability, and (z^n)' = n z^{n-1}, (e^z)' = e^z.

theorem rules (f g : ℂ → ℂ) (f' g' z : ℂ) (hf : HasDerivAt f f' z) (hg : HasDerivAt g g' z) :

Differentiability at a single point is of little use. The useful notion is differentiability on an open set, which is what holomorphy means and what the rest of the chapter assumes.


Definition 8 (Holomorphic function) A function is holomorphic on an open set D if it is complex differentiable at every point of D; it is holomorphic at a point if it is holomorphic on some neighbourhood of it. The third exercise uses the Cauchy-Riemann equations, stated next, to show that holomorphic functions of constant modulus are constant. Read the theorem first and then return to it.

Exercise 27 (Holomorphic functions with constant modulus) Show that a holomorphic function on a domain with |f| constant is itself constant. (Use the Cauchy-Riemann equations of Theorem 1 once you have read them.)

The direction-independence of the complex derivative can be written as a pair of partial differential equations. These are the Cauchy-Riemann equations, the computational criterion for holomorphy.


Theorem 1 (Cauchy-Riemann equations) Write f(x + iy) = u(x, y) + iv(x, y) with u, v real. If f is complex differentiable at z_0 then the partial derivatives of u and v exist there and satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}, with f'(z_0) = u_x + iv_x. Conversely, if u, v are continuously differentiable on an open set and satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations there, then f is holomorphic on it. The equations say that the real Jacobian of (x, y)
\mapsto (u, v) has the form \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}, the matrix of multiplication by a +
ib = f' (Example 3).

def check(f):

    u, v = g.real_part().simplify_full(), g.imag_part().simplify_full()
    cr = bool((diff(u, x) - diff(v, y)).simplify_full() == 0) and bool((diff(u, y) + diff(v, x)).simplify_full() == 0)

The second exercise rewrites the equations with the Wirtinger derivatives. The slogan that a holomorphic function does not depend on \bar z becomes a literal statement.

Exercise 29 (The Wirtinger form) Define the operators \partial_z = \tfrac12(\partial_x - i\partial_y) and \partial_{\bar z} = \tfrac12(\partial_x +
i\partial_y). Show that the Cauchy-Riemann equations are equivalent to \partial_{\bar z} f = 0, and that then f' = \partial_z f. Check both on f = z^2 and on f = z\bar z.







NoteSolution





\partial_{\bar z}(u + iv) = \tfrac12\bigl[(u_x - v_y) + i(u_y + v_x)\bigr], which vanishes exactly when both Cauchy-Riemann equations hold; then \partial_z f = \tfrac12\bigl[(u_x + v_y) + i(v_x - u_y)\bigr] = u_x + iv_x =
f'. Treating z and \bar z as independent variables, \partial_{\bar z}(z^2) = 0 and \partial_z(z^2) = 2z, while \partial_{\bar z}(z\bar z) = z \neq 0 except at the origin (Exercise 23).

Exercise 32 (The mean value property) Assuming Cauchy’s integral formula (Theorem 3), show that a harmonic function on a disc equals at the centre the average of its values on any concentric circle inside the disc, and deduce that it cannot have a strict local maximum.

d\theta; its real part is the mean value property. If u(z_0) were strictly larger than all nearby values, the average over a small circle would be strictly smaller than u(z_0), contradicting the property.

The matrix form of the Cauchy-Riemann equations says that a holomorphic map acts locally as a rotation-scaling. Such maps preserve angles, which is the geometric content of holomorphy.


Definition 10 (Conformal map) A map f between open subsets of the plane is conformal at z_0 if it preserves the angle (including its orientation) between any two smooth curves through z_0. A holomorphic f with f'(z_0) \neq 0 is conformal at z_0: to first order it multiplies displacements by the complex number f'(z_0), a rotation by \arg f'(z_0) combined with a scaling by |f'(z_0)|. Conversely a continuously differentiable orientation-preserving conformal map is holomorphic with non-vanishing derivative. A bijective holomorphic map with holomorphic inverse between two domains is a conformal equivalence.

The second example is a Möbius transformation that maps the real line to the unit circle. These maps are the conformal equivalences of the disc and the half-plane.

Example 35 (A Möbius transformation) f(z) = \dfrac{z - i}{z + i} is holomorphic on \mathbb{C}\setminus\{-i\} with f'(z) = 2i/(z + i)^2 \neq 0. Maps of the form (az + b)/(cz + d) with ad - bc \neq 0 are the Möbius transformations; they send circles and lines to circles and lines.

Integrating a holomorphic function along a curve depends only on the endpoints when the function has a primitive, and Cauchy’s theorem says that it always does locally; the integral formula then expresses a holomorphic function inside a closed curve by its values on the curve, from which infinite differentiability, the Taylor series of Section 1.4 and Liouville’s theorem follow.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 6).

Definition 11 (Contour) A contour is a continuous, piecewise continuously differentiable map \gamma : [a, b] \to \mathbb{C}, together with its orientation (the direction of increasing t); its image is also called the contour. It is closed if \gamma(a) = \gamma(b) and simple if it does not cross itself except possibly at the endpoints. A simple closed contour separates the plane into a bounded interior and an unbounded exterior (the Jordan curve theorem), and it is positively oriented if the interior lies to the left as one travels along it (counter-clockwise for a circle). The reversed contour -\gamma is t \mapsto \gamma(a + b - t), and the length of \gamma is L(\gamma) = \int_a^b |\gamma'(t)|\,dt.

With contours defined, we can integrate along them. The contour integral is the natural generalisation of the Riemann integral, and the existence of a primitive makes it depend only on the endpoints.


Definition 12 (Contour integral) The contour integral of a continuous f along \gamma : [a, b] \to \mathbb{C} is \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz = \int_a^b f\bigl(\gamma(t)\bigr)\,\gamma'(t)\,dt, a complex number computed as two real Riemann integrals (The Riemann integral). It is unchanged by orientation-preserving reparametrisation, changes sign under reversal, \int_{-\gamma} f = -\int_\gamma f, and obeys the ML estimate \bigl|\int_\gamma f\,dz\bigr| \leq M L(\gamma) when |f| \leq M on \gamma. If f =
F' for a holomorphic F (a primitive) on an open set containing \gamma, then \int_\gamma f\,dz =
F(\gamma(b)) - F(\gamma(a)), which vanishes for closed \gamma. A closed contour integral is written \oint_\gamma.

The vanishing of closed integrals of functions with a primitive is now promoted to a theorem about all holomorphic functions. Cauchy’s theorem is the central result of complex analysis.


Theorem 2 (Cauchy’s theorem) Let \gamma be a simple closed contour and f holomorphic on an open set containing \gamma and its interior. Then \oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 0. More generally, if f is holomorphic on a domain D and \gamma can be continuously deformed within D to another closed contour \gamma' (or to a point), then \oint_\gamma f\,dz = \oint_{\gamma'} f\,dz (or 0): closed contour integrals of holomorphic functions depend only on the deformation class of the contour within the domain of holomorphy. Equivalently, a holomorphic function on a disc has a primitive there.

Exercise 48 (A wrong answer from a symbolic integrator) Sage’s symbolic integrate of the parametrised form of \oint_{|z| = 1} dz/(z - 3) returns -2\pi i, whereas Cauchy’s theorem gives 0 and numerical integration agrees. Find the error.

Cauchy’s theorem applied to f(z)/(z - z_0) gives a formula for the values of a holomorphic function inside a contour. Differentiating under the integral gives all derivatives at once.


Theorem 3 (Cauchy’s integral formula) Let \gamma be a positively oriented simple closed contour and f holomorphic on an open set containing \gamma and its interior. Then for every z_0 in the interior f(z_0) = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\,dz, \qquad f^{(n)}(z_0) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma
\frac{f(z)}{(z - z_0)^{n+1}}\,dz. In particular a holomorphic function is infinitely complex differentiable, and on a disc of radius r about z_0 on which |f| \leq M it satisfies the Cauchy estimates |f^{(n)}(z_0)| \leq n!\,M/r^n.

The second exercise completes the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra. The bound on 1/p uses compactness of discs, from Compact and connected spaces.

Exercise 53 (Factorising a polynomial completely) Complete the argument of Example 53: show that 1/p is bounded when p has no zeros, and that a polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity.







NoteSolution





For p(z) = a_n z^n + \dots + a_0 with a_n \neq 0, |p(z)| \geq |a_n||z|^n - \sum_{k<n}|a_k||z|^k \geq
\tfrac12|a_n||z|^n for |z| \geq R large, so |1/p| \leq 2/(|a_n|R^n) there; on the compact disc |z| \leq R the continuous function 1/p is bounded (Compact and connected spaces). Hence 1/p is bounded, entire if p has no zero, thus constant, which is absurd for n \geq 1. Given a root z_1, p(z) = (z - z_1)q(z) with \deg q = n -
1 by polynomial division, and induction on the degree gives n roots with multiplicity.

The third exercise proves the growth version of the theorem using the Taylor series of the next section. Only finitely many Taylor coefficients can survive the estimates.

Exercise 54 (Growth and degree) Prove the general form of Liouville’s theorem: an entire f with |f(z)| \leq C(1 + |z|)^n is a polynomial of degree at most n. (Apply the Cauchy estimates on circles of radius r \to \infty and use the Taylor series of Definition 13.)

Definition 13 (Taylor series) A power series about z_0 is \sum_{n \geq 0} a_n (z - z_0)^n; it converges absolutely for |z - z_0| < R and diverges for |z - z_0| > R, where R \in [0, \infty] is the radius of convergence, 1/R = \limsup |
a_n|^{1/n} (the root test of Series). Inside the disc of convergence the sum is holomorphic and may be differentiated term by term. Conversely, if f is holomorphic on the disc |z - z_0| < R, then on that disc f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{f^{(n)}(z_0)}{n!}(z - z_0)^n, its Taylor series, with coefficients given by Cauchy’s integral formula; the radius of convergence is at least the distance from z_0 to the nearest point where f fails to be holomorphic.

The third exercise derives the Taylor expansion from the integral formula. The geometric series does the work, and the Cauchy estimates reappear as bounds on the coefficients.

Exercise 60 (The Taylor expansion from the integral formula) Derive the Taylor series of f on |z - z_0| < r by expanding \frac1{w - z} = \frac1{(w - z_0)}\cdot\frac1{1 -
(z - z_0)/(w - z_0)} in Cauchy’s formula over |w - z_0| = r, and deduce |a_n| \leq M/r^n when |f| \leq M on the circle.







NoteSolution





For |z - z_0| < r = |w - z_0| the geometric series \sum_n (z - z_0)^n/(w - z_0)^{n+1} converges uniformly in w on the circle, so it may be integrated term by term: f(z) = \sum_n (z - z_0)^n\cdot\frac1{2\pi i}\oint

Taylor series describe a function near a point where it is holomorphic. Near a singular point, or on a ring between two singularities, one needs negative powers as well, and the resulting two-sided expansion is unique on each annulus.


Definition 14 (Laurent series) If f is holomorphic on the annulus r < |z - z_0| < R, then there it equals its Laurent series f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n (z - z_0)^n, \qquad a_n = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z - z_0| = \rho} \frac{f(z)}{(z -
z_0)^{n+1}}\,dz \quad (r < \rho < R), converging absolutely on the annulus; the coefficients are unique, and the part with n < 0 is the principal part. The same function has different Laurent series on different annuli about the same point.

The third exercise proves the uniqueness of the Laurent coefficients from the circle integrals. The orthogonality of Exercise 57 is exactly what is needed.

Exercise 63 (Uniqueness of the coefficients) Show that if f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} b_n (z - z_0)^n on an annulus, with the series converging uniformly on each circle inside it, then b_n equals the coefficient a_n of Definition 14.







NoteSolution





Multiply by (z - z_0)^{-m-1} and integrate over a circle in the annulus, exchanging sum and integral by uniform convergence: \oint f(z)(z - z_0)^{-m-1}\,dz = \sum_n b_n\oint (z - z_0)^{n-m-1}\,dz = 2\pi i\,b_m by Proposition 3 (only n = m survives). Hence b_m = a_m: however a Laurent expansion is found, by partial fractions, substitution or division, it is the Laurent expansion.

A point where a function is not defined but around which it is holomorphic is classified by its principal part. Three cases arise, from the harmless to the wild, and the classification decides what the residue theorem can do.


Definition 15 (Isolated singularity) A point z_0 is an isolated singularity of f if f is holomorphic on a punctured disc 0 < |z - z_0| < r but not defined (or not holomorphic) at z_0. According to the principal part of the Laurent series on the punctured disc, the singularity is removable (no negative powers: f extends holomorphically to z_0), a pole of order m (finitely many, the lowest being a_{-m}(z - z_0)^{-m} with a_{-m} \neq 0; then |f(z)|
\to \infty as z \to z_0), or essential (infinitely many). A function holomorphic on a domain except for poles is meromorphic; a simple pole is one of order 1.

Of all the Laurent coefficients, one has a special role. The coefficient of 1/(z - z_0) is the only one that a closed contour integral around z_0 detects, and it can be computed without finding the whole series.


Definition 16 (Residue) The residue of f at an isolated singularity z_0 is the coefficient a_{-1} of its Laurent series on a punctured disc about z_0, \operatorname{Res}_{z = z_0} f = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint f(z)\,dz over a small positively oriented circle. At a simple pole \operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f = \lim_{z \to z_0}(z - z_0)f(z), and if f = g/h with g(z_0) \neq 0, h(z_0) = 0, h'(z_0) \neq 0, then \operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f = g(z_0)/h'(z_0); at a pole of order m, \operatorname{Res}_{z = z_0} f = \frac1{(m - 1)!}\lim_{z \to z_0}\frac{d^{m-1}}{dz^{m-1}}\Bigl[(z - z_0)^m f(z)\Bigr].

Cauchy’s theorem for a function with finitely many isolated singularities inside the contour is the residue theorem. The contour is shrunk onto small circles around the singularities, each contributing 2\pi i times its residue.


Theorem 4 (Residue theorem) Let \gamma be a positively oriented simple closed contour and f holomorphic on an open set containing \gamma and its interior except at finitely many points z_1, \dots, z_k inside \gamma. The third exercise treats a pole on the contour, which requires an indentation. The half-residue rule it produces is the one behind principal-value integrals and the i\epsilon prescription.

Exercise 75 (\int_{-\infty}^\infty \sin x/x\,dx = \pi) Integrate e^{iz}/z over the contour consisting of [-R, -\epsilon], the small clockwise semicircle of radius \epsilon above 0, [\epsilon, R] and the large arc C_R. Show that the large arc contributes nothing as R \to \infty (accept Jordan’s lemma), that the small arc contributes -i\pi as \epsilon \to 0, and conclude.







NoteSolution





The contour encloses no singularity, so the total is 0. On the small arc z = \epsilon e^{i\theta}, \theta from \pi to 0: \int e^{iz}\,dz/z = \int_\pi^0 e^{i\epsilon e^{i\theta}}\,i\,d\theta \to -i\pi. Hence \lim\int_{|x| > \epsilon} e^{ix}\,dx/x = i\pi; the real part is a principal value of an odd function, zero, and the imaginary part gives \int_{-\infty}^\infty \sin x/x\,dx = \pi. A simple pole on the contour contributes half a residue, with the sign fixed by the direction of the indentation.

Analytic continuation, the Gamma and Beta functions, the zeta function in outline, Wick rotation as a contour deformation. A holomorphic function is determined by its values on any small set with a limit point, so a formula valid on a half-plane defines a function far beyond it; the Gamma and zeta functions are the standard examples, and the rotation of an integration contour from the real to the imaginary axis, Wick rotation, is the same principle applied to integrals.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 7-8).

Definition 17 (Analytic continuation) Let f be holomorphic on a domain D_1 and D_2 \supset D_1 a larger domain. An analytic continuation of f to D_2 is a holomorphic function on D_2 that agrees with f on D_1. By the identity theorem, two functions holomorphic on a domain that agree on a set with a limit point in the domain (a segment, a small disc, a convergent sequence) agree everywhere on it; hence an analytic continuation, if it exists, is unique. The continuation may fail to exist (a natural boundary) or may depend on the path along which it is carried out, in which case the continued function is many-valued and has branch points (Definition 6).

The factorial is defined on the non-negative integers. The Gamma function interpolates it by an integral that converges on a half-plane, and analytic continuation then extends it to the whole plane minus a sequence of poles.


Definition 18 (Gamma function) The Gamma function is \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt for \operatorname{Re} z > 0, where the integral converges and defines a holomorphic function. Integration by parts gives the recursion \Gamma(z + 1)
= z\Gamma(z), so \Gamma(n + 1) = n! for integers n \geq 0. Rewriting the recursion as \Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z +
1)/z continues \Gamma to \operatorname{Re} z > -1, then to \operatorname{Re} z > -2, and so on: \Gamma is meromorphic on \mathbb{C} with simple poles at z = 0, -1, -2, \dots of residue (-1)^n/n! at -n, and no zeros. It satisfies the reflection formula \Gamma(z)\Gamma(1 - z) = \pi/\sin\pi z, whence \Gamma(\tfrac12)
= \sqrt\pi.

The Riemann zeta function is the archetype of a function defined by a series on a half-plane and continued beyond it. Its values at negative integers, finite numbers assigned to divergent sums, are what zeta-function regularisation uses.


Definition 20 (Zeta function) The Riemann zeta function is \zeta(s) = \sum_{n \geq 1} n^{-s} for \operatorname{Re} s > 1, where the series converges absolutely (Series) and defines a holomorphic function. It has the Euler product \zeta(s) = \prod_p (1 - p^{-s})^{-1} over the primes, and it continues analytically to a meromorphic function on \mathbb{C} with a single simple pole at s = 1 of residue 1, satisfying the functional equation \zeta(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin(\tfrac{\pi s}2)\Gamma(1 - s)\zeta(1 - s). The continuation is outlined in Example 86; its values include \zeta(2) = \pi^2/6, \zeta(0) = -\tfrac12, \zeta(-1) = -
\tfrac1{12} and \zeta(-2n) = 0 for n \geq 1.

An integral over the real line of a function holomorphic in a sector can be moved to another ray through the origin. Rotating the real axis to the imaginary axis is called Wick rotation, and it converts oscillatory integrals into decaying ones.


Definition 21 (Wick rotation) Let f be holomorphic on an open set containing the closed first and third quadrants of the k^0-plane, except possibly at infinity, with |k^0 f(k^0)| \to 0 uniformly as |k^0| \to \infty in those quadrants. The Wick rotation is the identity \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(k^0)\,dk^0 = i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(ik^4)\,dk^4, obtained from Cauchy’s theorem on the closed contour made of the real axis, the imaginary axis traversed downward and two arcs at infinity in the first and third quadrants: the arcs vanish by the ML estimate and the contour encloses no singularity. The substitution k^0 = ik^4 (or t = -i\tau in position space) is the rotation to Euclidean signature: a Minkowski square (k^0)^2 - \mathbf{k}^2 becomes -\bigl((k^4)^2 +
\mathbf{k}^2\bigr), minus a Euclidean square.

The third integrative exercise evaluates the time-dependent propagator from the i\epsilon-displaced poles. Which pole contributes depends on the sign of the time, and the answer explains the Feynman prescription.

Exercise 99 (The propagator in time) Evaluate G(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \dfrac{dk^0}{2\pi}\,\dfrac{e^{-ik^0 t}}{(k^0)^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon} for t >
0 and for t < 0 by closing the contour in the half-plane where e^{-ik^0 t} decays (Exercise 89), and show that G(t) = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-iE|t|} as \epsilon \to 0. Which pole contributes for each sign of t, and what does the answer say about the frequencies that propagate forward and backward in time?







NoteSolution





The poles are k^0 = E - i\delta and k^0 = -E + i\delta with \delta = \epsilon/2E (Example 88). For t > 0, |e^{-ik^0 t}| = e^{t\operatorname{Im} k^0} decays in the lower half-plane, so close below (clockwise): G = \dfrac1{2\pi}\cdot(-2\pi i)\operatorname{Res}_{E - i\delta} = -i\,\dfrac{e^{-iEt}}{2E} in the limit. For t <
0 close above and pick up -E + i\delta: G = \dfrac1{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi i\cdot\dfrac{e^{iEt}}{-2E} = -i\,\dfrac{e^{-iE|t|}}{2E}. Hence G(t) = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-iE|t|}: the positive-frequency pole k^0 = +E propagates forward in time and the negative-frequency pole k^0 = -E backward, which is the content of the Feynman prescription and the reason the i\epsilon is placed as it is. The Wick-rotated version, t = -i\tau, is G = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-E|\tau|}, a decaying Euclidean propagator, consistent with Proposition 6 at \tau = 0 after the factor i from dk^0 =
i\,dk^4 is included.

title: Complex analysis
text:
The field \mathbb{C}, modulus and argument, the exponential and the logarithm, branches and branch cuts. The six notions of this section are the vocabulary of the chapter; the single proposition at its end, on the roots of unity, exercises all of them on explicit numbers.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 1-2, Ch. 4).






Figure 1: The complex plane. Left: z = 2 + i, its conjugate \bar z = 2 - i, its modulus |z| = \sqrt 5, its argument, and the six sixth roots of unity on the unit circle. Right: the imaginary part of the principal logarithm, \operatorname{Arg} z \in (-\pi, \pi], which jumps by 2\pi across the branch cut along the negative real axis. Generated by figures/complex_plane.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.




Definition 1 (Complex number) A complex number is a pair of real numbers written z = x + iy, with x = \operatorname{Re} z the real part, y = \operatorname{Im} z the imaginary part and i a symbol with i^2 = -1. Complex numbers are added componentwise and multiplied by expanding and using i^2 = -1: (x + iy)(u + iv) = (xu - yv) + i(xv + yu). With these operations the set \mathbb{C} of complex numbers is a field: every z \neq 0 has an inverse. The complex conjugate of z is \bar z = x - iy; conjugation respects sums and products, \overline{z + w} = \bar
z + \bar w and \overline{zw} = \bar z \bar w. As a real vector space (Vector spaces) \mathbb{C} is \mathbb{R}^2 with basis 1, i, and z is the point (x, y) of the complex plane (Figure 1).

NoteExamples





The definition is best absorbed by computing. The first example multiplies and divides two concrete numbers, and shows the one trick that division needs: clearing the denominator with its conjugate.

Example 1 (A product and a quotient) (2 + i)(3 - i) = 6 - 2i + 3i - i^2 = 7 + i, and \dfrac{1}{2 + i} = \dfrac{2 - i}{(2 + i)(2 - i)} = \dfrac{2 -
i}{5}: to divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which makes the denominator real.

The next example looks at what the new symbol i buys. Negative numbers acquire square roots, and polynomials that were irreducible over the reals split into linear factors.

Example 2 (Square roots of negative numbers) (\pm 2i)^2 = -4, so -4 has the two square roots \pm 2i; more generally every non-zero complex number has exactly two square roots, w and -w (Definition 6 below says which one deserves the name \sqrt z). x^2 + 1 = (x + i)(x - i) factorises over \mathbb{C} though not over \mathbb{R}.

The third example gives complex multiplication a geometric meaning that the chapter will use repeatedly. A complex number acts on the plane as a matrix of a very special shape, a rotation combined with a scaling.

Example 3 (Complex numbers as 2 \times 2 real matrices) The map x + iy \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} x & -y \\ y & x \end{pmatrix} turns sums into sums and products into matrix products (i becomes the rotation by 90^\circ, whose square is -1); the determinant of the matrix is x^2 +
y^2 = |z|^2 and its transpose represents \bar z. Multiplication by a fixed z is thus a rotation-scaling of the plane, the geometric fact behind Definition 10.

NoteExercises





The first exercise is pure practice with the arithmetic rules. It also introduces Sage’s exact Gaussian rationals, which will serve as the computational ground for most of the chapter.

Exercise 1 (Products, quotients and conjugates) Compute (2 + i)(3 - i), (1 + i)/(1 - i) and (1 + i)^8, and check on these numbers that \overline{zw} = \bar
z \bar w.







NoteSolution





(2 + i)(3 - i) = 7 + i; (1 + i)/(1 - i) = (1 + i)^2/2 = i; (1 + i)^2 = 2i, so (1 + i)^8 = (2i)^4 = 16. Sage works in the Gaussian rationals \mathbb{Q}(i) exactly:

z, w = 2 + i, 3 - i

print("(1 + i)/(1 - i) =", (1 + i)/(1 - i))
print("(1 + i)^8 =", (1 + i)^8)
print("conj(z w) == conj(z) conj(w):", (z*w).conjugate() == z.conjugate()*w.conjugate())
print("|z w| = |z| |w| (squared moduli, exact):", (z*w).norm() == z.norm()*w.norm(), " |z|^2 =", z.norm(), " |w|^2 =", w.norm())

The second exercise derives the small identities that convert between the Cartesian description (x, y) and the pair (z, \bar z). They are used silently in every later computation with real and imaginary parts.

Exercise 2 (Real and imaginary parts from the conjugate) Show that \operatorname{Re} z = \tfrac12(z + \bar z), \operatorname{Im} z = \tfrac1{2i}(z - \bar z), z \bar z
= x^2 + y^2, and that z is real exactly when z = \bar z.







NoteSolution





With z = x + iy: z + \bar z = 2x, z - \bar z = 2iy, and z\bar z = (x + iy)(x - iy) = x^2 - i^2 y^2 = x^2 +
y^2. z = \bar z means 2iy = 0, that is, y = 0. These identities let one translate any statement about (x, y) into one about (z, \bar z), which is how the Cauchy-Riemann equations are written as \partial f/\partial
\bar z = 0 in Exercise 29.

Having the arithmetic, we need a notion of size. The modulus measures the distance of a point from the origin and turns the complex plane into the metric space on which limits, continuity and open sets make sense.


Definition 2 (Modulus) The modulus (or absolute value) of z = x + iy is |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt{z \bar z}, the Euclidean length of the vector (x, y). It is multiplicative, |zw| = |z||w|, and satisfies the triangle inequality |z + w| \leq |z| + |w|; |z - w| is the distance between the points z and w, so \mathbb{C} is a metric space with the open discs D(z_0, r) = \{z : |z - z_0| < r\} as basic open sets (the topology of Topological spaces). A set is open, closed, compact or connected in \mathbb{C} exactly when it is so in \mathbb{R}^2; a domain is a non-empty open connected set.

The exponential is the most important function of the chapter. Defined by its power series, it ties the polar form to the arithmetic of \mathbb{C} through Euler’s formula and makes trigonometry a chapter of complex analysis.


Definition 4 (Complex exponential) The complex exponential is e^z = \exp z = \sum_{n \geq 0} z^n/n!, a series that converges absolutely for every z (compare the ratio test of Series); equivalently, by multiplying the series, e^{x + iy} = e^x(\cos
y + i\sin y) (Euler’s formula). It satisfies e^{z + w} = e^z e^w, never vanishes, has |e^{x + iy}| = e^x and \arg e^{x + iy} \ni y, and is periodic with period 2\pi i. The polar form becomes z = r e^{i\theta}. The trigonometric and hyperbolic functions are defined from it: \cos z = \tfrac12(e^{iz} + e^{-iz}), \sin z =
\tfrac1{2i}(e^{iz} - e^{-iz}), \cosh z = \tfrac12(e^z + e^{-z}), \sinh z = \tfrac12(e^z - e^{-z}).

Definition 5 (Complex logarithm) A logarithm of z \neq 0 is any w with e^w = z; the logarithms of z form the set \log z = \ln|z| +

\operatorname{Log} z}; for integer a all values agree, for a = 1/n there are n values, the n-th roots.

The second exercise characterises exactly when the principal logarithm is additive. The answer identifies the right half-plane as a region where no bookkeeping of branches is needed.

Exercise 14 (When does \operatorname{Log}(zw) = \operatorname{Log} z + \operatorname{Log} w?) Show that the principal logarithm is additive exactly when \operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w \in (-\pi,
\pi], and deduce that it is additive whenever \operatorname{Re} z > 0 and \operatorname{Re} w > 0.







NoteSolution





\ln|zw| = \ln|z| + \ln|w| always, and \operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w is an argument of zw; it is the principal one exactly when it lies in (-\pi, \pi]. Hence \operatorname{Log} is additive on the right half-plane, where it is also continuous and, as Section 1.2 shows, holomorphic.

The repeated appearance of a choice among many values deserves a name. A branch is a continuous selection of one value, and a branch cut is the price paid for it.


Definition 6 (Branch) Let F be a many-valued function such as \log or z^{1/n}. A branch of F on a domain D is a continuous function f : D \to \mathbb{C} with f(z) \in F(z) for every z \in D. A branch point is a point around which no branch exists on any punctured neighbourhood (circling it once changes the value), and a branch cut is a curve removed from the plane so that a branch exists on the remainder; the principal branch of \log and of z^a uses the cut (-\infty, 0], with branch point 0. The branch of \sqrt z on \mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty, 0] with \sqrt 1 = 1 is the principal square root.

Exercise 17 (A branch of the logarithm on the slit plane) Define a branch of \log on \mathbb{C}\setminus[0, +\infty) with \log(-1) = i\pi, give its values at i and -i, and compare them with the principal values.

The third exercise builds a branch of \sqrt{z^2 - 1} that looks like z at infinity. Such branches are the ones used in dispersion relations, where the discontinuity across the cut carries the physics.

Exercise 18 (A branch of \sqrt{z^2 - 1} behaving like z at infinity) Show that f(z) = z\sqrt{1 - 1/z^2}, with the principal square root, is a branch of \sqrt{z^2 - 1} on \mathbb{C}\setminus[-1, 1], that f(z) = z + O(1/z) as |z| \to \infty, and compute its values just above and just below the cut at z = 0.







NoteSolution





1 - 1/z^2 lies on (-\infty, 0] exactly when 1/z^2 \geq 1, that is, z \in [-1, 1]; off that segment the principal root is continuous, and f(z)^2 = z^2 - 1. For large |z|, \sqrt{1 - 1/z^2} = 1 - \tfrac1{2z^2} +
\dots, so f(z) = z - \tfrac1{2z} + \dots. At z = \pm i\epsilon, 1 - 1/z^2 = 1 + 1/\epsilon^2 > 0, so f(\pm
i\epsilon) = \pm i\epsilon\sqrt{1 + 1/\epsilon^2} \to \pm i: the branch jumps from i to -i across the cut at 0, by the amount 2i that makes the discontinuity integrals of Section 1.4 work.

The second exercise generalises the vanishing sum to arbitrary powers of the roots. The result is the discrete orthogonality relation behind the discrete Fourier transform.

Exercise 20 (Sums of powers of the roots) Prove that for n \geq 2 and \omega = e^{2\pi i/n}, \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega^{km} equals n if n divides m and 0 otherwise.







NoteSolution





If n \mid m then \omega^m = 1 and every term is 1. Otherwise \omega^m \neq 1 and the geometric sum is (1 - \omega^{mn})/(1 - \omega^m) = 0 since \omega^{mn} = (\omega^n)^m = 1. This orthogonality of the discrete exponentials is the finite version of \int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(m - n)\theta}\,d\theta = 2\pi\delta_{mn} in Exercise 57.

title: Complex analysis
text:
The complex derivative, the Cauchy-Riemann equations, harmonic functions and conformal maps. A function of a complex variable is differentiable when its difference quotient has a limit that does not depend on the direction of approach; this single requirement, written out in real and imaginary parts, is the pair of Cauchy-Riemann equations, and it forces the real and imaginary parts to be harmonic and the map to preserve angles.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 4).






Figure 2: Holomorphic functions seen in two ways. Left: domain colouring of f(z) = (z - 1)/(z^2 + 1), hue encoding \arg f(z) and brightness |f(z)|; the zero at z = 1 and the poles at z = \pm i are the points where all hues meet. Right: the image of the Cartesian grid under z \mapsto z^2; the image curves still meet at right angles, since the map is conformal away from z = 0. Generated by figures/domain_colouring.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.




Definition 7 (Complex derivative) A function f : D \to \mathbb{C} on an open set D is complex differentiable at z_0 \in D if the limit f'(z_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)}{h}, \qquad h \in \mathbb{C}, exists; f'(z_0) is the complex derivative. The limit is over complex h, so the quotient must approach the same value along every direction. The sum, product, quotient and chain rules hold with the same proofs as in Continuity and differentiability, and (z^n)' = n z^{n-1}, (e^z)' = e^z.

/-- The sum, product and quotient rules for the complex derivative. -/
theorem rules (f g : ℂ → ℂ) (f' g' z : ℂ) (hf : HasDerivAt f f' z) (hg : HasDerivAt g g' z) :
    HasDerivAt (fun w => f w + g w) (f' + g') z ∧
      HasDerivAt (fun w => f w * g w) (f' * g z + f z * g') z ∧
      (g z ≠ 0 → HasDerivAt (fun w => f w / g w) ((f' * g z - f z * g') / g z ^ 2) z)

/-- The chain rule for the complex derivative. -/

    HasDerivAt (fun w => g (f w)) (g' * f') z

Differentiability at a single point is of little use. The useful notion is differentiability on an open set, which is what holomorphy means and what the rest of the chapter assumes.


Definition 8 (Holomorphic function) A function is holomorphic on an open set D if it is complex differentiable at every point of D; it is holomorphic at a point if it is holomorphic on some neighbourhood of it. A function holomorphic on all of \mathbb{C} is entire. Sums, products and compositions of holomorphic functions are holomorphic, and so are quotients away from the zeros of the denominator.

The third exercise uses the Cauchy-Riemann equations, stated next, to show that holomorphic functions of constant modulus are constant. Read the theorem first and then return to it.

Exercise 27 (Holomorphic functions with constant modulus) Show that a holomorphic function on a domain with |f| constant is itself constant. (Use the Cauchy-Riemann equations of Theorem 1 once you have read them.)







NoteSolution





If |f| = 0 then f = 0. Otherwise u^2 + v^2 = c > 0; differentiating, u u_x + v v_x = 0 and u u_y + v v_y =

The direction-independence of the complex derivative can be written as a pair of partial differential equations. These are the Cauchy-Riemann equations, the computational criterion for holomorphy.


Theorem 1 (Cauchy-Riemann equations) Write f(x + iy) = u(x, y) + iv(x, y) with u, v real. If f is complex differentiable at z_0 then the partial derivatives of u and v exist there and satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}, with f'(z_0) = u_x + iv_x. Conversely, if u, v are continuously differentiable on an open set and satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations there, then f is holomorphic on it. The equations say that the real Jacobian of (x, y)
\mapsto (u, v) has the form \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}, the matrix of multiplication by a +
ib = f' (Example 3).

The second exercise rewrites the equations with the Wirtinger derivatives. The slogan that a holomorphic function does not depend on \bar z becomes a literal statement.

Exercise 29 (The Wirtinger form) Define the operators \partial_z = \tfrac12(\partial_x - i\partial_y) and \partial_{\bar z} = \tfrac12(\partial_x +
i\partial_y). Show that the Cauchy-Riemann equations are equivalent to \partial_{\bar z} f = 0, and that then f' = \partial_z f. Check both on f = z^2 and on f = z\bar z.







NoteSolution





\partial_{\bar z}(u + iv) = \tfrac12\bigl[(u_x - v_y) + i(u_y + v_x)\bigr], which vanishes exactly when both Cauchy-Riemann equations hold; then \partial_z f = \tfrac12\bigl[(u_x + v_y) + i(v_x - u_y)\bigr] = u_x + iv_x =
f'. Treating z and \bar z as independent variables, \partial_{\bar z}(z^2) = 0 and \partial_z(z^2) = 2z, while \partial_{\bar z}(z\bar z) = z \neq 0 except at the origin (Exercise 23).

The third exercise draws two rigidity consequences from the equations. Real-valued holomorphic functions and holomorphic functions with vanishing derivative are both constant.

Exercise 30 (Holomorphic functions with real values) Prove that a holomorphic function on a domain whose values are all real is constant, and that a holomorphic function whose derivative vanishes identically is constant.







NoteSolution





If v = 0 then u_x = v_y = 0 and u_y = -v_x = 0, so u is constant on the connected open set (a function with vanishing gradient is constant along every path, Calculus on \mathbb{R}^n). If f' = u_x + iv_x = 0 then u_x = v_x
= 0 and, by the equations, u_y = v_y = 0, so both u and v are constant.

Definition 9 (Harmonic function) A twice continuously differentiable real function u on an open subset of \mathbb{R}^2 is harmonic if it satisfies Laplace’s equation \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0. The matrix form of the Cauchy-Riemann equations says that a holomorphic map acts locally as a rotation-scaling. Such maps preserve angles, which is the geometric content of holomorphy.


Definition 10 (Conformal map) A map f between open subsets of the plane is conformal at z_0 if it preserves the angle (including its orientation) between any two smooth curves through z_0. A holomorphic f with f'(z_0) \neq 0 is conformal at z_0: to first order it multiplies displacements by the complex number f'(z_0), a rotation by \arg f'(z_0) combined with a scaling by |f'(z_0)|. Conversely a continuously differentiable orientation-preserving conformal map is holomorphic with non-vanishing derivative. A bijective holomorphic map with holomorphic inverse between two domains is a conformal equivalence.

The second example is a Möbius transformation that maps the real line to the unit circle. These maps are the conformal equivalences of the disc and the half-plane.

The third exercise generalises the angle doubling at a critical point. The order of vanishing of the derivative is the factor by which angles are multiplied.

Exercise 36 (Angle multiplication at a critical point) Show that if f is holomorphic near z_0 with f'(z_0) = \dots = f^{(n-1)}(z_0) = 0 and f^{(n)}(z_0) \neq 0 (assume the Taylor expansion of Definition 13), then f multiplies the angles between curves through z_0 by n.







NoteSolution





f(z) - f(z_0) = c(z - z_0)^n\bigl(1 + O(z - z_0)\bigr) with c = f^{(n)}(z_0)/n! \neq 0. Along a curve leaving z_0 in the direction e^{i\alpha}, f(z) - f(z_0) \approx c\,t^n e^{in\alpha} leaves f(z_0) in the direction \arg c + n\alpha. Two curves at angle \beta - \alpha are mapped to curves at angle n(\beta - \alpha): z^2 at the origin doubles angles (Example 34), z^3 triples them.

title: Complex analysis
text:
Contour integrals, Cauchy’s theorem, Cauchy’s integral formula and Liouville’s theorem. Integrating a holomorphic function along a curve depends only on the endpoints when the function has a primitive, and Cauchy’s theorem says that it always does locally; the integral formula then expresses a holomorphic function inside a closed curve by its values on the curve, from which infinite differentiability, the Taylor series of Section 1.4 and Liouville’s theorem follow.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 6).






Figure 3: Contours. Left: the positively oriented unit circle |z| = 1, enclosing the pole of 1/z and not that of 1/(z - 3). Right: the closed semicircular contour [-R, R] + C_R used for real integrals, enclosing the pole i of 1/(1 + z^2) and the poles e^{i\pi/4}, e^{3i\pi/4} of 1/(1 + z^4) in the upper half-plane, but not -i. Generated by figures/contours_poles.sage.







Definition 11 (Contour) A contour is a continuous, piecewise continuously differentiable map \gamma : [a, b] \to \mathbb{C}, together with its orientation (the direction of increasing t); its image is also called the contour. It is closed if \gamma(a) = \gamma(b) and simple if it does not cross itself except possibly at the endpoints. A simple closed contour separates the plane into a bounded interior and an unbounded exterior (the Jordan curve theorem), and it is positively oriented if the interior lies to the left as one travels along it (counter-clockwise for a circle). The reversed contour -\gamma is t \mapsto \gamma(a + b - t), and the length of \gamma is L(\gamma) = \int_a^b |\gamma'(t)|\,dt.

With contours defined, we can integrate along them. The contour integral is the natural generalisation of the Riemann integral, and the existence of a primitive makes it depend only on the endpoints.


Definition 12 (Contour integral) The contour integral of a continuous f along \gamma : [a, b] \to \mathbb{C} is \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz = \int_a^b f\bigl(\gamma(t)\bigr)\,\gamma'(t)\,dt, a complex number computed as two real Riemann integrals (The Riemann integral). It is unchanged by orientation-preserving reparametrisation, changes sign under reversal, \int_{-\gamma} f = -\int_\gamma f, and obeys the ML estimate \bigl|\int_\gamma f\,dz\bigr| \leq M L(\gamma) when |f| \leq M on \gamma. If f =
F' for a holomorphic F (a primitive) on an open set containing \gamma, then \int_\gamma f\,dz =
F(\gamma(b)) - F(\gamma(a)), which vanishes for closed \gamma. A closed contour integral is written \oint_\gamma.

The vanishing of closed integrals of functions with a primitive is now promoted to a theorem about all holomorphic functions. Cauchy’s theorem is the central result of complex analysis.


Theorem 2 (Cauchy’s theorem) Let \gamma be a simple closed contour and f holomorphic on an open set containing \gamma and its interior. Then \oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 0. More generally, if f is holomorphic on a domain D and \gamma can be continuously deformed within D to another closed contour \gamma' (or to a point), then \oint_\gamma f\,dz = \oint_{\gamma'} f\,dz (or 0): closed contour integrals of holomorphic functions depend only on the deformation class of the contour within the domain of holomorphy. Equivalently, a holomorphic function on a disc has a primitive there.

Exercise 48 (A wrong answer from a symbolic integrator) Sage’s symbolic integrate of the parametrised form of \oint_{|z| = 1} dz/(z - 3) returns -2\pi i, whereas Cauchy’s theorem gives 0 and numerical integration agrees. Find the error.

Cauchy’s theorem applied to f(z)/(z - z_0) gives a formula for the values of a holomorphic function inside a contour. Differentiating under the integral gives all derivatives at once.


Theorem 3 (Cauchy’s integral formula) Let \gamma be a positively oriented simple closed contour and f holomorphic on an open set containing \gamma and its interior. Then for every z_0 in the interior f(z_0) = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{z - z_0}\,dz, \qquad f^{(n)}(z_0) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma
\frac{f(z)}{(z - z_0)^{n+1}}\,dz. In particular a holomorphic function is infinitely complex differentiable, and on a disc of radius r about z_0 on which |f| \leq M it satisfies the Cauchy estimates |f^{(n)}(z_0)| \leq n!\,M/r^n.

The third exercise derives the Cauchy estimates and tests their sharpness on the exponential. The bound is weak, but it is what Liouville’s theorem needs.

Exercise 51 (The Cauchy estimates) Derive |f^{(n)}(z_0)| \leq n!\,M/r^n from the derivative formula and the ML estimate, and apply it to f = e^z at z_0 = 0 with r = 1 and n = 10 to bound 1 = f^{(10)}(0) (how good is the bound?).

The Cauchy estimates have an immediate consequence for functions holomorphic on the whole plane. Growth at infinity controls the degree, and boundedness forces constancy.


Corollary 1 (Liouville’s theorem) A bounded entire function is constant. More generally an entire function with |f(z)| \leq C(1 + |z|)^n for all z is a polynomial of degree at most n. (From the Cauchy estimates with r \to \infty: every derivative of order > n vanishes.)

The second example is the classical proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra. A polynomial without zeros would have a bounded entire reciprocal.

Example 53 (The fundamental theorem of algebra) If a non-constant polynomial p had no zero, 1/p would be entire and bounded (it tends to 0 at infinity), hence constant: a contradiction. The second exercise completes the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra. The bound on 1/p uses compactness of discs, from Compact and connected spaces.

Exercise 53 (Factorising a polynomial completely) Complete the argument of Example 53: show that 1/p is bounded when p has no zeros, and that a polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity.







NoteSolution





For p(z) = a_n z^n + \dots + a_0 with a_n \neq 0, |p(z)| \geq |a_n||z|^n - \sum_{k<n}|a_k||z|^k \geq
\tfrac12|a_n||z|^n for |z| \geq R large, so |1/p| \leq 2/(|a_n|R^n) there; on the compact disc |z| \leq R the continuous function 1/p is bounded (Compact and connected spaces). Hence 1/p is bounded, entire if p has no zero, thus constant, which is absurd for n \geq 1. Given a root z_1, p(z) = (z - z_1)q(z) with \deg q = n -
1 by polynomial division, and induction on the degree gives n roots with multiplicity.

The third exercise proves the growth version of the theorem using the Taylor series of the next section. Only finitely many Taylor coefficients can survive the estimates.

Exercise 54 (Growth and degree) Prove the general form of Liouville’s theorem: an entire f with |f(z)| \leq C(1 + |z|)^n is a polynomial of degree at most n. (Apply the Cauchy estimates on circles of radius r \to \infty and use the Taylor series of Definition 13.)

title: Complex analysis
text:
Taylor and Laurent series, poles, the residue theorem and real integrals computed by residues. Cauchy’s integral formula expands a holomorphic function in a power series on every disc where it is holomorphic, and in a two-sided series on every annulus; the coefficient of 1/(z - z_0) in the latter, the residue, is all that a closed contour integral sees, and the residue theorem turns the evaluation of integrals into algebra.
For more on this topic, see Magnus (2023, Ch. 3) and Yu (2022, Ch. 5, Ch. 9).






Figure 4: Laurent series of f(z) = 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)). Left: the three regions |z| < 1, 1 < |z| < 2 and |z| > 2 on which f has three different expansions, separated by circles through the poles. Right: the error |S_N(z) - f(z)| of the partial sums of the annulus expansion at z = 1.5i, decreasing geometrically with N. Generated by figures/laurent_series.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.




Definition 13 (Taylor series) A power series about z_0 is \sum_{n \geq 0} a_n (z - z_0)^n; it converges absolutely for |z - z_0| < R and diverges for |z - z_0| > R, where R \in [0, \infty] is the radius of convergence, 1/R = \limsup |
a_n|^{1/n} (the root test of Series). Inside the disc of convergence the sum is holomorphic and may be differentiated term by term. Conversely, if f is holomorphic on the disc |z - z_0| < R, then on that disc f(z) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{f^{(n)}(z_0)}{n!}(z - z_0)^n, its Taylor series, with coefficients given by Cauchy’s integral formula; the radius of convergence is at least the distance from z_0 to the nearest point where f fails to be holomorphic.

Definition 14 (Laurent series) If f is holomorphic on the annulus r < |z - z_0| < R, then there it equals its Laurent series f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n (z - z_0)^n, \qquad a_n = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z - z_0| = \rho} \frac{f(z)}{(z -
z_0)^{n+1}}\,dz \quad (r < \rho < R), converging absolutely on the annulus; the coefficients are unique, and the part with n < 0 is the principal part. The same function has different Laurent series on different annuli about the same point.

The third exercise proves the uniqueness of the Laurent coefficients from the circle integrals. The orthogonality of Exercise 57 is exactly what is needed.

Exercise 63 (Uniqueness of the coefficients) Show that if f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} b_n (z - z_0)^n on an annulus, with the series converging uniformly on each circle inside it, then b_n equals the coefficient a_n of Definition 14.

Hence b_m = a_m: however a Laurent expansion is found, by partial fractions, substitution or division, it is the Laurent expansion.

A point where a function is not defined but around which it is holomorphic is classified by its principal part. Three cases arise, from the harmless to the wild, and the classification decides what the residue theorem can do.


Definition 15 (Isolated singularity) A point z_0 is an isolated singularity of f if f is holomorphic on a punctured disc 0 < |z - z_0| < r but not defined (or not holomorphic) at z_0. According to the principal part of the Laurent series on the punctured disc, the singularity is removable (no negative powers: f extends holomorphically to z_0), a pole of order m (finitely many, the lowest being a_{-m}(z - z_0)^{-m} with a_{-m} \neq 0; then |f(z)|
\to \infty as z \to z_0), or essential (infinitely many). A function holomorphic on a domain except for poles is meromorphic; a simple pole is one of order 1.

Of all the Laurent coefficients, one has a special role. The coefficient of 1/(z - z_0) is the only one that a closed contour integral around z_0 detects, and it can be computed without finding the whole series.


Definition 16 (Residue) The residue of f at an isolated singularity z_0 is the coefficient a_{-1} of its Laurent series on a punctured disc about z_0, \operatorname{Res}_{z = z_0} f = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint f(z)\,dz over a small positively oriented circle. At a simple pole \operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f = \lim_{z \to z_0}(z - z_0)f(z), and if f = g/h with g(z_0) \neq 0, h(z_0) = 0, h'(z_0) \neq 0, then \operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f = g(z_0)/h'(z_0); at a pole of order m, \operatorname{Res}_{z = z_0} f = \frac1{(m - 1)!}\lim_{z \to z_0}\frac{d^{m-1}}{dz^{m-1}}\Bigl[(z - z_0)^m f(z)\Bigr].

Cauchy’s theorem for a function with finitely many isolated singularities inside the contour is the residue theorem. The contour is shrunk onto small circles around the singularities, each contributing 2\pi i times its residue.


Theorem 4 (Residue theorem) Let \gamma be a positively oriented simple closed contour and f holomorphic on an open set containing \gamma and its interior except at finitely many points z_1, \dots, z_k inside \gamma. Then \oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i\sum_{j = 1}^k \operatorname{Res}_{z = z_j} f.

The third exercise treats a pole on the contour, which requires an indentation. The half-residue rule it produces is the one behind principal-value integrals and the i\epsilon prescription.

Exercise 75 (\int_{-\infty}^\infty \sin x/x\,dx = \pi) Integrate e^{iz}/z over the contour consisting of [-R, -\epsilon], the small clockwise semicircle of radius \epsilon above 0, [\epsilon, R] and the large arc C_R. Show that the large arc contributes nothing as R \to \infty (accept Jordan’s lemma), that the small arc contributes -i\pi as \epsilon \to 0, and conclude.







NoteSolution





The contour encloses no singularity, so the total is 0. On the small arc z = \epsilon e^{i\theta}, \theta from \pi to 0: \int e^{iz}\,dz/z = \int_\pi^0 e^{i\epsilon e^{i\theta}}\,i\,d\theta \to -i\pi. Hence \lim\int_{|x| > \epsilon} e^{ix}\,dx/x = i\pi; the real part is a principal value of an odd function, zero, and the imaginary part gives \int_{-\infty}^\infty \sin x/x\,dx = \pi. A simple pole on the contour contributes half a residue, with the sign fixed by the direction of the indentation.
