title: Complex analysis
text:
Analytic continuation, the Gamma and Beta functions, the zeta function in outline, Wick rotation as a contour deformation. A holomorphic function is determined by its values on any small set with a limit point, so a formula valid on a half-plane defines a function far beyond it; the Gamma and zeta functions are the standard examples, and the rotation of an integration contour from the real to the imaginary axis, Wick rotation, is the same principle applied to integrals.
For more on this topic, see Yu (2022, Ch. 7-8).






Figure 5: The Gamma function and Wick rotation. Left: \Gamma(x) on the real line, with its poles at 0, -1, -2, \dots and the values \Gamma(n + 1) = n!. Right: the poles \pm(E - i\epsilon) of 1/(k^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon) and the counter-clockwise rotation of the real k^0 axis onto the imaginary axis k^0 = ik^4 through the two quadrants that contain no pole. Generated by figures/gamma_function.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.




Definition 17 (Analytic continuation) Let f be holomorphic on a domain D_1 and D_2 \supset D_1 a larger domain. An analytic continuation of f to D_2 is a holomorphic function on D_2 that agrees with f on D_1. By the identity theorem, two functions holomorphic on a domain that agree on a set with a limit point in the domain (a segment, a small disc, a convergent sequence) agree everywhere on it; hence an analytic continuation, if it exists, is unique. The continuation may fail to exist (a natural boundary) or may depend on the path along which it is carried out, in which case the continued function is many-valued and has branch points (Definition 6).

/-- The identity theorem: two functions holomorphic on a connected open set `U` that agree on a set accumulating at
a point `z₀ ∈ U` agree on `U`. -/

    (hf : DifferentiableOn ℂ f U) (hg : DifferentiableOn ℂ g U) (z₀ : ℂ) (hz₀ : z₀ ∈ U)
    (h : ∃ᶠ z in 𝓝[≠] z₀, f z = g z) : EqOn f g U

NoteExamples





The first example is the geometric series, whose sum formula makes sense far beyond the disc of convergence. The continuation is the rational function, not the series.

Example 76 (The geometric series) \sum_{n \geq 0} z^n converges only on |z| < 1, where it equals 1/(1 - z); the latter is holomorphic on \mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\} and is the unique analytic continuation of the series. The value -1 at z = 2 belongs to the continuation, not to the divergent series 1 + 2 + 4 + \dots; the zeta function below is defined by the same mechanism.

The second example shows how real identities propagate to the complex plane. Any identity between entire functions that holds on the real axis holds everywhere.

The same argument transfers every trigonometric identity, and the functional equation e^{z + w} = e^z e^w, from \mathbb{R} to \mathbb{C}.

The factorial is defined on the non-negative integers. The Gamma function interpolates it by an integral that converges on a half-plane, and analytic continuation then extends it to the whole plane minus a sequence of poles.


Definition 18 (Gamma function) The Gamma function is \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt for \operatorname{Re} z > 0, where the integral converges and defines a holomorphic function. Integration by parts gives the recursion \Gamma(z + 1)
= z\Gamma(z), so \Gamma(n + 1) = n! for integers n \geq 0. Rewriting the recursion as \Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z +
1)/z continues \Gamma to \operatorname{Re} z > -1, then to \operatorname{Re} z > -2, and so on: \Gamma is meromorphic on \mathbb{C} with simple poles at z = 0, -1, -2, \dots of residue (-1)^n/n! at -n, and no zeros. It satisfies the reflection formula \Gamma(z)\Gamma(1 - z) = \pi/\sin\pi z, whence \Gamma(\tfrac12)
= \sqrt\pi.

The Riemann zeta function is the archetype of a function defined by a series on a half-plane and continued beyond it. Its values at negative integers, finite numbers assigned to divergent sums, are what zeta-function regularisation uses.


Definition 20 (Zeta function) The Riemann zeta function is \zeta(s) = \sum_{n \geq 1} n^{-s} for \operatorname{Re} s > 1, where the series converges absolutely (Series) and defines a holomorphic function. It has the Euler product \zeta(s) = \prod_p (1 - p^{-s})^{-1} over the primes, and it continues analytically to a meromorphic function on \mathbb{C} with a single simple pole at s = 1 of residue 1, satisfying the functional equation \zeta(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin(\tfrac{\pi s}2)\Gamma(1 - s)\zeta(1 - s). The continuation is outlined in Example 86; its values include \zeta(2) = \pi^2/6, \zeta(0) = -\tfrac12, \zeta(-1) = -
\tfrac1{12} and \zeta(-2n) = 0 for n \geq 1.

Example 87 (“1 + 2 + 3 + \dots = -\tfrac1{12}”) The series \sum n diverges; \zeta(-1) = -\tfrac1{12} is the value at s = -1 of the analytic continuation of \sum n^{-s}. Concretely, \sum_{n \geq 1} n e^{-\epsilon n} = \dfrac{e^{-\epsilon}}{(1 - e^{-\epsilon})^2} =

The second exercise derives the Euler product from unique factorisation. Expanding each factor as a geometric series and multiplying out produces every integer exactly once.

Exercise 86 (The Euler product) Show that for \operatorname{Re} s > 1, \prod_{p \leq N}(1 - p^{-s})^{-1} = \sum' n^{-s}, the sum over integers whose prime factors are all at most N, and deduce the Euler product as N \to \infty.

(1 - p^{-s})^{-1} = \sum_{k \geq 0} p^{-ks}; multiplying finitely many absolutely convergent series, the product is \sum p_1^{-k_1 s}\cdots p_r^{-k_r s} over all exponent tuples, that is, \sum n^{-s} over the n whose factorisation uses only p_1, \dots, p_r, each n once by unique factorisation. As N \to \infty every n is included and the tail \sum_{n > N}|n^{-s}| tends to 0.

An integral over the real line of a function holomorphic in a sector can be moved to another ray through the origin. Rotating the real axis to the imaginary axis is called Wick rotation, and it converts oscillatory integrals into decaying ones.


Definition 21 (Wick rotation) Let f be holomorphic on an open set containing the closed first and third quadrants of the k^0-plane, except possibly at infinity, with |k^0 f(k^0)| \to 0 uniformly as |k^0| \to \infty in those quadrants. The Wick rotation is the identity \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(k^0)\,dk^0 = i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(ik^4)\,dk^4, obtained from Cauchy’s theorem on the closed contour made of the real axis, the imaginary axis traversed downward and two arcs at infinity in the first and third quadrants: the arcs vanish by the ML estimate and the contour encloses no singularity. The substitution k^0 = ik^4 (or t = -i\tau in position space) is the rotation to Euclidean signature: a Minkowski square (k^0)^2 - \mathbf{k}^2 becomes -\bigl((k^4)^2 +
\mathbf{k}^2\bigr), minus a Euclidean square.

Exercise 95 (The other prescription) Repeat the residue computation for 1/(k^2 - E^2 - i\epsilon) and show that the integral is +i\pi/E; explain why the Wick rotation for this integrand is clockwise, k^0 = -ik^4.







NoteSolution





Now the poles are E + i\delta (first quadrant) and -E - i\delta (third); closing above picks up 2\pi
i/(2E) = i\pi/E. The first and third quadrants contain poles, so the counter-clockwise rotation is forbidden; the second and fourth are free, and rotating clockwise, k^0 = -ik^4, gives -i\int dk^4/\bigl(-(k^4)^2 - E^2\bigr) =
i\pi/E. The two prescriptions are complex conjugates of each other, as the integrands are.

theorem pole_quadrants_conj (M ε : ℝ) (hM : 0 < M) (hε : 0 < ε) (c : ℂ) (hc : c ^ 2 = M + ε * I) :
    (0 < c.re ∧ 0 < c.im) ∨ (c.re < 0 ∧ c.im < 0)

theorem euclidean_side_clockwise (E : ℝ) (hE : 0 < E) :
    (E : ℂ) * (-I * ∫ k : ℝ, 1 / ((-I * k) ^ 2 - (E : ℂ) ^ 2)) = π * I

/-- The two prescriptions are complex conjugates: `∫ dk/(k² - E² - iε) = conj ∫ dk/(k² - E² + iε)`. -/
theorem prescriptions_conj (E ε : ℝ) :
    ∫ k : ℝ, 1 / ((k : ℂ) ^ 2 - E ^ 2 - ε * I) = (starRingEnd ℂ) (∫ k : ℝ, 1 / ((k : ℂ) ^ 2 - E ^ 2 + ε * I))

Explicit roots c of c^2 = M + i eps (2 + i, -2 - i, 3 + i); Lean checks c^2 and the quadrant by norm_num; Sage integrates the propagator with the opposite prescription and compares with 2 pi i/(2E + 2 i delta); Sage takes delta -> 0+ in 2 pi i/(2E + 2 i delta) and compares with i pi/E; Sage integrates -i/((-i k)^2 - E^2) over R and compares with i pi/E; Sage integrates both prescriptions over R and compares one with the conjugate of the other.



The third exercise rotates the Gaussian path-integral weight. It shows that Wick rotation also fixes the convergence of real-time Gaussian integrals.

Exercise 96 (A Gaussian with an i\epsilon) Evaluate \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{\frac i2(a + i\epsilon)x^2}\,dx for a > 0, \epsilon > 0, both by completing the rotation to x = e^{i\pi/4}u and by analytic continuation of \int e^{-\frac12\lambda x^2}\,dx =
\sqrt{2\pi/\lambda} in \lambda; identify the branch of the square root.







NoteSolution





\lambda = -i(a + i\epsilon) = \epsilon - ia has positive real part, so the Gaussian formula continues to it: \sqrt{2\pi/(\epsilon - ia)} \to \sqrt{2\pi/a}\,e^{i\pi/4} as \epsilon \to 0, with the principal branch (the continuation starts from \lambda > 0 and never crosses the cut). The rotation gives e^{i\pi/4}\int
e^{-\frac12 a u^2}\,du = e^{i\pi/4}\sqrt{2\pi/a}, the same value; the i\epsilon makes the original integral absolutely convergent, which the rotation then evaluates.

title: Complex analysis
text:
NoteExercises





The three exercises of this section combine several sections of the chapter. The first evaluates a Fourier transform by shifting a contour, the second integrates around a branch cut with a keyhole contour and produces the reflection formula of the Gamma function, and the third derives the time-dependent propagator from the residues of the i\epsilon-displaced poles. The first integrative exercise is the shifted Gaussian. Cauchy’s theorem on a rectangle moves the integration line into the complex plane, where the integral becomes the familiar real one.

Exercise 97 (The Fourier transform of a Gaussian) Show that \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}e^{ikx}\,dx = \sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-k^2/2} for real k by completing the square and shifting the contour from \operatorname{Im} x = 0 to \operatorname{Im} x = k (Cauchy’s theorem of Section 1.3 on a rectangle); confirm with Sage. Why is a Gaussian its own Fourier transform?







NoteSolution





-x^2/2 + ikx = -(x - ik)^2/2 - k^2/2. The integrand e^{-(x - ik)^2/2} is entire, and on the vertical sides of the rectangle [-R, R] \times [0, k] it is bounded by e^{-R^2/2 + k^2/2} \to 0, so by Theorem 2 \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-(x - ik)^2/2}\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-u^2/2}\,du = \sqrt{2\pi} (Example 79 with u^2 = 2t). The transform of e^{-x^2/2} is \sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}, the same Gaussian up to the normalisation: the Gaussian is an eigenfunction of the Fourier transform. Sage’s integrate agrees, and the Gaussian integral itself is \Gamma(\tfrac12)\sqrt2:

x = var("x", domain="real"); k = var("k", domain="real")
ft = integrate(exp(-x^2/2)*exp(I*k*x), x, -oo, oo)
print("Fourier transform:", ft.simplify_full())
print("equals sqrt(2 pi) e^{-k^2/2}:", bool((ft - sqrt(2*pi)*exp(-k^2/2)).simplify_full() == 0))
print("integral of e^{-x^2/2}:", integrate(exp(-x^2/2), x, -oo, oo), "= Gamma(1/2) sqrt(2) =", (gamma(1/2)*sqrt(2)).simplify_full())
Output:
Fourier transform: sqrt(2)*sqrt(pi)*e^(-1/2*k^2)
equals sqrt(2 pi) e^{-k^2/2}: True
integral of e^{-x^2/2}: sqrt(2)*sqrt(pi) = Gamma(1/2) sqrt(2) = sqrt(2)*sqrt(pi)










TipVerification

/-- Completing the square: `-x²/2 + ikx = -(x - ik)²/2 - k²/2`. -/
theorem complete_square (x k : ℝ) : -(x : ℂ) ^ 2 / 2 + I * k * x = -((x : ℂ) - I * k) ^ 2 / 2 - (k : ℂ) ^ 2 / 2
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.complete_square in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- On the vertical sides of the rectangle `[-R, R] × [0, k]` the integrand `e^{-z²/2}` is bounded by
`e^{-R²/2 + k²/2}`. -/
theorem vertical_side_bound (R t k : ℝ) (ht : |t| ≤ |k|) :
    ‖Complex.exp (-((R : ℂ) + t * I) ^ 2 / 2)‖ ≤ Real.exp (-R ^ 2 / 2 + k ^ 2 / 2)
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.vertical_side_bound in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- The shifted Gaussian integral: `∫ e^{-(x - ik)²/2} dx = √(2π)` (Cauchy's theorem on the rectangle, in mathlib's
form for a Gaussian with complex shift). -/
theorem shifted_gaussian (k : ℝ) : ∫ x : ℝ, Complex.exp (-((x : ℂ) - I * k) ^ 2 / 2) = ((2 * π : ℝ) : ℂ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℂ)
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.shifted_gaussian in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- The Fourier transform of the Gaussian: `∫ e^{-x²/2} e^{ikx} dx = √(2π) e^{-k²/2}`. -/
theorem gaussian_fourier (k : ℝ) :
    ∫ x : ℝ, Complex.exp (-(x : ℂ) ^ 2 / 2) * Complex.exp (I * k * x) =
      ((2 * π : ℝ) : ℂ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℂ) * Complex.exp (-(k : ℂ) ^ 2 / 2)
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.gaussian_fourier in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- The Gaussian integral `∫ e^{-b u²} du = Γ(½)/√b` for `b > 0` (at `b = ½`: `√(2π) = Γ(½)√2`). -/
theorem gaussian_gamma (b : ℝ) (hb : 0 < b) : ∫ u : ℝ, Real.exp (-b * u ^ 2) = Real.Gamma (1 / 2) / √b
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.gaussian_gamma in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises

The second integrative exercise integrates a many-valued function around its branch cut. The discontinuity across the cut, the residue at a pole and the Beta function combine to prove the reflection formula of the Gamma function.

Exercise 98 (A keyhole contour and the reflection formula) For 0 < a < 1 evaluate I(a) = \int_0^\infty \dfrac{x^{a-1}}{1 + x}\,dx by integrating z^{a-1}/(1 + z), with the branch \arg z \in (0, 2\pi) (Definition 6), over the keyhole contour that runs along the upper side of the positive real axis, around a large circle, back along the lower side and around a small circle about 0. Deduce from Definition 19 that \Gamma(a)\Gamma(1 - a) = \pi/\sin\pi a, and check I(\tfrac13) =
2\pi/\sqrt3 with Sage.







NoteSolution





On the upper side z^{a-1} = x^{a-1}; on the lower side \arg z = 2\pi and z^{a-1} = x^{a-1}e^{2\pi i(a-1)} =
x^{a-1}e^{2\pi ia}, traversed in the opposite direction. The large circle contributes O(R^{a-1}) \to 0 and the small one O(\epsilon^a) \to 0. The only pole inside is z = -1 = e^{i\pi}, with residue e^{i\pi(a-1)} = -
e^{i\pi a} (Definition 16). By Theorem 4, (1 - e^{2\pi ia})I(a) = -2\pi i\,e^{i\pi a}, so I(a) =
\dfrac{-2\pi i}{e^{-i\pi a} - e^{i\pi a}} = \dfrac{\pi}{\sin\pi a}. The rational form of the Beta function gives I(a) = B(a, 1 - a) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(1 - a)/\Gamma(1), which is the reflection formula; at a = \tfrac13 both sides equal 2\pi/\sqrt3 (Exercise 79):

x = var("x", domain="positive"); a = var("a")
assume(a > 0); assume(a < 1)
I13 = integrate(x^(1/3 - 1)/(1 + x), x, 0, oo)
print("a = 1/3: integral =", I13, "  pi/sin(pi/3) =", (pi/sin(pi/3)).simplify_full(), "  B(1/3, 2/3) =", beta(1/3, 2/3), "  numerically", I13.n(), beta(1/3, 2/3).n())
Ia = integrate(x^(a - 1)/(1 + x), x, 0, oo)
print("general a in (0, 1): integral =", Ia, "  equals B(a, 1 - a):", bool((Ia - beta(a, 1 - a)).simplify_full() == 0), "  equals pi/sin(pi a) at a = 1/3, 1/7, 9/10:", all(abs((Ia - pi/sin(pi*a)).subs(a=v).n()) < 1e-12 for v in (1/3, 1/7, 9/10)))
print("residue of z^(a-1)/(1 + z) at z = -1 = e^{i pi}: e^{i pi (a - 1)} = -e^{i pi a}; (1 - e^{2 pi i a}) I = -2 pi i e^{i pi a} gives I = pi/sin(pi a):", bool(((-2*pi*I*exp(I*pi*a))/(1 - exp(2*pi*I*a)) - pi/sin(pi*a)).exponentialize().simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
a = 1/3: integral = 2/3*sqrt(3)*pi   pi/sin(pi/3) = 2/3*sqrt(3)*pi   B(1/3, 2/3) = beta(1/3, 2/3)   numerically 3.62759872846844 3.62759872846844
general a in (0, 1): integral = beta(-a + 1, a)   equals B(a, 1 - a): True   equals pi/sin(pi a) at a = 1/3, 1/7, 9/10: True
residue of z^(a-1)/(1 + z) at z = -1 = e^{i pi}: e^{i pi (a - 1)} = -e^{i pi a}; (1 - e^{2 pi i a}) I = -2 pi i e^{i pi a} gives I = pi/sin(pi a): True

/-- On the lower side of the cut `arg z = 2π`: `x^{a-1} e^{2πi(a-1)} = x^{a-1} e^{2πia}`. -/
theorem lower_side_phase (a : ℝ) : Complex.exp (2 * π * I * (a - 1)) = Complex.exp (2 * π * I * a)
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.lower_side_phase in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- The residue of `z^{a-1}/(1 + z)` at `z = -1 = e^{iπ}` is `e^{iπ(a-1)} = -e^{iπa}`. -/
theorem keyhole_residue (a : ℝ) : Complex.exp (π * I * (a - 1)) = -Complex.exp (π * I * a)
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.keyhole_residue in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- Solving the keyhole relation `(1 - e^{2πia}) I = -2πi e^{iπa}`: since `-2πi e^{iπa} sin πa = π(1 - e^{2πia})`,
`I = -2πi e^{iπa}/(1 - e^{2πia}) = π/sin πa` whenever `sin πa ≠ 0`. -/
theorem keyhole_solve (a : ℝ) :
    -2 * π * I * Complex.exp (π * I * a) * (Real.sin (π * a) : ℂ) = π * (1 - Complex.exp (2 * π * I * a))
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.keyhole_solve in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- The reflection formula `Γ(a)Γ(1 - a) = π/sin πa` (mathlib's form, for every complex `a`). -/
theorem reflection (a : ℂ) (ha : ∀ n : ℤ, a ≠ n) :
    Complex.Gamma a * Complex.Gamma (1 - a) * Complex.sin (π * a) = π
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.reflection in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises


/-- At `a = ⅓`: `π/sin(π/3) = 2π/√3`. -/
theorem keyhole_third : π / Real.sin (π * (1 / 3)) = 2 * π / √3
KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises.keyhole_third in KaluzaKlein/PartI/ComplexAnalysis/Exercises.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.ComplexAnalysis.Exercises

Sage. lower_side_phase at (0); ((1 / 3)); ((1 / 2)) (3 evaluated by Sage in exact or 128-bit interval arithmetic); keyhole_residue at (0); ((1 / 3)); ((1 / 2)) (3 evaluated by Sage in exact or 128-bit interval arithmetic); ideal_membership.sage: Gröbner cofactors expressing lhs - rhs through the relations used (i² = -1, (√k)² = k, the stated identities), checked by linear_combination; reflection at ((1 / 2)); ((1 / 3)); ((1 / 2 + 2 * Complex.I)) (3 evaluated by Sage in exact or 128-bit interval arithmetic); ca-num-ring.sage: the expansion of lhs - rhs to the zero polynomial, checked by ring1.



The third integrative exercise evaluates the time-dependent propagator from the i\epsilon-displaced poles. Which pole contributes depends on the sign of the time, and the answer explains the Feynman prescription.

Exercise 99 (The propagator in time) Evaluate G(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \dfrac{dk^0}{2\pi}\,\dfrac{e^{-ik^0 t}}{(k^0)^2 - E^2 + i\epsilon} for t >
0 and for t < 0 by closing the contour in the half-plane where e^{-ik^0 t} decays (Exercise 89), and show that G(t) = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-iE|t|} as \epsilon \to 0. Which pole contributes for each sign of t, and what does the answer say about the frequencies that propagate forward and backward in time?







NoteSolution





The poles are k^0 = E - i\delta and k^0 = -E + i\delta with \delta = \epsilon/2E (Example 88). For t > 0, |e^{-ik^0 t}| = e^{t\operatorname{Im} k^0} decays in the lower half-plane, so close below (clockwise): G = \dfrac1{2\pi}\cdot(-2\pi i)\operatorname{Res}_{E - i\delta} = -i\,\dfrac{e^{-iEt}}{2E} in the limit. For t <
0 close above and pick up -E + i\delta: G = \dfrac1{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi i\cdot\dfrac{e^{iEt}}{-2E} = -i\,\dfrac{e^{-iE|t|}}{2E}. Hence G(t) = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-iE|t|}: the positive-frequency pole k^0 = +E propagates forward in time and the negative-frequency pole k^0 = -E backward, which is the content of the Feynman prescription and the reason the i\epsilon is placed as it is. The Wick-rotated version, t = -i\tau, is G = -\dfrac{i}{2E}e^{-E|\tau|}, a decaying Euclidean propagator, consistent with Proposition 6 at \tau = 0 after the factor i from dk^0 =
i\,dk^4 is included.

title: Fourier analysis
text:
Fourier analysis decomposes a function into modes: a periodic function into the harmonics e^{inx}, a function on the line into the plane waves e^{ikx}, a function on the sphere into the spherical harmonics Y_{lm}, and a function on a compact group into the matrix coefficients of its irreducible representations. In each case the modes are the eigenfunctions of a Laplacian, they are orthogonal for a natural inner product, the coefficients of a function are inner products with the modes, and the sum of the squares of the coefficients is the square of the norm of the function. The chapter develops this circle of ideas in four sections. Fourier series treats periodic functions on the circle, their coefficients, the Dirichlet kernel and the Gibbs phenomenon, the convergence theorems and Parseval’s identity, with the square wave and the sawtooth as running examples. The Fourier transform passes from the circle to the line, with the Gaussian as the central example, the convolution theorem, Plancherel’s theorem and the uncertainty inequality, which says that a function and its transform cannot both be narrow. Distributions gives a meaning to the delta function and its derivatives, to the Fourier transform of 1 and of \delta, and to the principal value 1/x, the objects that make the formal manipulations of the first two sections rigorous. Harmonic analysis on the sphere and on compact groups describes the spherical harmonics as eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on S^2 and as the spin-l representations of SU(2), states the Peter-Weyl theorem, and ends with the mode expansion of a function on a coset space G/H, the general setting in which a field on a compact space is expanded in modes. Each definition is followed by three examples of increasing complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions; each section ends with a proposition that collects its explicit values, and the quoted theorems (Dirichlet’s convergence theorem, Plancherel, the uncertainty inequality, Peter-Weyl) are stated with their hypotheses and argued in the text. The real analysis assumed is that of Series, The Riemann integral and Multiple integrals and convergence of functions, the complex analysis that of Contour integration and Series and residues, the orthogonal functions and the delta of Boundary value and Sturm-Liouville problems and Green’s functions, and the representation theory of SU(2) that of Weights and the representations of su(2); the normalisations fixed here, \hat f(k) = \int f(x)e^{-ikx}dx with inverse f(x) =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(k)e^{ikx}dk and c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-inx}dx on the circle, are used throughout the book.


A function on the circle is a periodic function on the line, and the harmonics e^{inx} are the simplest periodic functions of all. This section defines periodic functions and their Fourier coefficients, studies the partial sums through the Dirichlet kernel, states the convergence theorems of Dirichlet and of the L^2 theory, and proves Parseval’s identity, with the square wave and the sawtooth of Figure 1 as running examples whose coefficients, partial sums and overshoot are collected in Proposition 1.
For more on this topic, see Arrigo (2023, Ch. 4).






Figure 1: Partial Fourier sums S_1, S_3, S_9, S_{29} of the square wave \operatorname{sgn} x (left) and of the sawtooth x (right) on (-\pi, \pi). The sums converge to the function away from the jumps, to the midpoint 0 at the jumps, and overshoot by about 9\% of the jump next to it however many terms are taken: the Gibbs phenomenon, with the limiting overshoot 1.179 marked. Generated by figures/fourier_square_wave.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


Before anything can be expanded in harmonics one needs the class of functions that live on the circle. The definition below fixes periodicity, the standard period 2\pi, the way a function on an interval is extended, and the finite sums of harmonics that will approximate everything else.


Definition 1 (Periodic function) A function f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} is periodic with period T > 0 if f(x + T) = f(x) for all x; it is then determined by its values on any interval of length T, and after the rescaling x \mapsto 2\pi x/T one may take T = 2\pi, which is assumed from now on. A 2\pi-periodic function is the same thing as a function on the circle S^1 = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}, and a function given on [0, 2\pi) or on (-\pi, \pi] has a unique periodic extension. A trigonometric polynomial of degree N is a finite sum \sum_{|n| \leq N} c_n
e^{inx}, equivalently \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^N (a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx); a periodic function is piecewise continuous if it has at most finitely many jumps per period, with one-sided limits f(x^\pm) at each, and piecewise C^1 if the same holds for f'.

The harmonics themselves are the first periodic functions to look at, and the only subtlety is which period one means. The first example records that e^{inx} has the smaller period 2\pi/n as well as 2\pi, which is why all harmonics live on the same circle.

Example 1 (The harmonics) \sin nx, \cos nx and e^{inx} are 2\pi-periodic for every integer n, and 2\pi/|n| is their smallest period when n \neq 0: a function with period T also has period kT for every positive integer k. The constant function is periodic with every period, and e^{inx} = \cos nx + i\sin nx relates the complex and the real harmonics.

Example 2 (The square wave and the sawtooth) The square wave is the periodic extension of \operatorname{sgn} x from (-\pi, \pi), and the sawtooth that of f(x) = x from (-\pi, \pi) (Figure 1). Both are piecewise C^1: the square wave jumps by 2 at every multiple of \pi, the sawtooth by -2\pi at the odd multiples of \pi, where f(\pi^-) = \pi and f(\pi^+) = -\pi. The extension of |x| from (-\pi, \pi) is continuous, since |{-\pi}| = |\pi|, but its derivative jumps at the multiples of \pi.

Deciding whether a sum of periodic functions is periodic is a question about the ratio of the periods, and the answer is negative when the ratio is irrational. The first exercise works this out, which is also the reason why only integer multiples of a basic frequency appear in a Fourier series.

Exercise 1 (Periods of sums) Show that \sin x + \sin 2x is 2\pi-periodic, that \sin x + \sin(x/2) has smallest period 4\pi, and that \sin x + \sin\sqrt2\,x is not periodic at all.







NoteSolution





Both terms of the first sum have period 2\pi. For the second, \sin(x/2) has smallest period 4\pi and \sin

A periodic function integrated over any interval of one period gives the same number, which is what makes the coefficients below independent of the interval chosen. The third exercise proves this and uses it to show that the integral of a product of two periodic functions is a periodic function of the shift between them.

Exercise 3 (Integrals over a period) Prove that \int_a^{a + 2\pi} f(x)\,dx is independent of a for a piecewise continuous 2\pi-periodic f, and deduce that F(t) = \int_0^{2\pi} f(x)g(x - t)\,dx is 2\pi-periodic in t for periodic f, g.







NoteSolution





\frac{d}{da}\int_a^{a + 2\pi} f = f(a + 2\pi) - f(a) = 0 at every point where f is continuous, by the fundamental theorem of calculus (The Riemann integral), and the integral is a continuous function of a, so it is constant. For F, substitute y = x - t: F(t) = \int_{-t}^{2\pi - t} f(y + t)g(y)\,dy, and y \mapsto f(y +
t)g(y) is periodic, so by the first part the integral equals \int_0^{2\pi} f(y + t)g(y)\,dy, which is visibly 2\pi-periodic in t. This is the periodicity of the convolution on the circle, the form in which the partial sums are written in Definition 3.

The coefficients of a periodic function are its inner products with the harmonics, and everything rests on the fact that distinct harmonics are orthogonal. The definition fixes the normalisation of the coefficients once and for all, in the complex form and in the real form, and records the orthogonality relation that makes them the right numbers.


Definition 2 (Fourier coefficient) The Fourier coefficients of a piecewise continuous 2\pi-periodic f are 
c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\,e^{-inx}\,dx, \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z},
 and the Fourier series of f is \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} c_n e^{inx}, written f \sim \sum c_n e^{inx} until its convergence is settled. In real form f \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n \geq 1}(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx) with a_n = \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\cos nx\,dx and b_n = \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\sin nx\,dx, related by c_n =
\tfrac12(a_n - ib_n) and c_{-n} = \tfrac12(a_n + ib_n) for n \geq 1, c_0 = a_0/2. The coefficients are the inner products c_n = \langle e^{inx}, f\rangle/2\pi for \langle g, f\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}\bar g f\,dx, and the orthogonality of the modes 
\int_0^{2\pi} e^{inx}\,e^{-imx}\,dx = 2\pi\,\delta_{nm}
\tag{1} shows that the coefficients of a trigonometric polynomial are its given coefficients and that c_n is the unique choice making f - c_n e^{inx} orthogonal to e^{inx} (Definition 14 of Differential equations).

Whether and how the series represents the function is decided by its partial sums, and the partial sums have a closed form as an integral of the function against a kernel. The definition introduces the Dirichlet kernel, records its two properties, and names the overshoot visible in Figure 1.


Definition 3 (Partial Fourier sum) The partial Fourier sum of order N of f is S_N f(x) = \sum_{|n| \leq N} c_n e^{inx}. Inserting the coefficients and exchanging sum and integral, 
S_N f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} D_N(x - y)\,f(y)\,dy, \qquad D_N(t) = \sum_{|n| \leq N} e^{int} =
\frac{\sin\bigl((N + \tfrac12)t\bigr)}{\sin(t/2)},
\tag{2} where D_N is the Dirichlet kernel: an even trigonometric polynomial with \frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi D_N =
1 and D_N(0) = 2N + 1, which concentrates at 0 as N grows but is not positive and has \int_{-\pi}^\pi|D_N|
\to \infty like \log N. Near a jump of f the partial sums overshoot the one-sided limit by a fixed fraction of the jump that does not decrease with N, the Gibbs phenomenon.

Replacing the partial sums by their averages removes the negative lobes of the kernel and with them the Gibbs phenomenon. The third exercise introduces the Fejér kernel and proves its positivity, the key to Fejér’s theorem that the averaged sums of every continuous function converge uniformly.

Exercise 9 (The Fejér kernel) Define the Cesàro means \sigma_N f = \frac{1}{N + 1}\sum_{n=0}^N S_n f. Show that \sigma_N f = \frac1{2\pi}\int
F_N(x - y)f(y)\,dy with F_N(t) = \frac{1}{N + 1}\sum_{n=0}^N D_n(t) = \frac{1}{N + 1}\frac{\sin^2((N +
1)t/2)}{\sin^2(t/2)}, that F_N \geq 0 with \frac1{2\pi}\int F_N = 1, and deduce that |\sigma_N f| \leq
\sup|f|: the Cesàro means never overshoot.







NoteSolution





Averaging the integral formula for S_n f gives the one for \sigma_N f with the averaged kernel. With s =
\sin(t/2), \sum_{n=0}^N\sin((n + \tfrac12)t) = \operatorname{Im}\sum_n e^{i(n + 1/2)t} =
\operatorname{Im}\frac{e^{it/2}(e^{i(N+1)t} - 1)}{e^{it} - 1} = \operatorname{Im}\frac{e^{i(N+1)t} -
1}{2is} = \frac{1 - \cos((N + 1)t)}{2s} = \frac{\sin^2((N + 1)t/2)}{s}, and dividing by (N + 1)s gives F_N, visibly non-negative. Its integral is the average of the integrals of the D_n, each 2\pi. Then |\sigma_N
f(x)| \leq \frac1{2\pi}\int F_N(x - y)|f(y)|\,dy \leq \sup|f|, since F_N \geq 0 integrates to 2\pi. A positive kernel of unit mass concentrating at 0 is an approximate identity, and \sigma_N f \to f uniformly for continuous f (Fejér’s theorem), with no Gibbs overshoot.

The question of when the Fourier series equals the function has several answers depending on what one asks of f and in what sense the limit is taken. The theorem below collects the three that are used throughout the book, the pointwise theorem of Dirichlet, uniform convergence under absolute summability, and the L^2 theorem, with the proof of the first sketched through the Dirichlet kernel.


Theorem 1 (Convergence of Fourier series) Let f be 2\pi-periodic. (i) (Dirichlet) If f is piecewise C^1, then S_N f(x) \to \tfrac12\bigl(f(x^+) +
f(x^-)\bigr) at every x, in particular S_N f(x) \to f(x) at points of continuity. (ii) If \sum|c_n| <
\infty, which holds when f is continuous and piecewise C^1, the series converges absolutely and uniformly (Definition 19 of Real analysis) to a continuous function, which equals f at its points of continuity. (iii) (Riesz-Fischer) If \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2 < \infty then \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f - S_N f|^2\,dx \to 0, and conversely every square-summable sequence (c_n) is the coefficient sequence of such an f; Carleson’s theorem adds that the series of a square-integrable function converges to it at almost every point. Sketch of (i). By Equation 2 and the evenness of D_N, S_N f(x) - \tfrac12(f(x^+) + f(x^-)) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi D_N(t)\bigl[f(x + t) +
f(x - t) - f(x^+) - f(x^-)\bigr]dt; the bracket divided by \sin(t/2) is piecewise continuous on [0, \pi] because f is piecewise C^1, so the integral is a Fourier coefficient of a piecewise continuous function at frequency N + \tfrac12 and tends to 0 by the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma (Exercise 11). Statement (ii) is the Weierstrass M-test (Series), and (iii) follows from Parseval’s identity (Theorem 2).

The square wave satisfies the hypotheses of Dirichlet’s theorem, and its series shows both conclusions at once: convergence to the function away from the jumps and to the midpoint at them. The first example records this, and notes that the convergence cannot be uniform.

For g = 1 on [c, d] the integral is (\cos\lambda c - \cos\lambda d)/\lambda, of absolute value at most 2/\lambda, so the statement holds for step functions. A piecewise continuous g is Riemann integrable, so for every \varepsilon > 0 there is a step function s with \int_a^b|g - s| < \varepsilon (Definition 11 of Real analysis, lower sums). Then |\int g\sin\lambda t| \leq |\int (g - s)\sin\lambda t| + |\int s\sin\lambda t| \leq \varepsilon +
|\int s\sin\lambda t|, and the second term is below \varepsilon for \lambda large; so the limit superior is at most 2\varepsilon for every \varepsilon. The same argument works with \cos\lambda t and e^{i\lambda t}, and shows c_n \to 0 for every piecewise continuous periodic f.

Differentiating a Fourier series term by term is legitimate when the result converges uniformly, and illegitimate when it does not, even though both series look equally formal. The third exercise contrasts |x|, whose differentiated series is the square wave, with the sawtooth, whose differentiated series diverges everywhere.

The sum of the squares of the coefficients equals the mean square of the function, which is the Pythagorean theorem in infinitely many dimensions. The theorem states this identity in both forms together with the finite inequality of Bessel and the best-approximation property that explains why Fourier coefficients are the right choice.


Theorem 2 (Parseval’s identity) For a 2\pi-periodic f with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2 < \infty, 
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(x)|^2\,dx = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}|c_n|^2, \qquad \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,dx =
\frac{|a_0|^2}{2} + \sum_{n \geq 1}\bigl(|a_n|^2 + |b_n|^2\bigr),
\tag{3} and more generally \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\bar f g\,dx = \sum_n\bar c_n(f)c_n(g). Argument. For a trigonometric polynomial T = \sum_{|n| \leq N} t_n e^{inx}, Equation 1 gives \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f -
T|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 - \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 + \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n - t_n|^2, so S_N f is the  best approximation** of f in mean square among trigonometric polynomials of degree N, and Bessel’s inequality \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 holds for every N. Equality in the limit is the statement that \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f - S_N f|^2 \to 0, which holds because trigonometric polynomials approximate every such f in mean square (by Fejér’s theorem for continuous f and by approximation of f with continuous functions in general); the polarised form follows by applying the identity to f + g and f + ig.

The coefficients of a function with jumps are sums of integrals over the pieces on which it is smooth. The first example computes them for the square wave and explains why they are exact rational multiples of 1/\pi.

Example 16 (Coefficients of piecewise functions) The square wave is -1 on (-\pi, 0) and 1 on (0, \pi), so a_n = 0 by oddness and b_n =
\frac1\pi\bigl(-\int_{-\pi}^0\sin nx\,dx + \int_0^\pi\sin nx\,dx\bigr). Each of the two integrals equals (1 - \cos n\pi)/n, an integer divided by n, so b_n = \frac{2(1 - (-1)^n)}{\pi n} is a rational multiple of 1/\pi: 4/(\pi n) for odd n, for instance 4/(3\pi) for n = 3, and 0 for even n. Summing up to N = 5 gives S_5 = \frac4\pi(\sin x + \tfrac13\sin 3x + \tfrac15\sin 5x).

A function on [0, \pi] can be expanded in sines alone or in cosines alone, by extending it to (-\pi, \pi) as an odd or an even function. The third exercise connects these half-range expansions with the Dirichlet modes of Boundary value and Sturm-Liouville problems and explains which one converges better.

A function vanishing at both ends, such as \sin x or x(\pi - x), has an odd extension that is continuous, and then the sine series converges uniformly too.

A function on the whole line has no period, and the discrete harmonics e^{inx} are replaced by the continuum of plane waves e^{ikx} with the sum over n replaced by an integral over k. This section defines the transform and its inverse, computes it for the box, the two-sided exponential and the Gaussian, proves the convolution theorem, states Plancherel’s theorem and the uncertainty inequality, and ends with a proposition that collects the explicit transforms; the figure shows the trade-off between the width of a Gaussian and the width of its transform.
For more on this topic, see Aliev and Lara (2024, Ch. 8), Arrigo (2023, Ch. 6) and Borodzik et al. (2019, Ch. 2).

The Fourier transform of an integrable function is its inner product with every plane wave at once, a function of the wave number k. The definition fixes the normalisation used throughout the book, lists the rules that make the transform computable, and records the heuristic that it is a Fourier series whose period has gone to infinity.


Definition 4 (Fourier transform) For f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} with \int_{-\infty}^\infty|f| < \infty (absolutely integrable), the Fourier transform is 
\hat f(k) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,e^{-ikx}\,dx, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R},
\tag{4} a bounded continuous function with |\hat f(k)| \leq \int|f| and \hat f(k) \to 0 as |k| \to \infty (Riemann-Lebesgue). It obeys the translation rule \widehat{f(x - a)} = e^{-ika}\hat f(k), the modulation rule \widehat{e^{iax}f} = \hat f(k - a), the scaling rule \widehat{f(\lambda x)} = \hat
f(k/\lambda)/|\lambda|, the derivative rule \widehat{f'} = ik\hat f when f is C^1 with f, f' integrable, and the multiplication rule \widehat{xf} = i\,\hat f\,' when xf is integrable; a Schwartz function, smooth with all derivatives decaying faster than any power, has a Schwartz transform. Heuristically, f on [-L, L] has the series \sum_n c_n e^{i\pi nx/L} with 2Lc_n = \hat f(\pi n/L), and as L \to \infty the sum over the wave numbers k_n = \pi n/L spaced by \pi/L becomes \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(k)e^{ikx}dk, which is the inversion formula of Theorem 3.

A function is recovered from its transform by the inverse integral, with the factor 1/2\pi placed in the inverse in this book. The theorem states the inversion formula under a hypothesis that covers the examples, sketches the proof by Gaussian regularisation, and records the duality that the transform of a transform is the reflected function.


Theorem 3 (Fourier inversion) If f and \hat f are both absolutely integrable and f is continuous, then 
f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\hat f(k)\,e^{ikx}\,dk
\tag{6} for every x; if f is only piecewise C^1 the right side converges, as \lim_{L \to \infty}\int_{-L}^L, to \tfrac12(f(x^+) + f(x^-)). In particular \hat{\hat f}(x) = 2\pi f(-x) (duality). The step in the inversion argument that needs real analysis is the convergence of the Gaussian regularisation, an approximate identity. The second exercise proves it, which is the same estimate that makes the delta function a limit of Gaussians in Section 1.3.

Exercise 23 (Gaussian regularisation) Let G_\varepsilon(x) = e^{-x^2/2\varepsilon}/\sqrt{2\pi\varepsilon}. Show that \int G_\varepsilon = 1, that for every \delta > 0, \int_{|y| > \delta}G_\varepsilon(y)\,dy \to 0 as \varepsilon \to 0, and that \int
f(x - y)G_\varepsilon(y)\,dy \to f(x) for every bounded f continuous at x.







NoteSolution





\int G_\varepsilon = 1 is the Gaussian integral; substituting y = \sqrt\varepsilon\,u, \int_{|y| >
\delta}G_\varepsilon = \int_{|u| > \delta/\sqrt\varepsilon}e^{-u^2/2}du/\sqrt{2\pi} \to 0 as the lower limit goes to infinity. Then \int f(x - y)G_\varepsilon(y)dy - f(x) = \int[f(x - y) - f(x)]G_\varepsilon(y)dy; split at |y| = \delta, where \delta is chosen so that |f(x - y) - f(x)| < \eta for |y| < \delta: the inner part is at most \eta and the outer part at most 2\sup|f|\int_{|y| > \delta}G_\varepsilon \to 0. So the limit superior is at most \eta for every \eta > 0.

The duality \hat{\hat f} = 2\pi f(-x) means that the transform applied four times is (2\pi)^2 times the identity, so its eigenvalues are the four fourth roots of (2\pi)^2. The third exercise identifies the first two eigenfunctions, the Gaussian and the Gaussian times x, which begin the Hermite functions.

Exercise 24 (Eigenfunctions of the transform) Show from the duality that the only possible eigenvalues of f \mapsto \hat f are \pm\sqrt{2\pi} and \pm i\sqrt{2\pi}, verify with Sage that e^{-x^2/2} and xe^{-x^2/2} are eigenfunctions with eigenvalues \sqrt{2\pi} and -i\sqrt{2\pi}, and find the eigenvalue of (2x^2 - 1)e^{-x^2/2}.

Multiplying transforms corresponds to an operation on the functions themselves, the convolution, which is also how a function is smoothed or averaged. The definition introduces it, states the convolution theorem in both directions, and names the smoothing property that makes approximate identities work.


Definition 5 (Convolution) The convolution of two integrable functions is 
(f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x - y)\,g(y)\,dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(y)\,g(x - y)\,dy,
 commutative and associative, integrable with \int|f * g| \leq \int|f|\int|g|. The convolution theorem states 
\widehat{f * g} = \hat f\,\hat g, \qquad \widehat{fg} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\,\hat f * \hat g,
\tag{7} the first for integrable f, g and the second when f, g and their transforms are integrable. Convolution smooths: f * g is as differentiable as the better of f and g, with (f * g)' = f' * g = f * g'; and convolving with a family of non-negative functions of unit integral concentrating at 0 (an approximate identity, such as the Gaussians of Exercise 23) returns f in the limit.

The theorem is also the statement that the transform preserves inner products, and the Hermite functions of Exercise 24 show it in action: orthogonal eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues. The third example makes this explicit and notes what unitarity says about the eigenvalues.

Example 30 (Orthogonality of the Hermite functions) e^{-x^2/2} and xe^{-x^2/2} are orthogonal, \int xe^{-x^2}dx = 0 by oddness, and so are their transforms \sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2} and -ik\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}, as the polarised identity requires. Exercise 31 (The proof in detail) Justify each step of the proof of Theorem 5, extend it to the uncentred case with means \bar x and \bar

The product of widths does not change under scaling, translation or modulation, which is why the inequality has a universal constant. The third exercise proves this invariance and uses it to reduce every Gaussian to the standard one.

Exercise 33 (Invariance of the product) Show that \Delta x\,\Delta k is unchanged when f(x) is replaced by f(\lambda x), by f(x - a) (with the centred definitions about the new mean) or by e^{ibx}f(x), and deduce from the single case e^{-x^2/2} that every Gaussian has product \tfrac12.

Under f(\lambda x), the substitution u = \lambda x gives (\Delta x)^2 \mapsto (\Delta x)^2/\lambda^2, while the transform becomes \hat f(k/\lambda)/|\lambda| and (\Delta k)^2 \mapsto \lambda^2(\Delta k)^2; the product is unchanged. A translation shifts \bar x by a and leaves |\hat f| unchanged (the phase e^{-ika} has modulus 1), so both centred widths are unchanged; a modulation shifts \bar k by b and leaves |f| unchanged. Every Gaussian Ce^{i\bar kx}e^{-(x - \bar x)^2/2\sigma^2} is obtained from e^{-x^2/2} by scaling, translating and modulating, so its product equals that of e^{-x^2/2}, which is \tfrac12 by Example 31 with \sigma = 1.

A computer stores a function by finitely many samples, and the integrals of the coefficients and of the transform become finite sums. On N equally spaced samples of a period the harmonics e^{inx} become the N-th roots of unity, and the orthogonality of Equation 1 becomes an exact identity between finite sums; the definition records the resulting transform, which is exact and invertible in its own right (Izaac and Wang 2018, secs. 8.3.1–8.3.3).


Definition 6 (Discrete Fourier transform) The discrete Fourier transform of (f_0, \dots, f_{N - 1}) \in \mathbb{C}^N is the sequence 
F_m = \sum_{n = 0}^{N - 1}f_n\,e^{-2\pi imn/N}, \qquad m \in \mathbb{Z},
\tag{10} which is N-periodic, F_{m + N} = F_m, so that F_0, \dots, F_{N - 1} determine it. The discrete orthogonality \sum_{m = 0}^{N - 1}e^{2\pi im(l - n)/N} = N\delta_{ln} for 0 \leq l, n < N gives the inversion f_n =
\frac1N\sum_{m = 0}^{N - 1}F_me^{2\pi imn/N} and the discrete Parseval identity \sum_n|f_n|^2 =
\frac1N\sum_m|F_m|^2. For real f_n, F_{N - m} = \overline{F_m}, so F_0 and (for even N) F_{N/2} =
\sum_n(-1)^nf_n are real and about half of the F_m carry the information. If f_n = f(2\pi n/N) are samples of a trigonometric polynomial f(x) = \sum_{|k| < N/2}c_ke^{ikx}, then F_m = Nc_m for |m| < N/2: the transform of the samples computes the Fourier coefficients of Definition 2 exactly, the index m and m - N standing for the same wave number.

Proposition 2 (Sampling and aliasing)

The transforms, rules and inequalities of this section are collected in one proposition. Every item is an exact integral over the line, valid under sign conditions on the parameters; the widths are exact rational multiples of \sigma and the products are exact numbers.


Proposition 3 (Transforms of the Gaussian, the box and the exponential) \widehat{e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}} = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2} and the inverse integral returns the Gaussian; \hat\chi_a = 2\sin ak/k and \widehat{e^{-a|x|}} = 2a/(a^2 + k^2); \widehat{f'} = ik\hat f for the Gaussian; \chi_a * \chi_a is the triangle (2a - |x|)_+, with \int_{x - a}^a dy = 2a - x on [0, 2a], and its transform is (2\sin ak/k)^2; Plancherel for the box, \frac{1}{2\pi}\int4\sin^2ak/k^2\,dk = 2a = \int\chi_a^2; \Delta x = \sigma/\sqrt2, \Delta k = 1/\sigma\sqrt2 and \Delta x\Delta k = \tfrac12 for the Gaussian, and \Delta x\Delta k = 1/\sqrt2 for e^{-a|x|}.

NoteExamples





Each transform of the proposition is an improper integral, and it converges only under conditions on the parameters. The first example states these conditions for the exponential and the Gaussian and shows what goes wrong without them.

Example 40 (Assumptions for improper integrals) \int_0^\infty e^{-ax}e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{1}{a + ik} converges exactly when \operatorname{Re}(a + ik) > 0, which for real k means a > 0; adding the integral over (-\infty, 0), which is \frac{1}{a - ik}, gives \widehat{e^{-a|x|}} = \frac{2a}{a^2 + k^2}. For a \leq 0 the function does not decay and the integral diverges, although the right-hand side still makes sense: the formula is not the transform of anything there. For the Gaussian the integral converges for every complex k once \sigma > 0, and \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2} holds for complex k as well, both sides being analytic in k.

The convolution rule can be tested on two boxes, where both sides are elementary. The second example computes the triangle from the convolution integral, transforms it piece by piece and recovers the square of the sinc.

Example 41 (The convolution rule for two boxes) For 0 \leq x \leq 2a the boxes [-a, a] and [x - a, x + a] overlap in [x - a, a], so (\chi_a * \chi_a)(x) =
\int_{x - a}^a dy = 2a - x, and by evenness the convolution is the triangle (2a - |x|)_+. Its transform is \int_{-2a}^0(2a + x)e^{-ikx}dx + \int_0^{2a}(2a - x)e^{-ikx}dx = 2\int_0^{2a}(2a - x)\cos kx\,dx = \frac{2 -
2\cos 2ak}{k^2}, and 2 - 2\cos 2ak = 4\sin^2ak turns this into (2\sin ak/k)^2 = \hat\chi_a^2, as Equation 7 requires.

The widths are ratios of second moments to integrals, and each moment is a Gaussian-type or a Lorentzian-type integral with a closed form. The third example lists the four integrals behind the two uncertainty products.

Example 42 (The widths as moment integrals) For the Gaussian, \int x^2e^{-x^2/\sigma^2} = \sigma^3\sqrt\pi/2 over \int e^{-x^2/\sigma^2} = \sigma\sqrt\pi gives \sigma^2/2, and \int k^2\cdot2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2} over \int2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2} gives 1/2\sigma^2; for the exponential, \int x^2e^{-2a|x|} = 1/2a^3 over 1/a and \int4a^2k^2/(a^2 + k^2)^2 =
2\pi a over 2\pi/a. The squared products are \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2} = \tfrac14 and \tfrac{1}{2a^2}\cdot a^2 = \tfrac12, so \Delta x\Delta k = \tfrac12 and 1/\sqrt2.

The damped cosine is the function whose transform is the sum of two Lorentzians, the line shape of a damped oscillator. The first exercise computes its transform in Sage and locates the two peaks.

Exercise 40 (The damped cosine) Compute the transform of e^{-a|x|}\cos bx with Sage, show that it is the sum of two Lorentzians centred at k =
\pm b, and find the width at half maximum of each peak for a \ll b.







NoteSolution





By the modulation rule, \frac{a}{a^2 + (k - b)^2} + \frac{a}{a^2 + (k + b)^2}; each Lorentzian a/(a^2 + (k \mp
b)^2) has maximum 1/a and drops to half of it at |k \mp b| = a, so the full width at half maximum is 2a, the decay rate:

x, k, a, b = var("x k a b")
assume(a > 0); assume(b > 0); assume(k, "real")
F = integrate(exp(-a * abs(x)) * cos(b * x) * exp(-I * k * x), x, -oo, oo).simplify_full()
L = a / (a ** 2 + (k - b) ** 2) + a / (a ** 2 + (k + b) ** 2)
print("transform:", F)
print("equals a/(a^2 + (k - b)^2) + a/(a^2 + (k + b)^2):", bool((F - L).simplify_full() == 0))
peak = a / (a ** 2 + (k - b) ** 2)

The delta function of Definition 24 of Differential equations, the transform of the constant function, and the derivative of a function with a jump are not functions, but they are all linear functionals on smooth test functions, and that is the definition that makes the formal computations of physics rigorous. This section defines test functions and distributions, their derivatives and Fourier transforms, and the principal value, with the figure showing two sequences of functions that converge to the delta; the identities obtained along the way are collected in the proposition at the end.

Right: the Fourier kernels \delta_L(x) = \sin(Lx)/(\pi x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^Le^{ikx}dk, also of unit integral, oscillating more and more rapidly as L \to \infty while their action on every test function tends to its value at 0. A distribution is defined by what it does to nice functions, so the first thing to fix is the class of nice functions. The definition introduces the two standard classes, the smooth functions of compact support and the rapidly decreasing functions of Schwartz, and what it means for a sequence of them to converge.


Definition 7 (Test function) A test function is a smooth function \varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} that vanishes outside a bounded interval (compact support); the space of test functions is written \mathcal{D}. A Schwartz function is a smooth function such that x^m\varphi^{(n)}(x) is bounded for all m, n \geq 0 (all derivatives decay faster than any power); the space of Schwartz functions is \mathcal{S} \supset \mathcal{D}, and it is closed under differentiation, multiplication by polynomials and the Fourier transform (Exercise 44). A sequence \varphi_j \to \varphi in \mathcal{S} if \sup_x|x^m(\varphi_j - \varphi)^{(n)}| \to 0 for every m, n, and in \mathcal{D} if moreover all \varphi_j vanish outside one fixed interval. The same definitions apply on \mathbb{R}^n with multi-indices.

The Fourier transform exchanges decay with smoothness, which is why the Schwartz space, with both, is the natural home of the transform. The third example makes the exchange explicit through the rules of Definition 4.

Example 45 (Decay against smoothness) By the derivative and multiplication rules, \widehat{\varphi^{(n)}} = (ik)^n\hat\varphi and \widehat{x^m\varphi}

A distribution is a continuous linear functional on test functions, and every locally integrable function is one by integration; the delta is the simplest one that is not. The definition fixes the vocabulary, the notion of convergence of distributions, and the fact that the delta is a limit of functions.


Definition 8 (Distribution) A distribution is a linear map T : \mathcal{D} \to \mathbb{C}, written T(\varphi) or \langle T,
\varphi\rangle, that is continuous: T(\varphi_j) \to T(\varphi) whenever \varphi_j \to \varphi in \mathcal{D}. A tempered distribution is a continuous linear map \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{C}; it restricts to a distribution, and tempered distributions are the ones with Fourier transforms. Every locally integrable f of at most polynomial growth defines the regular tempered distribution T_f(\varphi) = \int f\varphi\,dx, and f is identified with T_f; the Dirac delta is \delta(\varphi) = \varphi(0), and \delta_a(\varphi) =
\varphi(a) is written \delta(x - a) (Definition 24 of Differential equations). Distributions T_j converge to T if T_j(\varphi)
\to T(\varphi) for every test function; the point of the definition is that a sequence of functions can converge as distributions to something that is not a function, as g_\varepsilon \to \delta in Figure 3.

Exercise 47 (The delta is not a function) Prove that there is no locally integrable f with \int f\varphi = \varphi(0) for all test functions \varphi, and show that if a distribution T satisfies T(\varphi) = 0 whenever \varphi vanishes near 0 and T(\varphi) depends only on \varphi(0), then T = c\,\delta.

A periodic array of deltas is a tempered distribution, and its Fourier series is the formal series of Exercise 12 with all coefficients equal. The third exercise proves this identity, which is Poisson summation in distributional form.

Exercise 48 (The Dirac comb) Show that \text{Ш}(x) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\delta(x - 2\pi n) is a tempered distribution and that \text{Ш} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}e^{inx} as distributions, that is, \sum_n\varphi(2\pi n) =

Every distribution has derivatives of all orders, defined by moving the derivative onto the test function with a sign, as integration by parts suggests. The definition records this, the product with a smooth function, and the Leibniz rule, with the identity x\delta' = -\delta as the first non-obvious consequence.


Definition 9 (Distributional derivative) The derivative of a distribution T is the distribution T'(\varphi) = -T(\varphi'), so that T^{(n)}(\varphi)
= (-1)^nT(\varphi^{(n)}); for a C^1 function f this agrees with the classical derivative, since \int
f\varphi'\,dx = -\int f'\varphi\,dx with no boundary terms. The product of T with a smooth function \psi of polynomial growth (with all derivatives) is (\psi T)(\varphi) = T(\psi\varphi), and the Leibniz rule (\psi T)' = \psi'T + \psi T' holds. Differentiation is continuous: T_j \to T implies T_j' \to T', so a convergent sequence of functions may be differentiated term by term as distributions, whatever happens to the classical derivatives.

The delta in three dimensions is what the Laplacian of 1/r produces, and writing it in spherical coordinates connects the flux computation of Proposition 9 of Differential equations with the distributional derivative. The third exercise asks for this identity and for its Fourier-space form.

Exercise 60 (\nabla^2(1/r) = -4\pi\delta^3) Show that \nabla^2\frac1r = -4\pi\delta^3(\mathbf x) as distributions on \mathbb{R}^3 by integrating \frac1r\nabla^2\varphi over the exterior of a small ball and using Green’s identity, and deduce the Fourier transform \widehat{1/r} = 4\pi/k^2 from the derivative rule.

\nabla^2\frac1r(\varphi) = \int\frac1r\nabla^2\varphi\,d^3x = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\int_{r >
\varepsilon}\frac1r\nabla^2\varphi. Green’s second identity on V = \{r > \varepsilon\} reads \int_V(u\nabla^2\varphi -
\varphi\nabla^2u) = \oint_{\partial V}(u\,\partial_n\varphi - \varphi\,\partial_nu)\,dS with n the outward normal of V, which on the sphere r = \varepsilon points towards the origin, so \partial_n = -\partial_r. With u = 1/r, harmonic in V, and \partial_r(1/r) = -1/r^2, the surface integral is \oint\bigl(-\tfrac1\varepsilon\partial_r\varphi -
\varphi\cdot\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\bigr)\varepsilon^2d\Omega = -\oint(\varepsilon\,\partial_r\varphi + \varphi)\,d\Omega
\to -4\pi\varphi(0); so \nabla^2\frac1r = -4\pi\delta^3, the flux statement of Proposition 9 of Differential equations in distributional form. Transforming, -k^2\widehat{1/r} = -4\pi\hat\delta^3 = -4\pi, so \widehat{1/r} = 4\pi/k^2, the m \to 0 limit of the Yukawa transform 4\pi/(k^2 + m^2) of Exercise 42.

The circle is the simplest compact space, and Fourier series are the expansion of functions on it in the eigenfunctions of d^2/dx^2; the sphere and the compact Lie groups are the next cases, and the same structure reappears with the Laplacian replaced by the Laplacian of the round metric and the harmonics by the spherical harmonics or the matrix coefficients of the irreducible representations. This section defines the Laplacian on S^2 and the spherical harmonics, connects them to the spin-l representations of SU(2) of Weights and the representations of su(2), states the Peter-Weyl theorem, and describes the mode expansion of a function on a coset space G/H; the figure shows the harmonics for l \leq 3, and the eigenvalue equations, the orthonormality and the representation-theoretic identities are collected in the proposition at its end.
For more on this topic, see Aliev and Lara (2024, Ch. 7).

A function on the sphere has a Laplacian, the angular part of the Laplacian of \mathbb{R}^3, and its eigenfunctions are the modes of the sphere. The definition gives the operator in spherical coordinates, its relation to the three-dimensional Laplacian, its symmetry, and the angular momentum operators that generate the rotations and square to minus the Laplacian.


Definition 12 (Laplacian on the sphere) The Laplacian on the unit sphere S^2, in the spherical coordinates (\theta, \varphi) of the round metric d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2, is 
\Delta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Bigl(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Bigr) +
\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\varphi^2},
\tag{15} the angular part of the Laplacian of \mathbb{R}^3: \nabla^2 = \partial_r^2 + \frac2r\partial_r + \frac{1}{r^2}\Delta. It is symmetric and non-positive for the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_{S^2}\bar fg\,d\Omega with d\Omega = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi, so its eigenvalues are real and \leq 0 and eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues are orthogonal (Exercise 63); and it commutes with rotations, since the round metric is rotation invariant. The angular momentum operators L_z = -i\partial_\varphi and L_\pm =
e^{\pm i\varphi}(\pm\partial_\theta + i\cot\theta\,\partial_\varphi) generate the rotations about the z-axis and the raising and lowering of m, satisfy the \mathfrak{su}(2) relations [L_z, L_\pm] = \pm L_\pm, [L_+, L_-]
= 2L_z of Weights and the representations of su(2), and their Casimir is \mathbf L^2 = L_z^2 + \tfrac12(L_+L_- + L_-L_+) = -\Delta.

The function \cos\theta, the height z restricted to the sphere, is the first non-constant eigenfunction, and its eigenvalue is read off from the formula. The first example computes it and the eigenvalues of the other two coordinate functions.

Example 61 (The coordinate functions) \Delta\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(-\sin^2\theta) = -2\cos\theta, so z = \cos\theta is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue -2 = -l(l + 1) for l = 1. The same holds for x = \sin\theta\cos\varphi and y =
\sin\theta\sin\varphi (Exercise 61): \Delta(\sin\theta\cos\varphi) = \frac{\cos\varphi}{\sin\theta}
\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\cos\theta) - \frac{\sin\theta\cos\varphi}{\sin^2\theta} = \cos\varphi\Bigl(\frac{\cos
2\theta}{\sin\theta} - \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\Bigr) = -2\sin\theta\cos\varphi. The three coordinate functions span the eigenspace of -2, a three-dimensional space on which rotations act as on vectors.

Exercise 61 (Applying the Laplacian) Compute \Delta f with Sage for f = \cos^2\theta, f = \sin\theta\cos\varphi and f = \sin^2\theta\cos2\varphi, decide which are eigenfunctions, and decompose the one that is not into eigenfunctions.







NoteSolution





\sin\theta\cos\varphi and \sin^2\theta\cos2\varphi are eigenfunctions with eigenvalues -2 and -6 (they are the restrictions of x and of x^2 - y^2); \cos^2\theta = z^2 is not, since z^2 = \tfrac13(2z^2 - x^2 -
y^2) + \tfrac13r^2 is the sum of a harmonic quadratic and \tfrac13: \Delta\cos^2\theta = 2 - 6\cos^2\theta =
-6(\cos^2\theta - \tfrac13), so \cos^2\theta = \tfrac13 + (\cos^2\theta - \tfrac13) with eigenvalues 0 and -6:

th, ph = var("theta phi")
lap = lambda f: diff(sin(th) * diff(f, th), th) / sin(th) + diff(f, ph, 2) / sin(th) ** 2
for name, f, lam in [("cos^2 theta", cos(th) ** 2, None), ("sin theta cos phi", sin(th) * cos(ph), -2), ("sin^2 theta cos 2phi", sin(th) ** 2 * cos(2 * ph), -6)]:
    L = lap(f).simplify_full()
    if lam is None:
        print(name, ": Delta f =", L.trig_reduce(), "; not proportional to f")
    else:
        print(name, ": Delta f =", L, "; eigenvalue", lam, ":", bool((L - lam * f).simplify_full() == 0))
f0 = SR(1) / 3; f2 = cos(th) ** 2 - SR(1) / 3
print("cos^2 theta = 1/3 + (cos^2 theta - 1/3) with Delta(1/3) = 0 and Delta(cos^2 theta - 1/3) = -6 (cos^2 theta - 1/3):", bool(lap(f0) == 0) and bool((lap(f2) + 6 * f2).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:

sin theta cos phi : Delta f = -2*cos(phi)*sin(theta) ; eigenvalue -2 : True
sin^2 theta cos 2phi : Delta f = 6*(2*sin(phi)^2 - 1)*sin(theta)^2 ; eigenvalue -6 : True
cos^2 theta = 1/3 + (cos^2 theta - 1/3) with Delta(1/3) = 0 and Delta(cos^2 theta - 1/3) = -6 (cos^2 theta - 1/3): True

The splitting of the three-dimensional Laplacian into radial and angular parts is a chain-rule computation, and the second exercise asks for it. It is the step that connects harmonic polynomials with eigenfunctions on the sphere.

Exercise 62 (Radial and angular parts) Derive \nabla^2 = \partial_r^2 + \frac2r\partial_r + \frac{1}{r^2}\Delta with \Delta as in Equation 15 from the spherical coordinates x = r\sin\theta\cos\varphi, y = r\sin\theta\sin\varphi, z = r\cos\theta, using the general formula \nabla^2f = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\partial_i(\sqrt g\,g^{ij}\partial_jf) for the metric dr^2 + r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2).







NoteSolution





The metric is diagonal with g_{rr} = 1, g_{\theta\theta} = r^2, g_{\varphi\varphi} = r^2\sin^2\theta and \sqrt g = r^2\sin\theta, so \nabla^2f = \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\bigl[\partial_r(r^2\sin\theta\,\partial_rf) +
\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f) + \partial_\varphi(\tfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\varphi f)\bigr] =
\frac{1}{r^2}\partial_r(r^2\partial_rf) + \frac{1}{r^2}\Delta f, and \frac{1}{r^2}\partial_r(r^2\partial_rf) =
\partial_r^2f + \frac2r\partial_rf. The formula \nabla^2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\partial_i\sqrt g g^{ij}\partial_j itself follows from the change of variables formula applied to \int\nabla f\cdot\nabla\varphi = -\int\varphi
\nabla^2f (Theorem 7 of Real analysis), and the Laplacian of Equation 15 is the same formula for the round metric alone.

The symmetry of the Laplacian for the inner product on the sphere is an integration by parts with no boundary, and it is what makes the eigenvalue problem self-adjoint. The third exercise proves it and derives the sign of the eigenvalues and the orthogonality of eigenfunctions.

Exercise 63 (Symmetry of the Laplacian) Show that \int_{S^2}\bar g\,\Delta f\,d\Omega = -\int_{S^2}\bigl(\partial_\theta\bar g\,\partial_\theta f +
\tfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi\bar g\,\partial_\varphi f\bigr)d\Omega = \int_{S^2}\overline{\Delta g}\,f\,d\Omega for smooth f, g, and deduce that every eigenvalue of \Delta is real and non-positive, that 0 is an eigenvalue only for the constants, and that eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.







NoteSolution





\int\bar g\,\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f)\,d\theta\,d\varphi = -\int\partial_\theta\bar g\,
\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f\,d\theta\,d\varphi since \sin\theta vanishes at \theta = 0, \pi, and \int\bar g\,\partial_\varphi^2f\,d\varphi = -\int\partial_\varphi\bar g\,\partial_\varphi f\,d\varphi by periodicity in \varphi; together with the factor \sin\theta of d\Omega this gives the middle expression, which is symmetric under exchanging f and g up to conjugation, hence the right side. With g = f an eigenfunction, \lambda\int|f|^2 = -\int(|\partial_\theta f|^2 + \tfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}|\partial_\varphi f|^2) \leq
0, with equality only if f is constant; and for eigenfunctions f, g with eigenvalues \lambda \neq \mu, \lambda\langle g, f\rangle = \langle g, \Delta f\rangle = \langle\Delta g, f\rangle = \mu\langle g, f\rangle forces \langle g, f\rangle = 0. This is the Sturm-Liouville argument of Theorem 2 of Differential equations in two variables.

The eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on the sphere are the spherical harmonics, products of an associated Legendre function of \cos\theta and a Fourier mode in \varphi. The definition fixes their normalisation and phase, records the eigenvalue equations for \Delta, L_z and L_\pm, and states their completeness, the analogue of the convergence theorems for Fourier series.


Definition 13 (Spherical harmonic) For l = 0, 1, 2, \dots and m = -l, \dots, l the spherical harmonic is 
Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) = (-1)^m\sqrt{\frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}\frac{(l - m)!}{(l + m)!}}\;P_l^m(\cos\theta)\,e^{im\varphi},
\qquad P_l^m(u) = (1 - u^2)^{m/2}\frac{d^m}{du^m}P_l(u) \ (m \geq 0),
\tag{16} with P_l the Legendre polynomial of Definition 16 of Differential equations, Y_{l,-m} = (-1)^m\overline{Y_{lm}}, and the Condon-Shortley phase (-1)^m as in Sage’s spherical_harmonic. They satisfy \Delta Y_{lm} = -l(l + 1)Y_{lm}, L_zY_{lm} = mY_{lm} and L_\pm Y_{lm} = \sqrt{(l \mp m)(l \pm m + 1)}\,Y_{l,m \pm 1}; they are orthonormal, \int_{S^2}\overline{Y_{lm}}Y_{l'm'}\,d\Omega = \delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'}; and they are complete: every square-integrable function on the sphere has the expansion 
f(\theta, \varphi) = \sum_{l \geq 0}\sum_{m = -l}^{l}f_{lm}Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi), \qquad f_{lm} =
\int_{S^2}\overline{Y_{lm}}\,f\,d\Omega,
\tag{17} convergent in mean square, uniformly if f is smooth, with Parseval’s identity \int|f|^2d\Omega =
\sum_{lm}|f_{lm}|^2. The 2l + 1 harmonics of degree l span the eigenspace of -l(l + 1), which is the spin-l representation of SU(2) (Definition 22 of Lie groups and Lie algebras) under rotations, with Y_{lm} the weight vector of weight m; Y_{l0} = \sqrt{(2l + 1)/4\pi}\,P_l(\cos\theta) is the rotationally symmetric one about the z-axis.

The sum over m of Y_{lm}(\mathbf n)\overline{Y_{lm}(\mathbf n')} depends only on the angle between the two directions, which is the rotation invariance of the eigenspaces made explicit. The third example states the addition theorem, checks it for l = 1, and gives its most important application.

Example 66 (The addition theorem) \sum_{m = -l}^lY_{lm}(\theta, \varphi)\overline{Y_{lm}(\theta', \varphi')} = \frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}P_l(\cos\gamma), where \cos\gamma = \cos\theta\cos\theta' + \sin\theta\sin\theta'\cos(\varphi - \varphi') is the cosine of the angle between the two directions; for l = 1 the left side is \frac{3}{4\pi}\cos\gamma (Proposition 6). The left side is the kernel of the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace of -l(l +
1), so it must be rotation invariant, hence a function of \gamma alone, and an eigenfunction of degree l in each argument, hence cP_l(\cos\gamma); the constant follows from \theta = \theta'. Combined with \frac{1}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|} = \sum_l\frac{r_<^l}{r_>^{l + 1}}P_l(\cos\gamma) it gives the multipole expansion of the Coulomb potential (Exercise 83).

Exercise 64 (Expansions in Sage) Expand \sin^2\theta\cos2\varphi and \cos^2\theta in spherical harmonics with Sage by computing f_{lm} for l

\sin^2\theta\cos2\varphi = \sqrt{\tfrac{8\pi}{15}}(Y_{22} + Y_{2,-2}), a pure l = 2 function, and \cos^2\theta

th, ph = var("theta phi")
Y = lambda l, m: spherical_harmonic(l, m, th, ph)
def coeff(f, l, m):
    return integrate(integrate((conjugate(Y(l, m)) * f).simplify_full() * sin(th), ph, 0, 2 * pi), th, 0, pi).simplify_full()
for name, f in [("sin^2 theta cos 2phi", sin(th) ** 2 * cos(2 * ph)), ("cos^2 theta", cos(th) ** 2)]:
    cs = {(l, m): coeff(f, l, m) for l in range(3) for m in range(-l, l + 1)}
    nz = {key: v for key, v in cs.items() if v != 0}
    print(name, ": non-zero f_lm =", nz)
    rec = sum(v * Y(l, m) for (l, m), v in nz.items())
    print("  expansion reproduces the function:", bool((rec - f).simplify_full().trig_reduce() == 0) or bool(abs((rec - f).subs({th: 0.7, ph: 1.3}).n()) < 1e-12))

The orthogonality of the harmonics has two sources, the symmetry of the Laplacian for different l and the Fourier orthogonality for different m, while the normalisation is a Legendre integral. The second exercise assembles these three facts into a proof.

Exercise 65 (Proof of orthonormality) Prove \int\overline{Y_{lm}}Y_{l'm'}d\Omega = \delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'}: for m \neq m' from the \varphi integral, for l \neq l' from Exercise 63, and for l = l', m = m' from \int_{-1}^1(P_l^m)^2du
= \frac{2}{2l + 1}\frac{(l + m)!}{(l - m)!} (which may be assumed) and Equation 16.







NoteSolution





The integrand contains e^{i(m' - m)\varphi}, whose integral over [0, 2\pi] vanishes for m \neq m' by Equation 1. For m = m' and l \neq l' the two functions are eigenfunctions of the symmetric operator \Delta with distinct eigenvalues -l(l + 1) \neq -l'(l' + 1), hence orthogonal. For l = l', m =
m': \int|Y_{lm}|^2d\Omega = \frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}\frac{(l - m)!}{(l + m)!}\cdot2\pi\int_{-1}^1(P_l^m(u))^2du with u
= \cos\theta, du = -\sin\theta\,d\theta, and the Legendre integral gives exactly 1. For m = 0 this is the normalisation \int P_l^2 = 2/(2l + 1) of Proposition 5 of Differential equations.

The addition theorem of Example 66 separates the directions of two points in 1/|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|, and integrating it against a localised density expands the potential of the density far away into spherical harmonics. The proposition states this expansion, defines the multipole moments as its coefficients, and relates the first three to the charge, the dipole moment and the quadrupole tensor of electrostatics (Maggiore 2023, sec. 6.1, eqs. (6.5)-(6.29)).


Proposition 5 (The multipole expansion) Let \rho be an integrable function on \mathbb{R}^3 vanishing for |\mathbf x| > d (or a finite sum of point charges q_a\delta^3(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_a) with |\mathbf x_a| \leq d), and \Phi(\mathbf x) = \int\frac{\rho(\mathbf
x')}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|}d^3x', the solution of \nabla^2\Phi = -4\pi\rho of Exercise 60. For r =
|\mathbf x| > d, with \mathbf x = r\mathbf n, 
\Phi(\mathbf x) = \sum_{l = 0}^\infty\sum_{m = -l}^l\frac{4\pi}{2l + 1}\,q_{lm}\,\frac{Y_{lm}(\mathbf n)}{r^{l + 1}},
\qquad q_{lm} = \int\rho(\mathbf x')\,r'^l\,\overline{Y_{lm}(\mathbf n')}\,d^3x' ,
\tag{18} converging absolutely and uniformly on r \geq r_0 > d; the numbers q_{lm} are the multipole moments of \rho, and each term is a harmonic function for r > 0. In Cartesian form, 
\Phi(\mathbf x) = \frac qr + \frac{\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n}{r^2} + \frac{Q_{ij}n_in_j}{2r^3} + O(r^{-4}), \qquad q =
\int\rho, \quad \mathbf d = \int\rho\,\mathbf x, \quad Q_{ij} = \int\rho\,(3x_ix_j - r^2\delta_{ij}) ,
\tag{19} with q_{00} = q/\sqrt{4\pi}, q_{10} = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\,d_z, q_{1, \pm1} = \mp\sqrt{3/8\pi}\,(d_x \mp id_y) and q_{20}
= \sqrt{5/16\pi}\,Q_{zz}; the quadrupole tensor Q_{ij} is symmetric and traceless, with five independent components like the q_{2m}. Proof. For r' \leq d < r, the Legendre expansion of 1/|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'| quoted in Example 66 (and proved in Exercise 83) and the addition theorem give \frac{1}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|} = \sum_{lm}\frac{4\pi}{2l + 1}\frac{r'^l}{r^{l + 1}}Y_{lm}(\mathbf n)\overline{Y_{lm}(\mathbf
n')}, and the l-th term is bounded by d^l/r_0^{l + 1}, because \sum_m|Y_{lm}|^2 = (2l + 1)/4\pi and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bound the sum over m; integrating term by term against \rho gives Equation 18. By Equation 15, \nabla^2(R(r)Y_{lm}) = (R'' + 2R'/r - l(l + 1)R/r^2)Y_{lm}, which vanishes for R =

The moments are computed about an origin, and moving the origin changes them, although the potential does not change. The second example finds how the dipole moment changes and when it does not (Maggiore 2023, sec. 6.1, eqs. (6.21)-(6.25)).

The gradient of the dipole term is the field of a dipole, with the characteristic angular pattern of field lines leaving one end and entering the other. The third example computes it from Equation 19.

Example 69 (The field of a dipole) With \partial_ir = n_i and \partial_in_j = (\delta_{ij} - n_in_j)/r, -\partial_i\frac{d_jn_j}{r^2} =

n - \mathbf d}{r^3}. On the axis, \mathbf n = \pm\mathbf d/|\mathbf d|, it is 2\mathbf d/r^3, along the dipole; in the equatorial plane, \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf d = 0, it is -\mathbf d/r^3, opposite to it and half as strong. In Heaviside-Lorentz units the electrostatic potential is \Phi/4\pi and in SI units \Phi/4\pi\varepsilon_0, so the electric field of a dipole is this vector divided by 4\pi or 4\pi\varepsilon_0; it falls like r^{-3}, one power faster than the Coulomb field.

On a compact group the role of the harmonics is played by the matrix elements of the irreducible unitary representations, and the role of the orthogonality of modes by Schur’s orthogonality relations. The definition introduces the matrix coefficients, the characters, the invariant integration they are orthogonal for, and the Wigner functions of SU(2) in Euler angles.


Definition 14 (Matrix coefficient) For a compact Lie group G and a unitary representation D of dimension d on \mathbb{C}^d (Definition 16 of Group theory), the matrix coefficients are the functions D_{ij}(g) = \langle e_i, D(g)e_j\rangle on G, and the character is \chi(g) = \operatorname{tr}D(g) = \sum_iD_{ii}(g), a function constant on conjugacy classes (a class function). The Haar measure dg is the unique measure on G invariant under left and right translations with \int_Gdg = 1; for SU(2) in the Euler-angle parametrisation g(\varphi, \theta,
\psi) = e^{-i\varphi J_z}e^{-i\theta J_y}e^{-i\psi J_z} with 0 \leq \varphi < 2\pi, 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi, 0
\leq \psi < 4\pi it is dg = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi/16\pi^2. The Schur orthogonality relations state that for irreducible unitary representations D^r, D^s, 
\int_GD^r_{ij}(g)\,\overline{D^s_{kl}(g)}\,dg = \frac{\delta_{rs}\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}}{d_r}, \qquad
\int_G\chi_r\bar\chi_s\,dg = \delta_{rs},

The Haar measure of SU(2) is determined by its invariance, and the Euler-angle formula can be checked against left translations. The first exercise verifies the two easy invariances and the normalisation, and identifies the measure with the volume form of the round S^3.

Exercise 70 (The Haar measure of SU(2)) Show that dg = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi/16\pi^2 has total mass 1, is invariant under left multiplication by e^{-i\alpha J_z} (which shifts \varphi) and right multiplication by e^{-i\beta J_z} (which shifts \psi), and is proportional to the volume form of the round metric on S^3 \cong SU(2); why is this enough to identify it with the Haar measure?







NoteSolution





\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi\int_0^{4\pi}d\psi = 2\cdot2\pi\cdot4\pi = 16\pi^2. Left multiplication by e^{-i\alpha J_z} sends (\varphi, \theta, \psi) to (\varphi + \alpha, \theta, \psi) and right multiplication by e^{-i\beta J_z} to (\varphi, \theta, \psi + \beta); d\varphi and d\psi are invariant under shifts, and \sin\theta\,d\theta does not involve them. The Euler angles are coordinates on S^3 in which the round metric is \tfrac14(d\theta^2 + d\varphi^2 + d\psi^2 + 2\cos\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi), with volume form \tfrac18\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi; the round metric is bi-invariant (it is the Killing form up to scale, Definition 4 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles), so its volume form is bi-invariant, and the Haar measure is unique, so the two agree after normalisation. Invariance under the one-parameter subgroups generated by J_z alone would not suffice; the bi-invariance of the metric supplies the rest.

vals = {}
