The matrix coefficients of all irreducible representations together form a complete orthogonal system on the group, which is the theorem of Peter and Weyl, the Fourier theory of compact groups. The theorem states it in three forms, as a basis, as an expansion, and as a decomposition of the regular representation, and records the two instances that this chapter is about.


Theorem 6 (The Peter-Weyl theorem) Let G be a compact Lie group and let \{D^r\} be a complete set of pairwise inequivalent irreducible unitary representations, of dimensions d_r. (i) The functions \sqrt{d_r}\,D^r_{ij}, over all r, i, j, form an orthonormal basis of the square-integrable functions on G: every such f has the expansion 
f(g) = \sum_rd_r\sum_{i, j = 1}^{d_r}\hat f^r_{ji}D^r_{ij}(g), \qquad \hat f^r = \int_Gf(g)\,D^r(g)^{-1}\,dg,
\tag{21} convergent in mean square, with \int|f|^2dg = \sum_rd_r\operatorname{tr}(\hat f^r{}^\dagger\hat f^r) (Parseval), uniformly if f is smooth. (ii) The characters \chi_r form an orthonormal basis of the square-integrable class functions. (iii) Under left translation (L_hf)(g) = f(h^{-1}g) the space of functions on G decomposes as \bigoplus_r(D^r)^{\oplus d_r}, each irreducible representation occurring as many times as its dimension, the d_r copies being spanned by the columns j of D^r_{ij}. Statement (i) contains Fourier series (G = U(1), D^n = e^{in\varphi}, d_n = 1) and the expansion of functions on SU(2) in Wigner functions; the spherical harmonics are the special case of functions on SU(2) independent of \psi (Definition 15). Argument. Orthonormality is Equation 20. Completeness is the content of the theorem: the convolution operators f \mapsto \int k(g^{-1}h)f(h)dh with continuous k are compact and self-adjoint for k(g^{-1}) =
\overline{k(g)}, their eigenspaces are finite-dimensional and invariant under translation, hence sums of matrix coefficients, and they approximate the identity as k runs through an approximate identity; the spectral theorem of the next chapter then gives the density of the matrix coefficients.

A function on a coset space G/H is a function on G that is constant along the cosets, and the Peter-Weyl expansion restricted to such functions keeps only the matrix coefficients whose right index is invariant under H. The definition states this and works out what it says for the sphere, where it reproduces the spherical harmonics, and records how the Laplacian acts on each mode.


Definition 15 (Mode expansion on a coset space) Let H \subset G be a closed subgroup of a compact Lie group and G/H the coset space (Definition 2 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles). A function on G/H is a function f on G with f(gh) = f(g) for all h \in H, and the Peter-Weyl expansion of such an f contains only the coefficients D^r_{ij} whose index j runs over an orthonormal basis of the H-singlets in D^r, the vectors v with D^r(h)v = v for all h \in H (the trivial representation in the restriction of D^r to H, Branching rules): the mode expansion on G/H is 
f(gH) = \sum_rd_r\sum_{i = 1}^{d_r}\sum_{j \in \text{singlets}}\hat f^r_{ji}\,D^r_{ij}(g),
\tag{22} so each irreducible representation r of G contributes to the functions on G/H as many copies of r as the number n_r of H-singlets in r, and the Laplacian of a G-invariant metric on a symmetric coset acts on the modes of type r by minus the Casimir, \Delta D^r_{ij} = -C_2(r)D^r_{ij}, in the normalisation in which C_2 =
j(j + 1) for SU(2). For S^2 = SU(2)/U(1) with U(1) = \{e^{-i\psi J_z}\}, the singlets of spin j are the weight vectors with n = 0, one for every integer j = l and none for half-integer j; the modes are D^l_{m0}
(\varphi, \theta, \psi) = \sqrt{4\pi/(2l + 1)}\,\overline{Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi)}, independent of \psi, and Equation 22 is the expansion Equation 17 in spherical harmonics with eigenvalues -l(l +
1).

Counting singlets is the computation that decides which representations appear on a coset space, and for the sphere it is a one-line inspection of the weights. The first exercise does it for S^2 and for the real projective plane, where an additional reflection halves the spectrum.

Exercise 76 (Counting singlets) Show that the restriction of the spin-j representation of SU(2) to U(1) = \{e^{-i\psi J_z}\} contains the trivial representation once if j is an integer and not at all if j is a half-integer; then determine which Y_{lm} are functions on \mathbb{RP}^2 = S^2/\{\pm1\}, the sphere with antipodal points identified.







NoteSolution





e^{-i\psi J_z} acts on the weight vector of weight n by e^{-in\psi}, \psi \in [0, 4\pi), and this is trivial exactly when n = 0; the weights of spin j are j, j - 1, \dots, -j, which contain 0 exactly when j is an integer, once (Definition 22 of Lie groups and Lie algebras). So the functions on S^2 carry every integer spin once and no half-integer spin, as Definition 15 states. The antipodal map \mathbf n \mapsto -\mathbf n is (\theta, \varphi) \mapsto (\pi - \theta, \varphi + \pi), under which Y_{lm} \mapsto (-1)^lY_{lm} (parity of the harmonic polynomial of degree l), so the functions on \mathbb{RP}^2 are spanned by the Y_{lm} with even l, the eigenvalues -l(l + 1) = 0, -6, -20, \dots with multiplicities 1, 5, 9, \dots.

The multiplicity of an eigenvalue of the Laplacian on G/H is the number of singlets times the dimension, a form of the Frobenius reciprocity theorem; on the group itself it is the square of the dimension. The third exercise derives these counts and the eigenvalues on S^3.

Exercise 78 (Degeneracies on G/H) Show from Equation 22 that the modes of type r on G/H span a space of dimension n_rd_r, so that the eigenvalue -C_2(r) of the Laplacian has multiplicity \sum_{r : C_2(r) = \lambda}n_rd_r; apply this to S^2 and to S^3, and derive the eigenvalues -n(n + 2) of the round unit S^3 from the Casimir and the relation between the bi-invariant metric and the round one.

For fixed r the index i takes d_r values and j takes n_r values, and the D^r_{ij} are linearly independent by Schur orthogonality, so the modes of type r span n_rd_r dimensions; different r with the same Casimir add up. On S^2, n_l = 1 and d_l = 2l + 1, so -l(l + 1) has multiplicity 2l + 1; on S^3, n_j = d_j = 2j + 1 and -C_2(j) has multiplicity (2j + 1)^2. The eigenvalue equation is proved for an explicit harmonic by applying the Laplacian of Equation 15 and simplifying, and the ladder relation by applying L_+. The first example does both for l = 1.

Example 79 (Simplifying to zero) For Y_{10} \propto \cos\theta, \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta\cos\theta) = -
\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta\sin^2\theta = -2\cos\theta, so \Delta Y_{10} + 2Y_{10} = 0. For Y_{11}
\propto \sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi} the \theta part gives \frac{\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta} and the \varphi part -\frac{1}{\sin\theta}, which add up to -2\sin\theta by \cos^2\theta - 1 = -\sin^2\theta: again \Delta Y_{11} + 2Y_{11} = 0. With L_+ = e^{i\varphi}(\partial_\theta + i\cot\theta\,\partial_\varphi), L_+Y_{10} = -\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{4\pi}}\sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi} = \sqrt2\,Y_{11}, the ladder relation with \sqrt{(1 - 0)(1 + 0 + 1)} = \sqrt2.

The number of independent harmonic polynomials of degree l is computed by linear algebra over the rationals, without any reference to the sphere. The second example explains the rank computation that gives 2l + 1.

Example 80 (Counting harmonic polynomials) The monomials x^ay^bz^c with a + b + c = l number \binom{l + 2}{2}, and the Laplacian maps their span onto the polynomials of degree l - 2, of dimension \binom{l}{2}: the matrix of \nabla^2 in these bases over \mathbb{Q} has full rank \binom{l}{2}, so its kernel has dimension \binom{l + 2}{2} -
\binom{l}{2} = 2l + 1. This is the dimension of the spin-l representation, obtained here without representation theory.

The identity d^1(\theta) = e^{-i\theta J_y} can be proved without computing a matrix exponential, through the defining differential equation and initial condition, which characterise the exponential uniquely. The third example does this and records the other matrix identities.

Example 81 (The Wigner matrix by its differential equation) e^{-i\theta J_y} is the unique solution of d' = -iJ_yd with d(0) = 1 (Definition 11 of Lie groups and Lie algebras), so it suffices that the explicit d^1(\theta) of Example 72 satisfies both: d^1(0) = 1 is immediate, and differentiating the entries gives d' + iJ_yd = 0. The same matrix satisfies d^1(d^1)^T = 1 and \det d^1 = 1, the spin-1 matrices satisfy their commutation relations, and assembling D^1 = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\varphi}, 1, e^{i\varphi})\,d^1\,\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\psi}, 1,
e^{i\psi}) gives a matrix whose middle column is \sqrt{4\pi/3}\,\overline{Y_{1m}}.

Exercise 81 (The ladder coefficient) Using [L_z, L_\pm] = \pm L_\pm, L_-= L_+^\dagger for the inner product on the sphere, and \mathbf L^2 = L_-L_+ +

\leq 3 numerically in Sage, and explain why the same function has the Fourier representation \frac{1}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|} = \frac{1}{2\pi^2}\int\frac{e^{i\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf x - \mathbf x')}}{k^2}d^3k.







NoteSolution





|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|^2 = r^2 + r'^2 - 2rr'\cos\gamma = r_>^2(1 - 2ut + t^2) with u = \cos\gamma and t =
r_</r_> < 1, so \frac{1}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|} = \frac{1}{r_>}\sum_lP_l(\cos\gamma)t^l by the generating function, which converges for t < 1 (Definition 6 of Real analysis; the generating function itself follows from Rodrigues’ formula or from the recursion of Proposition 5 of Differential equations). The addition theorem of Example 66 replaces P_l(\cos\gamma) by \frac{4\pi}{2l + 1}\sum_mY_{lm}(\mathbf n)\overline{Y_{lm}(\mathbf n')}. The Fourier form is the inverse transform of \widehat{1/r} = 4\pi/k^2 (Exercise 60) translated to \mathbf x', \frac{1}{(2\pi)^3}\int\frac{4\pi}{k^2}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf x - \mathbf x')}d^3k: the two expansions are the harmonic analysis of the same Green’s function on the sphere and on the line, respectively. Numerically, the truncation at l \leq 3 has error of order t^4:

th, ph, th2, ph2 = var("theta phi theta2 phi2")
Y = lambda l, m, t, p: spherical_harmonic(l, m, t, p)
r1, r2 = 1, 3
n1 = (sin(0.4) * cos(1.1), sin(0.4) * sin(1.1), cos(0.4)); n2 = (sin(2.0) * cos(-0.7), sin(2.0) * sin(-0.7), cos(2.0))
cosg = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(n1, n2))
exact = (1 / sqrt(r1 ** 2 + r2 ** 2 - 2 * r1 * r2 * cosg)).n(digits=12)
leg = sum(QQ(r1) ** l / QQ(r2) ** (l + 1) * legendre_P(l, cosg) for l in range(4)).n(digits=12)
sph = sum(4 * pi / (2 * l + 1) * QQ(r1) ** l / QQ(r2) ** (l + 1) * sum(Y(l, m, 0.4, 1.1) * conjugate(Y(l, m, 2.0, -0.7)) for m in range(-l, l + 1)) for l in range(4)).n(digits=12)
print("1/|x - x'| =", exact)
print("Legendre sum, l <= 3:", leg, "; spherical-harmonic sum, l <= 3:", sph.real(), "(imaginary part", abs(sph.imag()).n(digits=2), ")")
print("the two truncations agree:", bool(abs(leg - sph.real()) < 1e-10), "; error of the truncation", abs(exact - leg).n(digits=2), "; next term bound (r</r>)^4/r> =", (QQ(r1) ** 4 / QQ(r2) ** 5).n(digits=2))
t = var("t")
gen = taylor(1 / sqrt(1 - 2 * cosg * t + t ** 2), t, 0, 3)
print("generating function: coefficients of t^l are P_l(cos gamma) for l <= 3:", all(bool(abs(gen.coefficient(t, l) - legendre_P(l, cosg)) < 1e-12) for l in range(4)))

A Fourier series on [-L, L] becomes the Fourier transform as L \to \infty: the coefficients sample the transform, the sum becomes a Riemann sum for the inversion integral, and the Dirichlet kernel becomes the delta sequence \sin(Lx)/\pi x. The third exercise makes each of these three statements precise and checks the first two in Sage for a Gaussian.

Exercise 84 (From Fourier series to the Fourier transform) For f a Schwartz function and L > 0, let c_n^{(L)} = \frac{1}{2L}\int_{-L}^Lf(x)e^{-i\pi nx/L}dx be the coefficients of the 2L-periodic extension of f|_{[-L, L]}. Show that 2Lc_n^{(L)} \to \hat f(\pi n/L) as L \to \infty with exponentially small error for a Gaussian, that \sum_nc_n^{(L)}e^{i\pi nx/L} is the Riemann sum of \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(k)e^{ikx}dk with step \pi/L, that Parseval on [-L, L] becomes Plancherel, and that the Dirichlet kernel of the interval, \frac{1}{2L}\sum_{|n| \leq N}e^{i\pi nx/L}, tends to \sin(Kx)/\pi
x when N, L \to \infty with \pi N/L \to K; compare the partial sums with the Gaussian in Sage for L = 3, 6.







NoteSolution





2Lc_n^{(L)} = \int_{-L}^Lf(x)e^{-ik_nx}dx with k_n = \pi n/L differs from \hat f(k_n) by \int_{|x| > L}fe^{-ik_nx}, bounded by \int_{|x| > L}|f|, which for f = e^{-x^2/2} is below e^{-L^2/2}. Then \sum_nc_n^{(L)}e^{ik_nx} =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_n\hat f(k_n)e^{ik_nx}\,\Delta k with \Delta k = \pi/L, up to the exponentially small errors, a Riemann sum (Definition 11 of Real analysis) of the inversion integral Equation 6, which converges to it as \Delta k \to 0 since \hat f is Schwartz. Parseval on [-L, L], \frac{1}{2L}\int_{-L}^L|f|^2 =
\sum_n|c_n^{(L)}|^2 = \frac{1}{(2L)^2}\sum_n|\hat f(k_n)|^2 + \dots, becomes \int|f|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_n|\hat
f(k_n)|^2\Delta k \to \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|\hat f|^2, which is Equation 8. Finally \frac{1}{2L}\sum_{|n| \leq
N}e^{ik_nx} = \frac{1}{2L}\frac{\sin((N + \frac12)\pi x/L)}{\sin(\pi x/2L)} by Equation 2, and for L
\to \infty with \pi N/L \to K the denominator is \approx\pi x/2L, giving \frac{\sin Kx}{\pi x}, the kernel of Figure 3. For a Gaussian with L = 3 the periodic images already contribute less than e^{-9/2}, and the partial sums with N = 10 match f to four decimals:

x = var("x")
f = exp(-x ** 2 / 2); fhat = lambda k: sqrt(2 * pi) * exp(-k ** 2 / 2)
for L in [3, 6]:
    c = lambda n: integrate(f * exp(-I * pi * n * x / L), x, -L, L) / (2 * L)
    errs = [abs(2 * L * c(n) - fhat(pi * n / L)).n(digits=3) for n in range(0, 4)]
    print("L =", L, ": |2L c_n - fhat(pi n/L)| for n = 0..3:", errs, "; bound exp(-L^2/2) =", exp(-L ** 2 / 2).n(digits=3))
    S = sum(c(n) * exp(I * pi * n * x / L) for n in range(-10, 11))
    err = max(abs((S - f).subs(x=xv)).n() for xv in [0, 0.5, 1, 2, L / 2])
    print("  max |S_10 - f| at sample points:", err.n(digits=3))
    parseval = (sum(abs(c(n)) ** 2 for n in range(-10, 11)) * 2 * L).n(digits=8)
    print("  2L sum |c_n|^2 =", parseval, "vs int f^2 = sqrt(pi) =", sqrt(pi).n(digits=8))

title: Fourier analysis
text:
A function on the circle is a periodic function on the line, and the harmonics e^{inx} are the simplest periodic functions of all. This section defines periodic functions and their Fourier coefficients, studies the partial sums through the Dirichlet kernel, states the convergence theorems of Dirichlet and of the L^2 theory, and proves Parseval’s identity, with the square wave and the sawtooth of Figure 1 as running examples whose coefficients, partial sums and overshoot are collected in Proposition 1.
For more on this topic, see Arrigo (2023, Ch. 4).






Figure 1: Partial Fourier sums S_1, S_3, S_9, S_{29} of the square wave \operatorname{sgn} x (left) and of the sawtooth x (right) on (-\pi, \pi). The sums converge to the function away from the jumps, to the midpoint 0 at the jumps, and overshoot by about 9\% of the jump next to it however many terms are taken: the Gibbs phenomenon, with the limiting overshoot 1.179 marked. Generated by figures/fourier_square_wave.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


Before anything can be expanded in harmonics one needs the class of functions that live on the circle. The definition below fixes periodicity, the standard period 2\pi, the way a function on an interval is extended, and the finite sums of harmonics that will approximate everything else.


Definition 1 (Periodic function) A function f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} is periodic with period T > 0 if f(x + T) = f(x) for all x; it is then determined by its values on any interval of length T, and after the rescaling x \mapsto 2\pi x/T one may take T = 2\pi, which is assumed from now on. A 2\pi-periodic function is the same thing as a function on the circle S^1 = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}, and a function given on [0, 2\pi) or on (-\pi, \pi] has a unique periodic extension. A trigonometric polynomial of degree N is a finite sum \sum_{|n| \leq N} c_n
e^{inx}, equivalently \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^N (a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx); a periodic function is piecewise continuous if it has at most finitely many jumps per period, with one-sided limits f(x^\pm) at each, and piecewise C^1 if the same holds for f'.

The harmonics themselves are the first periodic functions to look at, and the only subtlety is which period one means. The first example records that e^{inx} has the smaller period 2\pi/n as well as 2\pi, which is why all harmonics live on the same circle.

Example 1 (The harmonics) \sin nx, \cos nx and e^{inx} are 2\pi-periodic for every integer n, and 2\pi/|n| is their smallest period when n \neq 0: a function with period T also has period kT for every positive integer k. The constant function is periodic with every period, and e^{inx} = \cos nx + i\sin nx relates the complex and the real harmonics.

Deciding whether a sum of periodic functions is periodic is a question about the ratio of the periods, and the answer is negative when the ratio is irrational. The first exercise works this out, which is also the reason why only integer multiples of a basic frequency appear in a Fourier series.

Exercise 1 (Periods of sums) Show that \sin x + \sin 2x is 2\pi-periodic, that \sin x + \sin(x/2) has smallest period 4\pi, and that \sin x + \sin\sqrt2\,x is not periodic at all.







NoteSolution





Both terms of the first sum have period 2\pi. For the second, \sin(x/2) has smallest period 4\pi and \sin
x has period 4\pi too, so the sum has period 4\pi; it has no smaller one, since a period T of the sum would give \sin(x + T) + \sin((x + T)/2) = \sin x + \sin(x/2) for all x, and comparing the values at x = 0 and the second derivatives at x = 0 forces \sin T + \sin(T/2) = 0 and \sin T + \tfrac14\sin(T/2) = 0, hence \sin T = \sin(T/2) = 0 and T \in 4\pi\mathbb{Z}. For the third, a period T would make f(x) = \sin x +
\sin\sqrt2 x satisfy f(T) = f(0) = 0 and f''(T) = 0, that is, \sin T + \sin\sqrt2 T = 0 and \sin T +
2\sin\sqrt2 T = 0, so \sin T = \sin\sqrt2 T = 0, T = m\pi and \sqrt2 T = n\pi with integers m, n \neq 0, contradicting the irrationality of \sqrt2.

A periodic function integrated over any interval of one period gives the same number, which is what makes the coefficients below independent of the interval chosen. The third exercise proves this and uses it to show that the integral of a product of two periodic functions is a periodic function of the shift between them.

Exercise 3 (Integrals over a period) Prove that \int_a^{a + 2\pi} f(x)\,dx is independent of a for a piecewise continuous 2\pi-periodic f, and deduce that F(t) = \int_0^{2\pi} f(x)g(x - t)\,dx is 2\pi-periodic in t for periodic f, g.







NoteSolution

The coefficients of a periodic function are its inner products with the harmonics, and everything rests on the fact that distinct harmonics are orthogonal. The definition fixes the normalisation of the coefficients once and for all, in the complex form and in the real form, and records the orthogonality relation that makes them the right numbers.


Definition 2 (Fourier coefficient) The Fourier coefficients of a piecewise continuous 2\pi-periodic f are 
c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\,e^{-inx}\,dx, \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z},
 and the Fourier series of f is \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} c_n e^{inx}, written f \sim \sum c_n e^{inx} until its convergence is settled. In real form f \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n \geq 1}(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx) with a_n = \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\cos nx\,dx and b_n = \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\sin nx\,dx, related by c_n =
\tfrac12(a_n - ib_n) and c_{-n} = \tfrac12(a_n + ib_n) for n \geq 1, c_0 = a_0/2. The coefficients are the inner products c_n = \langle e^{inx}, f\rangle/2\pi for \langle g, f\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}\bar g f\,dx, and the orthogonality of the modes 
\int_0^{2\pi} e^{inx}\,e^{-imx}\,dx = 2\pi\,\delta_{nm}
\tag{1} shows that the coefficients of a trigonometric polynomial are its given coefficients and that c_n is the unique choice making f - c_n e^{inx} orthogonal to e^{inx} (Definition 14 of Differential equations).

Exercise 5 (Complex and real coefficients) Derive c_n = \tfrac12(a_n - ib_n) and c_{-n} = \tfrac12(a_n + ib_n) for n \geq 1, show that f is real if and only if c_{-n} = \bar c_n for all n, and that f is even (odd) if and only if all b_n (all a_n) vanish.

Whether and how the series represents the function is decided by its partial sums, and the partial sums have a closed form as an integral of the function against a kernel. The definition introduces the Dirichlet kernel, records its two properties, and names the overshoot visible in Figure 1.


Definition 3 (Partial Fourier sum) The partial Fourier sum of order N of f is S_N f(x) = \sum_{|n| \leq N} c_n e^{inx}. Inserting the coefficients and exchanging sum and integral, 
S_N f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} D_N(x - y)\,f(y)\,dy, \qquad D_N(t) = \sum_{|n| \leq N} e^{int} =
\frac{\sin\bigl((N + \tfrac12)t\bigr)}{\sin(t/2)},
\tag{2} where D_N is the Dirichlet kernel: an even trigonometric polynomial with \frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi D_N =
1 and D_N(0) = 2N + 1, which concentrates at 0 as N grows but is not positive and has \int_{-\pi}^\pi|D_N|
\to \infty like \log N. Near a jump of f the partial sums overshoot the one-sided limit by a fixed fraction of the jump that does not decrease with N, the Gibbs phenomenon.

The closed form of the Dirichlet kernel is a geometric sum, and its two properties follow from the sum and from the orthogonality relation. The first exercise asks for the derivation, which is the only computation needed to analyse pointwise convergence.

Exercise 7 (The closed form of D_N) Derive \sum_{|n| \leq N} e^{int} = \sin((N + \tfrac12)t)/\sin(t/2), and show that \frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi
D_N = 1 and D_N(0) = 2N + 1.







NoteSolution





With q = e^{it} \neq 1, \sum_{n=-N}^N q^n = q^{-N}\frac{q^{2N+1} - 1}{q - 1} = \frac{q^{N + 1/2} - q^{-N -
1/2}}{q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}} = \frac{2i\sin((N + \tfrac12)t)}{2i\sin(t/2)}. Integrating the sum term by term, only n = 0 survives by Equation 1, giving 2\pi; at t = 0 every term is 1 and there are 2N + 1 of them, in agreement with the limit \sin((N + \tfrac12)t)/\sin(t/2) \to (2N + 1) as t \to 0.

Replacing the partial sums by their averages removes the negative lobes of the kernel and with them the Gibbs phenomenon. The third exercise introduces the Fejér kernel and proves its positivity, the key to Fejér’s theorem that the averaged sums of every continuous function converge uniformly.

Exercise 9 (The Fejér kernel) Define the Cesàro means \sigma_N f = \frac{1}{N + 1}\sum_{n=0}^N S_n f. Show that \sigma_N f = \frac1{2\pi}\int
F_N(x - y)f(y)\,dy with F_N(t) = \frac{1}{N + 1}\sum_{n=0}^N D_n(t) = \frac{1}{N + 1}\frac{\sin^2((N +
1)t/2)}{\sin^2(t/2)}, that F_N \geq 0 with \frac1{2\pi}\int F_N = 1, and deduce that |\sigma_N f| \leq
\sup|f|: the Cesàro means never overshoot.







NoteSolution





Averaging the integral formula for S_n f gives the one for \sigma_N f with the averaged kernel. With s =
\sin(t/2), \sum_{n=0}^N\sin((n + \tfrac12)t) = \operatorname{Im}\sum_n e^{i(n + 1/2)t} =
\operatorname{Im}\frac{e^{it/2}(e^{i(N+1)t} - 1)}{e^{it} - 1} = \operatorname{Im}\frac{e^{i(N+1)t} -
1}{2is} = \frac{1 - \cos((N + 1)t)}{2s} = \frac{\sin^2((N + 1)t/2)}{s}, and dividing by (N + 1)s gives F_N, visibly non-negative. Its integral is the average of the integrals of the D_n, each 2\pi. Then |\sigma_N
f(x)| \leq \frac1{2\pi}\int F_N(x - y)|f(y)|\,dy \leq \sup|f|, since F_N \geq 0 integrates to 2\pi. A positive kernel of unit mass concentrating at 0 is an approximate identity, and \sigma_N f \to f uniformly for continuous f (Fejér’s theorem), with no Gibbs overshoot.

The question of when the Fourier series equals the function has several answers depending on what one asks of f and in what sense the limit is taken. The theorem below collects the three that are used throughout the book, the pointwise theorem of Dirichlet, uniform convergence under absolute summability, and the L^2 theorem, with the proof of the first sketched through the Dirichlet kernel.


Theorem 1 (Convergence of Fourier series) Let f be 2\pi-periodic. (i) (Dirichlet) If f is piecewise C^1, then S_N f(x) \to \tfrac12\bigl(f(x^+) +
f(x^-)\bigr) at every x, in particular S_N f(x) \to f(x) at points of continuity. (ii) If \sum|c_n| <
\infty, which holds when f is continuous and piecewise C^1, the series converges absolutely and uniformly (Definition 19 of Real analysis) to a continuous function, which equals f at its points of continuity. (iii) (Riesz-Fischer) If \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2 < \infty then \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f - S_N f|^2\,dx \to 0, and conversely every square-summable sequence (c_n) is the coefficient sequence of such an f; Carleson’s theorem adds that the series of a square-integrable function converges to it at almost every point. Sketch of (i). By Equation 2 and the evenness of D_N, S_N f(x) - \tfrac12(f(x^+) + f(x^-)) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi D_N(t)\bigl[f(x + t) +
f(x - t) - f(x^+) - f(x^-)\bigr]dt; the bracket divided by \sin(t/2) is piecewise continuous on [0, \pi] because f is piecewise C^1, so the integral is a Fourier coefficient of a piecewise continuous function at frequency N + \tfrac12 and tends to 0 by the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma (Exercise 11). Statement (ii) is the Weierstrass M-test (Series), and (iii) follows from Parseval’s identity (Theorem 2).

The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma is the analytic engine of Dirichlet’s theorem: the Fourier coefficients of an integrable function tend to zero. The second exercise proves it for piecewise continuous functions by approximation with step functions, the case needed above, where the frequency need not be an integer.

Exercise 11 (The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma) Prove that \int_a^b g(t)\sin(\lambda t)\,dt \to 0 as \lambda \to \infty for every piecewise continuous g on [a, b], first for a step function and then in general.







NoteSolution





For g = 1 on [c, d] the integral is (\cos\lambda c - \cos\lambda d)/\lambda, of absolute value at most 2/\lambda, so the statement holds for step functions. A piecewise continuous g is Riemann integrable, so for every \varepsilon > 0 there is a step function s with \int_a^b|g - s| < \varepsilon (Definition 11 of Real analysis, lower sums). Then |\int g\sin\lambda t| \leq |\int (g - s)\sin\lambda t| + |\int s\sin\lambda t| \leq \varepsilon +
|\int s\sin\lambda t|, and the second term is below \varepsilon for \lambda large; so the limit superior is at most 2\varepsilon for every \varepsilon. The same argument works with \cos\lambda t and e^{i\lambda t}, and shows c_n \to 0 for every piecewise continuous periodic f.

The sum of the squares of the coefficients equals the mean square of the function, which is the Pythagorean theorem in infinitely many dimensions. The theorem states this identity in both forms together with the finite inequality of Bessel and the best-approximation property that explains why Fourier coefficients are the right choice.


Theorem 2 (Parseval’s identity) For a 2\pi-periodic f with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2 < \infty, 
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(x)|^2\,dx = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}|c_n|^2, \qquad \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,dx =
\frac{|a_0|^2}{2} + \sum_{n \geq 1}\bigl(|a_n|^2 + |b_n|^2\bigr),
\tag{3} and more generally \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\bar f g\,dx = \sum_n\bar c_n(f)c_n(g). Argument. For a trigonometric polynomial T = \sum_{|n| \leq N} t_n e^{inx}, Equation 1 gives \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f -
T|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 - \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 + \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n - t_n|^2, so S_N f is the  best approximation** of f in mean square among trigonometric polynomials of degree N, and Bessel’s inequality \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 holds for every N. Equality in the limit is the statement that \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f - S_N f|^2 \to 0, which holds because trigonometric polynomials approximate every such f in mean square (by Fejér’s theorem for continuous f and by approximation of f with continuous functions in general); the polarised form follows by applying the identity to f + g and f + ig.

The best-approximation identity is the heart of the argument for Parseval and deserves its own derivation. The second exercise expands the mean-square error of an arbitrary trigonometric polynomial and reads off the two consequences.

Exercise 14 (Best approximation in mean square) Prove that \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f - \sum_{|n| \leq N}t_n e^{inx}|^2\,dx = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 -

NoteSolution





Expanding |f - T|^2 = |f|^2 - \bar fT - f\bar T + |T|^2 and integrating, \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\bar fT = \sum t_n\bar
c_n by the definition of c_n, and \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|T|^2 = \sum|t_n|^2 by Equation 1; so the error is \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 - \sum(t_n\bar c_n + \bar t_nc_n - |t_n|^2) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 -
\sum|c_n|^2 + \sum|c_n - t_n|^2 after completing the square. The last sum is non-negative and zero only for t_n
= c_n, which gives the minimality; taking t_n = c_n and using that the error is non-negative gives Bessel’s inequality.

The coefficients of a function with jumps are sums of integrals over the pieces on which it is smooth. The first example computes them for the square wave and explains why they are exact rational multiples of 1/\pi.

Example 16 (Coefficients of piecewise functions) The square wave is -1 on (-\pi, 0) and 1 on (0, \pi), so a_n = 0 by oddness and b_n =

A function on [0, \pi] can be expanded in sines alone or in cosines alone, by extending it to (-\pi, \pi) as an odd or an even function. The third exercise connects these half-range expansions with the Dirichlet modes of Boundary value and Sturm-Liouville problems and explains which one converges better.

Exercise 18 (Half-range expansions) Show that a function f on [0, \pi] has a sine series \sum b_n\sin nx with b_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\sin
nx and a cosine series \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum a_n\cos nx with a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\cos nx, identify them with the expansions in the Dirichlet and Neumann eigenfunctions of -d^2/dx^2 on [0, \pi], and explain why the cosine series of f(x) = x converges uniformly while the sine series does not.







NoteSolution





The odd extension f_o(-x) = -f(x) has a_n = 0 and b_n = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi f_o\sin nx =
\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\sin nx; the even extension has b_n = 0 and a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\cos nx. The sines \sin nx are the eigenfunctions of -d^2/dx^2 with u(0) = u(\pi) = 0 and the cosines those with u'(0)
= u'(\pi) = 0 (Theorem 2 of Differential equations, Exercise 61 of Differential equations), so the half-range series are the eigenfunction expansions of the two boundary value problems. The odd extension of f(x) = x is the sawtooth, discontinuous at \pm\pi, with coefficients 2(-1)^{n+1}/n and non-uniform convergence; the even extension is |x|, continuous, with coefficients O(1/n^2) and uniform convergence (Example 11). A function vanishing at both ends, such as \sin x or x(\pi - x), has an odd extension that is continuous, and then the sine series converges uniformly too.

title: Fourier analysis
text:
A function on the whole line has no period, and the discrete harmonics e^{inx} are replaced by the continuum of plane waves e^{ikx} with the sum over n replaced by an integral over k. This section defines the transform and its inverse, computes it for the box, the two-sided exponential and the Gaussian, proves the convolution theorem, states Plancherel’s theorem and the uncertainty inequality, and ends with a proposition that collects the explicit transforms; the figure shows the trade-off between the width of a Gaussian and the width of its transform.
For more on this topic, see Aliev and Lara (2024, Ch. 8), Arrigo (2023, Ch. 6) and Borodzik et al. (2019, Ch. 2).

The Fourier transform of an integrable function is its inner product with every plane wave at once, a function of the wave number k. The definition fixes the normalisation used throughout the book, lists the rules that make the transform computable, and records the heuristic that it is a Fourier series whose period has gone to infinity.


Definition 4 (Fourier transform) For f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} with \int_{-\infty}^\infty|f| < \infty (absolutely integrable), the Fourier transform is 
\hat f(k) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,e^{-ikx}\,dx, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R},
\tag{4} a bounded continuous function with |\hat f(k)| \leq \int|f| and \hat f(k) \to 0 as |k| \to \infty (Riemann-Lebesgue). It obeys the translation rule \widehat{f(x - a)} = e^{-ika}\hat f(k), the modulation rule \widehat{e^{iax}f} = \hat f(k - a), the scaling rule \widehat{f(\lambda x)} = \hat
f(k/\lambda)/|\lambda|, the derivative rule \widehat{f'} = ik\hat f when f is C^1 with f, f' integrable, and the multiplication rule \widehat{xf} = i\,\hat f\,' when xf is integrable; a Schwartz function, smooth with all derivatives decaying faster than any power, has a Schwartz transform. Heuristically, f on [-L, L] has the series \sum_n c_n e^{i\pi nx/L} with 2Lc_n = \hat f(\pi n/L), and as L \to \infty the sum over the wave numbers k_n = \pi n/L spaced by \pi/L becomes \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(k)e^{ikx}dk, which is the inversion formula of Theorem 3.

NoteExamples





The box function is the simplest integrable function, and its transform is the first appearance of the sinc function. The first example computes it and reads off the slow decay that goes with the jumps.

Example 19 (The box) For the box \chi_a = 1 on [-a, a] and 0 outside, \hat\chi_a(k) = \int_{-a}^a e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{e^{-ika} -
e^{ika}}{-ik} = \frac{2\sin ak}{k} (Proposition 3), with \hat\chi_a(0) = 2a the area of the box. The transform decays only like 1/|k| and is not absolutely integrable, the counterpart of the 1/n decay of the square wave’s coefficients: a jump in f costs a power of k in \hat f.

The two-sided exponential is continuous with a kink, and its transform is the Lorentzian, decaying one power faster than the sinc. The second example integrates the two half-lines separately and adds the results.

Example 20 (The two-sided exponential) For f(x) = e^{-a|x|} with a > 0, \hat f(k) = \int_0^\infty e^{-(a + ik)x}dx + \int_{-\infty}^0 e^{(a -
ik)x}dx = \frac{1}{a + ik} + \frac{1}{a - ik} = \frac{2a}{a^2 + k^2} (Proposition 3), the  Lorentzian**, decaying like 1/k^2 because f is continuous with a jump in f'. It is integrable, so the inversion formula applies at every point (Example 22).

The Gaussian is the central example of the chapter: its transform is again a Gaussian, with the inverse width. The third example derives this by completing the square and shifting the contour, and notes the special role of \sigma = 1.

Example 21 (The Gaussian) For g_\sigma(x) = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}, completing the square gives -\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2} - ikx = -
\frac{(x + ik\sigma^2)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\sigma^2k^2}{2}, so 
\hat g_\sigma(k) = e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x + ik\sigma^2)^2/2\sigma^2}dx =
\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2},
\tag{5} where the shifted integral equals the Gaussian integral \sigma\sqrt{2\pi} of The Riemann integral because the integrand is entire and the horizontal line \operatorname{Im} x = -k\sigma^2 can be moved to the real axis (Theorem 2 of Complex analysis, Exercise 97 of Complex analysis). A Gaussian of width \sigma transforms to a Gaussian of width 1/\sigma (Figure 2), and for \sigma = 1 the function reproduces itself up to the factor \sqrt{2\pi}: e^{-x^2/2} is an eigenfunction of the transform (Exercise 24).

The five rules of the definition are each a one-line substitution or integration by parts, and knowing them is what makes transforms computable without integrating. The first exercise asks for the derivations, with attention to the hypotheses on the derivative rule.

Exercise 19 (The transform rules) Prove the translation, modulation, scaling, derivative and multiplication rules of Definition 4, and use them to find the transforms of e^{-(x - 3)^2/2}, e^{-2|x|}\cos 5x and x e^{-x^2/2} from the examples.

f(k - a) directly; y = \lambda x gives \int f(\lambda x)e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{1}{|\lambda|}\int
f(y)e^{-i(k/\lambda)y}dy, the absolute value from the reversed limits when \lambda < 0. A function supported on a half-line has a transform that extends to the complex plane on one side, a property the next chapters’ Green’s functions depend on. The second exercise computes the transform of the one-sided exponential and locates its pole, with Sage handling the integral.

Exercise 20 (The one-sided exponential) Compute the transform of f(x) = \theta(x)e^{-ax} (a > 0, \theta the step function), show that it extends to a holomorphic function of k in the half-plane \operatorname{Im} k < a, which contains the whole lower half-plane, with a pole at k = ia, and check the transform and its real and imaginary parts with Sage.







NoteSolution





\hat f(k) = \int_0^\infty e^{-(a + ik)x}dx = \frac{1}{a + ik} = \frac{a - ik}{a^2 + k^2}, whose real part is half the Lorentzian of Example 20 and whose imaginary part -k/(a^2 + k^2) is odd. The integral converges whenever \operatorname{Re}(a + ik) = a - \operatorname{Im} k > 0, and the result 1/(a + ik) is holomorphic there, its only pole k = ia lying on the boundary line \operatorname{Im} k = a of the region; in general a function vanishing for x < 0 has a transform holomorphic in the lower half-plane \operatorname{Im} k
< 0, the origin of the retarded prescription of Green’s functions:

x, k, a = var("x k a")

The Gaussian transform can be obtained without any contour shifting, by turning the derivative and multiplication rules into a differential equation for \hat g. The third exercise asks for this derivation, which generalises to every function satisfying a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients.

Exercise 21 (The Gaussian transform by a differential equation) Show that g = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2} satisfies \sigma^2g' + xg = 0, transform this equation using the rules to obtain \hat g\,' = -\sigma^2k\hat g, and solve it to recover Equation 5; then explain why the same method gives the transform of e^{-ax^2} for complex a with \operatorname{Re} a > 0.

g' = -(x/\sigma^2)g is the equation. Transforming, \sigma^2\,ik\hat g + i\hat g\,' = 0, that is, \hat g\,' = -
\sigma^2k\hat g, whose solution is \hat g(k) = \hat g(0)e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2} with \hat g(0) = \int g =

A function is recovered from its transform by the inverse integral, with the factor 1/2\pi placed in the inverse in this book. The theorem states the inversion formula under a hypothesis that covers the examples, sketches the proof by Gaussian regularisation, and records the duality that the transform of a transform is the reflected function.


Theorem 3 (Fourier inversion) If f and \hat f are both absolutely integrable and f is continuous, then 
f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\hat f(k)\,e^{ikx}\,dk
\tag{6} for every x; if f is only piecewise C^1 the right side converges, as \lim_{L \to \infty}\int_{-L}^L, to \tfrac12(f(x^+) + f(x^-)). In particular \hat{\hat f}(x) = 2\pi f(-x) (duality). k^2/2}e^{ik(x - y)}dk\,dy = \int f(y)\frac{e^{-(x - y)^2/2\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{2\pi\varepsilon}}dy, the convolution of f with a Gaussian of unit integral and width \sqrt\varepsilon, which tends to f(x) as \varepsilon \to 0 at points of continuity (Exercise 23); the left side tends to \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f e^{ikx} by dominated convergence since \hat f is integrable. The piecewise C^1 case uses the kernel \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^Le^{ik(x - y)}dk = \frac{\sin L(x - y)}{\pi(x - y)} in place of the Gaussian, as in Dirichlet’s theorem.

Multiplying transforms corresponds to an operation on the functions themselves, the convolution, which is also how a function is smoothed or averaged. The definition introduces it, states the convolution theorem in both directions, and names the smoothing property that makes approximate identities work.


Definition 5 (Convolution) The convolution of two integrable functions is 
(f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x - y)\,g(y)\,dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(y)\,g(x - y)\,dy,
 commutative and associative, integrable with \int|f * g| \leq \int|f|\int|g|. The convolution theorem states 
\widehat{f * g} = \hat f\,\hat g, \qquad \widehat{fg} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\,\hat f * \hat g,
\tag{7} the first for integrable f, g and the second when f, g and their transforms are integrable. Convolution smooths: f * g is as differentiable as the better of f and g, with (f * g)' = f' * g = f * g'; and convolving with a family of non-negative functions of unit integral concentrating at 0 (an approximate identity, such as the Gaussians of Exercise 23) returns f in the limit.

Parseval’s identity for the line says that the transform preserves the squared integral, up to the factor 2\pi of the normalisation. Theorem 4 (Plancherel’s theorem) If f is absolutely and square integrable, then \hat f is square integrable and 
\int_{-\infty}^\infty|f(x)|^2\,dx = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty|\hat f(k)|^2\,dk, \qquad

The theorem is also the statement that the transform preserves inner products, and the Hermite functions of Exercise 24 show it in action: orthogonal eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues. The third example makes this explicit and notes what unitarity says about the eigenvalues.

Example 30 (Orthogonality of the Hermite functions) e^{-x^2/2} and xe^{-x^2/2} are orthogonal, \int xe^{-x^2}dx = 0 by oddness, and so are their transforms \sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2} and -ik\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}, as the polarised identity requires. More generally, since f \mapsto \hat f/\sqrt{2\pi} is unitary, its eigenvalues \lambda/\sqrt{2\pi} \in \{1, -i, -1, i\} have modulus 1, which is what Exercise 24 found, and eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues are automatically orthogonal, as for every unitary or self-adjoint operator (Linear algebra).

A function and its transform cannot both be concentrated: the product of their widths is bounded below, with the Gaussian as the unique extremal case. The theorem defines the widths as standard deviations, states the bound, and proves it with one integration by parts and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.


Theorem 5 (The uncertainty inequality) For a C^1 function f with f, xf, f' square integrable, define the widths \Delta x and \Delta k by (\Delta x)^2 = \int x^2|f|^2dx\big/\!\int|f|^2dx and (\Delta k)^2 = \int k^2|\hat f|^2dk\big/\!\int|\hat
f|^2dk (the centred case; in general replace x by x - \bar x and k by k - \bar k). Then 
\Delta x\,\Delta k \geq \tfrac12,
\tag{9} with equality if and only if f is a Gaussian Ce^{-x^2/2\sigma^2} (times e^{i\bar kx} in the uncentred case). Proof. By Plancherel and the derivative rule, \int k^2|\hat f|^2 = \int|\widehat{f'}|^2 = 2\pi\int|f'|^2 and \int|\hat f|^2 = 2\pi\int|f|^2, so (\Delta k)^2 = \int|f'|^2/\int|f|^2. Integrating by parts, \int|f|^2 = \int\frac{d}{dx}(x)|f|^2 = -\int x(\bar f f' + f\bar f') = -2\operatorname{Re}\int x\bar ff', the boundary term vanishing since x|f|^2 \to 0; by Cauchy-Schwarz \int|f|^2 \leq 2\bigl(\int x^2|f|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\int|f'|^2\bigr)^{1/2}, which is Equation 9. Equality requires f' = -cxf with c > 0 real, whose solutions are the Gaussians.

Exercise 33 (Invariance of the product) Show that \Delta x\,\Delta k is unchanged when f(x) is replaced by f(\lambda x), by f(x - a) (with the centred definitions about the new mean) or by e^{ibx}f(x), and deduce from the single case e^{-x^2/2} that every Gaussian has product \tfrac12.

A computer stores a function by finitely many samples, and the integrals of the coefficients and of the transform become finite sums. On N equally spaced samples of a period the harmonics e^{inx} become the N-th roots of unity, and the orthogonality of Equation 1 becomes an exact identity between finite sums; the definition records the resulting transform, which is exact and invertible in its own right (Izaac and Wang 2018, secs. 8.3.1–8.3.3).


Definition 6 (Discrete Fourier transform) The discrete Fourier transform of (f_0, \dots, f_{N - 1}) \in \mathbb{C}^N is the sequence 
F_m = \sum_{n = 0}^{N - 1}f_n\,e^{-2\pi imn/N}, \qquad m \in \mathbb{Z},
\tag{10} which is N-periodic, F_{m + N} = F_m, so that F_0, \dots, F_{N - 1} determine it. The discrete orthogonality \sum_{m = 0}^{N - 1}e^{2\pi im(l - n)/N} = N\delta_{ln} for 0 \leq l, n < N gives the inversion f_n =
\frac1N\sum_{m = 0}^{N - 1}F_me^{2\pi imn/N} and the discrete Parseval identity \sum_n|f_n|^2 =
\frac1N\sum_m|F_m|^2. For real f_n, F_{N - m} = \overline{F_m}, so F_0 and (for even N) F_{N/2} =
\sum_n(-1)^nf_n are real and about half of the F_m carry the information. If f_n = f(2\pi n/N) are samples of a trigonometric polynomial f(x) = \sum_{|k| < N/2}c_ke^{ikx}, then F_m = Nc_m for |m| < N/2: the transform of the samples computes the Fourier coefficients of Definition 2 exactly, the index m and m - N standing for the same wave number.

The proposition makes this precise on the circle and on the line, using the Poisson summation formula of Exercise 30, and deduces the sampling theorem (Izaac and Wang 2018, secs. 8.1–8.1.2, 8.4).


Proposition 2 (Sampling and aliasing)

\Delta x\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}f(n\Delta x)\,e^{-ikn\Delta x} = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}\hat f\Big(k + \frac{2\pi
j}{\Delta x}\Big), \qquad k \in \mathbb{R} ,
\tag{11} the aliasing formula: the Riemann sum for \hat f(k) adds the copies of \hat f shifted by multiples of 2\pi/\Delta x.

The convolution rule can be tested on two boxes, where both sides are elementary. The second example computes the triangle from the convolution integral, transforms it piece by piece and recovers the square of the sinc.

Example 41 (The convolution rule for two boxes) For 0 \leq x \leq 2a the boxes [-a, a] and [x - a, x + a] overlap in [x - a, a], so (\chi_a * \chi_a)(x) =
\int_{x - a}^a dy = 2a - x, and by evenness the convolution is the triangle (2a - |x|)_+. Its transform is \int_{-2a}^0(2a + x)e^{-ikx}dx + \int_0^{2a}(2a - x)e^{-ikx}dx = 2\int_0^{2a}(2a - x)\cos kx\,dx = \frac{2 -
2\cos 2ak}{k^2}, and 2 - 2\cos 2ak = 4\sin^2ak turns this into (2\sin ak/k)^2 = \hat\chi_a^2, as Equation 7 requires.

The widths are ratios of second moments to integrals, and each moment is a Gaussian-type or a Lorentzian-type integral with a closed form. The third example lists the four integrals behind the two uncertainty products.

Example 42 (The widths as moment integrals) For the Gaussian, \int x^2e^{-x^2/\sigma^2} = \sigma^3\sqrt\pi/2 over \int e^{-x^2/\sigma^2} = \sigma\sqrt\pi gives \sigma^2/2, and \int k^2\cdot2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2} over \int2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2} gives 1/2\sigma^2; for the exponential, \int x^2e^{-2a|x|} = 1/2a^3 over 1/a and \int4a^2k^2/(a^2 + k^2)^2 =
2\pi a over 2\pi/a. The squared products are \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2} = \tfrac14 and \tfrac{1}{2a^2}\cdot a^2 = \tfrac12, so \Delta x\Delta k = \tfrac12 and 1/\sqrt2.

The damped cosine is the function whose transform is the sum of two Lorentzians, the line shape of a damped oscillator. The first exercise computes its transform in Sage and locates the two peaks.

Exercise 40 (The damped cosine) Compute the transform of e^{-a|x|}\cos bx with Sage, show that it is the sum of two Lorentzians centred at k =
\pm b, and find the width at half maximum of each peak for a \ll b.

By the modulation rule, \frac{a}{a^2 + (k - b)^2} + \frac{a}{a^2 + (k + b)^2}; each Lorentzian a/(a^2 + (k \mp
b)^2) has maximum 1/a and drops to half of it at |k \mp b| = a, so the full width at half maximum is 2a, the decay rate:

The hyperbolic secant is, like the Gaussian, its own transform up to scaling, and it is the shape of the soliton of several wave equations. The second exercise asks for its transform, which is a residue computation over the poles of \operatorname{sech}, with Sage as a numerical check.

Exercise 41 (The hyperbolic secant) Show that \widehat{\operatorname{sech} x} = \pi\operatorname{sech}(\pi k/2) by summing the residues of \operatorname{sech} z\,e^{-ikz} at z = i\pi(n + \tfrac12), n \geq 0, and check the formula numerically in Sage at a few values of k.

For k < 0 close the contour in the upper half-plane; \operatorname{sech} z = 1/\cosh z has simple poles at z_n = i\pi(n + \tfrac12) with residues 1/\sinh z_n = 1/(i\sin\pi(n + \tfrac12)) = (-1)^n/i, so \int\operatorname{sech} x\,e^{-ikx}dx = 2\pi i\sum_{n \geq 0}\frac{(-1)^n}{i}e^{\pi k(n + 1/2)} =
2\pi\frac{e^{\pi k/2}}{1 + e^{\pi k}} = \frac{\pi}{\cosh(\pi k/2)}, a geometric series since e^{\pi k} < 1; the case k > 0 follows by evenness. Sage’s symbolic integrator does not return this closed form, and the check is numerical:

In several variables the transform is taken in each coordinate, and a radial function has a radial transform. The third exercise works out the three-dimensional transform of a radial function as a one-dimensional sine transform and applies it to the Yukawa function of Proposition 9 of Differential equations.

Exercise 42 (Radial functions in three dimensions) Define \hat f(\mathbf k) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(\mathbf x)e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d^3x. Show that for a radial f(r) the transform is radial with \hat f(k) = \frac{4\pi}{k}\int_0^\infty f(r)\sin(kr)\,r\,dr, and use it to show that the transform of e^{-mr}/(4\pi r) is 1/(k^2 + m^2) and that of the Gaussian e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2} is (\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^3e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}.

= 2\pi\int_0^\infty f(r)r^2\frac{2\sin kr}{kr}dr. For the Yukawa function, \frac{4\pi}{k}\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-mr}}{4\pi
r}\sin(kr)\,r\,dr = \frac1k\operatorname{Im}\int_0^\infty e^{-(m - ik)r}dr = \frac1k\operatorname{Im}\frac{1}{m -
ik} = \frac{1}{k^2 + m^2}, the momentum-space Green’s function of Proposition 9 of Differential equations. For the Gaussian the three Cartesian integrals factorise and each gives \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2k_i^2/2} by Equation 5.

title: Fourier analysis
text:
The delta function of Definition 24 of Differential equations, the transform of the constant function, and the derivative of a function with a jump are not functions, but they are all linear functionals on smooth test functions, and that is the definition that makes the formal computations of physics rigorous. This section defines test functions and distributions, their derivatives and Fourier transforms, and the principal value, with the figure showing two sequences of functions that converge to the delta; the identities obtained along the way are collected in the proposition at the end.






Figure 3: Two sequences converging to the delta function. Left: the Gaussians g_\varepsilon(x) =
e^{-x^2/\varepsilon^2}/(\varepsilon\sqrt\pi) of unit integral, concentrating as \varepsilon \to 0. Right: the Fourier kernels \delta_L(x) = \sin(Lx)/(\pi x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^Le^{ikx}dk, also of unit integral, oscillating more and more rapidly as L \to \infty while their action on every test function tends to its value at 0. Generated by figures/delta_sequence.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


A distribution is defined by what it does to nice functions, so the first thing to fix is the class of nice functions. The definition introduces the two standard classes, the smooth functions of compact support and the rapidly decreasing functions of Schwartz, and what it means for a sequence of them to converge.


Definition 7 (Test function) A test function is a smooth function \varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} that vanishes outside a bounded interval (compact support); the space of test functions is written \mathcal{D}. A Schwartz function is a smooth function such that x^m\varphi^{(n)}(x) is bounded for all m, n \geq 0 (all derivatives decay faster than any power); the space of Schwartz functions is \mathcal{S} \supset \mathcal{D}, and it is closed under differentiation, multiplication by polynomials and the Fourier transform (Exercise 44). A sequence \varphi_j \to \varphi in \mathcal{S} if \sup_x|x^m(\varphi_j - \varphi)^{(n)}| \to 0 for every m, n, and in \mathcal{D} if moreover all \varphi_j vanish outside one fixed interval. The same definitions apply on \mathbb{R}^n with multi-indices.

The Fourier transform exchanges decay with smoothness, which is why the Schwartz space, with both, is the natural home of the transform. The third example makes the exchange explicit through the rules of Definition 4.

Example 45 (Decay against smoothness) By the derivative and multiplication rules, \widehat{\varphi^{(n)}} = (ik)^n\hat\varphi and \widehat{x^m\varphi}

The transform of a test function is Schwartz but never a test function, by the identity theorem for its entire extension.

A distribution is a continuous linear functional on test functions, and every locally integrable function is one by integration; the delta is the simplest one that is not. The definition fixes the vocabulary, the notion of convergence of distributions, and the fact that the delta is a limit of functions.


Definition 8 (Distribution) A distribution is a linear map T : \mathcal{D} \to \mathbb{C}, written T(\varphi) or \langle T,
\varphi\rangle, that is continuous: T(\varphi_j) \to T(\varphi) whenever \varphi_j \to \varphi in \mathcal{D}. A tempered distribution is a continuous linear map \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{C}; it restricts to a distribution, and tempered distributions are the ones with Fourier transforms. Every locally integrable f of at most polynomial growth defines the regular tempered distribution T_f(\varphi) = \int f\varphi\,dx, and f is identified with T_f; the Dirac delta is \delta(\varphi) = \varphi(0), and \delta_a(\varphi) =
\varphi(a) is written \delta(x - a) (Definition 24 of Differential equations). Distributions T_j converge to T if T_j(\varphi)
\to T(\varphi) for every test function; the point of the definition is that a sequence of functions can converge as distributions to something that is not a function, as g_\varepsilon \to \delta in Figure 3.

Which functions define tempered distributions is a matter of growth at infinity, since the test functions decay fast but not infinitely fast. The first example sorts the common functions into the tempered and the non-tempered.

Example 46 (Regular distributions) Polynomials, |x|^s for s > -1, \log|x|, bounded functions and periodic piecewise continuous functions are all tempered, since \int|f\varphi| \leq \sup|(1 + x^2)^N\varphi|\int|f|(1 + x^2)^{-N} is finite for N large; the step function \theta and the sign function are tempered. e^{x^2} and e^{|x|} define distributions on \mathcal{D} but not tempered ones, since \int e^{x^2}\varphi diverges for \varphi = e^{-x^2/2} and \int e^{|x|}\varphi diverges for \varphi = e^{-\sqrt{1 + x^2}}, both Schwartz functions; and 1/x is not locally integrable at 0, so it defines no regular distribution at all, a gap that Definition 10 fills.

Exercise 47 (The delta is not a function) Prove that there is no locally integrable f with \int f\varphi = \varphi(0) for all test functions \varphi, and show that if a distribution T satisfies T(\varphi) = 0 whenever \varphi vanishes near 0 and T(\varphi) depends only on \varphi(0), then T = c\,\delta.

Take \varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varphi(x/\varepsilon) with \varphi the bump of Example 43; then \int f\varphi_\varepsilon \to 0 as \varepsilon \to 0, since |\int f\varphi_\varepsilon| \leq

Every distribution has derivatives of all orders, defined by moving the derivative onto the test function with a sign, as integration by parts suggests. The definition records this, the product with a smooth function, and the Leibniz rule, with the identity x\delta' = -\delta as the first non-obvious consequence.


Definition 9 (Distributional derivative) The derivative of a distribution T is the distribution T'(\varphi) = -T(\varphi'), so that T^{(n)}(\varphi)
= (-1)^nT(\varphi^{(n)}); for a C^1 function f this agrees with the classical derivative, since \int
f\varphi'\,dx = -\int f'\varphi\,dx with no boundary terms. The product of T with a smooth function \psi of polynomial growth (with all derivatives) is (\psi T)(\varphi) = T(\psi\varphi), and the Leibniz rule (\psi T)' = \psi'T + \psi T' holds. Differentiation is continuous: T_j \to T implies T_j' \to T', so a convergent sequence of functions may be differentiated term by term as distributions, whatever happens to the classical derivatives.

The function 1/x is not locally integrable, but the odd part of a test function around 0 cancels its singularity, and the resulting functional is the distribution that appears in every dispersion relation. The definition introduces it, identifies it as the derivative of \log|x|, and records the Sokhotski-Plemelj formula that splits 1/(x \mp i0) into a principal value and a delta.


Definition 10 (Principal value) The principal value of 1/x is the tempered distribution 
\operatorname{PV}\frac1x(\varphi) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}dx =
\int_0^\infty\frac{\varphi(x) - \varphi(-x)}{x}dx,
\tag{12} the limit existing because the integrand of the last form is bounded near 0 by 2\sup|\varphi'|. It is the distributional derivative of \log|x|, it satisfies x\cdot\operatorname{PV}\frac1x = 1, and the Sokhotski-Plemelj formula states that, as distributions, 
\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\frac{1}{x \mp i\varepsilon} = \operatorname{PV}\frac1x \pm i\pi\delta(x),
\tag{13} since \frac{1}{x \mp i\varepsilon} = \frac{x}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2} \pm i\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2}, the real part tending to the principal value and the imaginary part being \pi times a delta sequence (Example 47). The same definition gives \operatorname{PV}\int_a^b\frac{\varphi(x)}{x - c}dx for a <
c < b by removing a symmetric interval around c.

The identification of the principal value as the derivative of the logarithm is what makes it unavoidable: a locally integrable function has a derivative, and this is it. The second exercise proves the identification and the product identity.

Exercise 53 (The derivative of \log|x|) Show that \log|x| is a tempered distribution and that its derivative is \operatorname{PV}\frac1x; show that x\cdot\operatorname{PV}\frac1x = 1 and that the general solution of xT = 1 is \operatorname{PV}\frac1x +
c\,\delta.







NoteSolution





\log|x| is locally integrable (\int_0^1|\log x|dx = 1) and of logarithmic growth, hence tempered. By definition, (\log|x|)'(\varphi) = -\int\log|x|\varphi'(x)dx = -\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\int_{|x| >
\varepsilon}\log|x|\varphi', and integrating by parts on each half-line, -\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\log|x|\varphi'
= \int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{\varphi}{x}dx + \log\varepsilon\,[\varphi(\varepsilon) - \varphi(-\varepsilon)]; the boundary term is O(\varepsilon\log\varepsilon) \to 0 and the integral tends to the principal value. (x\cdot
\operatorname{PV}\frac1x)(\varphi) = \lim\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{x\varphi(x)}{x}dx = \int\varphi, so the product is 1. If xT = 1 then x(T - \operatorname{PV}\frac1x) = 0, and a distribution S with xS = 0 satisfies S(\varphi) = 0 for every \varphi vanishing at 0 (write \varphi = x\psi with \psi smooth), so S(\varphi) depends only on \varphi(0) and S = c\delta by Exercise 47.

Exercise 54 (The finite part of 1/x^2) Define \operatorname{Pf}\frac{1}{x^2} = -\bigl(\operatorname{PV}\frac1x\bigr)'. Show that \operatorname{Pf}\frac{1}{x^2}(\varphi) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\Bigl[\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x^2}dx -

\varepsilon}\frac{\varphi'}{x}, and integrating by parts on each half-line gives \lim\bigl[\int_{|x| >
\varepsilon}\frac{\varphi}{x^2} + \frac{\varphi(\varepsilon) + \varphi(-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\cdot(-1)\bigr], where \varphi(\pm\varepsilon) = \varphi(0) \pm \varepsilon\varphi'(0) + O(\varepsilon^2) gives -2\varphi(0)/\varepsilon + O(\varepsilon); the symmetric form follows by pairing x with -x, the integrand being bounded near 0 by \sup|\varphi''|. -2\sqrt\pi, after integrating by parts (The Riemann integral).

Since the transform is a continuous bijection of the Schwartz space, it can be moved onto the test function, and every tempered distribution acquires a transform. The definition does this and lists the transforms of the delta, the constant, the plane wave and their derivatives, the dictionary used in every momentum-space computation.


Definition 11 (Fourier transform of a distribution) The Fourier transform of a tempered distribution T is the tempered distribution \hat T(\varphi) = T(\hat
\varphi), which agrees with Equation 4 for integrable f by Fubini, since \int f(x)\hat\varphi(x)dx =
\int\hat f(k)\varphi(k)dk. The rules of Definition 4 persist, \widehat{T'} = ik\hat T, \widehat{xT}
= i\hat T\,', \widehat{T(x - a)} = e^{-ika}\hat T, as does inversion \hat{\hat T} = 2\pi T(-x). The basic transforms are 
\hat\delta = 1, \qquad \hat 1 = 2\pi\delta(k), \qquad \widehat{e^{iax}} = 2\pi\delta(k - a), \qquad
\widehat{\delta^{(n)}} = (ik)^n, \qquad \widehat{x^n} = 2\pi i^n\delta^{(n)}(k),
\tag{14} and the second of these is the identity \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-ikx}dx = 2\pi\delta(k) that physicists use to enforce momentum conservation; the Fourier series of a periodic function f = \sum c_ne^{inx} is its transform \hat f = 2\pi\sum_nc_n\delta(k - n), a sum of deltas at the integers.

The transform rules extend to distributions by moving everything onto the test function, and the second exercise asks for the derivations of the two most used ones. It then applies them to obtain the transforms of x^n and of the derivatives of the delta.

Exercise 56 (Rules for distributions) Prove \widehat{T'} = ik\hat T and \widehat{xT} = i\hat T\,' for tempered distributions from the corresponding rules on Schwartz functions, and deduce \widehat{\delta^{(n)}} = (ik)^n and \widehat{x^n} = 2\pi

\widehat{T'}(\varphi) = T'(\hat\varphi) = -T(\hat\varphi\,'), and the multiplication rule for \varphi gives \hat\varphi\,' = -i\,\widehat{x\varphi}, so -T(\hat\varphi\,') = T(\widehat{ix\varphi}) = \hat T(ix\varphi) =
(ik\hat T)(\varphi) after renaming the variable. Similarly \widehat{xT}(\varphi) = T(x\hat\varphi), and the derivative rule \widehat{\varphi'} = ik\hat\varphi gives k\hat\varphi = \widehat{-i\varphi'}, so T(x\hat\varphi) =
\hat T(-i\varphi') = -i\hat T(\varphi') = i\hat T\,'(\varphi). Iterating the first on \hat\delta = 1 gives (ik)^n; iterating the second on \hat1 = 2\pi\delta gives \widehat{x^n} = i^n\cdot2\pi\delta^{(n)}.

The damped transform is \frac{1}{\varepsilon + ik} - \frac{1}{\varepsilon - ik} = \frac{-2ik}{\varepsilon^2 +

title: Fourier analysis
text:
The circle is the simplest compact space, and Fourier series are the expansion of functions on it in the eigenfunctions of d^2/dx^2; the sphere and the compact Lie groups are the next cases, and the same structure reappears with the Laplacian replaced by the Laplacian of the round metric and the harmonics by the spherical harmonics or the matrix coefficients of the irreducible representations. This section defines the Laplacian on S^2 and the spherical harmonics, connects them to the spin-l representations of SU(2) of Weights and the representations of su(2), states the Peter-Weyl theorem, and describes the mode expansion of a function on a coset space G/H; the figure shows the harmonics for l \leq 3, and the eigenvalue equations, the orthonormality and the representation-theoretic identities are collected in the proposition at its end.
For more on this topic, see Aliev and Lara (2024, Ch. 7).






Figure 4: The real parts of the spherical harmonics Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) for l \leq 3 and 0 \leq m \leq l, on the rectangle 0 \leq \varphi \leq 2\pi (horizontal), 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi (vertical): l - m counts the nodal circles of constant \theta and m the oscillations in \varphi, so that each Y_{lm} has l nodal lines in all. Generated by figures/spherical_harmonics.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.


A function on the sphere has a Laplacian, the angular part of the Laplacian of \mathbb{R}^3, and its eigenfunctions are the modes of the sphere. The definition gives the operator in spherical coordinates, its relation to the three-dimensional Laplacian, its symmetry, and the angular momentum operators that generate the rotations and square to minus the Laplacian.


Definition 12 (Laplacian on the sphere) The Laplacian on the unit sphere S^2, in the spherical coordinates (\theta, \varphi) of the round metric d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2, is 
\Delta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Bigl(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Bigr) +
\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\varphi^2},
\tag{15} the angular part of the Laplacian of \mathbb{R}^3: \nabla^2 = \partial_r^2 + \frac2r\partial_r + \frac{1}{r^2}\Delta. It is symmetric and non-positive for the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_{S^2}\bar fg\,d\Omega with d\Omega = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi, so its eigenvalues are real and \leq 0 and eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues are orthogonal (Exercise 63); and it commutes with rotations, since the round metric is rotation invariant. The angular momentum operators L_z = -i\partial_\varphi and L_\pm =
e^{\pm i\varphi}(\pm\partial_\theta + i\cot\theta\,\partial_\varphi) generate the rotations about the z-axis and the raising and lowering of m, satisfy the \mathfrak{su}(2) relations [L_z, L_\pm] = \pm L_\pm, [L_+, L_-]
= 2L_z of Weights and the representations of su(2), and their Casimir is \mathbf L^2 = L_z^2 + \tfrac12(L_+L_- + L_-L_+) = -\Delta.

The splitting of the three-dimensional Laplacian into radial and angular parts is a chain-rule computation, and the second exercise asks for it. It is the step that connects harmonic polynomials with eigenfunctions on the sphere.

Exercise 62 (Radial and angular parts) Derive \nabla^2 = \partial_r^2 + \frac2r\partial_r + \frac{1}{r^2}\Delta with \Delta as in Equation 15 from the spherical coordinates x = r\sin\theta\cos\varphi, y = r\sin\theta\sin\varphi, z = r\cos\theta, using the general formula \nabla^2f = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\partial_i(\sqrt g\,g^{ij}\partial_jf) for the metric dr^2 + r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2).

\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f) + \partial_\varphi(\tfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\varphi f)\bigr] =

The symmetry of the Laplacian for the inner product on the sphere is an integration by parts with no boundary, and it is what makes the eigenvalue problem self-adjoint. The third exercise proves it and derives the sign of the eigenvalues and the orthogonality of eigenfunctions.

Exercise 63 (Symmetry of the Laplacian) Show that \int_{S^2}\bar g\,\Delta f\,d\Omega = -\int_{S^2}\bigl(\partial_\theta\bar g\,\partial_\theta f +
\tfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi\bar g\,\partial_\varphi f\bigr)d\Omega = \int_{S^2}\overline{\Delta g}\,f\,d\Omega for smooth f, g, and deduce that every eigenvalue of \Delta is real and non-positive, that 0 is an eigenvalue only for the constants, and that eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

\int\bar g\,\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f)\,d\theta\,d\varphi = -\int\partial_\theta\bar g\,
\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta f\,d\theta\,d\varphi since \sin\theta vanishes at \theta = 0, \pi, and \int\bar g\,\partial_\varphi^2f\,d\varphi = -\int\partial_\varphi\bar g\,\partial_\varphi f\,d\varphi by periodicity in \varphi; together with the factor \sin\theta of d\Omega this gives the middle expression, which is symmetric under exchanging f and g up to conjugation, hence the right side. With g = f an eigenfunction, \lambda\int|f|^2 = -\int(|\partial_\theta f|^2 + \tfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta}|\partial_\varphi f|^2) \leq
0, with equality only if f is constant; and for eigenfunctions f, g with eigenvalues \lambda \neq \mu, \lambda\langle g, f\rangle = \langle g, \Delta f\rangle = \langle\Delta g, f\rangle = \mu\langle g, f\rangle forces \langle g, f\rangle = 0. This is the Sturm-Liouville argument of Theorem 2 of Differential equations in two variables.

The eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on the sphere are the spherical harmonics, products of an associated Legendre function of \cos\theta and a Fourier mode in \varphi. The definition fixes their normalisation and phase, records the eigenvalue equations for \Delta, L_z and L_\pm, and states their completeness, the analogue of the convergence theorems for Fourier series.


Definition 13 (Spherical harmonic) For l = 0, 1, 2, \dots and m = -l, \dots, l the spherical harmonic is 
Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) = (-1)^m\sqrt{\frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}\frac{(l - m)!}{(l + m)!}}\;P_l^m(\cos\theta)\,e^{im\varphi},

The sum over m of Y_{lm}(\mathbf n)\overline{Y_{lm}(\mathbf n')} depends only on the angle between the two directions, which is the rotation invariance of the eigenspaces made explicit. The third example states the addition theorem, checks it for l = 1, and gives its most important application.

Example 66 (The addition theorem) \sum_{m = -l}^lY_{lm}(\theta, \varphi)\overline{Y_{lm}(\theta', \varphi')} = \frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}P_l(\cos\gamma), where \cos\gamma = \cos\theta\cos\theta' + \sin\theta\sin\theta'\cos(\varphi - \varphi') is the cosine of the angle between the two directions; for l = 1 the left side is \frac{3}{4\pi}\cos\gamma (Proposition 6). The left side is the kernel of the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace of -l(l +
1), so it must be rotation invariant, hence a function of \gamma alone, and an eigenfunction of degree l in each argument, hence cP_l(\cos\gamma); the constant follows from \theta = \theta'. Combined with \frac{1}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|} = \sum_l\frac{r_<^l}{r_>^{l + 1}}P_l(\cos\gamma) it gives the multipole expansion of the Coulomb potential (Exercise 83).

The orthogonality of the harmonics has two sources, the symmetry of the Laplacian for different l and the Fourier orthogonality for different m, while the normalisation is a Legendre integral. The second exercise assembles these three facts into a proof.

Exercise 65 (Proof of orthonormality) Prove \int\overline{Y_{lm}}Y_{l'm'}d\Omega = \delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'}: for m \neq m' from the \varphi integral, for l \neq l' from Exercise 63, and for l = l', m = m' from \int_{-1}^1(P_l^m)^2du

NoteSolution

m': \int|Y_{lm}|^2d\Omega = \frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}\frac{(l - m)!}{(l + m)!}\cdot2\pi\int_{-1}^1(P_l^m(u))^2du with u
= \cos\theta, du = -\sin\theta\,d\theta, and the Legendre integral gives exactly 1. For m = 0 this is the normalisation \int P_l^2 = 2/(2l + 1) of Proposition 5 of Differential equations.

On a compact group the role of the harmonics is played by the matrix elements of the irreducible unitary representations, and the role of the orthogonality of modes by Schur’s orthogonality relations. The definition introduces the matrix coefficients, the characters, the invariant integration they are orthogonal for, and the Wigner functions of SU(2) in Euler angles.


Definition 14 (Matrix coefficient) For a compact Lie group G and a unitary representation D of dimension d on \mathbb{C}^d (Definition 16 of Group theory), the matrix coefficients are the functions D_{ij}(g) = \langle e_i, D(g)e_j\rangle on G, and the character is \chi(g) = \operatorname{tr}D(g) = \sum_iD_{ii}(g), a function constant on conjugacy classes (a class function). The Haar measure dg is the unique measure on G invariant under left and right translations with \int_Gdg = 1; for SU(2) in the Euler-angle parametrisation g(\varphi, \theta,
\psi) = e^{-i\varphi J_z}e^{-i\theta J_y}e^{-i\psi J_z} with 0 \leq \varphi < 2\pi, 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi, 0
\leq \psi < 4\pi it is dg = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi/16\pi^2. The Schur orthogonality relations state that for irreducible unitary representations D^r, D^s, 
\int_GD^r_{ij}(g)\,\overline{D^s_{kl}(g)}\,dg = \frac{\delta_{rs}\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}}{d_r}, \qquad
\int_G\chi_r\bar\chi_s\,dg = \delta_{rs},
\tag{20} the counterpart of Equation 1, proved from Schur’s lemma (Theorem 3 of Group theory) by averaging D^r(g)AD^s(g)^{-1} over G. For SU(2) the coefficients of the spin-j representation are the Wigner functions D^j_{mn}(\varphi,
\theta, \psi) = e^{-im\varphi}d^j_{mn}(\theta)e^{-in\psi} with d^j(\theta) = e^{-i\theta J_y} in the weight basis of Definition 22 of Lie groups and Lie algebras, and the characters are \chi_j(\theta) = \sum_{m = -j}^je^{im\theta} = \frac{\sin((2j +
1)\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)} for the class of rotations by the angle \theta.

The Haar measure of SU(2) is determined by its invariance, and the Euler-angle formula can be checked against left translations. The first exercise verifies the two easy invariances and the normalisation, and identifies the measure with the volume form of the round S^3.

Exercise 70 (The Haar measure of SU(2)) Show that dg = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi/16\pi^2 has total mass 1, is invariant under left multiplication by e^{-i\alpha J_z} (which shifts \varphi) and right multiplication by e^{-i\beta J_z} (which shifts \psi), and is proportional to the volume form of the round metric on S^3 \cong SU(2); why is this enough to identify it with the Haar measure?







NoteSolution





\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi\int_0^{4\pi}d\psi = 2\cdot2\pi\cdot4\pi = 16\pi^2. Left multiplication by e^{-i\alpha J_z} sends (\varphi, \theta, \psi) to (\varphi + \alpha, \theta, \psi) and right multiplication by e^{-i\beta J_z} to (\varphi, \theta, \psi + \beta); d\varphi and d\psi are invariant under shifts, and \sin\theta\,d\theta does not involve them. The Euler angles are coordinates on S^3 in which the round metric is \tfrac14(d\theta^2 + d\varphi^2 + d\psi^2 + 2\cos\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi), with volume form \tfrac18\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi\,d\psi; the round metric is bi-invariant (it is the Killing form up to scale, Definition 4 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles), so its volume form is bi-invariant, and the Haar measure is unique, so the two agree after normalisation. Invariance under the one-parameter subgroups generated by J_z alone would not suffice; the bi-invariance of the metric supplies the rest.

Characters are orthonormal for the Haar measure, and since they are class functions the integral reduces to one over the rotation angle with a specific weight. The third exercise derives this reduced form, verifies it with Sage, and uses it to decompose a tensor product.

Exercise 72 (Characters and the Weyl integration formula) Show that for a class function f on SU(2), \int_{SU(2)}f\,dg = \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}f(\theta)\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,d\theta, where \theta is the rotation angle (the Weyl integration formula for SU(2), which may be derived from the eigenvalues e^{\pm i\theta/2} of the matrix g); verify with Sage that the characters \chi_j, j \leq
\tfrac32, are orthonormal for this measure, and decompose \chi_{1/2}\chi_1 into characters.







NoteSolution





Every g \in SU(2) is conjugate to \operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta/2}, e^{-i\theta/2}) with \theta \in [0,
2\pi], and the Haar measure pushed forward to the angle is the Weyl measure \frac1\pi\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,d\theta
= \frac{1}{2\pi}(1 - \cos\theta)d\theta, the density of \theta for a uniformly random rotation, which integrates to 1. Then \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\chi_j\bar\chi_{j'}\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,d\theta = \delta_{jj'}, and \chi_{1/2}\chi_1 = 2\cos\tfrac\theta2(1 + 2\cos\theta) = \chi_{1/2} + \chi_{3/2}, that is, \tfrac12\otimes1 =
\tfrac12\oplus\tfrac32, whose coefficients are the integrals \frac1\pi\int\chi_{1/2}\chi_1\bar\chi_j\sin^2\tfrac\theta2:

The matrix coefficients of all irreducible representations together form a complete orthogonal system on the group, which is the theorem of Peter and Weyl, the Fourier theory of compact groups. The theorem states it in three forms, as a basis, as an expansion, and as a decomposition of the regular representation, and records the two instances that this chapter is about.


Theorem 6 (The Peter-Weyl theorem) Let G be a compact Lie group and let \{D^r\} be a complete set of pairwise inequivalent irreducible unitary representations, of dimensions d_r. (i) The functions \sqrt{d_r}\,D^r_{ij}, over all r, i, j, form an orthonormal basis of the square-integrable functions on G: every such f has the expansion 
f(g) = \sum_rd_r\sum_{i, j = 1}^{d_r}\hat f^r_{ji}D^r_{ij}(g), \qquad \hat f^r = \int_Gf(g)\,D^r(g)^{-1}\,dg,
\tag{21} convergent in mean square, with \int|f|^2dg = \sum_rd_r\operatorname{tr}(\hat f^r{}^\dagger\hat f^r) (Parseval), uniformly if f is smooth. (ii) The characters \chi_r form an orthonormal basis of the square-integrable class functions. (iii) Under left translation (L_hf)(g) = f(h^{-1}g) the space of functions on G decomposes as \bigoplus_r(D^r)^{\oplus d_r}, each irreducible representation occurring as many times as its dimension, the d_r copies being spanned by the columns j of D^r_{ij}. Statement (i) contains Fourier series (G = U(1), D^n = e^{in\varphi}, d_n = 1) and the expansion of functions on SU(2) in Wigner functions; the spherical harmonics are the special case of functions on SU(2) independent of \psi (Definition 15). Argument. Orthonormality is Equation 20. Completeness is the content of the theorem: the convolution operators f \mapsto \int k(g^{-1}h)f(h)dh with continuous k are compact and self-adjoint for k(g^{-1}) =
\overline{k(g)}, their eigenspaces are finite-dimensional and invariant under translation, hence sums of matrix coefficients, and they approximate the identity as k runs through an approximate identity; the spectral theorem of the next chapter then gives the density of the matrix coefficients.
