Exercise 46 (A constant radius) For constant \phi = R, show that Equation 8 is the \phi = 1 action with A replaced by RA and \hat\kappa^2 by \hat\kappa^2/R. Which combination is the four-dimensional Newton constant?







NoteSolution





With \phi = R: -\frac{2\pi R}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}(R_4 + \tfrac14R^2F^2), and R^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} is the Maxwell invariant of RA. So the action is the \phi = 1 action for (g, RA) with 2\pi/2\hat\kappa^2 replaced by 2\pi
R/2\hat\kappa^2, and the Newton constant is \kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2/2\pi R, the five-dimensional one divided by the circumference (Exercise 56). The rescaled field RA is the gauge field of the coordinate Ry, of period 2\pi
R (Exercise 16).

title: The Kaluza-Klein reduction
text:
The reduced action of Section 1.2 multiplies the curvature scalar by the scalar field, so the strength of gravity varies with the size of the circle. A rescaling of the four-dimensional metric by a power of \phi, a Weyl rescaling, moves that factor into a kinetic term for the scalar and leaves the Einstein-Hilbert action in its standard form. This section defines Weyl rescalings and their effect on curvature, the Jordan and Einstein frames, and the dilaton, following Overduin and Wesson (1997, sec. 3.6) and Duff (1994, sec. 2).


Two metrics that differ by a positive factor at each point have the same light cones and measure the same angles, but they assign different lengths and different curvatures. Rescaling is the tool that trades a field-dependent factor in front of the curvature for derivative terms of that factor.


Definition 11 (Weyl rescaling) A Weyl rescaling (conformal rescaling) of a metric is \tilde g_{\mu\nu} = \Omega(x)^2g_{\mu\nu} with a positive function \Omega: angles are preserved and lengths multiplied by \Omega. The inverse rescales by \Omega^{-2} and the volume element by \Omega^n in n dimensions, \sqrt{-\tilde g} = \Omega^n\sqrt{-g}.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





A rescaled sphere can be drawn as a surface whose profile follows \Omega. The first example is the one shown in Figure 3.

Example 46 (Rescaling the sphere) \tilde g = \Omega(\theta)^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2) with \Omega = 1 + \tfrac12\cos\theta: the left panel of Figure 3 shows the profile, stretched near the north pole and shrunk near the south; the curvature is no longer constant (right panel).

Many important metrics are rescalings of flat space. The second example lists two, one of which is used to test the curvature formula below.

Example 47 (Conformally flat metrics) \tilde g = \Omega^2\eta: every two-dimensional metric is locally of this form, and de Sitter space in conformal time is \Omega^2 = 1/(H\eta)^2 times Minkowski space; the rescaling of Example 50 is the \Omega = \Omega(t) case on the flat-slicing form.

Fields respond to a rescaling according to how many inverse metrics their action contains. The third example compares the Maxwell field with a scalar.

Example 48 (Minimally coupled fields) The Maxwell action \int\sqrt{-g}\,g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma} is invariant under Weyl rescalings in four dimensions (\Omega^4\Omega^{-4} = 1), while a massless scalar’s action \int\sqrt{-g}g^{\mu\nu}\partial\phi\partial\phi picks up \Omega^2: this is why the Maxwell term of Equation 8 keeps only the \phi^3 from the Jordan frame (Exercise 62).










NoteExercises





The first exercise derives the transformation of the inverse metric and of the volume element. These are the two facts used in every later computation.

Exercise 47 (Inverse and volume) Show that \tilde g^{\mu\nu} = \Omega^{-2}g^{\mu\nu} and \sqrt{|\tilde g|} = \Omega^n\sqrt{|g|} in n dimensions, and compute how \sqrt{-g}\,R would scale under a constant rescaling in four dimensions.







NoteSolution





\Omega^{-2}g^{\mu\lambda}\cdot\Omega^2g_{\lambda\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu, and \det(\Omega^2g) = \Omega^{2n}\det g because each of the n rows is multiplied by \Omega^2. For constant \Omega the Christoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor are unchanged and \tilde R =
\Omega^{-2}R, so \sqrt{-\tilde g}\tilde R = \Omega^4\Omega^{-2}\sqrt{-g}R = \Omega^2\sqrt{-g}R: the Einstein-Hilbert action is not scale invariant in four dimensions, and a constant rescaling changes the effective Newton constant by \Omega^{-2}.



The name “conformal” refers to the preservation of angles. The second exercise makes this precise and adds the light cones.

Exercise 48 (Angles and light cones) Show that a Weyl rescaling preserves the angle between two spacelike vectors and the set of null vectors. Is a geodesic of g a geodesic of \tilde g?







NoteSolution





\tilde g(u, v)/\sqrt{\tilde g(u, u)\tilde g(v, v)} = \Omega^2g(u, v)/(\Omega^2\sqrt{g(u, u)g(v, v)}), the same cosine, and \tilde g(v, v) =
\Omega^2g(v, v) vanishes exactly when g(v, v) does. Geodesics are not preserved in general: the Christoffel symbols change by \delta^\lambda_\mu\partial_\nu\ln\Omega + \delta^\lambda_\nu\partial_\mu\ln\Omega - g_{\mu\nu}\partial^\lambda\ln\Omega. Null geodesics are preserved as curves (with a different affine parameter), timelike ones are not: this is why “which frame do particles follow” is a real question (Example 53).



The Maxwell term is special in four dimensions. The third exercise finds the power of \Omega it picks up in other dimensions, with Sage.

Exercise 49 (The Maxwell term in n dimensions) Show that \sqrt{|g|}\,g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma} picks up \Omega^{n - 4} under g \to \Omega^2g, and check with Sage for n = 2, \dots, 5 with a generic metric and field strength.







NoteSolution





\Omega^n from the volume element and \Omega^{-4} from the two inverse metrics:

Om = var("Om"); assume(Om > 0)
for n in range(2, 6):
    g = matrix(SR, n, n, lambda i, j: var("g%d%d" % (min(i, j), max(i, j))))
    F = matrix(SR, n, n, lambda i, j: 0 if i == j else (var("F%d%d" % (i, j)) if i < j else -var("F%d%d" % (j, i))))
    gi = matrix(SR, n, n, lambda i, j: var("h%d%d" % (min(i, j), max(i, j))))   # g^{-1} as free symmetric symbols
    dens = lambda gi_: sum(gi_[a, c] * gi_[b, d] * F[a, b] * F[c, d] for a in range(n) for b in range(n) for c in range(n) for d in range(n))
    ratio_det = (Om^2 * g).det() / g.det()                       # = Om^{2n}, so sqrt ratio = Om^n
    ratio = (dens(gi / Om^2) / dens(gi)).simplify_full()
    print("n = %d: det ratio = %s, F^2 ratio = %s, density ratio = Om^%d" % (n, ratio_det.simplify_full(), ratio, n - 4))
    if n == 4:
        print("[PASS] in four dimensions sqrt|g| F^2 is Weyl invariant:", bool(ratio_det.simplify_full() == Om^8) and bool(ratio == Om^(-4)))
Output:
n = 2: det ratio = Om^4, F^2 ratio = Om^(-4), density ratio = Om^-2
n = 3: det ratio = Om^6, F^2 ratio = Om^(-4), density ratio = Om^-1
n = 4: det ratio = Om^8, F^2 ratio = Om^(-4), density ratio = Om^0
[PASS] in four dimensions sqrt|g| F^2 is Weyl invariant: True
n = 5: det ratio = Om^10, F^2 ratio = Om^(-4), density ratio = Om^1

Classical electromagnetism is conformally invariant only in four dimensions.






The curvature of a rescaled metric involves derivatives of \Omega. The formula is classical, and it is what turns the factor \phi in front of R into a kinetic term.


Definition 12 (Curvature under a Weyl rescaling) In four dimensions, for \tilde g = \Omega^2g, 
\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}\left(R - 6\,\Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega\right)
  = \Omega^{-2}\left(R - 6\,\Box\ln\Omega - 6\,g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\Omega\,\partial_\nu\ln\Omega\right),
\tag{9} with \Box = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu the d’Alembertian of g (Overduin and Wesson 1997, eq. 15), a formula valid in every signature since R and \Box change sign together under g \to -g; in n dimensions the coefficients are 2(n - 1) and (n - 1)(n - 2) (Proposition 6).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





In two dimensions the formula simplifies. The first example checks it on the rescaled sphere of Example 46. It is also the content of the right panel of the figure below.

Example 49 (Two dimensions) \tilde R = \Omega^{-2}(R - 2\Box\ln\Omega): for the rescaled sphere of Example 46 SageManifolds gives exactly this, with R = 2 (Figure 3). The absence of a (\partial\ln\Omega)^2 term is special to n = 2.

The four-dimensional formula is tested on a time-dependent rescaling of de Sitter space. The second example records the result of the direct computation.

Example 50 (De Sitter with \Omega(t)) For g de Sitter in flat slicing and \Omega = \Omega(t), computing \tilde R directly gives \Omega^{-2}R - 6\Omega^{-3}
\Box\Omega exactly, and Exercise 62 does the same for a static spherically symmetric metric with \Omega(r).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Checked by exact computation with SageManifolds in figures/kk_einstein_frame.sage.



A constant rescaling is the case without derivative terms. The third example isolates the first term of the formula. Dimensional analysis alone predicts it.

Example 51 (Constant \Omega) \tilde R = \Omega^{-2}R: curvature has dimension of inverse length squared, and a constant rescaling of lengths by \Omega divides it by \Omega^2, the first term of Equation 9; all the rest comes from the derivatives of \Omega.










NoteExercises











Figure 3: Weyl rescaling. Left: the unit sphere (dashed) and the profile of the rescaled metric \Omega^2g with \Omega = 1 +
\tfrac12\cos\theta. Right: the curvature scalar R = 2 of the sphere and \tilde R = \Omega^{-2}(R - 2\Box\ln\Omega) of the rescaled metric, computed with SageManifolds; the four-dimensional formula is checked on de Sitter space in the same script. Generated by figures/kk_einstein_frame.sage.



The two forms of Equation 9 are equivalent. The first exercise proves this, which is a small computation with the chain rule.

Exercise 50 (The logarithmic form) Show that \Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega = \Box\ln\Omega + g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\Omega\,\partial_\nu\ln\Omega, and hence that the two expressions in Equation 9 agree.







NoteSolution





\partial_\nu\ln\Omega = \Omega^{-1}\partial_\nu\Omega, so \nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\ln\Omega = \Omega^{-1}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\Omega - \Omega^{-2}\partial_\mu\Omega\,
\partial_\nu\Omega. Contracting with g^{\mu\nu}: \Box\ln\Omega = \Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega - (\partial\ln\Omega)^2, which is the identity. Multiplied by -6 it turns -6\Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega into -6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2.



The round sphere is conformally flat, through the stereographic projection. The second exercise uses the two-dimensional formula to recover its curvature from flat space.

Exercise 51 (The sphere from the plane) The stereographic metric of the unit sphere is \Omega^2(dx^2 + dy^2) with \Omega = 2/(1 + x^2 + y^2). Compute its curvature with SageManifolds and with the two-dimensional formula of Example 49.







NoteSolution





With R = 0 and the flat Laplacian \Delta (the Riemannian \Box), \tilde R = -2\Omega^{-2}\Delta\ln\Omega, and \Delta\ln\Omega = -4/(1 + x^2 + y^2)^2 = -\Omega^2:

M = Manifold(2, "M"); X = M.chart("x y"); x, y = X[:]
Om = 2 / (1 + x^2 + y^2)
g = M.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = Om^2; g[1, 1] = Om^2
R = g.ricci_scalar().expr().simplify_full()
lap = (diff(log(Om), x, 2) + diff(log(Om), y, 2)).simplify_full()
print("R of the stereographic metric:", R, "; Delta ln Omega =", lap)
print("[PASS] R = 2 = Omega^{-2}(0 - 2 Delta ln Omega):", bool(R == 2) and bool((-2 * lap / Om^2 - 2).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
R of the stereographic metric: 2 ; Delta ln Omega = -4/(x^4 + y^4 + 2*(x^2 + 1)*y^2 + 2*x^2 + 1)
[PASS] R = 2 = Omega^{-2}(0 - 2 Delta ln Omega): True

The curvature is 2, that of the unit sphere.



The coefficients of the formula depend on the dimension. The third exercise checks them for n = 3. A conformally flat metric with a one-variable factor suffices.

Exercise 52 (Three dimensions) Check with SageManifolds that \tilde g = \Omega(x)^2(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2) has \tilde R = \Omega^{-2}(-4(\ln\Omega)'' -
2((\ln\Omega)')^2), the n-dimensional formula with n = 3.







NoteSolution





With n = 3 the coefficients are 2(n - 1) = 4 and (n - 1)(n - 2) = 2:

M = Manifold(3, "M"); X = M.chart("x y z"); x, y, z = X[:]
Om = function("Omega")(x)
g = M.metric("g")
for i in range(3): g[i, i] = Om^2
R = g.ricci_scalar().expr()
L = log(Om)
target = (-4 * diff(L, x, 2) - 2 * diff(L, x)^2) / Om^2
print("R~ =", R.simplify_full())
print("[PASS] n = 3: R~ = Omega^{-2}(-4 (ln Omega)'' - 2 ((ln Omega)')^2) on flat space:", bool((R - target).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
R~ = 2*(diff(Omega(x), x)^2 - 2*Omega(x)*diff(Omega(x), x, x))/Omega(x)^4
[PASS] n = 3: R~ = Omega^{-2}(-4 (ln Omega)'' - 2 ((ln Omega)')^2) on flat space: True










The reduced action can be written with different four-dimensional metrics, related by Weyl rescalings by powers of \phi. The two common choices are named after the forms of the action they produce; the first is the one that comes directly out of the reduction.


Definition 13 (Jordan frame) The Jordan frame is the description in which the metric is the one appearing in the higher-dimensional ansatz: the reduced action Equation 8, -\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,\phi(R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2), with the scalar multiplying the curvature. In it the effective Newton constant is G/\phi, varying in space and time.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





Scalar-tensor theories of gravity were studied independently of Kaluza-Klein theory. The first example places the Jordan-frame action among them. The comparison fixes the value of the Brans-Dicke parameter.

Example 52 (Brans-Dicke theory) -\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,(\phi R - \omega\phi^{-1}(\partial\phi)^2), with (\partial\phi)^2 = g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial_\nu\phi, is the Brans-Dicke action in the signature (+, -, -, -), and the Kaluza-Klein scalar is the case \omega = 0 (Overduin and Wesson 1997, eq. 13); solar-system tests require \omega > 500, so the scalar must be stabilised by extra ingredients in any realistic model.

The frames differ in which metric measures lengths. The second example asks which one test particles follow. The answer depends on what the particle couples to.

Example 53 (Which metric do particles follow?) A five-dimensional geodesic projects to a four-dimensional curve that is a geodesic of neither frame in general; for the charged Kaluza-Klein black hole Duff (1994, 10) argues that the Weyl-rescaled metric e^{\sqrt3\phi}g_{\mu\nu} is the one coupling to a charged particle’s worldline. The choice of frame is a matter of which quantities are held fixed, not of physics (Overduin and Wesson 1997, sec. 3.7).

The scalar has no kinetic term in the Jordan frame. The third example notes this, which is what the Einstein frame repairs.

Example 54 (No kinetic term) The Jordan-frame action has no (\partial\phi)^2 term at all (Exercise 35): the scalar’s dynamics is entirely hidden in its coupling to R, and is revealed by the rescaling below.










NoteExercises





The first exercise reads off the effective gravitational coupling of the Jordan frame. It makes the statement “G/\phi” quantitative. The result is plotted in the figure of the dilaton couplings below.

Exercise 53 (The effective Newton constant) In the Jordan frame with A = 0, read off the coefficient of \sqrt{-g}R in Equation 8 and the effective Newton constant. By how much does gravity weaken where the circle is twice as large?







NoteSolution





The coefficient is -\frac{2\pi\phi}{2\hat\kappa^2}, which has the Einstein-Hilbert form -\frac{1}{16\pi G_{\text{eff}}} with 16\pi G_{\text{eff}} = 2\hat\kappa^2/(2\pi\phi), i.e. G_{\text{eff}} = G/\phi with G the value at \phi = 1. Where the circle is twice as large (\phi = 2) the effective Newton constant is halved: gravity is diluted over a larger internal volume, the mechanism of Exercise 56 applied point by point (Figure 4).



Neutral particles do not feel the gauge field. The second exercise asks which four-dimensional metric they follow when the circle has varying size.

Exercise 54 (Neutral particles) For A = 0, show that a five-dimensional geodesic with p_y = -\phi^2\dot y = 0 projects to a geodesic of the Jordan-frame metric g, and that a particle with p_y \neq 0 feels the force of Example 25.







NoteSolution





p_y = 0 means \dot y = 0, and the spacetime components of the geodesic equation reduce to \ddot x^\lambda +
\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = 0 with \hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} for A = 0: a geodesic of g, and since \hat g(\dot x, \dot x) = g(\dot x, \dot x) the affine parameters agree. For p_y \neq 0, \dot y = -p_y/\phi^2 and the term \hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy}\dot y^2 = \phi\partial^\lambda\phi\,p_y^2/\phi^4 gives \ddot x^\lambda + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = -
p_y^2\phi^{-3}\partial^\lambda\phi = \partial^\lambda(p_y^2/2\phi^2). For the spatial components \partial^i = -\partial_i, so the force points down the gradient of p_y^2/\phi^2, the square of the Jordan-frame Kaluza-Klein mass (Exercise 20 of Gauge symmetry and the Kaluza-Klein tower): towards larger circles.



The Kaluza-Klein scalar is a Brans-Dicke field with \omega = 0. The third exercise performs the frame change for any \omega, which shows which theories have a healthy scalar.

Exercise 55 (Brans-Dicke in the Einstein frame) Rescale g = \phi^{-1}g^E in the Brans-Dicke action of Example 52 and show that, up to a total derivative, it becomes \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g^E}(-R^E + (\omega + \tfrac32)(\partial_E\ln\phi)^2). For which \omega is the scalar not a ghost?







NoteSolution





The \phi R term gives Equation 10. For the kinetic term, \sqrt{-g} = \phi^{-2}\sqrt{-g^E} and g^{\mu\nu} =
\phi g_E^{\mu\nu}, so \sqrt{-g}\,\phi^{-1}g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi = \sqrt{-g^E}\,\phi^{-2}(\partial_E\phi)^2 =
\sqrt{-g^E}(\partial_E\ln\phi)^2. Altogether -\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\sqrt{-g^E}(R^E - \tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2 - \omega(\partial\ln\phi)^2) plus a total derivative. The kinetic term \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}(\omega + \tfrac32)(\partial\ln\phi)^2 has the healthy sign in (+, -, -, -) exactly when \omega > -\tfrac32; the Kaluza-Klein value \omega = 0 gives \tfrac32, as in Equation 11.






The Einstein frame is defined by the requirement that the coefficient of the curvature be constant. With Equation 9 this fixes the power of \phi in the rescaling and produces a kinetic term for the scalar.


Definition 14 (Einstein frame) The Einstein frame metric is g^E_{\mu\nu} = \phi\,g_{\mu\nu}, that is g = \Omega^2g^E with \Omega^2 = \phi^{-1}. By Equation 9 and Equation 4, 
\sqrt{-g}\,\phi R = \sqrt{-g^E}\left(R^E + 3\,\Box^E\ln\phi - \tfrac32\,g_E^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\phi\,\partial_\nu\ln\phi\right),
\tag{10} and dropping the total derivative the reduced action becomes 
\hat S = \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g^E}\left(-R^E + \tfrac32\,g_E^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\phi\,\partial_\nu\ln\phi
  - \tfrac14\phi^3F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}_E\right)
\tag{11} (Overduin and Wesson 1997, eq. 17): canonical gravity (-R, the sign of Equation 1 of General relativity), a scalar with a positive kinetic term, and Maxwell’s term -\tfrac14F^2 with a \phi-dependent coupling (Proposition 7).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The kinetic term comes from the derivative terms of the Weyl formula. The first example traces the factors. Its sign is the important point.

Example 55 (The kinetic term) \Omega = \phi^{-1/2} gives \ln\Omega = -\tfrac12\ln\phi, and the terms -6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 of Equation 9 become 3\Box\ln\phi - \tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2; the factors \sqrt{-g}\,\phi = \Omega^4\phi\sqrt{-g^E} =
\phi^{-1}\sqrt{-g^E} and \Omega^{-2} = \phi cancel exactly (Exercise 62); the overall -\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2} of the action then turns -\tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2 into the positive kinetic term of Equation 11, the sign a scalar must have in the signature (+, -, -, -) (Coordinates, indices and signature).

The Maxwell term is Weyl invariant in four dimensions, so it keeps the powers of \phi it had. The second example counts them.

Example 56 (The Maxwell term) \sqrt{-g}\,\phi\cdot\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma} = \phi^{-2}\sqrt{-g^E}\,\phi^3\,\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}
g_E^{\mu\rho}g_E^{\nu\sigma} = \phi^3\sqrt{-g^E}F^2_E: the dilaton coupling \phi^3.

In the Einstein frame the Newton constant is a constant. The third example relates it to the five-dimensional one. This is the relation that makes gravity weak in four dimensions.

Example 57 (Newton’s constant) In the Einstein frame the coefficient of R^E is the constant 1/2\kappa^2 with \kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2/2\pi: the four-dimensional Newton constant is the five-dimensional one divided by the circumference of the circle, G_4 = G_5/2\pi R for a circle of radius R (Overduin and Wesson 1997, eq. 10) (Exercise 56).










NoteExercises





The first exercise derives the relation between the two Newton constants for a circle of radius R. It is the relation used throughout The Kaluza-Klein tower.

Exercise 56 (Newton’s constant and the circle) With \hat S = -\frac{1}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int d^5x\sqrt{|\hat g|}\,\hat R and a circle 0 \leq y < 2\pi R, express the four-dimensional \kappa in terms of \hat\kappa and R.







NoteSolution





With \phi = R constant (the circle has circumference 2\pi R for 0 \leq y < 2\pi in Equation 1) the y integral gives 2\pi and the factor \phi = R: \hat S = -\frac{2\pi R}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,R_4 + \dots, so \kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2/2\pi R, that is G_4 = G_5/(2\pi R): gravity is weaker in four dimensions by the volume of the internal space, the mechanism of Arkani-Hamed et al. (1998) for large extra dimensions (Part VI). In Duff’s normalisation with 0 \leq my \leq 2\pi this is 2\pi\kappa^2 = m\hat\kappa^2 (Duff 1994, 5).



The power \phi^1 in g^E = \phi g was stated, not derived. The second exercise derives it as the unique power that makes the coefficient of the curvature constant.

Exercise 57 (Why \phi^1?) Write g = \phi^ag^E and find the power of \phi multiplying \sqrt{-g^E}R^E in \sqrt{-g}\,\phi R. Which a gives the Einstein frame?







NoteSolution





With \Omega^2 = \phi^a: \sqrt{-g} = \phi^{2a}\sqrt{-g^E} and R = \phi^{-a}(R^E + \dots) by Equation 9, so \sqrt{-g}\,\phi
R = \phi^{1 + a}\sqrt{-g^E}(R^E + \dots). The coefficient is constant for a = -1, g = \phi^{-1}g^E, as in Definition 14. In d dimensions the same count gives \phi^{1 + a(d - 2)/2} and a = -2/(d - 2) (Exercise 70).



The two frames assign different masses to the same particle. The third exercise relates them, which is needed to compare the Kaluza-Klein masses of The Kaluza-Klein tower in the two frames.

Exercise 58 (Masses in the two frames) A point particle of mass m in the Jordan frame has action -m\int d\tau_J with d\tau_J^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu. Show that its Einstein-frame mass is m\phi^{-1/2} for constant \phi, and apply this to the Jordan-frame Kaluza-Klein mass |n|/(R\phi).







NoteSolution





g = \phi^{-1}g^E gives d\tau_J = \phi^{-1/2}d\tau_E, so -m\int d\tau_J = -m\phi^{-1/2}\int d\tau_E: the Einstein-frame mass is m\phi^{-1/2}. For the Kaluza-Klein modes, |n|/(R\phi) \cdot \phi^{-1/2} = |n|/(R\phi^{3/2}), which is what the wave equation gives directly in Exercise 20 of Gauge symmetry and the Kaluza-Klein tower.






In the Einstein frame the scalar has a kinetic term with a non-standard normalisation. Rescaling the field to make it canonical defines the dilaton, and exposes the exponential coupling to the Maxwell term.


Definition 15 (Dilaton) The dilaton is the canonically normalised scalar \sigma = \sqrt3\ln\phi, in terms of which Equation 11 reads 
\hat S = \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g^E}\left(-R^E + \tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2 - \tfrac14e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2\right),
\tag{12} a massless scalar without potential coupled to the Maxwell term through e^{\sqrt3\sigma} (Duff 1994, eq. 8, with \sigma = -\phi_{\text{Duff}}).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The coefficient \sqrt3 is not a choice. The first example shows that it is forced by the normalisation of the kinetic term.

Example 58 (Fixing the normalisation) \tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2 = \tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2 requires \ln\phi = \sigma/\sqrt3, and then \phi^3 = e^{\sqrt3\sigma}: the coefficient \sqrt3 in the exponent is forced by the kinetic normalisation (Exercise 59).

The dilaton has no potential. The second example draws the consequence: the size of the circle is undetermined. This is the moduli problem of every compactification.

Example 59 (A flat direction) \sigma has no potential: every constant value is a vacuum, the radius of the circle is a modulus (a flat direction in the sense of Example 61 of Supersymmetry and supergravity), and the global shift \sigma \to \sigma + c with A \to e^{-\sqrt3c/2}A is a symmetry of Equation 12. Stabilising this modulus is the first problem of every compactification (Part VI).

The exponential coupling is characteristic of dimensional reduction. The third example compares it with other dilaton couplings. The value of the coupling distinguishes the theories.

Example 60 (The dilaton coupling a = \sqrt3) Dilaton black holes with e^{-a\sigma}F^2 have a = 0 for Reissner-Nordström, a = 1 for the string dilaton and a =
\sqrt3 for Kaluza-Klein (Duff 1994, 30); the extreme Kaluza-Klein black holes have the charge-to-mass ratio of the massive modes of The Kaluza-Klein tower.










NoteExercises











Figure 4: The couplings of the reduced theory as functions of the size \phi of the circle, with y \sim y + 2\pi R: the Jordan-frame Newton constant G/\phi (blue), the Einstein-frame gauge coupling e\phi^{-3/2} read off from -\tfrac14e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2 = -\tfrac14\phi^3F^2, which coincides with the Einstein-frame mass m_1R = \phi^{-3/2} of the first Kaluza-Klein mode (red; dashed, the Jordan-frame mass \phi^{-1}), and the ratio q_n/(\sqrt2\kappa m_n) = 1 (green), independent of \phi. The exponents are checked symbolically, the mass from the wave equation on \phi^{-1}\eta -
\phi^2dy^2 with SageManifolds. Generated by figures/kkr_couplings.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.
The first exercise derives Equation 12 from Equation 11. It is the computation behind Example 58. Only the normalisation of the kinetic term is needed.

Exercise 59 (The dilaton) Derive Equation 12 from Equation 11.







NoteSolution





With \phi = e^{c\sigma}, \ln\phi = c\sigma and \tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2 = \tfrac32c^2(\partial\sigma)^2, which equals \tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2 for c = 1/\sqrt3; then \phi^3 = e^{3c\sigma} = e^{\sqrt3\sigma}. The sign of \sigma is a convention: Duff (1994) writes e^{-\sqrt3\phi} with his \phi = -\sigma.



The shift symmetry of Example 59 is stated without proof. The second exercise verifies it and identifies the physical quantity it changes.

Exercise 60 (The shift symmetry) Show that Equation 12 is invariant under \sigma \to \sigma + c, A_\mu \to e^{-\sqrt3c/2}A_\mu, g^E fixed. How does the effective gauge coupling of Figure 4 change?







NoteSolution





R^E and (\partial\sigma)^2 do not change, and e^{\sqrt3(\sigma + c)}(e^{-\sqrt3c/2})^2F^2 = e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2. The symmetry changes the vacuum value of \phi = e^{\sigma/\sqrt3} by e^{c/\sqrt3} and hence the effective coupling e\phi^{-3/2} by e^{-\sqrt3c/2}, compensated by the rescaling of A: in the zero-mode theory the value of the gauge coupling is not fixed. It is fixed only by the charged massive modes, whose charges n/R are quantised (Definition 7 of Gauge symmetry and the Kaluza-Klein tower), so the symmetry is broken by the full tower.



The dilaton is sourced by the electromagnetic field. The third exercise derives its field equation and recovers the constraint of Example 28.

Exercise 61 (The dilaton equation) Derive the field equation of \sigma from Equation 12. Can \sigma be constant in a Coulomb field?







NoteSolution





With L = \tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2 - \tfrac14e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2, the Euler-Lagrange equation \nabla^E_\mu(\partial L/\partial(\partial_\mu\sigma)) = \partial
L/\partial\sigma gives \Box^E\sigma = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2. A Coulomb field has F^2 = -2E^2 \neq 0, so \Box\sigma
\neq 0 and \sigma cannot be constant: the electric field sources the dilaton, the Einstein-frame form of the inconsistency of Kaluza’s \phi = 1 (Example 28, Exercise 31).






The two propositions of this section are the curvature formula and the Einstein-frame identity. The first is the four-dimensional case of the Weyl formula, and the second rests on it.


Proposition 6 (The Weyl rescaling formula) In four dimensions \tilde R = \Omega^{-2}R - 6\Omega^{-3}\Box\Omega for \tilde g = \Omega^2g.







TipVerification





Veriphy. The ideal_membership shape, here closed by ring after unfolding, since the inverse metric is explicit; certificate pending.
Lean. KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Weyl.weyl_scalar, for a diagonal metric with arbitrary functions, a polynomial identity in the jets of g and \Omega.

/-- `R[Ω² g] = Ω⁻² R[g] - 6 Ω⁻³ □Ω` for a diagonal four-dimensional metric with arbitrary functions. -/
theorem weyl_scalar (gd : Fin 4 → ℝ) (dgd : Fin 4 → Fin 4 → ℝ) (ddgd : Fin 4 → Fin 4 → Fin 4 → ℝ)
    (W : ℝ) (dW : Fin 4 → ℝ) (ddW : Fin 4 → Fin 4 → ℝ) (hg : ∀ μ, gd μ ≠ 0) (hW : W ≠ 0) :
    (weylJets gd dgd ddgd W dW ddW).R4 =
      W⁻¹ ^ 2 * (diagJets gd dgd ddgd W dW ddW).R4 - 6 * W⁻¹ ^ 3 * (diagJets gd dgd ddgd W dW ddW).boxφ
KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Weyl.weyl_scalar in KaluzaKlein/AbelianKK/Weyl.lean, namespace KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Weyl

Sage. Checked by exact computation for general metrics with SageManifolds on de Sitter space with \Omega(t) (figures/kk_einstein_frame.sage) and on a static spherically symmetric metric with \Omega(r) (Exercise 62); the two-dimensional formula likewise on the sphere.










NoteExamples





De Sitter space is a rescaling of Minkowski space. The first example obtains its curvature from the formula with R =
0.

Example 61 (De Sitter from Minkowski) In conformal time \tau < 0, de Sitter space is \Omega^2\eta with \Omega = -1/(H\tau). With R = 0 and \Box\Omega =
\partial_\tau^2\Omega = -2/(H\tau^3), the formula gives \tilde R = -6\Omega^{-3}\Box\Omega = -6(-H\tau)^3 \cdot (-2)/(H\tau^3) = -12H^2, the curvature of de Sitter space in the signature (+, -, -, -) (Exercise 63).

Unlike the reduction formulas, the Weyl formula does not hold with the inverse metric as free symbols. The second example shows where the relation between g^{\mu\nu} and g_{\mu\nu} enters.

Example 62 (The true inverse is needed) With g^{\mu\nu} free the identity fails, while with the true inverse it holds: the derivation uses g^{\mu\lambda}g_{\lambda\nu} =
\delta^\mu_\nu, for instance in g^{\mu\nu}g_{\mu\nu} = 4, which produces the coefficient 6 = 2(n - 1) (Exercise 25). For a diagonal metric the inverse is explicit and the issue does not arise.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Weyl.weyl_scalar avoids the issue with a diagonal metric, whose inverse is explicit.
Sage. sage/kk_weyl.sage reports that with g^{\mu\nu} free the identity fails, while at random points with the true inverse it holds.



The formula is the same in every signature. The third example checks the claim made in the definition. The argument is the one used for the reduction formula in Exercise 34.

Example 63 (Independence of the signature) Under g \to -g (with \Omega fixed), \tilde g \to -\tilde g, R \to -R, \tilde R \to -\tilde R and \Box \to -\Box, so both sides of \tilde R = \Omega^{-2}R - 6\Omega^{-3}\Box\Omega change sign: the formula of a mostly-plus reference is the same formula, which is why Equation 9 could be quoted from Overduin and Wesson (1997) unchanged.










NoteExercises





The first exercise checks the formula on a static spherically symmetric metric and then the Einstein-frame identity. It tests both propositions on the same metric.

Exercise 62 (Weyl rescaling with SageManifolds) Check Equation 9 on a static spherically symmetric metric with \Omega(r), and then Equation 10 for g = \phi^{-1}g^E.







NoteSolution






M = Manifold(4, "M", structure="Lorentzian"); X = M.chart("t r th ph"); t, r, th, ph = X[:]
f = function("f")(r); Om = function("Omega")(r)
g = M.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = f; g[1, 1] = -1 / f; g[2, 2] = -r^2; g[3, 3] = -r^2 * sin(th)^2
gt = M.metric("gt")
for i in range(4): gt[i, i] = Om^2 * g[i, i].expr()
R = g.ricci_scalar().expr(); Rt = gt.ricci_scalar().expr()
nab = g.connection()
box = lambda s: (nab(nab(M.scalar_field(s)).up(g)).trace()).expr()
print("[PASS] R[Omega^2 g] = Omega^{-2} R[g] - 6 Omega^{-3} Box Omega on the diagonal metric with Omega(r):", bool((Rt - (R / Om^2 - 6 * box(Om) / Om^3)).simplify_full() == 0))
# Einstein frame: g = phi^{-1} gE, i.e. gE = phi g (Omega^2 = phi^{-1} rescales gE to g); gE plays the role of g~ above
phi = function("phi")(r)
gJ = M.metric("gJ")                     # Jordan-frame metric g = phi^{-1} gE with gE = the diagonal metric above
for i in range(4): gJ[i, i] = g[i, i].expr() / phi
RJ = gJ.ricci_scalar().expr()
lnphi = log(phi)
dln2 = sum(g.inverse()[i, i].expr() * diff(lnphi, X[i])^2 for i in range(4))
# sqrt(-g) = phi^{-2} sqrt(-gE) for g = phi^{-1} gE in four dimensions, so after dividing both sides by sqrt(-gE) the
# identity reads phi^{-1} R[g] = R_E + 3 Box_E ln phi - (3/2)(d_E ln phi)^2 (the common square root is cancelled
# analytically; Sage does not simplify sqrt(r^4 sin^2 th / phi^4) on its own)
print("[PASS] det g = phi^{-4} det gE for g = phi^{-1} gE:", bool((gJ.determinant().expr() - g.determinant().expr() / phi^4).simplify_full() == 0))
lhs = RJ / phi
rhs = R + 3 * box(lnphi) - 3 / 2 * dln2
print("[PASS] sqrt(-g) phi R[g] = sqrt(-gE) (R_E + 3 Box_E ln phi - (3/2)(d_E ln phi)^2) for g = phi^{-1} gE (both sides divided by sqrt(-gE)):", bool((lhs - rhs).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
[PASS] R[Omega^2 g] = Omega^{-2} R[g] - 6 Omega^{-3} Box Omega on the diagonal metric with Omega(r): True
[PASS] det g = phi^{-4} det gE for g = phi^{-1} gE: True
[PASS] sqrt(-g) phi R[g] = sqrt(-gE) (R_E + 3 Box_E ln phi - (3/2)(d_E ln phi)^2) for g = phi^{-1} gE (both sides divided by sqrt(-gE)): True




The second exercise verifies Example 61 with SageManifolds. It tests the sign of the curvature as well as the formula. Example 50 treats a different rescaling of the same space.

Exercise 63 (De Sitter space) Compute the curvature scalar of \Omega^2\eta, \Omega = -1/(H\tau), with SageManifolds and compare with the formula.







NoteSolution






M = Manifold(4, "M", structure="Lorentzian"); X = M.chart("tau x y z"); tau, x, y, z = X[:]
H = var("H"); assume(H > 0); assume(tau < 0)
Om = -1 / (H * tau)
g = M.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = Om^2
for i in (1, 2, 3): g[i, i] = -Om^2
R = g.ricci_scalar().expr().simplify_full()
print("R~ =", R)
print("[PASS] R~ = -12 H^2 = -6 Omega^{-3} d_tau^2 Omega:", bool(R == -12 * H^2) and bool((-6 * diff(Om, tau, 2) / Om^3 + 12 * H^2).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
R~ = -12*H^2
[PASS] R~ = -12 H^2 = -6 Omega^{-3} d_tau^2 Omega: True

In the signature (+, -, -, -) de Sitter space has R = -12H^2; in the mostly-plus signature the same space has R = +
12H^2 (Example 63).



Rescaling by \Omega and then by \Omega^{-1} must return the original curvature. The third exercise checks this consistency, which tests the derivative terms of the formula.

Exercise 64 (Rescaling back) Apply Equation 9 to g = \Omega^{-2}\tilde g, using \tilde\Box f = \Omega^{-2}(\Box f + 2g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\Omega\,\partial_\nu f) in four dimensions, and show that it returns R.







NoteSolution





With \ln\Omega^{-1} = -\ln\Omega: R = \Omega^2(\tilde R + 6\tilde\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\tilde\partial\ln\Omega)^2). Here \tilde\Box\ln\Omega =
\Omega^{-2}(\Box\ln\Omega + 2(\partial\ln\Omega)^2) and (\tilde\partial\ln\Omega)^2 = \Omega^{-2}(\partial\ln\Omega)^2, and \Omega^2\tilde R = R -
6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2. Altogether R - 6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 + 6\Box\ln\Omega + 12(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 -
6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 = R.






The second proposition is the Einstein-frame identity. Its general proof is the algebra of Example 55 applied to Proposition 6; it turns the reduced action into the Einstein-frame action.


Proposition 7 (The Einstein-frame identity) Equation 10 holds for g = \phi^{-1}g^E; it follows from Proposition 6 by the algebra of Example 55.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Checked by exact computation with SageManifolds on a static spherically symmetric g^E and \phi(r) (Exercise 62); the general case follows from Proposition 6 by the algebra of Example 55, argued in the text.










NoteExamples





For constant \phi the identity is the constant rescaling of Example 51. The first example checks this case. It shows that the Einstein frame is then a mere change of units.

Example 64 (Constant \phi) For constant \phi, g^E = \phi g has \sqrt{-g^E} = \phi^2\sqrt{-g} and R^E = \phi^{-1}R, so \sqrt{-g^E}R^E = \phi\sqrt{-g}R, and the derivative terms vanish: Equation 10 reduces to an identity between constants, and the Einstein frame is a change of units by \sqrt\phi.

The identity contains a total derivative that disappears from the action. The second example writes it. It is the reason the identity and the action differ by one term.

Example 65 (The boundary term) 3\sqrt{-g^E}\Box^E\ln\phi = 3\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g^E}g_E^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\ln\phi) by Exercise 35 applied to g^E, a total derivative; the only trace of the rescaling in the action is the kinetic term -\tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2.

In cosmology the two frames give different expansion histories. The third example, checked in Exercise 65, states the identity for a homogeneous metric.

Example 66 (A cosmological metric) For g^E = dt^2 - a(t)^2d\vec x^2 and \phi = \phi(t), R^E = -6(\dot a^2 + a\ddot a)/a^2, \Box^E\ln\phi = a^{-3}\partial_t(a^3\partial_t\ln\phi) and (\partial\ln\phi)^2 = (\partial_t\ln\phi)^2; the identity then expresses the curvature of the Jordan metric \phi^{-1}g^E, whose scale factor is a/\sqrt\phi, through these.










NoteExercises





The first exercise verifies Example 66 with SageManifolds. It is a check of the identity on a family of metrics different from that of Exercise 62.

Exercise 65 (The identity on a cosmology) Verify Equation 10 for g^E = dt^2 - a(t)^2(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2) and \phi = \phi(t) with SageManifolds.







NoteSolution





Both sides divided by \sqrt{-g^E} = a^3 (with \sqrt{-g} = \phi^{-2}a^3):

M = Manifold(4, "M", structure="Lorentzian"); X = M.chart("t x y z"); t, x, y, z = X[:]
a = function("a")(t); phi = function("phi")(t)
gE = M.metric("gE"); gE[0, 0] = 1
for i in (1, 2, 3): gE[i, i] = -a^2
g = M.metric("g")
for i in range(4): g[i, i] = gE[i, i].expr() / phi
RE = gE.ricci_scalar().expr(); R = g.ricci_scalar().expr()
nab = gE.connection(); L = M.scalar_field(log(phi))
boxL = nab(nab(L).up(gE)).trace().expr()
dL2 = diff(log(phi), t)^2                                # gE^{tt} = 1
print("R_E =", RE.simplify_full())
print("[PASS] phi^{-1} R[g] = R_E + 3 Box_E ln phi - (3/2)(d ln phi)^2 on the FRW metric:", bool((R / phi - (RE + 3 * boxL - 3 / 2 * dL2)).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
R_E = -6*(diff(a(t), t)^2 + a(t)*diff(a(t), t, t))/a(t)^2
[PASS] phi^{-1} R[g] = R_E + 3 Box_E ln phi - (3/2)(d ln phi)^2 on the FRW metric: True




The sign of the kinetic term decides whether the scalar is physical. The second exercise shows that it is fixed by the Weyl formula and not by the signature of the circle, while the Maxwell sign is not.

Exercise 66 (A timelike circle) Replace the ansatz by g + \phi^2(dy + A)^2 in the signature (+, -, -, -) for g, so that the circle is timelike. Using Exercise 34, find the reduced curvature scalar and the signs of the scalar and Maxwell kinetic terms in the Einstein frame.







NoteSolution





Every term of the reduction depends on \phi^2, except \phi^{-1}\Box\phi = \Box\ln\phi + (\partial\ln\phi)^2, which depends only on \ln\phi^2; so \phi^2 \to -\phi^2 gives \hat R = R - \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 - \tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi, while \sqrt{|\hat g|} =
\phi\sqrt{-g} is unchanged. The Einstein-frame rescaling acts only on \sqrt{-g}\,\phi R, so the scalar kinetic term keeps its healthy sign, but the Maxwell term becomes +\tfrac14\phi^3F^2: the photon is a ghost with negative energy. A second time direction is excluded for this reason; the spacelike circle is forced.



The Jordan and Einstein metrics of a cosmology have different scale factors. The third exercise relates them and the corresponding proper times.

Exercise 67 (Two scale factors) For g^E = dt^2 - a_E(t)^2d\vec x^2 and \phi = \phi(t), write the Jordan metric g = \phi^{-1}g^E in the form d\tau_J^2 -
a_J(\tau_J)^2d\vec x^2. If the circle shrinks, which scale factor grows faster?







NoteSolution





g = \phi^{-1}dt^2 - \phi^{-1}a_E^2d\vec x^2, so d\tau_J = \phi^{-1/2}dt and a_J = \phi^{-1/2}a_E. If \phi decreases, \phi^{-1/2} increases and a_J/a_E grows: a shrinking circle makes the Jordan-frame universe expand faster than the Einstein-frame one. The Kasner solution of Exercise 69 is an example, with a_J \propto \sqrt t and a_E \propto
t^{1/4}.

title: The Kaluza-Klein reduction
text:
NoteExercises





The three exercises below combine the three sections of the chapter. The first two follow an exact five-dimensional vacuum solution through the whole reduction, from the ansatz to the Einstein frame; the third repeats the reduction in an arbitrary number of dimensions.

Exercise 68 (The Kaluza-Klein black hole) The product of the Schwarzschild metric with a circle, f\,dt^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2 - dw^2 with f = 1 - 2m/r, is a five-dimensional vacuum solution, the black string. (a) Boost it along the circle, t = \cosh b\,t' + \sinh b\,w', w = \sinh b\,t' + \cosh b\,w', and read off \phi, A_\mu and the Jordan metric g_{\mu\nu} with Equation 2. (b) Check with SageManifolds that the five-dimensional metric is Ricci flat and that the four-dimensional fields satisfy the equations of Example 42 and of Exercise 37. (c) Write the Einstein-frame metric. (d) Why is the boosted string not the same five-dimensional space as the unboosted one, although the two are related by a coordinate change?







NoteSolution






With c = \cosh b, s = \sinh b: \hat g_{ww} = fs^2 - c^2 = -\phi^2 gives \phi^2 = 1 + \frac{2m}{r}s^2; \hat g_{tw} =
(f - 1)sc = -\phi^2A_t gives A_t = \frac{2m}{r}\frac{sc}{\phi^2}; and g_{tt} = \hat g_{tt} + \phi^2A_t^2 = f/\phi^2, the other components being those of Schwarzschild: g = \phi^{-2}f\,dt^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2, an electric potential and a scalar that tends to 1 at infinity. (b) The checks, the dilaton equation in the form \phi\Box\phi = \tfrac12\Box\phi^2 -
(\partial\phi)^2 to avoid square roots:


m, b = var("m b"); assume(m > 0)
c, s = cosh(b), sinh(b)
M5 = Manifold(5, "M5", structure="Lorentzian"); X5 = M5.chart(r"t r th ph:\phi w"); t, r, th, ph, w = X5[:]
f = 1 - 2 * m / r
G = M5.metric("G")
G[0, 0] = f * c^2 - s^2; G[0, 4] = (f - 1) * s * c; G[4, 4] = f * s^2 - c^2
G[1, 1] = -1 / f; G[2, 2] = -r^2; G[3, 3] = -r^2 * sin(th)^2
print("[PASS] the boosted black string is Ricci flat:", all(bool(G.ricci()[i, j].expr().simplify_full() == 0) for i in range(5) for j in range(i, 5)))
phi2 = (-G[4, 4].expr()).simplify_full(); At = (-G[0, 4].expr() / phi2).simplify_full()
print("phi^2 =", phi2, "; A_t =", At)
print("[PASS] phi^2 = 1 + (2m/r) sinh^2 b and g_tt = G_tt + phi^2 A_t^2 = f/phi^2:", bool((phi2 - 1 - 2 * m / r * s^2).simplify_full() == 0) and bool((G[0, 0].expr() + phi2 * At^2 - f / phi2).simplify_full() == 0))
M = Manifold(4, "M", structure="Lorentzian"); X = M.chart(r"t r th ph:\phi"); t, r, th, ph = X[:]
P2 = (1 + 2 * m / r * s^2); phi = sqrt(P2); A_t = 2 * m / r * s * c / P2
g = M.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = f / P2; g[1, 1] = -1 / f; g[2, 2] = -r^2; g[3, 3] = -r^2 * sin(th)^2
gi = g.inverse(); nab = g.connection()
Af = M.one_form(); Af[0] = A_t
F = Af.exterior_derivative()
F2 = sum(F[i, j].expr() * F[k, l].expr() * gi[i, k].expr() * gi[j, l].expr() for i in range(4) for j in range(4) for k in range(4) for l in range(4))
boxphi = nab(nab(M.scalar_field(phi)).up(g)).trace().expr()
print("F^2 =", F2.simplify_full())
# phi Box phi = (1/2) Box phi^2 - (d phi)^2 with (d phi)^2 = (d phi^2)^2/(4 phi^2): rational in r, no square roots
boxP2 = nab(nab(M.scalar_field(P2)).up(g)).trace().expr()
dphi2 = sum(gi[i, j].expr() * diff(P2, X[i]) * diff(P2, X[j]) for i in range(4) for j in range(4)) / (4 * P2)
print("[PASS] R_yy = 0: phi Box phi = (1/2) Box phi^2 - (d phi)^2 = -(1/4) phi^4 F^2:", bool((boxP2 / 2 - dphi2 + P2^2 * F2 / 4).simplify_full() == 0))
Fu = F.up(g, 0).up(g, 1)                                 # F^{mu nu}
divF = nab(Fu).trace(0, 2)                                # nabla_l F^{l nu}
lhs = [sum(g[n, k].expr() * divF[k].expr() for k in range(4)) for n in range(4)]      # nabla^l F_{l mu}
Fmix = [[sum(F[mu, k].expr() * gi[k, l].expr() for k in range(4)) for l in range(4)] for mu in range(4)]
rhs = [3 / phi * sum(diff(phi, X[l]) * Fmix[mu][l] for l in range(4)) for mu in range(4)]
print("[PASS] R_{mu y} = A_mu R_yy: nabla^l F_{l mu} = 3 phi^{-1} d_l phi F_mu^l:", all(bool((lhs[mu] - rhs[mu]).simplify_full() == 0) for mu in range(4)))
R4 = g.ricci_scalar().expr()
print("[PASS] R5 = 0: R4 = -(3/4) phi^2 F^2:", bool((R4 + 3 / 4 * P2 * F2).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
[PASS] the boosted black string is Ricci flat: True
phi^2 = (2*m*sinh(b)^2 + r)/r ; A_t = 2*m*cosh(b)*sinh(b)/(2*m*sinh(b)^2 + r)
[PASS] phi^2 = 1 + (2m/r) sinh^2 b and g_tt = G_tt + phi^2 A_t^2 = f/phi^2: True
F^2 = -8*m^2*cosh(b)^2*sinh(b)^2/(8*m^3*r*sinh(b)^6 + 12*m^2*r^2*sinh(b)^4 + 6*m*r^3*sinh(b)^2 + r^4)
[PASS] R_yy = 0: phi Box phi = (1/2) Box phi^2 - (d phi)^2 = -(1/4) phi^4 F^2: True
[PASS] R_{mu y} = A_mu R_yy: nabla^l F_{l mu} = 3 phi^{-1} d_l phi F_mu^l: True
[PASS] R5 = 0: R4 = -(3/4) phi^2 F^2: True


g^E = \phi g = \phi^{-1}f\,dt^2 - \phi(f^{-1}dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2), with \phi = (1 + \frac{2m}{r}\sinh^2b)^{1/2}: the electrically charged dilaton black hole with coupling a = \sqrt3 (Example 60). (d) The boost mixes t with the periodic coordinate w, so it is not a globally defined coordinate change on \mathbb{R}_t \times S^1_w: the identification w \sim w + 2\pi L becomes (t', w') \sim (t' - 2\pi Ls, w' + 2\pi Lc). Locally the two metrics are isometric, globally they are different spaces, which is why the reduction produces a charged black hole from an uncharged string; the charge is the momentum along the circle, \propto mcs.




The second exercise reduces a cosmological solution. It shows the dilaton rolling, the Jordan and Einstein frames disagreeing about the expansion, and the vacuum equations at work.

Exercise 69 (A Kasner universe with a shrinking circle) The five-dimensional Kasner metric dt^2 - \sum_it^{2p_i}(dx^i)^2 - t^{2q}dw^2 is Ricci flat when 3p + q = 1 and 3p^2 + q^2
= 1 for p_1 = p_2 = p_3 = p. (a) Find the non-trivial solution and identify \phi, A and the Jordan metric. (b) Use Equation 7 and Equation 6 to predict \Box\phi and R for it, and check with SageManifolds. (c) Find the Einstein-frame metric and its scale factor as a function of its proper time. Which kind of matter produces this expansion in four-dimensional cosmology?







NoteSolution






q = 1 - 3p and 3p^2 + (1 - 3p)^2 = 1 give 12p^2 = 6p, so p = \tfrac12, q = -\tfrac12 (the other root p = 0, q = 1 is flat space in Milne coordinates). Then \phi = t^{-1/2}, the circle shrinking, A = 0, and g = dt^2 - t\,d\vec
x^2. (b) \hat R_{yy} = \phi\Box\phi = 0 and \hat R = R - 2\phi^{-1}\Box\phi = 0 predict \Box\phi = 0 and R = 0. (c) g^E =
\phi g = t^{-1/2}dt^2 - t^{1/2}d\vec x^2: proper time \tau = \int t^{-1/4}dt = \tfrac43t^{3/4} and a_E = t^{1/4} =
(3\tau/4)^{1/3}:


M5 = Manifold(5, "M5", structure="Lorentzian"); X5 = M5.chart("t x y z w"); t, x, y, z, w = X5[:]
assume(t > 0)
G = M5.metric("G"); G[0, 0] = 1
for i in (1, 2, 3): G[i, i] = -t
G[4, 4] = -1 / t
print("[PASS] the Kasner metric with exponents (1/2, 1/2, 1/2, -1/2) is Ricci flat:", all(bool(G.ricci()[i, j].expr().simplify_full() == 0) for i in range(5) for j in range(i, 5)))
M = Manifold(4, "M", structure="Lorentzian"); X = M.chart("t x y z"); t, x, y, z = X[:]
g = M.metric("g"); g[0, 0] = 1
for i in (1, 2, 3): g[i, i] = -t
phi = t^(-1 / 2)
nab = g.connection(); box = nab(nab(M.scalar_field(phi)).up(g)).trace().expr().simplify_full()
R4 = g.ricci_scalar().expr().simplify_full()
print("Box phi =", box, "; R4 =", R4)
print("[PASS] Box phi = 0 and R4 = 0, as R_yy = phi Box phi = 0 and R5 = R4 - (2/phi) Box phi = 0 require:", bool(box == 0) and bool(R4 == 0))
tau = var("tau"); assume(tau > 0)
tau_of_t = integrate(t^(-1 / 4), t, 0, t)                  # proper time of gE = phi g: d tau = t^{-1/4} dt
aE2 = phi * t                                             # spatial scale factor squared of gE: t^{1/2}
t_of_tau = (3 * tau / 4)^(4 / 3)                         # inverse of tau = (4/3) t^{3/4}
assert bool((tau_of_t.subs(t=t_of_tau) - tau).simplify_full() == 0)
aE = (t_of_tau)^(1 / 4)                                   # a_E = sqrt(phi t) = t^{1/4}
print("tau(t) =", tau_of_t, "; a_E(tau)^3 =", (aE^3).canonicalize_radical())
print("[PASS] the Einstein-frame scale factor grows as tau^{1/3}: a_E = (3 tau/4)^{1/3}:", bool((aE^12 - (3 * tau / 4)^4).canonicalize_radical() == 0) and bool((aE2 - sqrt(t)).simplify_full() == 0))
Output:
[PASS] the Kasner metric with exponents (1/2, 1/2, 1/2, -1/2) is Ricci flat: True
Box phi = 0 ; R4 = 0
[PASS] Box phi = 0 and R4 = 0, as R_yy = phi Box phi = 0 and R5 = R4 - (2/phi) Box phi = 0 require: True
tau(t) = 4/3*t^(3/4) ; a_E(tau)^3 = 3/4*tau
[PASS] the Einstein-frame scale factor grows as tau^{1/3}: a_E = (3 tau/4)^{1/3}: True

a \propto \tau^{1/3} is the expansion of a flat universe filled with stiff matter, p = \rho, which is what a homogeneous massless scalar is: in the Einstein frame the shrinking circle appears as the kinetic energy of the rolling dilaton, \sigma = \sqrt3\ln\phi = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\ln t. In the Jordan frame the scale factor is \sqrt t instead (Exercise 67).



The third exercise repeats the chapter in d + 1 dimensions. It shows which numbers in the chapter are special to four dimensions.

Exercise 70 (Reduction from d + 1 to d dimensions) Take the ansatz Equation 1 with a d-dimensional metric g. (a) Find \det\hat g and the volume element. (b) Assuming that Equation 7 holds in every dimension (the jet computation never uses d = 4), write the reduced action. (c) Find the Einstein-frame rescaling g = \phi^ag^E, using the n-dimensional Weyl formula of Definition 12. (d) Show that the canonical dilaton is \sigma = \sqrt{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)}\,\ln\phi and that the Maxwell term becomes -\tfrac14e^{a\sigma}F^2 with a = \sqrt{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)}. Check d = 4. What goes wrong for d = 2?







NoteSolution






\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g (Exercise 15) and \sqrt{|\hat g|} = \phi\sqrt{|g|}. (b) -\frac{2\pi}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int
d^dx\sqrt{|g|}\,\phi(R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2), the \Box\phi term being a total derivative as before. (c) With \Omega^2 = \phi^a, \sqrt{|g|}\,\phi R = \phi^{ad/2}\phi\,\phi^{-a}\sqrt{|g^E|}(R^E + \dots), constant coefficient for a(d - 2)/2 = -1: g =
\phi^{-2/(d - 2)}g^E. (d) With \ln\Omega = -\ln\phi/(d - 2) the term -(d - 1)(d - 2)(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 of the Weyl formula gives -\frac{d - 1}{d - 2}(\partial\ln\phi)^2 inside the bracket, hence the kinetic term \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\frac{d - 1}{d - 2}(\partial\ln\phi)^2
= \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2 for \sigma = \sqrt{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)}\ln\phi. The Maxwell term picks up \Omega^{d - 4} (Exercise 49): \phi^3\phi^{-(d - 4)/(d - 2)} = \phi^{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)} = e^{a\sigma} with a = \frac{2(d - 1)}{d -
2}\big/\sqrt{\frac{2(d - 1)}{d - 2}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(d - 1)}{d - 2}}. For d = 4: \sigma = \sqrt3\ln\phi, a = \sqrt3 and the weight \phi^3, as in Definition 15. For d = 2 the exponent -2/(d - 2) is undefined: two-dimensional gravity is Weyl invariant (\sqrt g R is a total derivative) and no rescaling can remove \phi, which survives as a dilaton-gravity theory.

title: Isometries and gauge fields
text:
Kaluza’s fifth dimension produced one gauge field, the photon, because the circle has one symmetry: the rotation generated by the Killing vector \partial_y (Part III, Gauge invariance from the fifth dimension). The Standard Model needs twelve gauge fields and three non-commuting gauge groups, and the natural question, first asked by DeWitt, is whether a larger internal space with a larger symmetry group can produce them all from geometry. This chapter answers the first half of the question. Replacing the circle by an internal space with a non-abelian group of isometries, the sphere S^2 with its three rotations being the running example, the off-diagonal components of the metric become one gauge field per Killing vector, and the coordinate changes along the Killing vectors become Yang-Mills gauge transformations whose structure constants are those of the isometry algebra.
The chapter has two sections. The first, on the ansatz, recalls the Killing vectors of the internal space (Part I, Flows and Killing vectors), writes the non-abelian Kaluza-Klein ansatz on M_4 \times M_k and inverts it; the inverse is a statement about block matrices that holds for every internal space at once. The second derives the gauge transformation from the Lie derivative of the metric along spacetime-dependent isometries and identifies the gauge algebra with the opposite of the Killing algebra, the Lie algebra of the isometry group of Lie groups and Lie algebras. The geometric picture behind both is that of a fibre bundle with structure group G (Fibre bundles), and the sphere is the simplest coset space SO(3)/SO(2) of Coset spaces. The next chapter reduces the curvature scalar and meets the consistency problem. Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions.


Replacing the circle by a sphere replaces the single Killing vector \partial_y by the three Killing vectors of SO(3), and the single gauge field by three: the gauge group of the reduced theory is the isometry group of the internal space. This section sets up the non-abelian Kaluza-Klein ansatz on M_4 \times S^2, the sphere of Part I as SO(3)/SO(2), following Duff (1994, sec. 5) and Overduin and Wesson (1997, sec. 4.3); its block inverse holds for an arbitrary internal space.


The ansatz needs two ingredients from the internal space: a metric that fixes its size and shape, and the Killing vectors that generate its symmetries. The definition collects both and fixes the sign with which the internal metric enters the higher-dimensional metric of signature (+, -, \dots, -).


Definition 1 (Internal space with isometries) An internal space is a compact Riemannian manifold (M_k, \gamma) with positive-definite metric \gamma_{mn}(y) and a group G of isometries generated by Killing vectors K_a = K^m_a\partial_m (Definition 77 of Differential geometry), a = 1, \dots, \dim G, closing into the Lie algebra of G, [K_a, K_b] = f_{ab}{}^cK_c (Definition 78 of Differential geometry). The compactification is M_4 \times M_k, and the Kaluza-Klein ansatz couples the Killing vectors to gauge fields on M_4. Inside the full metric the internal block is h_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}, so that \hat g has signature (+, -, \dots, -) (Coordinates, indices and signature); the geometry of M_k itself, its Killing vectors and its curvature R_\gamma, is that of the positive metric \gamma.







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





The round two-sphere is the example the whole of this Part returns to. Its three Killing vectors were found in Part I, and their brackets fix the structure constants that will reappear in the gauge transformation.

Example 1 (The sphere) S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2) with the round metric d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2 and the three Killing vectors Equation 54 of Differential geometry, K_1 = -\sin\varphi\,\partial_\theta - \cot\theta\cos\varphi\,\partial_\varphi, K_2 = \cos\varphi\,\partial_\theta -
\cot\theta\sin\varphi\,\partial_\varphi, K_3 = \partial_\varphi, with [K_a, K_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}K_c (Equation 56 of Differential geometry, Proposition 31 of Differential geometry): f_{ab}{}^c = -\epsilon_{abc}, the algebra \mathfrak{so}(3) (Exercise 1).

The circle of Part III is the degenerate case with a one-dimensional abelian isometry group. Keeping it in view checks every formula of this chapter, because each must reduce to its Part III counterpart.

Example 2 (The circle) S^1 with \gamma = \phi^2 (h = -\phi^2) and the single Killing vector K = \partial_y, f = 0: the ansatz of Five-dimensional gravity and the Kaluza-Klein ansatz is the case \dim G = 1, and every formula below reduces to Part III when K^m_a = 1.

Flat tori and group manifolds show that the number of Killing vectors is not tied to the dimension of the space. A torus has as many as dimensions, a group manifold twice as many, and a coset as many as the group that acts on it.

Example 3 (Tori and group manifolds) T^k has the k commuting Killing vectors \partial_{y^m} and gauge group U(1)^k; a group manifold G has 2\dim G Killing vectors, the left- and right-invariant fields of Maurer-Cartan forms, and gauge group G \times
G; a coset G/H has the \dim G Killing vectors of G acting on the left (Duff 1994, 14). The number of gauge fields is \dim G, not the number of internal dimensions.










NoteExercises











Figure 1: The non-abelian ansatz on M_4 \times S^2: a row of sphere fibres along a spacetime direction x, each carrying the tangent field \xi = A^a_\mu(x)K_a (red arrows) that tilts the fibre relative to the base, here with A^1 growing and A^3 oscillating with x. The brackets [K_a, K_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}K_c and the inner products K_a\cdot
K_b = \delta_{ab} - n_an_b are checked symbolically. Generated by figures/s2_gauge_fields.sage.



Interactive figure (drag to rotate or zoom); the static version is above.
The first exercise recomputes the brackets and inner products of the sphere’s Killing vectors in the chart. It is the input for every later computation on M_4 \times S^2, so it is worth checking once by machine.

Exercise 1 (The Killing algebra of the sphere) Verify the brackets and the inner products of the three Killing vectors with Sage.







NoteSolution






th, ph = var("th ph")
K = [vector([-sin(ph), -cot(th) * cos(ph)]), vector([cos(ph), -cot(th) * sin(ph)]), vector([0, 1])]
n = vector([sin(th) * cos(ph), sin(th) * sin(ph), cos(th)])
def lc(a, b, c): return Permutation([a + 1, b + 1, c + 1]).sign() if len({a, b, c}) == 3 else 0
def bracket(U, V): return vector([sum(U[k] * diff(V[m], [th, ph][k]) - V[k] * diff(U[m], [th, ph][k]) for k in range(2)) for m in range(2)])
print("[K_1, K_2] =", bracket(K[0], K[1]).apply_map(lambda e: e.simplify_full()), " and -K_3 =", -K[2])
print("[PASS] [K_a, K_b] = -eps_abc K_c:", all((bracket(K[a], K[b]) + sum(lc(a, b, c) * K[c] for c in range(3))).apply_map(lambda e: e.simplify_full()).is_zero() for a in range(3) for b in range(3)))
h = diagonal_matrix([1, sin(th)^2])
G = matrix(SR, 3, 3, lambda a, b: (K[a] * h * K[b]).simplify_full())
print("K_a . K_b ="); print(G)
print("[PASS] K_a . K_b = delta_ab - n_a n_b:", (G - (identity_matrix(3) - n.column() * n.row())).apply_map(lambda e: e.simplify_full()).is_zero())
print("[PASS] the Killing vectors are tangent to the sphere and the matrix K_a . K_b has rank 2 (one combination, n^a K_a, vanishes at each point):", G.rank() == 2 and (sum(n[a] * K[a] for a in range(3))).apply_map(lambda e: e.simplify_full()).is_zero())
Output:
[K_1, K_2] = (0, -1)  and -K_3 = (0, -1)
[PASS] [K_a, K_b] = -eps_abc K_c: True
K_a . K_b =
[cos(ph)^2*cos(th)^2 + sin(ph)^2      -cos(ph)*sin(ph)*sin(th)^2        -cos(ph)*cos(th)*sin(th)]
[     -cos(ph)*sin(ph)*sin(th)^2 cos(th)^2*sin(ph)^2 + cos(ph)^2        -cos(th)*sin(ph)*sin(th)]
[       -cos(ph)*cos(th)*sin(th)        -cos(th)*sin(ph)*sin(th)                       sin(th)^2]
[PASS] K_a . K_b = delta_ab - n_a n_b: True
[PASS] the Killing vectors are tangent to the sphere and the matrix K_a . K_b has rank 2 (one combination, n^a K_a, vanishes at each point): True

In the chart the Killing vectors look complicated, but in the ambient space they are the familiar rotation fields. The second exercise pushes them forward to \mathbb{R}^3, as in the interactive figure, and rederives the brackets from the cross product.

Exercise 2 (The Killing vectors in \mathbb{R}^3) Show that the push-forward of K_a by the embedding \vec n(\theta, \varphi) is \vec e_a \times \vec n. Writing \vec e_a \times \vec x = L_a\vec x with (L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}, use the bracket of linear vector fields, [L\vec x, M\vec x] = (ML - LM)\vec x, to rederive [K_a, K_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}K_c, and compute (\vec e_a \times \vec n)
\cdot (\vec e_b \times \vec n).







NoteSolution





For K_3 = \partial_\varphi the push-forward is \partial_\varphi\vec n = (-\sin\theta\sin\varphi, \sin\theta\cos\varphi, 0) =
\vec e_3 \times \vec n; the other two follow in the same way. For linear fields X = L\vec x, Y = M\vec x, the bracket X^j\partial_jY - Y^j\partial_jX is ML\vec x - LM\vec x; since [L_a, L_b] = \epsilon_{abc}L_c as matrices, the fields have the opposite bracket -\epsilon_{abc}, the sign that runs through this chapter. Finally (\vec e_a \times
\vec n)\cdot(\vec e_b \times \vec n) = \delta_{ab}(\vec n\cdot\vec n) - n_an_b = \delta_{ab} - n_an_b:

th, ph = var("th ph")
K = [vector([-sin(ph), -cot(th) * cos(ph)]), vector([cos(ph), -cot(th) * sin(ph)]), vector([0, 1])]
n = vector([sin(th) * cos(ph), sin(th) * sin(ph), cos(th)])
J = matrix(SR, 3, 2, lambda i, m: diff(n[i], [th, ph][m]))          # columns d n / d th, d n / d ph
e = identity_matrix(SR, 3).columns()
push = [(J * K[a]).simplify_full() for a in range(3)]
for a in range(3): print("push-forward of K_%d:" % (a + 1), push[a], "  e_%d x n:" % (a + 1), e[a].cross_product(n))
print("[PASS] the push-forward of K_a is e_a x n:", all((push[a] - e[a].cross_product(n)).simplify_full().is_zero() for a in range(3)))
# linear vector fields on R^3: X_a(x) = e_a x x = L_a x with the matrices (L_a)_{bc} = -eps_abc
x = vector(var("x1 x2 x3"))
def lc(a, b, c): return Permutation([a + 1, b + 1, c + 1]).sign() if len({a, b, c}) == 3 else 0
L = [matrix(QQ, 3, 3, lambda b, c: -lc(a, b, c)) for a in range(3)]
print("[PASS] e_a x x = L_a x with (L_a)_{bc} = -eps_abc:", all((L[a] * x - e[a].cross_product(x)).is_zero() for a in range(3)))
# for linear fields X = L x, Y = M x the vector-field bracket is [X, Y] = (M L - L M) x
br = lambda P, Q: Q * P - P * Q
print("[PASS] [X_a, X_b] = (L_b L_a - L_a L_b) x = -eps_abc X_c:", all(br(L[a], L[b]) == -sum(lc(a, b, c) * L[c] for c in range(3)) for a in range(3) for b in range(3)))
G = matrix(SR, 3, 3, lambda a, b: (e[a].cross_product(n) * e[b].cross_product(n)).simplify_full())
print("[PASS] (e_a x n).(e_b x n) = delta_ab - n_a n_b:", (G - (identity_matrix(3) - n.column() * n.row())).apply_map(lambda t: t.simplify_full()).is_zero())
Output:
push-forward of K_1: (0, -cos(th), sin(ph)*sin(th))   e_1 x n: (0, -cos(th), sin(ph)*sin(th))
push-forward of K_2: (cos(th), 0, -cos(ph)*sin(th))   e_2 x n: (cos(th), 0, -cos(ph)*sin(th))
push-forward of K_3: (-sin(ph)*sin(th), cos(ph)*sin(th), 0)   e_3 x n: (-sin(ph)*sin(th), cos(ph)*sin(th), 0)
[PASS] the push-forward of K_a is e_a x n: True
[PASS] e_a x x = L_a x with (L_a)_{bc} = -eps_abc: True
[PASS] [X_a, X_b] = (L_b L_a - L_a L_b) x = -eps_abc X_c: True
[PASS] (e_a x n).(e_b x n) = delta_ab - n_a n_b: True




The number of gauge fields depends on the isometry group, not on the dimension. The third exercise makes the comparison for the internal spaces met so far and for the three-sphere in two of its guises.

Exercise 3 (Counting) For the internal spaces S^1, T^2, S^2, S^3 = SU(2) and S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3), give the number of internal dimensions and the number of gauge fields.







NoteSolution





S^1: 1 dimension, 1 gauge field (U(1)); T^2: 2 and 2 (U(1)^2); S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2): 2 and 3 (SO(3)); S^3 as the group manifold SU(2): 3 dimensions and 6 gauge fields (SU(2) \times SU(2), the left and right actions); S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3): 3 and 6, the same space and the same isometry group SO(4) \cong
(SU(2) \times SU(2))/\mathbb{Z}_2 (Example 5 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles). The gauge group is the isometry group, whose dimension can exceed that of the space (Duff 1994, 14).









With the Killing vectors in hand, the circle ansatz generalises by replacing A_\mu\,dx^\mu in dy + A_\mu dx^\mu by the vector-valued one-form K^m_aA^a_\mu dx^\mu. The internal metric stays fixed, so that the only new fields are the gauge fields, one for each Killing vector.


Definition 2 (Non-abelian Kaluza-Klein ansatz) The non-abelian ansatz on M_4 \times M_k is 
d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}(x)\,dx^\mu dx^\nu - \gamma_{mn}(y)\left(dy^m + K^m_a(y)A^a_\mu(x)\,dx^\mu\right)\left(dy^n + K^n_b(y)A^b_\nu(x)\,dx^\nu\right),
\tag{1} with components \hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} - \gamma_{mn}K^m_aK^n_bA^a_\mu A^b_\nu, \hat g_{\mu m} = -\gamma_{mn}K^n_aA^a_\mu, \hat g_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}, that is \hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} + h_{mn}K^m_aK^n_bA^a_\mu A^b_\nu, \hat g_{\mu m} = h_{mn}K^n_aA^a_\mu, \hat g_{mn} = h_{mn} in terms of the internal block h = -\gamma (Duff 1994, eq. 27, with the signature converted; Overduin and Wesson 1997, eq. 31): one gauge field A^a_\mu per Killing vector, the internal metric fixed, and no scalars (the generalisation with y-dependent internal metric brings in the scalar fields of The reduction of the curvature scalar, which Part V treats in its own way).







TipVerification





Veriphy. Pending.
Lean. Pending.
Sage. Pending.










NoteExamples





On the sphere the mixed components can be written out from the three Killing vectors. They depend on the point of the sphere, unlike the circle’s -\phi^2A_\mu, and this dependence is what the next chapter has to cope with.

Example 4 (On the sphere) With Example 1, \hat g_{\mu\theta} = -K^\theta_aA^a_\mu = \sin\varphi A^1_\mu - \cos\varphi A^2_\mu and \hat g_{\mu\varphi} = -\sin^2\theta K^\varphi_aA^a_\mu = \sin\theta\cos\theta(\cos\varphi A^1_\mu + \sin\varphi A^2_\mu) - \sin^2\theta A^3_\mu: the three gauge fields enter through the three Killing vectors, with \varphi-dependent coefficients.

Collecting the products K^m_aA^a_\mu into a single matrix makes the structure of the ansatz plain. It is the block form of Part III with the corner promoted from a number to a k \times k matrix.

Example 5 (In block form) With B^m{}_\mu = K^m_aA^a_\mu and h = -\gamma the metric is \begin{pmatrix} g + B^ThB & B^Th \\ hB & h \end{pmatrix}, the block form of Example 4 of The Kaluza-Klein reduction with the 1 \times 1 corner -\phi^2 replaced by the k \times k internal block h and the column -\phi^2A by hB (Proposition 1).

The one-forms in the brackets of the ansatz have a geometric meaning. They single out a horizontal direction at each point of the product, which is the defining property of a connection on a bundle.

Example 6 (The tilt as a connection) The one-forms dy^m + K^m_aA^a_\mu dx^\mu vanish on the horizontal directions \partial_\mu - K^m_aA^a_\mu\partial_m: moving along x^\mu one is carried along the fibre by the isometry generated by A^a_\mu K_a (Figure 1), a connection on the bundle M_4 \times S^2 \to M_4 with structure group SO(3) (Definition 18 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles), as A_\mu was a U(1) connection in Example 5 of Gauge theories.










NoteExercises





The first exercise expands the line element on the sphere and reads off its components. It also checks the horizontal-vector statement of Example 6, which says that the four-dimensional metric is what remains along the horizontal directions.

Exercise 4 (Reading off the components) Expand Equation 1 on S^2 with symbolic g_{\mu\nu} and A^a_\mu (two spacetime dimensions suffice), compare with Example 4, and show that the horizontal vectors e_\mu = \partial_\mu - B^m{}_\mu\partial_m are orthogonal to the fibre with \hat g(e_\mu, e_\nu) = g_{\mu\nu}.







NoteSolution





The components are half the second derivatives of d\hat s^2 with respect to the coordinate differentials. Since dy^m + B^m{}_\mu dx^\mu vanishes on e_\mu and the internal term is the only one that sees \partial_m, \hat g(e_\mu, \partial_m) = 0, and on e_\mu, e_\nu only g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu survives:

th, ph = var("th ph")
K = [vector([-sin(ph), -cot(th) * cos(ph)]), vector([cos(ph), -cot(th) * sin(ph)]), vector([0, 1])]
gam = diagonal_matrix(SR, [1, sin(th)^2])
g = matrix(SR, [[var("g00"), var("g01")], [var("g01"), var("g11")]])
A = matrix(SR, 3, 2, lambda a, mu: var("A%d%d" % (a + 1, mu)))
B = matrix(SR, 2, 2, lambda m, mu: sum(K[a][m] * A[a, mu] for a in range(3)))   # B^m_mu = K^m_a A^a_mu
dX = vector(var("dt dx dth dph"))
theta = vector([dX[2 + m] + sum(B[m, mu] * dX[mu] for mu in range(2)) for m in range(2)])
ds2 = (vector(dX[:2]) * g * vector(dX[:2]) - theta * gam * theta).expand()
G = matrix(SR, 4, 4, lambda i, j: (diff(ds2, dX[i], dX[j]) / 2).simplify_full())   # ds^2 = G_ij dX^i dX^j
print("ghat_{t th} =", G[0, 2].trig_reduce(), "   ghat_{t ph} =", G[0, 3].simplify_trig())
print("[PASS] ghat_{mu th} = sin(ph) A^1_mu - cos(ph) A^2_mu:", all(bool((G[mu, 2] - (sin(ph) * A[0, mu] - cos(ph) * A[1, mu])).simplify_full() == 0) for mu in range(2)))

Example 10 (A triangular factorisation) With L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ B & 1 \end{pmatrix}, the ansatz is \hat g = L^T\begin{pmatrix} g & 0 \\ 0 & h

The block inverse is therefore the same theorem in both signature conventions, and with g = 1, h = 1 it inverts L^TL, a matrix congruent to the identity (Example 10).

The derivation is a short computation with the Lie derivative. Its key step uses that the Killing vectors preserve the internal metric, so that the Lie derivative of a lowered Killing vector is again a combination of Killing vectors.

Example 16 (The derivation) \mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu m} = \xi^n\partial_n\hat g_{\mu m} + \partial_m\xi^n\hat g_{\mu n} + \partial_\mu\xi^nh_{nm} with \hat g_{\mu m} =
K_{ma}A^a_\mu (K_{ma} = h_{mn}K^n_a, h = -\gamma; every term is linear in h, so the sign of the internal block drops out): the last term is K_{ma}\partial_\mu\epsilon^a, and the first two are \epsilon^bA^a_\mu
(\mathcal{L}_{K_b}K_a)_m, the Lie derivative of the covector K_{ma} along K_b, which equals h_{mn}[K_b, K_a]^n =
f_{ba}{}^cK_{mc} because \mathcal{L}_{K_b}h = 0. Hence \delta\hat g_{\mu m} = K_{mc}(\partial_\mu\epsilon^c + f_{ba}{}^c\epsilon^bA^a_\mu), which is Equation 4 (Exercise 16).

The internal block of the ansatz must not change, or the form of the ansatz would not be preserved. That it does not is exactly the Killing property of the vectors along which the fibres are moved.

Example 17 (The internal block is unchanged) \mathcal{L}_\xi h_{mn} = \epsilon^a\mathcal{L}_{K_a}h_{mn} = 0 because the K_a are Killing (Proposition 30 of Differential geometry): the internal metric, and with it the size and shape of the sphere, is not a gauge degree of freedom.

For constant parameters the derivative term disappears and only the commutator term is left. It rotates the three gauge fields into each other like the components of a vector in three dimensions.

Example 18 (The commutator term) For constant \epsilon, \delta A^c = -f_{ab}{}^cA^a\epsilon^b is the adjoint action (Definition 9 of Lie groups and Lie algebras): on the sphere \delta A^c = \epsilon_{abc}A^a\epsilon^b, that is \delta\vec A = \vec A \times \vec\epsilon = -\vec\epsilon \times \vec A, a rotation of the three gauge fields into each other, as in Example 17 of Gauge theories. The right panel of Figure 2 shows \epsilon^3 turning A^1 into -A^2.

For the sphere the Killing brackets carry a minus sign, and the gauge transformation carries the opposite sign. The example explains where this comes from and why it is harmless.

Example 19 (\mathfrak{so}(3) from the sphere) f_{ab}{}^c = -\epsilon_{abc} from Equation 56 of Differential geometry, so the gauge transformation Equation 4 has structure constants -f_{ab}{}^c = +\epsilon_{abc}: the vector fields generating a left action of a group represent its Lie algebra with the opposite bracket (Exercise 2, Exercise 15), and the gauge algebra they induce is that of the rotation matrices themselves. The sign is a convention for the orientation of the generators, and K_a \to -K_a gives +\epsilon_{abc} with A^a \to -A^a: the field strength and the action are unchanged (Exercise 19).

When the isometries commute the commutator term disappears. A flat torus therefore gives several copies of Maxwell theory and nothing non-abelian, however many dimensions it has.

Example 20 (Abelian limits) For T^k the Killing vectors commute, f = 0, and Equation 4 is k copies of Equation 2 of Gauge symmetry and the Kaluza-Klein tower (with \epsilon \to -\epsilon, Exercise 13); the non-abelian structure needs non-commuting isometries, which a flat torus does not have.

On a coset space two groups play a role, the group acting and the isotropy group of a point. Only the first one becomes the gauge group of this ansatz.

Example 21 (Cosets and their isotropy) For G/H the Killing vectors of the left action give the full G, and the gauge group of the reduction is G, while the isotropy group H (Definition 3 of Homogeneous spaces and fibre bundles) is what the fields at a point of the fibre are charged under: the two roles that SO(3) and SO(2) play in the CSDR constraints of Part V.
